intro.heading: One grade, two completely different problems
paragraphs: Design Technology is the Diploma subject where a single reported grade hides two unrelated situations. There is a long internally assessed design project, built over months, assessed on a folder of evidence. And there are written papers that test core content, graphical interpretation, material properties and the ability to answer structured questions in the register an examiner expects. A student can be strong at one and weak at the other, and the report card will say 4 either way. Parents in Abu Dhabi are routinely told their child is doing fine in design and should work harder on the theory, which is a diagnosis that tells nobody what to do on Monday.

So this page is organised around collecting evidence for each half separately. For the papers, that means timed structured questions marked against the command terms, weekly, with the marks written down. For the project, it means a documented folder trail: what existed at each stage, what the criteria credit, what feedback was given, and what the student changed. Both are legible to a parent who has never drawn an orthographic projection, and together they answer the only question worth asking after six weeks, which is whether anything has moved.

Abu Dhabi students have a genuine content advantage in this subject and almost never use it. Design Technology asks about material selection, manufacturing, sustainability and the context a product is used in. They live in a place where thermal cycling is brutal, coastal humidity corrodes, ultraviolet exposure degrades polymers within a season and airborne sand abrades moving parts, where the emirate runs its own sustainable building rating system, and where heavy industry at Musaffah and aerospace composite manufacturing in Al Ain are local rather than theoretical. A student who justifies a material choice using conditions they can describe from experience writes better answers than one reciting a table.

The second local reality is logistical. Prototyping in an Abu Dhabi apartment is harder than the subject guide imagines, and component lead times into the UAE are genuinely slow if a part has to be ordered from abroad. Projects stall on that far more often than on imagination. A good tutor plans the project around what can actually be sourced and modelled in the time available, which is a practical judgement rather than a design one, and it is the reason some projects are rescued and others are not.

What we do is match an Abu Dhabi Design Technology student with a specialist, run lessons live online in Gulf Standard Time, and keep the marked evidence where a parent can read it.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-design-technology-home-t.programmesIntro: Design Technology is a Group 4 subject with a making component, which makes its preparation routes unusually varied. These are the stages our Abu Dhabi tutors work across.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Design Technology
programmes.description: The course this page is about. Students study the core design cycle, human factors, resource management, materials, production systems and sustainability, with additional Higher Level material, and complete an extended design project assessed against published criteria. Confirm the current paper structure, weightings and project requirements with your child's IB coordinator before any plan is written, since the specification has been revised and older material is still circulating.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi, Design Technology runs at a modest number of schools and the provision varies enormously: some have a workshop, a 3D printer and a specialist technician, others teach the subject in a classroom with CAD and no fabrication capacity at all. That difference changes what a realistic project looks like, so the first question a tutor should ask is what the school can actually make, not what the student would like to build.

programmes.name: MYP Design
programmes.description: The continuum route, and a strong one. MYP Design assesses inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution and evaluating, which is the design cycle in miniature. Students arriving from MYP Design already understand that documentation of thinking is what gets credited, which is the single hardest idea to teach a student who has only made things.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi's IB continuum schools in the eastern corridor supply most of the MYP intake. These students start ahead on the project and behind on the written papers, where timed structured questions are a new experience. Two or three sessions on paper technique early in Year 12 usually prevents a term of avoidable mid-band marks.

programmes.name: IGCSE Design and Technology
programmes.description: The British-track route. IGCSE Design and Technology covers materials, processes and graphical communication, and students arrive confident at drawing and at short written answers. The step up is justification: Diploma answers and project folders are credited for explaining why a decision was taken against alternatives, not for describing what was done.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi has a large British-curriculum population, so a sizeable share of Diploma Design Technology students come from IGCSE rather than MYP. They tend to produce attractive folders with thin analysis and strong exam recall with weak evaluation, which is the opposite profile to the MYP intake and needs the opposite first month.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-design-technology-home-t.subjectsIntro: Design Technology is usually taken alongside subjects that share part of its skill set. These are the pairings Abu Dhabi families ask about most, and what each one demands.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Assessed through written papers plus an extended design project. Marks are lost when the folder shows outcomes instead of reasoning, and when paper answers describe a process rather than justifying a choice against alternatives.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Supports the mechanisms, structures, energy and materials content directly. Students taking both find the stress, force and energy material in Design Technology straightforward and can usually explain a failure mode properly.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Underpins polymer behaviour, corrosion, composites and the degradation processes that matter in a Gulf climate. Useful for justifying material selection rather than asserting it.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: A common pairing for students who make things. Both require documented process, though Visual Arts credits intention and Design Technology credits performance against a specification.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Increasingly chosen with Design Technology by students building electronic or embedded products. The programming does not earn Design Technology marks, but it widens what a project can plausibly do.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The usual maths route. Geometry, trigonometry and modelling support dimensioning, tolerances and the quantitative parts of testing, which are commonly the weakest pages in a folder.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Pairs well for students interested in product development. Market analysis and the production and marketing content overlap, which makes the commercial sections of a folder easier to argue.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Supports the sustainability content with systems thinking and life-cycle reasoning, which is exactly the register the higher-mark sustainability answers require.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: Taken by many Abu Dhabi students alongside a Group 4 subject. Productive skills under time pressure carry the grade, so it competes for the written-practice hours a long design project has already eaten.

sections.heading: What the design folder is actually marked on
paragraphs: Families consistently expect the project to be marked on the quality of the final object. It is marked on documented reasoning. The folder has to show a need identified and supported, a specification with testable criteria, several genuinely different ideas rather than three variations of one, a development process where decisions are justified against alternatives, and testing against the specification that was written at the start. A beautiful prototype with no reasoning trail scores poorly. A modest prototype with a rigorous trail scores well.

That is why the evidence approach works so neatly in this subject. The criteria themselves define what should exist at each stage, so a parent can look at a folder and ask simple questions. Is there a specification with measurable criteria? Does the development section explain why option B was dropped? Is there testing that references those original criteria, or only a photograph of the finished thing? Those questions are answerable without any design training.

The table below sets out the stages, what gets credited, what examiners see too often, and the evidence to keep. We use it as the audit tool in the first project session. Most stalled Abu Dhabi projects turn out to be missing the specification and the justification pages rather than the making, and both can be reconstructed if the decisions were real even when they were never written down.

One warning about reconstruction. Writing up a decision that was genuinely taken at the time is legitimate; inventing a decision retrospectively is not, and it reads false to an examiner because the rest of the folder contradicts it. The honest route is to document what actually happened, including the dead ends, which the criteria reward more generously than students expect.

sections.heading: Material selection for a Gulf climate: content Abu Dhabi students can own
paragraphs: Material properties are examined every year and answered badly almost every year, because students recite a table of properties instead of justifying a choice in context. Abu Dhabi students can do better than that without any extra reading, because the local environment is a severe test case for most of the material behaviours on the syllabus.

Consider what a product outdoors here endures: surface temperatures far above air temperature, a daily thermal cycle that works joints loose, coastal humidity with salt that corrodes ferrous metals and some aluminium alloys, ultraviolet exposure that embrittles and discolours polymers within a season, and airborne sand that abrades surfaces and destroys unsealed bearings. Every one of those maps onto a syllabus concept: thermal expansion, fatigue, corrosion, degradation of polymers, wear and surface finish.

The table pairs the condition with its design consequence and with where it appears in assessment. The teaching point is the structure of the answer rather than the facts: name the condition, name the mechanism, state the consequence for the product's performance against its specification, then justify the choice against a named alternative. That shape converts a list of properties into an argument, which is what the higher mark bands ask for.

There is a second benefit for the project. Students designing an outdoor or semi-outdoor product here can test material behaviour cheaply and honestly, leaving a sample in sun for a fortnight and photographing the change. That is real testing against a specification criterion, it costs nothing, and it is far more credible in a folder than a claim copied from a materials website.

sections.heading: Prototyping in an Abu Dhabi apartment, and what counts as a model
paragraphs: A large share of stalled projects we see here stall for physical reasons, not creative ones. The student has no bench, no ventilation for finishing, nowhere to leave work in progress, and a component on order that will take three weeks to arrive from abroad. None of that is a failure of imagination, and the subject guide does not really acknowledge it. Planning around it is part of the job.

The key realisation is that models are assessed for what they test, not for how finished they look. A card and foam model that proves a mechanism clears its housing earns credit. A laser-cut acrylic enclosure that tests nothing earns very little. Students who understand that can do serious modelling on a dining table: scale sketch models for proportion, card for layout, foam for ergonomics and grip, 3D printing through the school for parts that must be dimensionally accurate, and digital modelling for anything that cannot be built at all.

Sourcing deserves planning rather than optimism. Components ordered internationally can take weeks to arrive, and a project that depends on one arriving is a project with a single point of failure. Where a part is genuinely necessary, order early and design a fallback. Where a part is decorative, drop it. The industrial area on the mainland side of the city and the model and hobby suppliers around it can often substitute something adequate within a day, which is worth more than the ideal component arriving after the deadline.

This is also where honest triage matters in a rescue block. If the remaining weeks do not allow the planned build, the right move is usually to scale the realisation down and spend the time on testing and evaluation, which carry marks that an unfinished prototype does not. Students resist this and are almost always better off for doing it.

sections.heading: The written papers, and why strong designers underperform on them
paragraphs: The written papers are the half of the grade that gets neglected, because a project with a deadline always feels more urgent than revision without one. The result is predictable: students who are genuinely capable designers walk into papers having never practised answering a structured question to time, and lose marks in ways that have nothing to do with their ability to design.

The three recurring losses are specific. Command terms are ignored, so a question asking for justification receives a description. Questions carrying data or an image are answered from general knowledge rather than from the material supplied, which is an immediate ceiling. And answers are written at the wrong length for the marks available, with a paragraph given to a two-mark item and a single line to a six-mark one.

All three respond to drilling rather than to teaching, which is good news in a crowded Year 13. Short, frequent, marked sets work better than occasional long sessions: twenty minutes of structured questions, marked against the command terms, twice a week. Because the content is already familiar from the project work, gains here are usually faster than in a content-heavy science.

Higher Level material needs its own slot. It is taught last, revised least and examined with the same precision as the core, and folding it into general revision reliably leaves it half-learned. We run it as a separate strand with separately marked questions from roughly ten weeks out, which also makes it visible in the evidence folder rather than invisible.

sections.heading: Sustainability with a local rating system: Estidama, Masdar and life-cycle thinking
paragraphs: Sustainability questions attract the vaguest answers in the subject, usually a sentence about recycling and a reference to renewable energy. The mark bands want life-cycle reasoning: where the material came from, what the manufacturing process consumed, what the product uses in service, what happens at end of life, and which trade-offs the designer accepted. Abu Dhabi students have unusually concrete material to work with.

The emirate operates its own sustainable building rating system, Estidama, with its Pearl ratings for development, which gives a student a locally specific framework to cite rather than a generic international one. Masdar City is a purpose-built low-carbon district where shading, orientation, passive cooling and transport choices are visible design decisions. The emirate's energy mix includes large-scale solar at Al Dhafra and nuclear generation at Barakah, which complicates the usual simple story about clean energy in a way that higher-band answers can exploit.

Used properly, this material changes the shape of an answer. Instead of asserting that a product is sustainable, a student can state which stage of the life cycle their decision addresses, what it costs elsewhere, and how it would be assessed under a named framework. That is the difference between a mid-band and a top-band sustainability response, and it transfers directly into the folder, where the sustainability justification pages are often the thinnest in the whole document.

A caution, because it matters in this market: cite frameworks and figures, do not invent them. If a student wants to reference a rating or a target, it needs a source they have read. Fabricated numbers are easy to spot and they discredit the pages around them, which is a disproportionate loss for a sentence the student did not need.

sections.heading: What Design Technology support costs in Abu Dhabi, including the extras
paragraphs: Published market rates for private tuition in the UAE run from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour at the budget online end, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, and AED 200 to 450 and above for IB and IGCSE specialists; one premium provider publishes AED 650. A Dubai rate survey puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors quoted up to AED 500. Those are the market's published figures, attributed to whoever published them, and not an IB Gram price list.

Design Technology has a second cost layer that no tutoring page mentions, and it catches Abu Dhabi families out: the project itself costs money. Materials, consumables, printing and plotting, a 3D printing allowance where the school charges one, components, and sometimes a CAD licence if the student wants to work at home on something the school does not provide. None of that is tutoring, all of it is real, and it should be budgeted before the project is planned rather than discovered halfway through.

The table lists the items we see most often with indicative AED figures, flagged clearly as indicative because prices vary by supplier and by what a school already covers. The useful discipline is to ask the school first what it provides, then design within that, and only then decide how much outside tutoring is actually needed. Families regularly buy weekly tutoring when the real obstacle was a plotter charge and three weeks of shipping.

On tutoring specifically, two questions make quotes comparable. Does the rate include written marking of timed questions, which is where the evidence comes from. And is the rate for online delivery, since in-home bands price travel inside the hour for identical teaching. IB Gram does not sell in-home visits in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India, and every UAE lesson is live online and one-to-one. We publish no tariff here, because the honest answer depends on the tutor and the number of sessions, and the free trial lesson exists to let you judge before paying.

sections.heading: Honesty when part of the work is an object, plus permits and school ethics
paragraphs: The academic-honesty boundary in Design Technology is harder to see than in an essay subject, because help can be physical. The rule is still clear. The student must generate the ideas, take the decisions, carry out the development, make or model the solution and write the folder. A tutor may teach the design cycle, explain what the criteria credit, challenge a specification that cannot be tested, review drawings, discuss manufacturing options and give written feedback on the student's own drafts. A tutor may not redesign the product, draw sheets for the folder, or build any part of the realisation.

Two grey areas come up repeatedly in Abu Dhabi, so it is worth being explicit. First, a parent with engineering skills helping in the garage: assistance must be acknowledged and must not become authorship, and anything beyond supervision needs to be declared to the supervising teacher. Second, commercial fabrication. Having a part cut or printed by a workshop in the industrial area is normally acceptable where the student specified it and the process is documented, and is not acceptable where the shop effectively designed or finished the product. If in doubt, ask the supervising teacher in writing and keep the answer.

On permits, the position is checkable. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers applicants including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so treat quoted amounts as unverified.

In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff also bar teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct points the same way. Since the design teacher is often the only Design Technology specialist a family knows, this is a practical constraint rather than a theoretical one, and it is a large part of why families here end up looking outside the emirate for a specialist at all.

faqs.question: My son's prototype is excellent but his Design Technology grade is mid-band. Why?
faqs.answer: Because the folder is marked on documented reasoning, not on the object. The criteria want a need supported by evidence, a specification with measurable criteria, genuinely different concepts, development where each decision is justified against alternatives, and testing against that original specification. A strong prototype with no reasoning trail scores poorly, while a modest one with a rigorous trail scores well. The other half of the explanation is usually the written papers, which get neglected because the project has a deadline and revision does not. Audit both before deciding what to buy.

faqs.question: Can a Design Technology project be completed in an Abu Dhabi apartment with no workshop?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided the project is chosen for it. Models earn marks for what they test, not for how finished they look, so card, foam and scale sketch models do real assessed work on a dining table. Anything needing dimensional accuracy can usually go through the school's 3D printer, and anything that cannot be built at all can be modelled digitally. What does not work is choosing a product that requires fabrication the student has no access to and then hoping. Plan around the school's actual capacity from the start.

faqs.question: How do component lead times into the UAE affect project planning?
faqs.answer: More than most students expect. A part ordered internationally can take weeks to arrive, and a project that depends on a single delivery has a single point of failure. The discipline is to order anything essential early and design a fallback, to drop decorative components entirely, and to check local suppliers and the industrial area on the mainland side of the city before ordering abroad, since an adequate substitute available tomorrow beats an ideal part arriving after the deadline. Build this into the timeline rather than discovering it at the worst moment.

faqs.question: How should an Abu Dhabi student answer a material selection question?
faqs.answer: By arguing, not listing. Name the condition the product faces, name the mechanism it drives, state the consequence for performance against the specification, then justify the choice against a named alternative. Local conditions make this easy to do convincingly: surface temperatures and thermal cycling, salt-laden coastal humidity, ultraviolet exposure that embrittles polymers within a season, and airborne sand that abrades surfaces and contaminates bearings. A student who reasons from conditions they can describe produces a higher-band answer than one reciting a properties table from memory.

faqs.question: What does a sustainability answer need to score in the top bands?
faqs.answer: Life-cycle reasoning with trade-offs stated. Where the material came from, what manufacturing consumed, what the product uses in service, what happens at end of life, and what the designer gave up to improve one of those. Abu Dhabi students can cite the emirate's own sustainable building rating system, the design decisions visible at Masdar City, and an energy mix that includes both large-scale solar and nuclear generation, which complicates the simple story in a way examiners reward. Cite frameworks and figures you have actually read, and never invent a number.

faqs.question: Where exactly is the line between help and authorship on the design project?
faqs.answer: The student must generate the ideas, take the decisions, carry out the development, make or model the solution and write the folder. A tutor may teach the design cycle, explain what the criteria credit, challenge an untestable specification, review drawings, discuss manufacturing options and give written feedback on the student's own drafts. A tutor may not redesign the product, draw folder sheets or build any part of the realisation. Keep every dated iteration; a documented development trail is both the best evidence of authorship and the most useful teaching record there is.

faqs.question: Can we have a part machined or printed by a workshop in Musaffah?
faqs.answer: Usually yes if the student specified it and the process is documented, and no if the workshop effectively designed or finished the product. Commercial processes are a normal part of real design, and using one is not inherently a problem; the assessment is of the student's thinking and decisions. The safe route is to write down the specification given to the shop, keep the drawings the student produced, and ask the supervising teacher in writing before committing. Keep their answer. The same applies to help from an engineer parent, which must be supervision rather than authorship and should be declared.

faqs.question: My daughter is strong at CAD and weak at the written papers. What should sessions do?
faqs.answer: Drill structured questions rather than teach content. The three recurring losses are ignoring the command term, answering from general knowledge instead of the data or image supplied, and writing at the wrong length for the marks available. All three respond to short frequent marked sets: twenty minutes twice a week, marked against the command terms, with the mark allocation used to decide answer length. Because the content is already familiar from project work, gains come faster here than in a content-heavy science, which makes it the cheapest improvement available in Year 13.

faqs.question: Does the school's facilities level change what tutoring can achieve?
faqs.answer: It changes the project, not the teaching. A school with a workshop, printer and technician supports a different scope of realisation from a school teaching the subject in a classroom with CAD only. A tutor cannot add fabrication capacity, so the useful contribution is designing within the real constraint and then protecting the marks that do not depend on making: research, specification, development reasoning, testing and evaluation. Ask the department what it provides and what it charges for before planning anything, and tell the tutor the answer in the first session.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a stalled Design Technology project usually need?
faqs.answer: Two or three if the problem is the specification or the justification pages, because those can be reconstructed from decisions that were genuinely taken even if never written down. Considerably more if the problem is that the chosen product cannot be built with available facilities, since that is a replan rather than a repair. The audit in the first session is what tells you which case you are in, and it is the reason we ask for the folder before quoting any plan. Honest triage recovers more marks than optimism about the original build.

faqs.question: Is Design Technology accepted as a science for university applications?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it must be checked rather than assumed. It sits in the Diploma's sciences group, but some engineering and physical science courses specify Physics, Chemistry or Mathematics and will not substitute Design Technology for them. Product design, industrial design, architecture, engineering foundation routes and many design-led programmes value it highly. Read the published entry requirements for the specific courses on your child's list, including UAE universities, during Year 12 while a subject change is still possible, and treat admissions pages as the authority over general advice.

faqs.question: Should the same tutor handle the folder and the written papers?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, because the two tracks inform each other: a student who can justify a material choice in a paper answer writes better development pages, and vice versa. What matters is that the tutor treats them as separate work with separate records, rather than letting the folder deadline swallow every session. Ask a candidate directly how they would split a term between the two, and whether the papers get marked question sets of their own. If the answer is vague, the project will take all the time, which is exactly the pattern that produced the mid-band grade in the first place.

faqs.question: Can sessions fit around the project deadline crunch and Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and both should be planned rather than improvised. In a deadline crunch we usually swap one weekly lesson for two shorter reviews, because written feedback on successive folder stages is more useful than a long conversation. During Ramadan school hours shorten and evenings reorganise around Iftar, so sessions move to post-Iftar slots from about 8.30pm or to weekend mornings for longer work. Since Ramadan currently falls inside the revision term for the May session, agreeing the pattern before the month begins protects the most valuable weeks in the course.

faqs.question: Why look for an online specialist rather than someone local to Khalifa City?
faqs.answer: Because Design Technology specialists are scarce in the emirate and the obvious local candidate is often unavailable to you: in Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. Searching within a short drive then narrows the field to generalists. Online matching keeps the subject specialism and removes travel from the price and the timetable, which is what makes a 6.30pm weekday slot workable. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses; every lesson here runs live over video with screen sharing for drawings and folder pages.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-design-technology-home-t.closingHeading: Send the folder as it stands
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-design-technology-home-t.closingBody: A Design Technology grade that will not move is usually two problems wearing one number, and the fastest way to separate them is an audit. Send the design folder in whatever state it is in, plus one timed question answer, and a specialist will tell you in writing which stages the criteria are not yet seeing and what the papers are costing. That is what the free trial lesson is for, and it happens before any payment. Tell us what the school can actually make and when the deadlines fall, and we will match an Abu Dhabi student with a specialist for live one-to-one online lessons in Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: Why a strong designer can still be a weak Design Technology candidate
paragraphs: An IB DP Design Technology tutor in Abu Dhabi is most often called in by a parent who has just seen a report that makes no sense to them. The child is good at this. The sketchbook is full, the renders are convincing, the prototype works. The predicted grade is a 4. Nothing has gone wrong with the child's ability; something has gone wrong with the translation between what they can do and what the assessment measures, and that gap is the whole job of a tutor in this subject.

Design Technology is assessed in two halves that reward different things. The written papers want technical precision: the correct term for a material property, the right stage of a design cycle, the specific reason a user trial produced that result. The design project wants documented evidence of a process, in order, with decisions justified at the point they were made. A student can be excellent at designing and poor at both, because neither is the same skill as designing.

This page is built around the components rather than around reassurance. It sets out what each written paper asks for, what the six core topics and the four additional higher level topics actually test, the stages of the design project where marks are lost in practice, and the specific constraints Abu Dhabi students work under: limited workshop time in some schools, apartment living with nowhere to build, and the perennial problem of finding real users to test a prototype with.

Delivery first, because it matters. IB Gram teaches UAE students one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time, with the student's sketchbook, CAD file or folder shared on screen. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are a service we run only in India. In a subject taught largely through looking at a student's own work and asking why they did it that way, a shared screen is closer to the real task than a tutor sitting beside them would be.

A word on what we will not do. The design project must be the student's own work from the first sketch to the last page of the folder. A tutor asks questions, teaches the technical content, points at a criterion the folder has not addressed, and marks a practice version so the student can see the gap themselves. A provider offering to supply drawings, a CAD model or finished folder pages is offering your child an academic-honesty investigation, and no grade is worth that. That boundary is also the reason this page spends more words on what the assessment wants than on what we sell: a parent who understands the components can judge any tutor's plan, including ours, and a parent who does not is buying reassurance by the hour.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-design-technology-tutor.programmesIntro: Design Technology is examined in the Diploma, but the habits it rewards are built far earlier. Here is what each IB stage contributes for an Abu Dhabi student heading towards it, and what support at each stage is actually for.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years covering six core topics, four more at Higher Level, and an individually designed and documented design project. Written papers test technical vocabulary and applied reasoning; the project tests whether a process was followed, recorded and justified. Students who treat the folder as a presentation of a finished product rather than a record of decisions lose marks at every stage.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi cohorts in this subject are small, and workshop provision varies widely between schools in the emirate. A student with limited machine time can still score well, because the assessment rewards documented reasoning rather than manufacturing quality, but the project has to be designed with the available facilities in mind from the start.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Middle Years Design is the closest preparation there is. Its inquiry, development, creation and evaluation cycle is the Diploma project in miniature, and a student who has been made to document decisions at this stage arrives in DP1 with the one habit the Diploma punishes hardest for lacking.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi schools run the Middle Years Design course well and several treat it as a making subject with light documentation. We check which a student has had, because a Year 11 who has never written a justified specification needs that taught before the project begins, not during it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No bearing on a Diploma grade, but the beginning of the habit: asking who something is for, and whether it worked. Primary support in Abu Dhabi is usually booked for literacy and mathematics, and design thinking appears through inquiry units rather than as a subject.
programmes.countryNote: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies sit alongside the licensed international curriculum in UAE private schools as a federal requirement, so a Primary timetable in the emirate is fuller than the same school's abroad. Session length is set accordingly.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A sensible route for students combining Diploma courses with a design, engineering or architecture-related career study. Design Technology taken within it is assessed against the same subject guide, so the tutoring work is identical.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is uncommon in Abu Dhabi, so families on this route rarely find anyone locally who has supported it. Online matching solves a problem that was only ever about distance rather than expertise.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-design-technology-tutor.subjectsIntro: Design Technology students in Abu Dhabi usually need one other subject supported in the same year, most often because the two share a skill. These are the Diploma courses our tutors cover alongside it.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: Six core topics, four additional at Higher Level, and a documented design project. Marks go missing on imprecise material and manufacturing vocabulary, on user trials reported without data, and on folders that show a finished product rather than the reasoning that produced it.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The usual companion for engineering applicants. Forces, materials, energy and electricity overlap directly with the core topics, and a student strong here writes better justifications for material and structural choices than one who is not.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The route most engineering and architecture programmes expect. Worth checking against each university's published requirement rather than assumed, because a few design and product-design degrees accept Applications and Interpretation.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Often the better fit for a design-led student, with statistics and modelling content that directly supports user research and testing data in the project. Check the requirement of each target course before choosing it.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pairs well for students designing anything with embedded electronics or an interface. The two subjects share the discipline of specifying before building, and students taking both can reuse a user-requirement analysis with the framing rewritten.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Shares drawing and presentation skill and almost nothing else in assessment terms. A student taking both must keep the two folders separate in purpose: one documents a design process, the other an artistic intention.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Underpins the materials content of the core topics, particularly polymers, composites and corrosion. Useful rather than required, and the usual difficulty is calculation layout rather than understanding.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Maps onto the higher level topics on innovation, markets and commercial production. Students taking both often write the strongest commercial justification sections in the cohort.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Written precision transfers straight into the folder. A student who can structure a paragraph and cut a sentence writes a tighter justification, and the folder has strict limits on how much can be said.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Design is a possible choice and a common stalling point, usually because the question is a product review rather than a researchable design question. Support is process coaching and reading what the student has already written.

sections.heading: What the written papers in Design Technology actually ask for
paragraphs: The written side of this subject catches out students who think of design as a practical discipline. A paper does not ask whether an idea is good. It asks for the correct term, the specific property, the named stage of a process, and a reason that follows from evidence. A student who writes a thoughtful paragraph where the command term asked them to outline a property of a material will score a fraction of what they know, every time.

Standard Level students sit two written papers and Higher Level students sit three, with the third drawing on the additional higher level topics. The multiple-choice element rewards coverage: there is nowhere to hide a topic that was skipped. The structured and extended-response work rewards precision, and this is where almost all of the recoverable marks in the written component sit for students who already understand the subject.

The table below sets out each component, what it genuinely tests, where Abu Dhabi students in our caseload lose marks, and what a session can do about it. Component weightings are deliberately left out because the guide has been revised and schools in the emirate adopted the revision at different points. Your child's IB coordinator holds the current figures, and those are the ones worth planning against rather than anything an agency publishes. What does not change between guide versions is the behaviour of the marking: a precise answer to the question asked scores, and an impressive answer to a question nobody asked does not.

sections.heading: The six core topics, and what each one punishes
paragraphs: The core of this subject runs across human factors and ergonomics, resource management and sustainable production, modelling, final production, innovation and design, and classic design. Each topic has a characteristic failure, and after a few years of marking you can predict which one a student will hit from the way they talk about their project. A student who says a product is ergonomic without mentioning percentile data has told you exactly which topic will cost them marks.

Human factors is the most misunderstood. Students treat anthropometric and percentile data as decoration to be added after the design is finished, when it is the evidence base the design should have been built on. Modelling is the second: physical, graphical and computer modelling each serve a distinct purpose, and a student who renders everything and tests nothing has modelled the appearance of a solution without ever modelling its function.

The table below is the version of this we use in a first session. It names each core topic, the idea students most often misread, and the kind of question that exposes it. The right-hand column is the useful one for a parent, because it turns a vague report comment about technical understanding into something specific that can be practised in an hour. Classic design deserves a separate warning. Students enjoy it, read about famous chairs and lamps, and then write an answer that lists products rather than arguing a case against the criteria the syllabus sets out. It is the topic where the gap between interest and marks is widest.

sections.heading: The additional higher level topics and the paper that tests them
paragraphs: Higher Level students take four further topics covering user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production. They are not harder in the sense of involving more difficult ideas. They are harder because they ask a student to reason commercially about design decisions, and most sixteen-year-olds have no instinct for production volume, market pull or the cost of retooling a line.

The characteristic Higher Level failure is treating these topics as extra content to be recalled rather than extra lenses to be applied. A question about commercial production does not want a definition of mass production; it wants a reasoned judgement about whether this product, at this volume, in this market, should be made this way. Students who have been taught the topics as vocabulary lists sit the paper and write definitions nobody asked for.

The practical advice we give Abu Dhabi families is to start the additional topics earlier than the school timetable suggests, and to practise them against past questions separately from core content. A student who revises everything together ends up revising the core twice and the higher level topics never, because the core feels more familiar. Dedicated higher level sessions in the spring term of DP1 are unglamorous and they are where the grade difference usually comes from. The other reason to start early is that the additional topics give a student better language for their own project. A folder that justifies a production process against a realistic batch size reads as the work of someone who has understood commercial production, and the same reasoning earns marks twice.

sections.heading: The design project: where the marks actually go missing
paragraphs: The design project is the largest single component in this subject and the one where the most marks are thrown away by capable students. The pattern is nearly always the same. The student designs well, builds something decent, and documents the journey afterwards from memory. The folder then reads as a story about a finished product rather than as evidence of decisions made at the time, and a moderator can only credit what is evidenced.

The second pattern is a specification that cannot be tested. A student who writes that their product should be durable, attractive and easy to use has written three things nobody can measure, which means the testing stage has nothing to test against and the evaluation has nothing to conclude. One hour spent turning those three words into measurable criteria in October removes a cascade of lost marks in March.

The table sets out the project stages, the failure we see most often at each, what evidence the folder actually needs, and what a tutor can legitimately do. That last column is bounded by IB academic-honesty rules: the student designs, draws, models, tests and writes. A tutor asks, teaches, checks and marks practice work. Nobody at IB Gram supplies a drawing, a CAD file or a page of folder text, and any provider who offers to is offering your child a malpractice investigation. The stage families underestimate most is the first one. A problem chosen to suit a product the student already wanted to make poisons every later stage, because the research cannot honestly support a conclusion that was reached before it started.

sections.heading: Renders are not marks: the evidence problem
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi students have excellent access to software and often to a decent school design suite, and that creates a specific hazard. Modern CAD makes a convincing image easy to produce, and a convincing image feels like progress. It is not progress in assessment terms unless it is a model that answered a question. A render showing what the product will look like answers nothing that the specification asked.

The fix is a habit rather than a skill, and it is cheap to install. Every time the student makes anything, they record three things: what question this was meant to answer, what the result was, and what they changed because of it. Three sentences and a photograph, taken at the time. A folder assembled from those records writes itself and scores for process; a folder assembled from memory in March cannot, because the evidence no longer exists.

This is also why folder review works far better spread across the year than concentrated at the end. A stage reviewed in week three can be redone in week four. The same stage reviewed in April cannot be redone at all, so the only thing a tutor can honestly do is help the student present what exists and warn them what it will cost. Families who book review hours early spend fewer of them, which is the opposite of how most tutoring is sold. It also changes what the student learns. A student told in October that their specification is untestable learns to write testable criteria; a student told the same thing in April learns only that they lost marks.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a subject built from other people's parts
paragraphs: Design is a borrowing discipline, and that makes the honesty rules in this subject less obvious than in an essay subject. A student who downloads a bearing from a component library, uses a generative tool to produce a mood-board image, or bases a mechanism on a product they dismantled has done nothing wrong. A student who does any of those things without acknowledging it has. The rule is simple to state and easy to breach by accident: anything that is not yours is credited, where it appears.

The second honesty question is help. A parent who is an engineer, an older sibling who can use the software, a technician who machines a part the student designed: all legitimate, all requiring acknowledgement of exactly what was contributed. The IB's concern is not that a student had support but that the work submitted is presented as entirely their own when it is not. Writing down who did what, as it happens, protects the student completely.

Our own boundary is stated on every page and we hold it. A tutor teaches the content, questions the decisions, checks a specification is testable, names a criterion the folder has not addressed, and marks a practice version. A tutor does not sketch, model, render or write any part of a submitted folder. Providers in this market do sell finished coursework, and the risk of using them sits entirely with your child, whose Diploma is the thing on the table.

sections.heading: Workshops, apartments and finding real users in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Three practical constraints shape design projects in this emirate. Workshop provision varies: some Abu Dhabi schools have well-equipped design suites with laser cutters and three-dimensional printers, others have a classroom with hand tools, and the difference is worth knowing before a student commits to a project that needs machining they cannot access. The assessment rewards documented reasoning rather than manufacturing quality, so a limited workshop is a design constraint rather than a grade ceiling.

The second is space. A large share of our Abu Dhabi students live in apartments on Al Reem Island, around the Corniche or in Al Raha Beach, with no outdoor area, limited storage and rules about noise and dust. The workable answer is almost always to reduce scale: a bench-scale model that tests the mechanism properly evidences more than a full-size object that was never tested because there was nowhere to put it.

The third is users, and it is the one students resist most. A design project needs real people to research with and test on, and inventing a user is the fastest way to lose marks across three stages at once. Abu Dhabi offers more than students notice: school sports squads, residents' facilities, a grandparent with limited grip strength, the cultural district's visitor flow, a building's waste and recycling arrangements. The table sets out options by constraint, with what each one makes possible. Permission is the only real barrier, and it is usually granted when a student asks properly: a short written request naming what will be observed, for how long, and what will happen to the notes afterwards tends to get a yes from a head of year.

sections.heading: Where Design Technology leads, and what it costs to support
paragraphs: Parents ask two questions at the end of every first conversation: does this subject close doors, and what will help cost. On the first, it depends entirely on the destination and should be checked against each university's own published requirement rather than against reputation. Engineering and architecture programmes typically want Mathematics and Physics at Higher Level, and Design Technology is a strong third rather than a substitute for either. Product design, industrial design and design engineering courses frequently value it directly and may ask for a portfolio in which the project is the centrepiece.

On cost, published market rates for Diploma specialist support in the UAE run from roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, with qualified subject tutors online quoted from about AED 150 to AED 300 and in-home visits from around AED 180 to AED 500 because travel sits inside the rate. Those are figures providers in this market have published, read in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list. Our own rate is quoted per 60 minutes in writing after a free trial lesson, with marking and a written session note inside it.

Equivalency is a separate matter and belongs to the Ministry of Education rather than to any tutoring provider. For the British track the published rule is five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. No IB points threshold has been verified for this project, so none is published here. Check moe.gov.ae or the attestation authority directly before planning subject choices around it.

faqs.question: What is actually on the written papers in Diploma Design Technology?
faqs.answer: Standard Level students sit two written papers and Higher Level students sit three. One is multiple-choice and tests coverage of every core topic, which means a topic quietly skipped during the course shows up immediately. The others use structured and extended-response questions that reward precise technical vocabulary, applied reasoning and obedience to the command term. The Higher Level paper draws on the four additional topics. Confirm the current weightings with your school's IB coordinator, because the guide has been revised and schools adopted the revision at different points.

faqs.question: Why does a student who understands ergonomics still lose marks on human factors questions?
faqs.answer: Because the questions want evidence rather than awareness. A student who writes that a handle is comfortable and well shaped has described an intention. The mark is for justifying a dimension against named anthropometric or percentile data, and for saying which user population that data describes. Students typically meet percentile tables once, treat them as something to mention, and never use them to make a decision. It is one of the quickest things to fix in this subject: one or two sessions of applying real data to the student's own project usually settles it.

faqs.question: When should a Higher Level student start the four additional topics?
faqs.answer: Earlier than the school timetable implies, and practised separately from core content. The additional topics cover user-centred design, sustainability, innovation and markets, and commercial production, and they ask for commercial judgement rather than recall. Students who revise everything together revise the familiar core twice and the additional topics never. Dedicated sessions in the spring term of DP1, built on past questions rather than notes, are unglamorous and tend to be where the grade difference in Higher Level cohorts actually comes from.

faqs.question: The folder looks impressive. Why would a moderator still mark it down?
faqs.answer: Because a moderator can only credit evidence, and a polished folder often documents a finished product rather than the decisions that produced it. If the renders were made after the design was settled, no model tested anything, and the evaluation describes the object rather than judging it against measurable criteria, the marks have nowhere to attach. The repair is habit rather than talent: record what each model was meant to answer, what happened, and what changed because of it, at the time, with a dated photograph.

faqs.question: What counts as evidence of development in a design folder?
faqs.answer: Something that answered a question. A sketch exploring three mechanisms is evidence. A card model that showed the hinge fouled at forty degrees is better evidence, because it produced a result and a change. A render of the final object is not evidence of development at all, however good it looks. The useful test is whether each piece of work in the folder is followed by a stated outcome and a decision. Where that chain is missing, the stage reads as presentation rather than development, and is credited accordingly.

faqs.question: Is it acceptable to use a component library or a generative image tool in the project?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided it is credited where it appears. Downloading a standard bearing, fastener or motor model is normal professional practice and nobody expects a student to model a screw thread from scratch. Using a generative tool for a mood-board image is likewise permitted if acknowledged. The breach is presenting any of it as the student's own work. The same applies to help from a parent, sibling or technician: record exactly what was contributed, as it happens, and the student is fully protected.

faqs.question: Our Abu Dhabi school has a very limited workshop. Does that cap the grade?
faqs.answer: No. The assessment rewards documented reasoning rather than manufacturing quality, so a student with hand tools and card can evidence as much as a student with a laser cutter, provided the project is designed for the facilities available. What does cap a grade is choosing a project that needs machining the student cannot access, then submitting drawings of something never built or tested. Choose the project around the workshop in the first weeks, and reduce scale rather than reduce ambition.

faqs.question: We live in an apartment on Al Reem Island with nowhere to build. What then?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scale and modularise. A bench-scale model that properly tests the mechanism evidences more than a full-size object that was never tested because there was nowhere to keep it. Work that produces dust or fumes belongs in the school design suite rather than a flat. Photograph each stage against a plain background as you go, because retrospective photography of a finished model cannot show development. Several of our strongest Abu Dhabi folders were produced entirely on a dining table.

faqs.question: Where can a student in Abu Dhabi find real users to test a prototype with?
faqs.answer: Closer than they think, and inventing a user is the fastest way to lose marks across three stages at once. School sports squads, a residents' gym or pool, building waste and recycling arrangements, a grandparent with limited grip strength, and visitor flow in the cultural district have all produced genuine primary research for students we work with. What matters is recording it: interview notes, dated observations, trial data with the conditions stated. Ask the school for permission before approaching staff or other students.

faqs.question: Does Design Technology count as a science for engineering applications?
faqs.answer: Usually not as a substitute for Physics. Engineering and architecture programmes typically expect Mathematics and Physics at Higher Level, with Design Technology as a strong third subject that evidences process and making. Product design, industrial design and design engineering courses often value it directly, and some ask for a portfolio in which the design project is the centrepiece. Check each university's own published entry requirements rather than relying on a general rule, and ideally before the Year 12 option sheet is signed.

faqs.question: How does a session work when the work being reviewed is a sketchbook and a CAD file?
faqs.answer: The student shares their screen or photographs the pages before the call, and the hour is spent on their own work with the tutor asking why each decision was made. For a CAD model the student drives the software while the tutor questions the geometry, the tolerances and what the model is meant to prove. It is closer to a design review in practice than to a lesson, and because the student operates everything themselves, nothing produced in the session is anyone else's work.

faqs.question: My son is in DP2 and the project has barely started. What is recoverable?
faqs.answer: More than families fear, and less than they hope. What is recoverable is a tight, small-scope problem with real primary research, a testable specification, and genuine development evidenced as it happens from now on. What cannot be recovered is development that should have been documented last year; a folder cannot acquire a history retrospectively. The honest plan is to narrow the project hard, document everything from this week forward, and accept that some stages will score on quality rather than on volume.

faqs.question: Does a Design Technology tutor need a UAE permit to teach my child online?
faqs.answer: A tutor resident in the UAE who gives private lessons, including online lessons, needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no schedule of amounts has been published. A tutor resident abroad is governed by their own jurisdiction. Ask any provider directly and expect a clear answer.

faqs.question: What does Diploma Design Technology support cost in the Abu Dhabi market?
faqs.answer: Published market figures for Diploma specialist support run from roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, with qualified subject tutors online quoted from about AED 150 to AED 300 and in-home visits from around AED 180 to AED 500 because travel is inside the rate. Those figures were read in October 2026 from providers in this market and are not an IB Gram price list. We quote per 60 minutes in writing after a free trial lesson, with marking and a written session note included, and no package is required to begin.

faqs.question: Should we book weekly sessions or a block of folder reviews?
faqs.answer: Both, in different proportions depending on the year. In DP1 the project is the priority and reviews timed to the school's internal deadlines use the fewest hours, because a stage reviewed early can still be redone. In DP2 the written papers usually need the weekly slot, since families have postponed them while the project absorbed attention. A student who has done neither by February of DP2 should expect to spend more hours for less movement than one who started in the autumn of DP1.

intro.heading: A course too new for folklore, which makes marked work the only honest evidence
paragraphs: Digital Society is the newest subject on most Abu Dhabi Diploma option sheets. It replaced Information Technology in a Global Society and reached its first examination sessions in 2024, which means something unusual for a family trying to judge progress: the normal signals are missing. There is no decade of past papers, no shelf of revision guides written by people who have marked thousands of scripts, and very few teachers in the Gulf who have taken three cohorts through it. A parent in Khalifa City asking whether a predicted 5 is fair has almost nothing external to compare it against.

That absence is exactly why this page is built around evidence. When the folklore does not exist, the only reliable information about a student's standing is written work marked against the published criteria and command terms, repeated often enough to show a trend. One mark on one school assessment tells you nothing. Six marked answers across six weeks, each with a criterion-level comment and a named target, tell you whether the student is getting better at the thing the examiner credits.

There is a second reason evidence matters more here than in an established subject. Digital Society punishes a very particular kind of competence. Students who are fluent with technology — who build things, who follow the industry, who can explain a recommendation algorithm better than their teacher — frequently sit in the middle of the mark range. The course does not reward knowing how a system works. It rewards making a claim about a digital system in a named context, supporting it with specific evidence, and following the implication for real people. That is a writing discipline, and marked writing is the only way to see whether it is developing.

Abu Dhabi has an advantage in this subject that is hardly ever used. The course is assessed through real contexts, and the emirate is full of them: a government services platform most residents use weekly, a toll system that reads number plates on every bridge onto the island, a technology cluster on Al Maryah Island, autonomous vehicle trials on Yas Island, and a planned city built as a sustainability experiment. A student who writes about a system their own family uses writes with specificity. A student who writes about an American social network they have read about writes in generalities, and generalities are where the marks go.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We hold no accreditation or endorsement from the IB, from ADEK or from any school named on this page, and we claim none. What we do is find a tutor who has taught this syllabus, run the lessons live online in Gulf Standard Time, and keep the marked work where a parent can read it.

sections.heading: Why the usual signals do not work for this subject
paragraphs: In an established Diploma subject, a parent has several independent ways to judge a grade. There is a long run of past papers with mark schemes, a teacher who has seen many cohorts, published grade descriptors everyone recognises, and a revision industry whose products have been tested on real students. Digital Society has almost none of that. The course is young, and in the Gulf the pool of teachers who have taken more than two cohorts through to examination is small.

The practical effect in Abu Dhabi is that internal marks drift. Two schools in the same corridor can be marking the same quality of work a band apart, and neither is being careless; they are both estimating. A family hears that their daughter is on a 5 and has no way of knowing whether that means a secure 5, an optimistic 6 or a pessimistic 4. In a cohort of three students, the internal ranking carries almost no information at all.

An external marker working to the published command terms is therefore worth more in this subject than in a subject with forty years of accumulated practice. The value is not that the tutor knows a secret standard. It is that the same person marks the same student's writing repeatedly, against the same published criteria, so you get a consistent reading over time instead of a series of unrelated estimates.

That is why every arrangement described on this page produces written marks. Not a verbal impression at the end of a lesson, which evaporates, but a criterion-level comment and a named target in writing, kept somewhere you can read it in March when the predicted grades come out and you need to decide whether to argue.

sections.heading: Concepts, content and contexts: how a question is actually built
paragraphs: Digital Society is organised in three parts, and almost every weak answer we mark has misread which part the question is pointing at. There are seven concepts, which are the lenses: change, expression, identity, power, space, systems, and values and ethics. There are content areas, which are the technical substance: data, algorithms, computers, networks, media and artificial intelligence. And there are contexts, which are the real-world domains the course asks you to think inside.

A question gives you some of those and expects you to supply the rest. A student who treats a question about recommendation systems as an opportunity to explain how recommendation systems work has answered the content area and ignored the concept and the context, which is where most of the marks sit. A student who names the concept, locates it in a specific context, and then uses the technical content as evidence has written the answer the examiner is looking for.

The table below is the working tool we use in early sessions. It is deliberately short, because the point is not to memorise it but to be able to apply it to an unseen question in twenty seconds. Once a student can reliably say which concept a question is about, which context it sits in, and what evidence they are going to use, their marks move without any new content being learned.

This is also the diagnostic that explains the strange pattern families notice: a child who reads widely about technology and scores in the middle. Breadth of reading supplies content. Marks come from the discipline of putting content to work inside a concept and a context, under time pressure, in the order the command term asks for.

sections.heading: The inquiry project: why an Abu Dhabi system beats a global one
paragraphs: The inquiry project is the component where the student has the most control and where outside help, correctly bounded, pays the most. The mark is largely determined before much writing happens, by two choices: which real digital issue or intervention is being investigated, and how the question is framed. A broad question about social media and teenagers produces a broad answer that cannot be supported. A narrow question about a specific system, with identifiable stakeholders and accessible evidence, produces an answer that can.

Abu Dhabi students are sitting on better material than they realise. The emirate runs a unified government services platform that most residents use for renewals and payments, a road toll system that reads plates automatically on the approaches to the island, a technology and startup cluster on Al Maryah Island, autonomous vehicle trials that have operated on Yas Island, a smart parking scheme across the city, and a purpose-built low-carbon district at Masdar City. Each of those is a digital system with real stakeholders, published information, and consequences a student can observe rather than imagine.

The advantage is not patriotism, it is evidence quality. A student writing about a system their family uses can describe the actual interface, the actual friction, the actual data being collected and the actual people affected. They can interview a user without arranging anything. Specificity of that kind is visible in a mark scheme that rewards supported claims, and it is the fastest available upgrade to a middling project.

What the tutor does here is bounded and worth stating plainly. They teach what the criteria reward, discuss candidate contexts, challenge a question that is too broad, and give written feedback on a draft the student has produced. They do not supply the investigation, rewrite sections into their own prose, or hand over a structure with the content filled in. The student must write their own project, and the record of what the tutor saw is kept in case anyone asks.

sections.heading: What to practise on when there are no past papers
paragraphs: This is the question every Abu Dhabi family asks within the first fortnight, and the honest answer is that you build a practice bank instead of inheriting one. The subject has specimen material and a small number of real sessions behind it, and that is not enough volume for a student who needs two timed answers a week for ten weeks. So the material gets made, which is a legitimate and well-established thing for a tutor to do in a new course.

Four sources carry most of the weight. The school's own assessments, which have the advantage of matching what the teacher will mark. The published command terms, which allow a tutor to generate questions in the exact register the papers use. Current reporting on digital systems, which supplies unseen stimulus material of the kind papers use. And the student's own inquiry project context, which can be re-interrogated through different concepts to produce a dozen distinct practice questions.

The table sets out what each source is good for and what it cannot do, because mixing them up is how revision time gets wasted. The common error is to treat news articles as content to be learned rather than as stimulus to be analysed. The second common error is practising only on the concepts the student finds interesting, which in Abu Dhabi tends to mean artificial intelligence and almost never means space or expression.

One warning about reproduction. A tutor should reference and link official subject documentation rather than circulating copies of it, and the same applies to papers and mark schemes. Reproducing that material is a copyright problem and, for unreleased papers, worse than that. The practice bank we build is written material, not photocopies.

sections.heading: Higher Level: writing about interventions without drifting into opinion
paragraphs: The Higher Level extension asks students to think about challenges in digital society and the interventions proposed to address them. It is the component with the least available practice material and the one where able students most often lose marks, because the task invites exactly the wrong instinct. Asked what should be done about algorithmic bias in recruitment, a bright seventeen-year-old writes an opinion piece. The marks are not in the opinion.

What is credited is treating an intervention as an object of analysis. A specific intervention, proposed or implemented by somebody identifiable, aimed at a specific challenge, with stakeholders who respond to it differently, and consequences that can be traced and evidenced. Whether the student personally approves is almost irrelevant. Whether they can show who the intervention helps, who it burdens, what it assumes, and where it has failed before is the whole task.

In practice the fix is a structure, drilled until it is automatic: name the challenge precisely, name the intervention and who proposed it, state the claim about its effect, give evidence with a source and a date, and follow the implication for named stakeholders. Students who learn that shape stop writing editorials within about three marked answers. Students who are never shown it tend to keep writing editorials into the examination.

Timing matters at Higher Level too. The extension cannot be revised the week before, because it is a habit rather than a body of content, and habits need short repeated practice over weeks. We run it as a separate strand from the Standard Level papers, with its own marking, from roughly ten weeks out.

sections.heading: What Digital Society support costs in Abu Dhabi, and what moves the number
paragraphs: Market rates for private tuition in the UAE span a very wide range, and most of the pages ranking for these searches publish no figure at all. For context, providers' own published prices run from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour at the budget online end, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, and AED 200 to 450 and above for IB and IGCSE specialists; one premium provider publishes AED 650. A Dubai rate survey puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors quoted up to AED 500. Those are the market's numbers, attributed to whoever published them, not an IB Gram tariff.

For Digital Society specifically, four things move where a quote sits in that range, and they are worth asking about directly rather than inferring from the headline rate. The table below sets them out. Scarcity is the biggest single factor: the pool of teachers who have examined this course is genuinely small, and a subject-matched tutor costs more than a generalist humanities tutor who will read the guide the night before.

The second factor families consistently underestimate is marking. An hour of lesson plus a properly marked timed answer is closer to ninety minutes of tutor work, and in a course with no past-paper archive the marking is most of the value. Two quotes that look twenty per cent apart may be forty per cent apart once you ask which one includes written marking and which does not.

The third is format. An in-home visit anywhere in the UAE carries the tutor's travel inside the rate, which is why the in-home bands sit higher for identical teaching. IB Gram does not sell in-home visits in the UAE at all; home visits are a service we run only in India, and every UAE lesson is delivered live online, one-to-one. The fourth factor is timing: the weeks immediately before a session are when specialists run out of slots, which is a scheduling constraint rather than a surcharge, and it is why late enquiries get a shorter list of names.
