sections.heading: Scarcity, not distance, sets the economics rate in this emirate
paragraphs: Travel explains why two Abu Dhabi families are quoted differently for the same in-home lesson. It does not explain why economics costs more than mathematics for both of them. The reason is supply: there are fewer Diploma economics specialists in this emirate than science or mathematics tutors, and fewer still who regularly mark data response and commentaries against the published criteria. A scarce subject commands a premium that a central address does not remove.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home visits are a service we run only in India. Standard Level Economics teaching for Abu Dhabi families is delivered one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time slots. On cost that has two consequences worth stating plainly. No travel sits inside the rate, so a family in Al Shamkha pays what a family in Al Bateen pays. And the supply constraint loosens, because the shortlist is economists who teach this syllabus rather than economists who will drive to your community at 17:30.

That second point is the one that matters most for this subject. In an in-home arrangement the scarcity and the travel multiply: the few available specialists take the shortest journeys first, and in the six weeks before mocks the peripheral communities are quoted highest and served last. Families in Al Falah, Al Shamkha and Al Samha regularly find the person who covered DP1 is unavailable exactly when DP2 matters. Removing distance from the equation removes that failure mode along with the premium attached to it.

sections.heading: What you are paying a person to do that your school cannot
paragraphs: Your school delivers 150 taught hours of Standard Level Economics, sets the internal commentary deadlines, approves the portfolio plan and applies the criteria your child is marked against. Paying for a second delivery of that content is the default purchase and the weakest one. The useful question is which jobs are structurally impossible for a teacher with several classes, because those are the jobs a paid hour genuinely adds something to.

Three qualify. Reading one student's commentary draft closely and asking the questions that send them back to it is the first: a teacher with thirty portfolio drafts cannot do it more than once per commentary, however willing they are. Marking one student's timed answer every week against the descriptors is the second. Diagnosing why a particular student's evaluation never reaches the upper descriptors is the third, because it requires looking at that student's writing repeatedly rather than at the class's.

Content coverage qualifies only in narrow cases: a mid-year arrival in Abu Dhabi, an extended absence, a change of teacher mid-unit, or a student who began the course with no economics background in a class taught as though everyone had one. Those gaps are real and cheap to close because they are specific. A family that identifies one and buys three hours has spent well. A family that buys twenty hours of general revision has paid twice for the same teaching. The test for any content hour is whether a school clinic your child can already attend would have covered it.

sections.heading: Marking is the product, so ask what an hour of it produces
paragraphs: In a coursework-and-essay subject, the thing you are actually buying is somebody's reading time. Marking a Paper 1 part (b) answer properly takes a tutor roughly as long as teaching the topic would: read it, place it against the descriptors, identify which available marks were not claimed and why, then write that in a form the student can act on. An hourly rate priced to exclude that will exclude it, and the student will produce less writing as a result, which is the opposite of what the subject needs.

So ask the question directly before booking: if my child writes one answer a week, is it marked inside the rate, and what do we receive? A clear answer sounds like this: the answer comes back with the descriptor level and the reason, the uncollected marks named, and one instruction for the next attempt. A vague answer about ongoing feedback usually means marking happens verbally in the next session if time allows, which is a different and cheaper product.

The same applies to commentary drafts. Reading an 800-word commentary against five criteria takes real time, and some providers bill per draft while others include two and charge for the third. Neither is unreasonable; what is unreasonable is finding out in the deadline week. Get it in writing, and treat a provider who cannot say how many drafts are included as having answered the question. The number that matters is not the hourly rate but the cost of getting one piece of writing read properly three times.

sections.heading: The invoice questions for a coursework-heavy subject
paragraphs: Some of these apply to any tutoring and some are specific to a subject with three deadlines inside it. Is the rate per hour or per session, and how long is a session? Is marking of timed answers included? How many commentary drafts does the block cover, and what is charged for an extra one? Does a package expire at the end of term, and do unused sessions carry forward? Is the commentary block priced differently from weekly teaching? What is the cancellation window, and does a late cancellation lapse or roll over?

On tax the honest answer is narrow: ask whether the quoted price includes VAT and get it in writing. This page does not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition fees, because doing so would need a Federal Tax Authority citation rather than a confident sentence, and more than one page in this market asserts a treatment without one. The protection is the same either way, which is a written quote that says whether the number is inclusive.

Where something is described as free, check the condition on the same screen as the word. The trial here is a 45-minute working session with no card details required, and that is the whole condition. Elsewhere, a free assessment may require a package purchase before the findings are released, or a free first lesson may be conditional on booking a month. Those are legitimate commercial choices and they are only a problem when the condition appears after the decision.

sections.heading: Equivalency, universities and why the economics grade is being chased
paragraphs: Part of the pressure behind a Standard Level Economics grade in Abu Dhabi is what comes after it. For families intending to study in the UAE, Ministry of Education equivalency of the school certificate is the process that matters, and it is worth understanding before paying anyone to chase a grade for the wrong reason. Equivalency is a Ministry process. It is not something a tutoring provider performs, guarantees or accelerates, and anyone suggesting otherwise is describing a regulatory process they do not operate.

For the British track the published requirements are specific: five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. For the American track, English proficiency is evidenced by IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, with mathematics requiring at least 450 in SAT Math.

For the IB there is no points threshold published here, because none has been read on a Ministry source. Any figure quoted at you for IB equivalency should be checked on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate's attestation channel rather than taken from a tutoring page, including this one. One ranking competitor in this market already publishes the wrong subject count for the British track, which is a useful reminder that confident numbers on tutoring websites are not sources. University admission requirements are a separate matter again, and each programme publishes its own.

sections.heading: When to stop paying, and what the last invoice should buy
paragraphs: Every tutoring arrangement should have a point at which it ends, and economics gives you clear signals. Stop when the component you bought the hours for has improved and the remaining weakness is in a different component that needs a different purchase. Stop when the student can place their own answer against the descriptors and say what is missing, because at that point they can practise without paying. Stop when the portfolio is submitted and the remaining work is revision the school is already running clinics for.

There is also a harder signal. If eight weeks of marked writing have produced no change in descriptor level on comparable questions, more of the same will not help. The right response is a different approach or a different tutor, not additional hours, and a provider who proposes additional hours as the first answer is not reading the evidence. Families in this market often double the spend at precisely the moment the evidence says to change direction.

The last invoice is worth spending deliberately. A single session that produces a written summary of what remains weak, which components it affects and what the student should practise without paying is better value than three more sessions of general revision. Ask for that explicitly. A provider who treats the end of an arrangement as a thing to be managed rather than planned has told you something about the arrangement itself. Set the review date when the block is agreed, so that stopping is a decision already scheduled rather than a conversation somebody has to start.

process.title: Say the budget and the component
process.description: Advice improves when both are on the table. A family with four sessions to spend should be told which four, and that answer is different from a plan for a term. If the student's weakness is the portfolio, the answer is a planning hour and draft feedback, which is a smaller purchase than most families arrive expecting.

process.title: A free 45-minute trial with no card required
process.description: A working session rather than a consultation that withholds its findings. The student attempts an answer or brings a commentary article, and you are told which rows of the component table apply, with an estimate of hours. If the honest answer is fewer hours than you planned, that is what you are told.

process.title: Agree what the rate includes, in writing
process.description: Specifically: whether marking timed answers is inside the hour, how many commentary drafts the block covers, what an extra draft costs, whether the figure includes VAT, and what happens to unused sessions. Every one of those has changed somebody's invoice in this market, usually in the deadline week.

process.title: Buy the block, not the subscription
process.description: Commentary support is scoped to the school's deadlines. Marked writing runs four to six weeks before mocks and ends. Paired sessions are available where two students at the same level want content and timed practice. Nothing renews by default, and a review date is set when the block is agreed.

process.title: Close the arrangement deliberately
process.description: The final session should produce a written summary: what remains weak, which components it affects, and what the student can practise without paying. That is better value than three more hours of general revision, and asking for it tells you quickly how a provider thinks about the end of an engagement.

whyPoints.title: Priced against the component weightings
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 is 30 per cent, Paper 2 is 40 and the portfolio is 30 at Standard Level. Spending is planned against those figures rather than against whatever the class is currently teaching, which is how an evenly spread budget ends up reaching the least responsive components.

whyPoints.title: The cheapest third of the grade named
whyPoints.description: The portfolio carries 30 per cent and most of its mark is decided at the planning stage. An hour or two spent allocating units, key concepts and articles across all three commentaries is the best-value purchase in the course, and it is the one most providers never mention.

whyPoints.title: Every figure sourced
whyPoints.description: Each AED band on this page names the provider or survey that published it and the year. Three of the most visible pages in this market publish no price at all and two quote in dollars, so a sourced band in dirhams is the minimum a parent should have before comparing offers.

whyPoints.title: Marking stated as part of the rate
whyPoints.description: In an essay and coursework subject the product is reading time. Whether marking of timed answers and commentary drafts sits inside the hour is the single question that decides whether a quote is comparable, and it is asked and answered before the first session.

whyPoints.title: The free options named
whyPoints.description: School clinics, the teacher's own guidance on the portfolio plan, the component breakdown behind a grade and a study group marking each other's answers all cost nothing. Paid hours are worth buying for what those cannot do, and a page that hides them is selling rather than advising.

whyPoints.title: No claims about our own results
whyPoints.description: No success rate, no average grade movement, no star rating. Equivalency is described and attributed to its source rather than presented as something we perform, and no IB points threshold is published here because none has been read on a Ministry source.

faqs.question: How much should we expect to spend on Standard Level Economics across two years in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Less than most families assume, if it is spent by component. Planning all three commentaries plus draft feedback runs roughly AED 600-1,800 at published bands and reaches the 30 per cent portfolio. Diagram accuracy adds AED 300-900. A four to six week marked-writing block before mocks is AED 600-1,800. That is a complete plan for well under the cost of two years of weekly sessions, which at Bestimate's 2026 monthly estimates of AED 600-1,200 would run into five figures across the Diploma.

faqs.question: Why is the portfolio the cheapest part of the economics grade to protect?
faqs.answer: Because most of its mark is decided before any writing, by choices that take an hour to get right. Which article, which unit, which key concept and which diagram are settled at the planning stage, and a poor choice there caps the mark whatever the prose does later. The portfolio is 30 per cent of the Standard Level grade and has no clock on it, so the work can be done calmly in term time. Planning all three together also stops units and concepts colliding, which is a common and entirely avoidable loss.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to buy economics help in DP1 or to wait for DP2 mock results?
faqs.answer: Cheaper in DP1, and by a wide margin. Early hours are planning hours: commentary allocation, diagram accuracy, a catch-up block if the student started with no economics. They are short, they are not urgent, and they protect components rather than rescuing them. Hours bought in the final six weeks before the session are the most expensive in the course, because the student has no time to practise what is taught and the available tutors are at their most committed. Waiting for mocks is reasonable only if nothing specific is already wrong.

faqs.question: What should an hour of economics essay marking actually produce?
faqs.answer: A specific document rather than encouragement. The answer should come back with the descriptor level it reaches, the reason for that placement, the available marks that were not claimed and why, the diagram corrected label by label, and one instruction for the next attempt. If what arrives is a score and a sentence of praise, the marking has not happened. Ask what marking produces before booking, because reading time is the product in this subject and it is also the thing most easily dropped from a cheap hour.

faqs.question: Are economics group classes in Abu Dhabi good value at Standard Level?
faqs.answer: For content, structured revision and keeping pace, yes, and the published group rates in this market start well below one-to-one. For the thing most Standard Level students actually need, which is somebody reading their own writing, no. A group teacher cannot mark thirty commentary drafts closely, which is the same constraint your school's economics teacher works under. The efficient combination is group or self-directed work for content with a small number of individual hours for marking and the portfolio.

faqs.question: Why do economics tutors quote more than science tutors in this emirate?
faqs.answer: Supply. There are fewer Diploma economics specialists in Abu Dhabi than science or mathematics tutors, and fewer again who regularly mark data response and commentaries against the published criteria. That premium is about scarcity rather than travel, so it does not disappear because you live centrally. In-home arrangements compound it, because the few available specialists take the shortest journeys first and the peripheral communities are quoted highest and served last in the weeks before mocks.

faqs.question: Does the Standard Level portfolio cost the same to support as the Higher Level one?
faqs.answer: Roughly the same in hours and more valuable at Standard Level. Both involve three commentaries of up to 800 words marked against the same lettered criteria, so the work a tutor does is comparable. The difference is weighting: the portfolio is 30 per cent of a Standard Level grade and 20 per cent at Higher Level, because Higher Level students also sit the policy paper. Pound for pound, commentary support buys more of the final grade for a Standard Level student than for a Higher Level one.

faqs.question: Should we pay for help choosing the commentary articles?
faqs.answer: Pay for the criteria, not for the choice. The selection is part of the assessed work, so a tutor teaches what an article must satisfy: recent enough, from a credible outlet, describing a mechanism rather than only an outcome, and narrow enough for one unit and one key concept. The student then brings candidates and the discussion is about whether each one meets the criteria. If a tutor simply hands over an article, the first and most consequential decision in the commentary stopped being the student's.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Abu Dhabi need a permit, and does that affect the price?
faqs.answer: A permit is required and it is free, so it should not affect the price. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years, with eligibility covering registered teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted at you. Ask; the answer is checkable.

faqs.question: Does Economics count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: Equivalency is assessed on the certificate rather than on one subject, and the published rules differ by curriculum. For the British track, five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one Advanced Level at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at E. For the American track, English via IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or SAT 450 in reading and writing, with SAT Math at 450 or above. For the IB, no points threshold is published here because none has been read on a Ministry source; check moe.gov.ae or the attestation channel.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for mock marking before the May session?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the marking produces descriptor-level reasoning rather than a score, and if there is enough time left to act on it. A marked mock that names the uncollected marks and gives one instruction per component is the highest-value single purchase in DP2, because it directs everything that follows. A mock returned with a grade and general advice is worth little at any price. Two to three hours is usually enough for a full Standard Level paper set, which at published bands is a modest and well-targeted spend.

faqs.question: If we can only afford four sessions, what should they be spent on?
faqs.answer: If the portfolio is unsubmitted: one session planning all three commentaries, two on draft feedback, one on diagram accuracy. That sequence reaches 30 per cent of the grade and the technical marks across both papers. If the portfolio is already in: one session marking a timed Paper 2 data response, one on the losses it reveals, one marking a Paper 1 part (b), one on evaluation structure. Four sessions spent on general content revision will reach almost nothing, because the school is already delivering that.

faqs.question: Do you charge extra for reading an additional commentary draft?
faqs.answer: Ask this of any provider, including us, and get the answer in writing before the block starts. Reading an 800-word commentary against five criteria takes real time, so some providers include two drafts and charge for a third while others price per draft. Neither practice is unreasonable; discovering the policy in deadline week is. The same applies to whether the block covers all three commentaries or one, because a quote covering a single commentary looks competitive next to one covering the whole portfolio.

faqs.question: How do we avoid paying for economics content the school is already teaching?
faqs.answer: Ask the school two questions first: which components is my child losing marks on, and where is the class against the scheme of work. Then buy only what a teacher with several classes structurally cannot provide, which is close reading of one student's drafts, weekly marking of one student's timed answers, and diagnosis of why that student's evaluation does not reach the upper descriptors. Content hours are worth buying only for a specific gap: an absence, a mid-year arrival, a change of teacher, or no prior economics in a class taught as though everyone has it.

faqs.question: When should we stop paying for economics support?
faqs.answer: When the component you bought the hours for has improved and the remaining weakness needs a different purchase. When the student can place their own answer against the descriptors and say what is missing, because they can then practise unpaid. When the portfolio is submitted and what remains is revision the school runs clinics for. And when eight weeks of marked writing have produced no change in descriptor level on comparable questions, at which point the answer is a different approach rather than more hours.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-economics-sl-home-tutor.closingHeading: Price the components before you price the hours
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-economics-sl-home-tutor.closingBody: Send the last economics answer your child wrote and say what you are prepared to spend. The free 45-minute session identifies which component is losing the marks, says which rows of the spending plan actually apply, and estimates the hours each would take. No card details are required to book it. If the conclusion is one planning hour and four marked answers rather than two years of weekly sessions, you will have that in writing and can take it to any provider in Abu Dhabi for comparison.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-economics-sl-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Standard Level Economics to Diploma students across Abu Dhabi. Each profile names the units covered, whether the tutor has supervised portfolio commentaries, and the papers they work on most. Ask any of them which command term costs their students the most marks.

intro.heading: What a Standard Level Economics tutor is actually working on
paragraphs: Standard Level Economics is a small, tightly defined assessment. Three components, four syllabus units, nine key concepts and a published set of command terms. There is no Paper 3 and there is no coursework beyond the portfolio. Once a family understands that shape, most of the vagueness around what a tutor does disappears, because every hour has to land in one of those three components or it is not doing anything.

Paper 1 is extended response. The student picks questions and writes, in two parts, with part (a) asking for explanation and part (b) for discussion or evaluation. Real-world examples are expected, which is the part Abu Dhabi students most often supply weakly: a general reference to inflation is not an example, and an example without a figure or a date attached does not read as one either. Diagrams are expected inside written answers, labelled, with the shift shown and the new position identified, and referred to in the prose.

Paper 2 is data response. The student is given an unseen extract and asked to use it. The dominant failure in this component across Abu Dhabi cohorts is not a knowledge failure at all: students paraphrase the extract and then set out the relevant theory beside it, without ever connecting the two. A question that says use the extract is asking for specific figures and specific quotations supporting specific claims. There are also calculation items, and a correct answer with no working forfeits method marks that a wrong answer with clear working sometimes keeps.

The portfolio is three commentaries of no more than 800 words each, assessed against lettered criteria. At Standard Level it carries 30% of the subject grade, which is more than at Higher Level, because there is no third paper diluting it. That is the single most useful thing a Standard Level family can know: the component with the clearest, most teachable mark scheme is also the one carrying the largest share of the grade, and it is the one most students treat as an afterthought.

There is one more thing a parent should know before reading further, and it concerns who may lawfully take the work. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. In Abu Dhabi there is a second layer: ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate, and its professional-ethics rules, as reported by Gulf News, bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. Those two rules together shrink the lawful local pool, and they are the reason the first question to ask any provider is about the permit rather than about the price.

This page works through each of those in the detail a parent needs: the units and what each one tests, the nine concepts and how they are examined, the command terms and what they are worth, where the marks go topic by topic, and what one session can realistically fix. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service we run only in India.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-economics-sl-tutor.programmesIntro: Standard Level Economics sits in Group 3 of the Diploma. The IB routes below determine what a student brings to it, and in Economics the difference between routes is unusually visible in the first term.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across two years plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Economics is organised into four units and nine key concepts, and at Standard Level is assessed through two written papers and a portfolio. The concepts are examinable rather than introductory: one has to be applied explicitly in each commentary and carries its own marks for doing so.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi, Standard Level Economics is often the larger of the two Group 3 economics-and-business options, with Business Management competing for the same choosers. Groups of fifteen to twenty are common at the island schools and much smaller at the newer mainland ones, which changes how many marked exemplars a student has seen before writing their own first commentary.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Individuals and Societies is assessed on knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. The critical-thinking criterion maps onto Paper 1 part (b) and onto commentary evaluation. What MYP does not supply is diagram mechanics, which is a drawing and labelling skill rather than an analytical one and is learned fastest by being taught directly.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Abu Dhabi school runs MYP to the end of Year 11, DP1 Economics students arrive with confident written argument and no prior exposure to supply and demand diagrams. That profile is predictable enough to plan for: the first sessions go to diagram mechanics, not to essay coaching.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A smaller IB route pairing a few DP courses with a career-related study and a reflective project. A CP student taking Standard Level Economics sits the same two papers and submits the same portfolio, without the Theory of Knowledge load competing for the same weeks as the commentary deadlines.
programmes.countryNote: The Career-related Programme is uncommon in Abu Dhabi, which means a CP Economics student usually has no classmate writing the same commentaries at the same time. With no peer work to compare against, a tutor's criterion-referenced feedback becomes the only external reading the draft gets before submission.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
programmes.description: An Extended Essay in Economics is a 4,000-word independent piece supervised at school, entirely separate from the portfolio and with its own authenticity record. Theory of Knowledge shares no content with Economics but competes directly for the weeks when commentaries are due.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools generally set internal core deadlines ahead of the IB's own windows, and in most years the Theory of Knowledge essay and the second or third commentary fall within the same fortnight. Planning a Standard Level Economics term without checking that collision is how a student ends up writing a commentary in two evenings.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-economics-sl-tutor.subjectsIntro: Standard Level Economics is the subject here. The ones listed after it are what Abu Dhabi students carry alongside it, each described by what it contributes to, or takes from, Economics performance.

subjects.name: Economics (Standard Level)
subjects.description: Two written papers and a portfolio. Paper 1 is extended response at 30%, Paper 2 data response at 40%, and the portfolio 30%. Four units and nine key concepts. Marks concentrate in three places: diagram use inside written answers, evidence drawn from the extract in Paper 2, and judgement in part (b) of Paper 1.

subjects.name: Economics (Higher Level)
subjects.description: Adds a third paper, a quantitative policy paper carrying 30% of the grade, and rebalances the weightings so the portfolio drops to 20%. A student moving up carries their portfolio work with them; a student moving down finds the portfolio suddenly worth proportionally more.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The usual alternative in Group 3 rather than a companion. Shared ground is thin: market structures, some stakeholder thinking, a little finance. The assessment instincts differ, and a student who writes good Business answers often writes under-evaluated Economics ones.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Supplies percentage change, index numbers, elasticity arithmetic and real-data interpretation, all of which appear in Paper 2 calculation items. The gap is usually transfer rather than knowledge: the student can do the maths and does not recognise it dressed as economics.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Produces algebraically confident students who are unpractised at applied calculation under time pressure and at writing working the way a mark scheme credits it. One targeted session on shown working usually recovers more marks than a week of general revision.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Overlaps Economics on development, trade and sustainability, and the overlap is substantial enough that the shared content can be taught once. The habits of using named places and real figures as evidence also transfer straight into Paper 1 real-world examples.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Shares intervention, trade blocs and development debates. It teaches students to weigh competing positions, which is exactly the habit Paper 1 part (b) rewards and the one most Standard Level Economics answers are missing.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Not an obvious pairing, but History trains the use of specific, dated evidence in support of an argument. Students taking both tend to produce stronger real-world examples in Economics, because they already know that an example without a date is not evidence.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Where Economics marks are being lost to disorganised writing rather than to economics, the problem belongs here. A tutor should be able to tell a family which of the two it is after reading one marked Paper 1 answer.

subjects.name: Extended Essay in Economics
subjects.description: Separate from the portfolio and supervised at school. A tutor can teach question framing, data sourcing and economic method, and comment on drafts the student has written. The text must be the student's own, and the school supervisor records authenticity as part of the assessment.

sections.heading: The four units, and what each one actually tests
paragraphs: Economics is not a long syllabus, and at Standard Level it is finishable in the time available, which is not true of every Diploma subject. The four units are sequential in most schools and they test quite different things, so a student can be strong in two and weak in two without that showing in an overall grade until mocks.

Unit 1 introduces the discipline: scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, the fundamental economic questions and the central concepts the rest of the course uses. Students and schools both treat it as warm-up, and it is where a surprising number of Paper 1 marks are lost later, because an answer that cannot define its terms precisely cannot score the terminology credit that sits under every question.

Unit 2, microeconomics, is the mechanical heart of the course and the unit where diagram technique either exists or does not. Demand and supply, elasticity, market failure, government intervention and market structures. It produces the most calculation items and the most diagram-based marks, and it is where a tutor can move a grade fastest, because the failures are concrete and the fixes are procedural.

Unit 3, macroeconomics, is where students who are fluent in micro often stall. The content is interconnected rather than sequential: a change in interest rates moves several variables at once, and questions ask about trade-offs between objectives rather than about single effects. Unit 4, the global economy, covers trade, exchange rates, economic integration and development, and it is the unit most students meet last and with the least practice. In Abu Dhabi it is also the unit where local material is most readily usable as real-world evidence.

sections.heading: The nine key concepts, and how they are examined
paragraphs: The nine key concepts are the most under-used part of the Standard Level course. Students meet them in the first week, write them in a margin, and then write two years of answers that never use them. They are examinable, and in the portfolio they carry marks in their own right.

The nine are scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence and intervention. Read as a list they look like topic labels. They are not topics; they are lenses. Equity and efficiency pull against each other in almost every intervention question. Interdependence is what makes a macroeconomic policy question hard. Change is what turns a static diagram into an analysis. A student who can organise an answer around a concept writes a different answer from one who recites the content.

In the portfolio, applying a concept is a specific requirement with marks attached, and it is the single most commonly forfeited credit in a first draft. The pattern is unmistakable: the concept is named in the opening sentence, and the remaining 780 words proceed as if it had never been mentioned. Applying a concept means the analysis is framed by it, the diagram is chosen because of it, and the evaluation returns to it.

In the written papers the concepts work differently. They are not asked about by name, but they are what a strong part (b) answer is organised around. A question on a minimum wage is an equity-against-efficiency question. A question on a subsidy is an intervention-and-sustainability question. Teaching a student to recognise which concept a question is really about is one of the few interventions that improves every answer they write for the rest of the course.

sections.heading: Standard Level assessment: three components, no Paper 3
paragraphs: The Standard Level assessment model is smaller than the Higher Level one and weighted differently, and the difference changes where a family should spend attention. There are two written papers and the portfolio, and no quantitative policy paper.

Paper 1 carries 30% of the subject grade and is extended response. The student chooses questions and answers in two parts. Part (a) asks for explanation, part (b) for discussion, evaluation or examination depending on the command term, and the marks are distributed so that a strong part (a) cannot rescue an absent part (b). Real-world examples are expected and are marked as evidence, which means they need enough specificity to function as evidence.

Paper 2 carries 40%, the largest single share, and is data response on an unseen extract. It includes definition items, explanation items, calculation items and a final extended question that asks the student to use the extract to evaluate something. Because it is unseen, it cannot be revised for directly; it can only be practised. That distinction is why a Standard Level plan that consists of reading notes produces no movement in Paper 2 at all.

The portfolio carries 30%, three percentage points more than the whole of Paper 1. Three commentaries, 800 words each, assessed against lettered criteria for a combined 45 marks including three marks for meeting the portfolio's own requirements. It is coursework, so it is the only component where a student can work slowly, with feedback, before submitting. Treating it as the easiest component to improve is correct. Treating it as the least important, which is what most students do, is not.

sections.heading: Command terms, and the marks they quietly decide
paragraphs: A command term is the instruction in the question, and in Economics it is worth more than the topic. A student who writes an accurate, well-organised, well-illustrated answer to the wrong command term has written something that cannot score the available marks, and nothing in the answer looks wrong. This is the failure families find hardest to believe and tutors find easiest to fix.

The terms cluster into levels. Define and list ask for recall and nothing else, and marks are lost by over-writing them. Explain and analyse ask for mechanism: a chain of consequence, usually best carried by a diagram. Discuss, evaluate and examine ask for judgement, which means weighing at least two positions and arriving somewhere, with the basis for the judgement stated. Calculate asks for working as well as an answer.

The costly confusion in Abu Dhabi cohorts is consistently between analyse and evaluate. An analysis that is perfect scores perhaps half of an evaluate question, because no judgement has been reached and no alternative has been weighed. Students in small Group 3 classes are especially prone to it, because they have seen few marked examples of the difference and the teacher's verbal feedback does not survive into the next essay.

The repair is mechanical and fast. A reusable evaluation structure, drilled against real part (b) questions, with the student required to produce the judgement sentence first and build towards it. Four to six sessions is normally enough to see it in the next marked paper, and it lifts marks across every topic at once rather than one, which is why it is the first thing a diagnostic looks for.

sections.heading: Why the portfolio matters more at Standard Level
paragraphs: At Standard Level the portfolio carries 30% of the subject grade. At Higher Level the same three commentaries carry 20%, because a third paper absorbs the difference. The work is identical and its value is not, and a Standard Level family that understands this has found the cheapest marks on the course.

Three commentaries, no more than 800 words each. Each draws on a different unit of the syllabus. Each uses a different source, published no earlier than one year before the commentary is written. Each applies one of the nine key concepts explicitly. The assessment is against lettered criteria: diagrams, terminology, application and analysis, key concept and evaluation, for fourteen marks per commentary, plus three marks across the portfolio for meeting those presentation requirements.

The losses are concentrated and predictable. The diagram is correct and the text never refers to it. The key concept is named once and abandoned. The evaluation is a summary rather than a judgement, usually because the word budget ran out: students write 700 words of analysis and 100 words of conclusion, when the criteria would reward the reverse balance. The three presentation marks are lost to an article published too long ago or a commentary a hundred words over the limit, both of which are avoidable with a checklist.

What a tutor does here needs stating precisely, because this is coursework. A tutor may teach diagram technique, explain what applying a key concept looks like, show what the top evaluation band contains, and comment criterion by criterion on a draft the student has written. A tutor may not supply text, may not select and summarise the article on the student's behalf, and may not revise a draft into a submission. The school supervisor keeps the authenticity record and the IB treats a breach as malpractice by the candidate, not by whoever caused it.

sections.heading: Using the UAE economy as evidence rather than as decoration
paragraphs: Paper 1 expects real-world examples and Paper 2 supplies its own extract, which means the quality of a student's evidence habit decides a meaningful share of their grade. Abu Dhabi students have an advantage here that most of them never use: they live in an economy that illustrates a large part of the syllabus directly.

An example counts as evidence when it names a place, a time and a number. A reference to government spending is not an example. A reference to a named infrastructure programme, in a stated year, with an order of magnitude attached, is. The difference is not sophistication, it is specificity, and it is learnable in a single session once a student sees the two versions side by side.

The local material is unusually rich. Subsidy and price-control questions, value added tax and its incidence, labour-market questions about an economy with a large expatriate workforce, exchange-rate questions about a currency pegged to the dollar, sovereign wealth and the economics of diversifying away from hydrocarbons, free zones as an application of trade theory. Each of those maps onto a specific part of Units 2, 3 or 4.

Two cautions. Use figures that can be sourced, from official or reputable published material, rather than numbers remembered from a classroom conversation; an invented figure is worse than no figure. And do not let a local example substitute for the theory it is meant to illustrate. The marks are for the economics; the example is what makes the economics credible. A commentary built on a UAE policy story still has to show the diagram, apply the concept and reach a judgement.

sections.heading: What one session can realistically fix
paragraphs: Families are entitled to know what an hour buys, and in Standard Level Economics the honest answer varies by a factor of ten depending on what the problem is. Some things genuinely move in one session. Others take a term and no provider should pretend otherwise.

Fixable in roughly one session: the mechanics of a single diagram type; the definition set from Unit 1; what applying a key concept means as opposed to naming one; how to write working so method marks are available; how to tell analyse from evaluate in a question stem. These are procedural, and they show up in the next piece of marked work.

Fixable in four to six sessions: evaluation structure in part (b); using an extract as evidence throughout a Paper 2 answer; the diagram set for a whole unit; the discipline of a real-world example with a figure and a date. These are habits rather than facts, which is why they take repetition against real questions and marked feedback rather than explanation.

Not fixable in a block at all: content gaps across two or more units; a writing problem that is a writing problem rather than an economics one; a student who does nothing between sessions. Those take a term, a different kind of help, or a different conversation. A tutor who tells a family which category their child is in before taking money is being more useful than one who agrees to everything, and the first session at no charge exists to produce that answer.

sections.heading: The rules around a paid Economics tutor in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Three things are worth a family's attention before booking, and none of them appears on the competitor pages measured in this research set. They concern who is permitted to tutor, what a tutor may touch, and what material may change hands.

On permission: private tutoring in the UAE runs on the MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, and open to registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so no amount should be quoted to you. In Abu Dhabi there is an additional layer: Gulf News reported that ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, which should be verified against ADEK's current policy document.

On what a tutor may touch: the portfolio is coursework and the Extended Essay is coursework. A tutor teaches, explains the criteria, and comments on drafts the student has produced. Supplying text, selecting and summarising the source, or revising a draft into something submittable is malpractice under IB rules, and the consequence falls on the candidate. One provider in this market sells completed internal assessments outright. A family should treat that offer as a warning about the provider rather than as a service.

On material: syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB. A tutor should reference them and point you to the official source. A provider advertising a library of downloadable mark schemes is describing a copyright problem, not a resource advantage. The legitimate version is a tutor who knows the criteria well enough to explain them without handing over a copy.

faqs.question: What exactly does Standard Level Economics assess, and in what proportions?
faqs.answer: Three components. Paper 1 is extended response and carries 30% of the subject grade, with questions answered in two parts and real-world examples expected. Paper 2 is data response on an unseen extract and carries 40%, the largest single share, and includes definition, explanation, calculation and extended items. The portfolio of three commentaries carries 30%. There is no Paper 3 at Standard Level; that component exists only at Higher Level. Confirm the current weightings against the subject guide your child's Diploma coordinator holds for their examination session.

faqs.question: Which Economics unit do Abu Dhabi students find hardest?
faqs.answer: Macroeconomics, consistently, and for a structural reason. Microeconomics is sequential and mechanical: a change moves a curve, the curve gives a new equilibrium, the diagram carries the argument. Macroeconomics is interconnected, so a single policy change moves several variables at once and questions ask about trade-offs between objectives rather than single effects. Students who are fluent in micro produce single-effect macro answers and lose the comparative marks. The fix is building chains of consequence and then weighing them, which takes practice on real questions rather than more notes.

faqs.question: How much does a command term like evaluate actually matter in Economics?
faqs.answer: Often a third of a question's marks. An evaluate question asks for a judgement, justified, with alternatives weighed. A student who produces a faultless analysis and stops before judging has written something with nothing visibly wrong with it that still cannot reach the higher band. This is the failure families find hardest to accept, because the answer reads well. It is also among the fastest things to repair: four to six sessions drilling a reusable evaluation structure against real part (b) questions usually shows in the next marked paper.

faqs.question: What is the difference between explain and analyse in an Economics answer?
faqs.answer: Both ask for mechanism, and the difference is how much of it has to be visible. Explain wants a chain of cause and effect: this happens, which causes that, which results in this. Analyse wants the same chain broken into its steps with the diagram doing real work, so each stage is identified and the movement between states is accounted for rather than asserted. The practical test on a marked script is whether the diagram is referred to in the prose. An unreferenced diagram almost always means analysis credit was left on the table.

faqs.question: Does the portfolio count for more if my child is at Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Yes. The three commentaries carry 30% of the subject grade at Standard Level against 20% at Higher Level, because the Higher Level model adds a third paper that absorbs the difference. The work is identical either way. For a Standard Level student that makes the portfolio worth more than the whole of Paper 1, and it is the only component where the student can work slowly with feedback before submitting. Treating it as the easiest place to improve a grade is correct; treating it as a formality is expensive.

faqs.question: Can my son use the UAE economy as a real-world example in Paper 1?
faqs.answer: Yes, and he should, because the local economy illustrates a large part of the syllabus directly. Value added tax and its incidence, a currency pegged to the dollar, free zones as an application of trade theory, subsidy policy, and a labour market with a large expatriate workforce all map onto specific syllabus content. Two conditions make it count. The example needs a place, a date and a figure that can be sourced, and it has to illustrate the theory rather than replace it. The diagram and the judgement still have to be there.

faqs.question: Does every Standard Level Economics answer need a diagram?
faqs.answer: Not every answer, but far more of them than students draw. Any question asking about a change in a market, a policy effect or a macroeconomic adjustment is a diagram question, and the marks are available for a diagram that is correctly labelled on both axes, shows the shift rather than describing it, identifies the new position, and is referred to in the text. Diagrams drawn as decoration earn nothing. This is the most mechanical skill on the course and usually the first thing a diagnostic session addresses.

faqs.question: My daughter understands elasticity but loses the calculation marks. Why?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the working is not written in the form the mark scheme credits. Calculation items award method marks for the steps as well as marks for the answer, so a correct number with nothing shown forfeits credit that a wrong number with clear working sometimes keeps. The other common cause is units and signs: an elasticity figure without a sign, or a percentage change calculated from the wrong base. Both are procedural problems rather than understanding problems, and both are usually fixed inside one session.

faqs.question: What can one Economics session actually fix?
faqs.answer: More than families expect for procedural problems and less than they hope for content gaps. In roughly one session: the mechanics of a single diagram type, the Unit 1 definition set, what applying a key concept means rather than naming one, and how to write working so method marks are available. In four to six: evaluation structure, using an extract as evidence throughout an answer, and the real-world example habit. Content gaps across two or more units take a term, and nobody should tell you otherwise before seeing marked work.

faqs.question: Will Standard Level Economics be accepted for a business degree at a UAE university?
faqs.answer: Requirements are set by individual faculties rather than by a single rule, and they vary between institutions and between countries. Many business and management programmes accept Economics at Standard Level, and several do not require Economics at all, preferring Mathematics at a particular level. The right source is the specific programme's published entry requirements and the school's university counsellor, with the actual offer conditions in front of you. Tutoring is not a requirement for admission anywhere, and any page implying otherwise is making a false-urgency claim about an admissions process.

faqs.question: How do market failure questions catch Standard Level students out?
faqs.answer: Three ways, all of them repeatable. The externality is identified but never shown on a diagram, so the welfare loss is asserted rather than demonstrated. The intervention is described without being weighed against alternatives, which costs the evaluation marks. And equity is treated as a synonym for equality, which changes the claim being made. Market failure questions are also where the efficiency and sustainability concepts do the most work, so a student who has been taught to organise an answer around a concept scores noticeably better on them.

faqs.question: Does online tuition work for a subject built on diagrams?
faqs.answer: It works particularly well, which is counter-intuitive until you have seen it. A shared screen lets a tutor draw a diagram, label it, move a curve and correct the student's version live, with both people looking at the same thing rather than at two sheets of paper. The annotated version is saved at the end of the session instead of going home in a folder. A data extract, a mark scheme and a diagram being built can all be on screen simultaneously, which is physically awkward at a dining table.

faqs.question: Do lessons happen at our home in Al Bateen, or is it all online?
faqs.answer: All online. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every Abu Dhabi lesson is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The honest case for it is reach rather than price: a Standard Level Economics specialist who knows the current syllabus, the portfolio criteria and the command-term distinctions is a narrow brief, and restricting the search to people who can drive to Al Bateen on a weekday evening narrows it a great deal further.

faqs.question: Is my child's Economics teacher allowed to tutor them privately for a fee?
faqs.answer: In Abu Dhabi, press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules indicates that private and charter school staff are prohibited from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct that bars the same arrangement. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it. Separately, any individual tutoring privately in the UAE needs the MoHRE permit, which is granted free of charge for two years. Ask a provider both questions directly and expect plain answers.

faqs.question: When should an Abu Dhabi Standard Level Economics student start outside support?
faqs.answer: Earlier than most families do, and the reason is specific to this subject. The things that move a Standard Level Economics grade fastest are mechanical: diagram technique, command-term recognition, shown working, the key-concept habit. All of them pay back across both papers and all three commentaries, so buying them in the first term of DP1 means every piece of work for the next two years is written better. Buying them in the DP2 spring means they arrive after the portfolio is submitted and most of the practice is done.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-economics-sl-tutor.closingBody: Standard Level Economics is two papers and a portfolio, and the marks sit in a small number of identifiable places: diagram use, command-term recognition, evidence drawn from an extract, and the three commentaries that carry 30% of the grade. Send one marked part (b) answer or one returned commentary, tell us which unit the school is teaching now, and take the first session at no charge. The written list it produces will tell you which repairs take one session and which take a term, which is the only sensible basis for deciding how much to buy.

intro.heading: A mark out of 20 is not feedback, and it is where every family starts
paragraphs: The single most common thing an Abu Dhabi parent brings to a first conversation about this subject is a returned script with a number on it and a sentence underneath. The number is 11, 12 or 13 out of 20. The sentence says the response needs more depth, or closer analysis, or better structure. Neither the number nor the sentence tells anybody what to do next, and a student who has been given the same comment three times has usually concluded that they are simply not good at English, which is almost never the problem.

Language and Literature is assessed against four criteria on every component, and they are not interchangeable. One asks whether the student has understood and interpreted the text. One asks whether they have analysed and evaluated how the writer's choices produce meaning. One asks whether the response is focused and organised. One asks about the quality of the language itself. A student can be strong on two and weak on two, and the aggregate mark hides which. Reading a marked script against the criterion letters turns a vague 12 into a specific, short list of things to practise.

That diagnosis almost always contradicts what the family expected. A student whose written English is fluent and idiomatic frequently scores badly on analysis and evaluation, because fluency encourages assertion rather than argument. A student whose English is second-language and slightly formal frequently scores well on understanding and loses marks on language. The two need opposite interventions, and giving both of them more essay practice produces no movement in either, which is how a term disappears.

What realistically moves is the subject of this page. Focus and organisation respond quickly, often within a few weeks, because the fix is structural and teachable. Analysis and evaluation move over a term, because the underlying skill is a habit of mind. Language moves slowly and unevenly. Knowledge of the set texts moves as fast as the student reads them. Setting a family's expectations against that reality is more useful than any promise, and nothing on this page promises a grade.

Abu Dhabi context matters in two ways. ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection ratings, and the schools here teach a wide spread of curricula, so cohorts in this subject often mix students who have been in English-medium education since Year 1 with students who joined at Year 9. Arabic, Islamic education and social studies also run alongside the licensed curriculum, which compresses the evening. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Support here is one-to-one over live video, with annotated scripts on a shared screen.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-l.programmesIntro: Where a student sat before DP1 predicts which criterion will be weak, more reliably than any diagnostic test. The routes below are the ones that feed English A in Abu Dhabi schools.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Language and Literature
programmes.description: MYP Language and Literature assesses analysing, organising, producing text and using language, which maps closely onto the Diploma's four criteria. Students arriving by this route generally understand that analysis means explaining how a choice produces an effect. What they often lack is the stamina for a sustained comparative argument under timed conditions, because MYP tasks are mostly produced over days rather than in ninety minutes.
programmes.countryNote: A minority of Abu Dhabi Diploma students come through MYP, concentrated in the schools running the full continuum. Those students usually need timed-condition practice rather than skill teaching, which is a shorter and cheaper intervention than most families expect when they book.

programmes.name: IGCSE First Language English and English Literature
programmes.description: First Language English rewards accurate reading, directed writing and controlled expression. English Literature adds essay writing on set texts. Both build real strengths, and both reward a style of answer the Diploma marks down: confident summary and well-expressed personal response. The Diploma wants the mechanism, not the reaction, and that adjustment is the whole of term one for many students.
programmes.countryNote: This is the majority route in Abu Dhabi, because the British-curriculum cohort in the emirate is large. The signature pattern in a first marked Diploma script from these students is a strong, readable essay scoring in the middle band on analysis and evaluation.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme English A: Language and Literature
programmes.description: The course studies literary works alongside non-literary texts. Paper 1 is a guided analysis of previously unseen non-literary material. Paper 2 is a comparative essay on literary works studied, written without the texts to hand. The individual oral examines a global issue through one literary and one non-literary extract. Higher Level adds a written essay on a work or text studied in class.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi cohorts in this subject are frequently mixed in a way that matters: students schooled in English since Year 1 sitting beside students who arrived at Year 9. One class, one set of texts, two completely different sets of weak criteria, and a teacher who cannot run both diagnoses at once.

programmes.name: Extended Essay in English
programmes.description: A 4,000-word research essay on a literary or language question, supervised in school and marked externally. The reliable failure is a question broad enough to invite a tour of a novel. Support is process coaching and feedback on drafts the student has produced, with the essay remaining their own work throughout.
programmes.countryNote: English is among the most popular Extended Essay subjects in Abu Dhabi schools, including with students who find the subject hardest, because the texts feel familiar. Those students need the analytical frame before the question, and their first block is usually spent there.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-l.subjectsIntro: English A rarely appears alone in a request. The subjects below are the ones most often booked alongside it by Abu Dhabi families, with what each assesses and where a Language and Literature student usually needs the help.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 guided analysis of unseen non-literary text, Paper 2 comparative essay on literary works, individual oral on a global issue, and at Higher Level a written essay. Marks leak to assertion without mechanism, comparison written as two separate accounts, and orals that describe an issue rather than examine it.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: The literature-only route: two papers on literary works, an individual oral and, at Higher Level, an essay. Students sometimes move between the two courses early in DP1, and the transferable skill is analysis of technique rather than familiarity with particular texts.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: A language-acquisition course with reading, listening, writing and an oral, aimed at students who are not studying English as a first language. A student struggling badly in English A is sometimes in the wrong course, and that is a conversation for the Diploma coordinator early in DP1.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: An exhibition of three objects with commentaries and a prescribed-title essay. The skills overlap heavily with English A: a claim, a counterclaim and a real example per paragraph is the structure that earns marks in both, and students who learn it in one subject usually improve in the other.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Papers on prescribed subjects and world history topics plus a historical investigation. Source evaluation in History is the same mental move as analysis and evaluation in English A, applied to a different kind of text, and the pairing is efficient to tutor together.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Arabic is mandatory in UAE private schools alongside the licensed international curriculum, with placement set by a student's background rather than preference. For an English A student it is usually the subject with the heaviest competing reading load.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Papers across approaches and options plus an internal investigation. It pairs commonly with English A in Abu Dhabi, and the investigation's write-up is where those students most often need structural help rather than content teaching.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Papers plus a research project at Higher Level. Students who take it alongside English A tend to be strong on structure and weak on nuance, and the transferable gain runs from English into Business rather than the other way.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Two papers with technology permitted, plus an exploration. Humanities-weighted Diploma students usually sit this route, and the exploration is where a tutor's involvement is strictly feedback on the student's own draft.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-l.regionsIntro: In this subject, area matters because of who is in the classroom. The notes below describe the school mix and the typical constraint on an evening session across Abu Dhabi.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Schools in this cluster tend to have long-settled, largely English-first intakes, so cohorts are less mixed than elsewhere in the emirate. The commonest diagnosis here is a fluent writer scoring in the middle band on analysis and evaluation.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: A transient, international residential population feeding several schools, which produces genuinely mixed English A classes. Students joining a Diploma cohort mid-course are more common here, and the first session is usually a straight diagnosis of which criterion is weak.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities with a long weekday-evening drive to the island. Sessions here work best after 18:00, once the school run has cleared, and the length of the evening is the main constraint on how much reading gets done between sessions.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: A dense school corridor with large year groups, which means big English A cohorts and less individual attention per script. Students from this cluster often arrive with four marked scripts and no idea which criterion is losing them marks.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Older island neighbourhoods near long-established schools with experienced English departments. Requests from here are more often about Paper 1 timing and the individual oral than about analysis, which is usually being taught well.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Newer campuses with a commuting intake. Mixed cohorts and set-text lists that vary by school, so the first thing a session establishes is which works the student is actually studying rather than which ones are common.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Central and residential, close to most island schools. The constraint here is the number of subjects stacked into an evening alongside the mandatory UAE subjects, which makes fortnightly sessions with reading between them a better fit than weekly ones.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Al Shamkha
regions.note: Mainland communities with the widest spread of prior schooling in any English A class in the emirate. Students here are the most likely to be sitting in the wrong course entirely, which is a question for the Diploma coordinator rather than for a tutor.

schoolClusters.city: Island and Saadiyat schools
schoolClusters.note: The longest-established international schools in the emirate, with experienced English departments and relatively settled intakes. Requests from this cluster concentrate on Paper 1 under timed conditions and on the individual oral, where the global issue is the usual stumbling block.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-language-and-l.modesIntro: The three arrangements below differ in what gets marked and how often. Which fits depends on what the existing marked scripts show rather than on the student's confidence.

modes.title: Marked-script diagnosis and repair
modes.description: A short block that starts by reading three or four of the student's own returned scripts against the criterion letters, names the one or two criteria actually losing the marks, and then works only on those. It is the cheapest useful purchase in this subject because it stops a family paying for general essay practice that treats every weakness identically.

modes.title: Component-by-component build through DP1
modes.description: A weekly or fortnightly slot that takes the four components in a sensible order rather than all at once: analysis skill first, then Paper 1 under time, then the comparative habit for Paper 2, then the oral. Spreading it this way costs more across the year than a block and produces steadier movement than cramming in DP2.

modes.description: Short, frequent sessions in the run-up to the May session, aimed at the things that still move late: Paper 1 timing and text-type confidence, Paper 2 question choice, and a rehearsed structure for the comparative argument. This block is explicit about what cannot be fixed late, which is unread set texts and weak language control.

sections.heading: Reading a marked Language and Literature script against the criterion letters
paragraphs: Every component in this course is marked on four criteria, and the aggregate mark conceals which one is costing the student. That is why a returned script with 12 out of 20 and a comment about depth is so useless as a guide to action: depth could mean the interpretation is thin, or the analysis is missing, or the structure has buried the argument, or the expression is imprecise. Those are four different problems with four different fixes and four very different timescales.

The first session in almost every block here is a read of three or four of the student's own scripts side by side, looking for the pattern rather than the incident. Patterns are easy to spot once you look for them. A student who consistently scores well on understanding and poorly on analysis is quoting accurately and then telling the examiner what the quotation means instead of how it works. A student strong on analysis and weak on focus has good observations arranged in the order they occurred to them. Each pattern has a drill attached to it.

The table below maps the criteria to what a mid-band script typically does and the single move that lifts it. Criterion letters, weightings and descriptors should be confirmed against the current subject guide and with your child's teacher; no figure in this project has been verified against ibo.org, which blocks automated requests, and the IB revises its guides. The point of the table is not the letters. It is that a vague mark becomes a short, specific list of things to practise.
bullets: Four criteria per component, scored separately and then aggregated

sections.heading: Paper 1: why strong readers lose marks on an unseen text
paragraphs: Paper 1 gives a student non-literary material they have never seen and a guiding question, and asks for an analysis. It is the component where confident readers most often underperform, and the reason is that confidence produces the wrong shape of answer. A capable student reads the text, forms an impression, and then writes an essay defending the impression with quotations. The criteria reward something narrower: showing how the text's construction creates its effect, with the guiding question kept in view throughout.

Text type is the second obstacle, and it bites harder in this emirate than people expect. Students schooled anywhere can analyse a newspaper opinion column. A public-information poster, a satirical cartoon, a charity appeal, a product advertisement or an infographic each have their own conventions, and a student who has never been taught to read those conventions analyses the words and ignores the design, the framing and the implied audience. Half the available analysis sits in what the text is for and who it addresses.

Timing is the third, and it is the most tractable. Almost every student's first timed attempt runs out of time having analysed a third of the text very well. The repair is a planning habit of a few minutes that identifies the three or four features actually worth writing about, and the discipline to leave the rest alone and say so. That habit is teachable in two or three sessions and it is the fastest reliable movement available in this course.
bullets: The guiding question has to shape the answer, not decorate it
Design, framing and implied audience carry as much analysis as the words do
A few minutes of planning beats an extra paragraph of writing
Three features analysed well beats eight features mentioned

sections.heading: Paper 2: the comparative essay most students write as two essays
paragraphs: Paper 2 asks for a comparative essay on literary works studied, written without the texts in front of the student. The failure is structural and extremely consistent: the student writes four paragraphs on the first work, four on the second, and a final paragraph noting that both deal with the theme. That is two essays with a sentence stapled to the end, and it caps the mark however good the individual observations are.

A comparative essay compares inside every paragraph. Each paragraph takes one aspect of the question and examines how both works handle it, which is harder to plan and much stronger to read. The planning habit that produces it takes a few minutes: choose three aspects, decide what each work does with each, and note where the two diverge most sharply, because divergence is where the argument lives. Students find this difficult for about three attempts and then find it easier than what they were doing before.

The second Paper 2 problem is question choice, which is a skill in itself. Students pick the question with the most familiar-looking wording rather than the one their texts can actually answer. Two minutes spent testing each option against the works studied prevents an essay that fights its own material for ninety minutes. Both of these are drills rather than knowledge, which is why Paper 2 often moves faster in a final term than Paper 1 does. The one thing no drill can supply is the texts themselves, which have to have been read and annotated by the student.

sections.heading: The individual oral: a global issue is not a topic
paragraphs: The individual oral asks a student to examine a global issue through one literary and one non-literary extract from works and texts studied. It is worth a substantial share of the grade at both levels and it is the component where students lose most marks for a reason that has nothing to do with speaking ability. They choose a topic rather than an issue.

A topic is a noun: migration, gender, climate, censorship. An issue is a claim about something contested, which the two extracts can be used to examine from different angles. A student who prepares a topic delivers ten minutes of commentary about two extracts that both happen to mention it. A student who prepares an issue delivers an argument in which each extract does different work. The difference is visible in the first thirty seconds and it is worth several marks.

Extract choice is the other half, and students reliably choose badly. They pick the extract they like best rather than the one with most to analyse, and they pick extracts that make the same point, which leaves nothing to examine. The strongest pairings pull against each other. Sessions on this component spend most of their time on the issue statement and the pairing, both of which are decided before any rehearsal happens, and then on cutting a rehearsed oral that always overruns at first. Students cut the analysis and keep the context, which shortens the oral and weakens it at the same time, so the cutting is worth doing with somebody watching.
