sections.heading: The unseen passage: what to do in the first four minutes
paragraphs: Paper 1 puts literary material in front of a student that they have never read, with a guiding question, and asks for an analysis. At Higher Level there are two passages to handle rather than one, which doubles the planning problem and halves the time available for each. It is the component where a well-read student can underperform badly and the one that responds fastest to teaching.

What goes wrong is almost always the opening move. The student reads, forms an impression, and begins writing at the top of the passage, working downward and commenting as they go. That produces a commentary rather than an argument, and it runs out of time around the midpoint. The alternative takes a few minutes and feels like wasted time until a student has tried it twice: read once for the shape, identify the single most interesting thing the passage is doing, and choose three or four moments that evidence it. Everything else gets deliberately ignored.

Verse and prose need different habits, and students are usually much weaker on verse. With a poem the structural features carry a large share of the available analysis: line endings, stanza shape, where the syntax breaks against the line, what the poem does in its last two lines that it was not doing earlier. With prose the equivalents are narrative distance, the handling of time, and whose consciousness the reader is placed inside. Students who learn to ask those questions stop needing to like a passage in order to write about it.
bullets: Read for shape first; start writing from a claim, not from line one

sections.heading: Works in translation, and why the list is not a free choice
paragraphs: A Literature works list is not assembled from favourites. The guide requires coverage across three areas of exploration and sets minimums for works in translation, literary forms, periods and regions, which is why a school's list can look eclectic to a parent. It is a compliance document as much as a reading list. Confirm the exact minimums with your child's teacher, since they change between guide editions and none has been verified here against ibo.org.

Works in translation cause most of the confusion in this emirate, and they also carry a specific opportunity. The confusion is that students assume a translated novel must be analysed through its original language, which they do not read, and conclude the task is impossible. It is not: the assessment works with the English text in front of them, and register, syntax and the choices visible in the translation are all legitimate analytical ground. The opportunity is that a student here may bring genuine context to a work from the Arab world or South Asia that a student elsewhere does not have.

The practical problem is simply volume. Nine works at Standard Level and thirteen at Higher Level, read properly and annotated, is a substantial quantity of reading for a student also carrying five other subjects, the core, and the mandatory UAE subjects. Students fall behind quietly, usually on the longest work and usually in the second term of DP1. The repair is a dated reading plan rather than more sessions, and that is a plan a family can hold a student to without any knowledge of the texts.

sections.heading: Paper 2: writing about two works with the texts taken away
paragraphs: Paper 2 is a comparative essay on works studied, written without the texts in the room. That single condition reshapes everything about preparation, and most students prepare as though it did not exist. They re-read, highlight, and arrive with a general familiarity that evaporates under time pressure into vague gestures at what happens in the book.

What survives the exam room is short, precise and rehearsed. A dozen quotations per work, each no longer than a line, each attached to a point it can be used to make, is worth more than a hundred pages of highlighting. Students resist building this because it feels mechanical, and it is, and it works. The second thing that survives is a comparative paragraph shape practised until it is automatic: one aspect of the question, both works examined on it, with the sharpest attention paid to where they diverge.

The failure to avoid is the two-essay structure, where the student writes four paragraphs on one work, four on the other, and a closing sentence noting a similarity. It caps the mark however good the observations are, because comparison is the assessed act. The table below sets out what a workable quotation bank looks like against what students usually bring to the exam, because the difference is more concrete than any advice about revision technique. The column worth reading is the third one, which describes what is actually left in a student's head after an hour of writing under pressure rather than what the revision felt like at the time. Most revision methods fail that test and feel excellent while they are happening.

sections.heading: The individual oral across two works, and the Higher Level essay
paragraphs: In Literature, the individual oral examines a global issue through two of the works studied, with one extract taken from each. Both extracts are literary, which makes the pairing decision different from the one a Language and Literature student faces, and it is where most of the available marks are won or lost before any rehearsal starts.

A global issue has to be a contested claim rather than a subject area. Migration, gender and power are topics, and a topic produces ten minutes in which both extracts simply illustrate the same point. An issue gives each extract different work to do: how inherited guilt is transmitted through family language, or how a narrator's authority is used to foreclose a reader's judgement. The pairing should create friction. Two extracts that agree with each other leave nothing to examine, and students reliably choose agreement because it feels safer.

The Higher Level essay has the same structural weakness and no question to lean on. The student generates a line of inquiry from one work and writes to a word count, so a broad inquiry produces a tour and a narrow one produces an argument. The useful session is spent shrinking the inquiry until it is small enough to be answered properly, which students experience as having their best idea confiscated and later recognise as the move that made the essay possible. Neither component can be rescued late, because both depend on a decision taken months earlier.
bullets: Both oral extracts are literary in this course, unlike the other English A
A global issue is an arguable claim, never a subject area
Choose extracts that pull against each other, not ones that agree

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go, and what a single session can repair
paragraphs: Every weak Literature script in this emirate loses marks in one of six recognisable ways, and the useful thing about that list is how unevenly the items respond to help. Two can be fixed in a session. Two take a term. Two cannot be fixed by tutoring at all, and a provider who pretends otherwise is selling a term of comfort.

The fixable-fast group is structural. An essay that opens with context and biography instead of a claim can be reshaped in one session, and the change is immediately visible in the mark. An essay that walks through a text chronologically can be reorganised around arguments with a planning drill of a few minutes. Both of these are habits picked up at IGCSE and both are unlearned quickly once named.

The slow group is the real work: replacing appreciation with mechanism, and writing comparatively rather than sequentially. Both are reflexes, and reflexes take a term of practice with feedback. The group tutoring cannot touch is unread works and weak language control. Reading is the student's own job and the only route to it. Language improves gradually and resists acceleration, and attempts to speed it up produce a more decorative version of the same imprecision. The table sorts all six, with an honest timescale against each. A family deciding whether to buy a term of sessions should look at which rows apply to their own child's scripts: two fast rows and a slow one make a strong case for a block, while a script failing mainly on unread works makes the case for a reading plan and no sessions at all.

sections.heading: The reading load against an Abu Dhabi school week
paragraphs: The hardest practical problem in this subject is arithmetic. A Diploma student carries six subjects, Theory of Knowledge, an Extended Essay and a creativity, activity and service commitment. In a UAE private school they also study Arabic, Islamic education and social studies alongside the licensed international curriculum. Into that week a Literature student has to fit nine or thirteen works, read properly enough to quote from memory in two years' time.

Nobody solves that by adding tutoring hours, and a provider who sells weekly sessions into an already-full week is adding to the problem. What works is a reading plan built backwards from the Paper 2 preparation period, dated, with the longest works placed in the holidays and the shortest in term time. Dividing a four-hundred-page novel across a half-term as twenty pages a night is unremarkable advice that very few students have ever actually been given.

Scheduling also has local shape. Ramadan shifts school hours and household routines across the UAE, and post-Iftar sessions usually work better than late-afternoon ones. Long weekends and the winter break are when the heavy reading realistically happens. For families in the outer communities, where the school run eats the end of the afternoon, a fortnightly session with reading in between produces more movement than a weekly session with nothing done between, and it costs half as much. The table below places the works across the two years so the holidays carry the weight they should, which is the single change that most often rescues a Literature student who has fallen quietly behind.

sections.heading: Quotation, paraphrase and the honesty line in a literature course
paragraphs: Literature carries an academic-honesty question that other subjects do not, because quoting other people's words is the actual task. The boundary is simple to state and worth stating to a student once, early. Quoting a primary text with a reference is the work. Quoting a critic with a reference is scholarship. Using a critic's argument without a reference is malpractice, and using a study guide's reading of a novel as though it were the student's own interpretation is the version of it that happens most often and most innocently.

The same boundary governs what any tutor may do. Feedback identifies a paragraph that is not working, asks whether a claim has been evidenced, and names a recurring habit. It does not improve the sentences in a piece that will be submitted, because the student's own expression is part of what is assessed. A provider offering a finished essay is offering something that risks the student's diploma while carrying none of that risk themselves, and one page ranking for these searches does exactly that.

Two further constraints hold across this site. Official syllabus documents, prescribed reading lists, past papers and mark schemes are referenced and linked rather than reproduced, because reproducing them is a copyright matter rather than a style choice. And nothing here promises a grade, a number of marks or an improvement in a predicted grade: a prediction is the subject teacher's professional judgement, made from the work in front of them, and no external tutor produces or validates one.
bullets: A referenced critic is scholarship; an unreferenced one is malpractice

sections.heading: The permit question, ADEK's ethics rules, and what the market charges
paragraphs: Anyone giving private lessons in the UAE needs a permit, and the rule is clear enough to check. Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 introduced the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is issued free of charge and valid for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in both sectors, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. The application route is MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service, listed with a two-working-day completion time and no fee.

Operating without the permit carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no schedule of amounts has been published, so none is quoted here. Separately, press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics framework describes a prohibition on Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school; verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on the detail. In a literature class, where the same teacher marks the oral and writes the prediction, that restriction is sensible on its own terms.

On price, the figures below come from providers' own published pages read in October 2026, because most competitor pages in this search publish no rate at all. Bestimate's 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 and specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level work at AED 200-450 and above. Unitors lists IB from AED 200. TutorChase publishes AED 270. Tutopiya starts around AED 33-52 and EdFlik from AED 45-65 at the university-student end. None of these is an IB Gram price list, and this page quotes them as the market rather than as ours.

process.title: Send the works list first
process.description: Before anything else, send the list of works your child's school is actually studying, with the areas of exploration if the school has mapped them. Lists differ sharply between Abu Dhabi campuses, and preparation aimed at a commonly taught novel the school did not choose is a wasted specialist hour.

process.title: Send two marked essays and say which are unread
process.description: Two returned pieces with the teacher's comments show the pattern, and an honest statement of which works have not been finished shapes everything else. The free trial lesson is then spent on a real diagnosis. One free trial lesson per student, booked without card details.

process.title: Agree the reading plan before the session plan
process.description: The first session produces a dated reading schedule with the longest works placed in the holidays. This is the part a parent can hold a student to without reading the books, and in this subject it does more for the grade than any additional hour of teaching.

process.title: Start with the component that needs no list
process.description: Unseen passage work depends on nothing the school chose, so it can begin immediately and it is the component that moves fastest. That gives a student an early visible improvement while the slower comparative work and the reading catch up behind it.

process.title: Re-measure under time, not in conversation
process.description: After three or four sessions, a fresh piece is written under exam conditions and marked against the same criteria as the school's. That produces a before and an after instead of an impression, and it reveals an unproductive arrangement at four weeks rather than at the end of a term.

whyPoints.title: The reading stays the student's job, and we say so
whyPoints.description: In a course assessed on works the student is meant to have read, sessions spent summarising novels are a specialist rate paid for a study guide. Blocks here are built around a dated reading plan the student follows, with the teaching aimed at what reading alone does not deliver.

whyPoints.title: Unseen passage work that does not depend on the school's list
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 is the component that moves fastest and needs nothing the school chose, so it can start on day one. Higher Level students drill two passages rather than one, because the planning problem at Higher Level is a time problem as much as a skill problem.

whyPoints.title: Quotation banks instead of re-reading
whyPoints.description: Paper 2 is written without the texts, so preparation that leaves a general familiarity behind is preparation that fails in the room. Twelve one-line quotations per work, each tagged to a point it can make, is mechanical, unglamorous and the highest-return method available.

whyPoints.title: Honest timescales, published on the page
whyPoints.description: Structure changes in a session. Comparative writing takes a term. Unread works take as long as the reading takes, and language control resists acceleration. Those differences are on this page so a family can decide where a term's money goes rather than being promised a general improvement.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted as the market's, with the source named
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure here is attributed to the provider or rate table that published it, with the month it was read. Three of the six competitor pages researched for this market publish no price at all and two quote in a currency UAE families do not transact in.

whyPoints.title: No accreditation claimed that we do not hold
whyPoints.description: IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no office in the UAE. It holds no approval, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and it neither supplies nor completes any assessed component.

faqs.question: How many works will my child actually have to read for this course?
faqs.answer: Nine at Standard Level and thirteen at Higher Level, drawn partly from a prescribed reading list and partly from the school's own choices, and spread across three areas of exploration with minimums for works in translation, literary forms, periods and regions. Confirm the exact counts with your child's teacher, because they vary between guide editions. The practical point is that this is a substantial reading load for a student also carrying five other subjects, the core, and the mandatory UAE subjects, and it needs a dated plan rather than good intentions.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a Literature tutor to our address in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Support here is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with unseen passages and marked essays annotated on a shared screen. For this subject the format works well, because the core activity is reading a passage together and marking it up, which is easier side by side on a screen than across a table. It also keeps the drive across the emirate out of the hour you pay for.

faqs.question: My child reads constantly but the Diploma essays are average. Why?
faqs.answer: Because wide reading produces good interpretation and the marks also require mechanism. A well-read student writes an assured essay explaining what a passage means and praising how well it is written. The criteria want the step in between: how the construction produces the effect, stated explicitly. These students usually score strongly on understanding and sit in the middle band on analysis. The drill is narrow and slightly tedious. For every technique named, write the sentence linking the choice to the effect before moving on, until the sentence appears without prompting.

faqs.question: How should a student revise for a Paper 2 they sit without the texts?
faqs.answer: Not by re-reading, which is the instinct and the worst return on the hours. Build twelve one-line quotations per work, each tagged to the point it can be used to make, and rehearse a comparative paragraph shape until it is automatic. Those two things survive an exam room; general familiarity does not. Three timed practice essays, marked and discussed, come next in value. Memorising a whole essay is actively risky, because it produces a confident answer to a question that was not asked, which examiners recognise instantly.

faqs.question: Is a work in translation harder to analyse if we do not read the original language?
faqs.answer: No, and this worry stops students engaging with a sizeable part of their own list. The assessment works with the English text in front of them. Register, syntax, imagery and the decisions visible on the translated surface are all legitimate analytical ground, and the course requires works in translation precisely so students read beyond one tradition. Students in this emirate sometimes have real context for works from the Arab world or South Asia that a student elsewhere lacks, and that context is an advantage in the oral and in the Extended Essay.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a global issue and a theme for the individual oral?
faqs.answer: A theme is a noun and a global issue is a contested claim. If both extracts simply illustrate the same noun, the oral becomes ten minutes of commentary and the marks are capped. An issue gives each extract different work: how inherited guilt is transmitted through family language, or how a narrator's authority forecloses a reader's judgement. Then choose extracts that pull against each other, because two that agree leave nothing to examine. Students reliably pick agreement because it feels safer, and it is the commonest reason a well-delivered oral underperforms.

faqs.question: My child has not finished three of the works. What do we do first?
faqs.answer: Say so, plan the reading, and start the tutoring on the component that does not depend on the list. Unseen passage work needs nothing the school chose, so it can begin immediately and it moves faster than anything else in the course. Meanwhile the reading gets a dated schedule with the longest work placed in a holiday. What does not work is paying a specialist rate for plot summaries of books the student could read themselves, which is where a surprising number of Literature arrangements quietly end up.

faqs.question: Does Higher Level Literature involve much more work than Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Yes, in two concrete ways rather than vaguely. Thirteen works instead of nine, which is a material difference in reading time across two years. And two unseen passages to analyse in Paper 1 rather than one, which makes the planning habit a time-management skill as well as an analytical one. Higher Level also adds a written essay developed from the student's own line of inquiry. For a student who reads willingly it is a reasonable load; for one already behind on the works list in DP1 it is worth an early conversation with the coordinator.

faqs.question: Can a tutor give my child their interpretation of a novel to use?
faqs.answer: They should not, and a student should be careful with study guides for the same reason. Using someone else's reading of a text as though it were your own is the most common academic-honesty breach in this subject, and it usually happens innocently. A referenced critic is scholarship and is welcome. An unreferenced one is malpractice. What a tutor can properly do is ask questions that make a student's own reading sharper, and give marking-style feedback on a draft the student has written, without improving the sentences in it.

faqs.question: Should my child be on Literature or Language and Literature?
faqs.answer: It depends on how they read and what interests them, and it is a decision for the Diploma coordinator rather than a tutor. Literature studies literary works only, sets unseen literary material in Paper 1, and demands sustained reading with no escape from the works. Language and Literature adds non-literary texts, sets unseen non-literary material, and demands familiarity with text types such as advertisements, cartoons and infographics. Neither is easier. A student who reads widely and willingly usually belongs in Literature; one drawn to media and persuasion usually does not.

faqs.question: How much reading can realistically be done during an Abu Dhabi term?
faqs.answer: Less than most plans assume, which is why the plan should be dated rather than aspirational. A Diploma student here carries six subjects, Theory of Knowledge, an Extended Essay, a service commitment, and Arabic, Islamic education and social studies alongside the licensed curriculum. Twenty pages a night in term time is realistic; four hundred pages in a half-term is not. The winter break and long weekends are where the longest works belong, and Ramadan shifts the whole household routine, so the reading schedule should be built around it rather than through it.

faqs.question: What does Literature support cost per hour in this emirate?
faqs.answer: Published figures from providers' own pages, read in October 2026, put specialist IB tutoring at roughly AED 200-450 an hour and above. Unitors lists IB from AED 200 and TutorChase publishes AED 270. Bestimate's 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 and specialist work at AED 200-450 and higher. Budget online options start around AED 33-65. None of those is an IB Gram price list. The useful comparison is not the rate but what the hour contains: a diagnosis of where the marks are going, or a conversation about a novel.

faqs.question: Which component is the best value to buy support for first?
faqs.answer: Unseen passage work, for three reasons. It depends on nothing the school chose, so it can start before any other preparation. It moves faster than any other part of the course, usually within a few weeks, which matters for a student who has concluded they are not good at English. And the habit it builds, reading for shape and then arguing from three evidenced moments, transfers directly into Paper 2 and the oral. Six to eight hours at Standard Level or eight to twelve at Higher Level covers it.

faqs.question: Do Literature tutors working with students in Abu Dhabi need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 introduced the MoHRE private tuition work permit, issued free of charge and valid for two years, with eligible applicants including registered school teachers, public and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's private tutor licensing service lists a two-working-day completion time and no fee. Tutoring without the permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no schedule of amounts is published, none is quoted here.

faqs.question: Can my child's own school English teacher tutor them privately for payment?
faqs.answer: In Abu Dhabi that is the arrangement to avoid. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics framework describes a prohibition on private and charter school staff giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct is reported to carry a similar restriction; the current wording should be verified against ADEK's own policy document. In Literature it is a poor idea for a second reason as well: the same teacher marks the individual oral and writes the predicted grade, and the conflict there is obvious to everybody involved.

faqs.question: What if no Literature specialist is available for the slot we need?
faqs.answer: You are told before anything is booked. Where no UAE-resident specialist is free for the time requested, the match comes from the wider pool of Diploma English tutors working to Gulf Standard Time, most often from India, in the same online format and on the same hourly basis, with the tutor's location stated upfront rather than discovered later. Several providers in this search route UAE families to non-UAE numbers without saying so. Flexibility helps considerably: a 19:30 slot reaches a materially larger pool than a fixed 17:00 one.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-literature-hom.closingHeading: Send the works list, then the marked essays
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-literature-hom.closingBody: An IB DP English A Literature home tutor in Abu Dhabi is worth paying for once two things are on the table: the works your child's school actually chose, and two returned essays with the teacher's comments on them. From those, the free trial lesson can name where the marks are going, which works still need reading, and which component to start with. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, the reading stays your child's own job, every word submitted stays their own work, and nothing on this page promises a grade.

intro.heading: Start by auditing the works, because that is where the hidden problems are
paragraphs: English A Literature is a reading course with an administrative skeleton, and the skeleton is where Abu Dhabi families lose marks they never knew were available. A Standard Level candidate studies nine literary works; a Higher Level candidate studies thirteen. Those works have to span literary forms, historical periods and regions of the world, and a proportion must be read in translation. Each component then draws on a defined subset of them. A student who has read everything attentively and cannot say which work is reserved for the oral and which pair is viable for the comparative essay is not short of literary insight. They are short of a spreadsheet.

This is the first thing we do, and it is the reason the page is built around evidence rather than encouragement. The opening session produces a written audit: every work, its form, its period, its region, whether it was read in translation, which component it is allocated to, and how well the student actually knows it as against how well they think they do. Parents in Khalifa City and on Al Reem Island routinely discover that their child has three novels and no poetry they could write about under time pressure, or that both works they intend to pair for the comparative essay are already committed elsewhere.

The audit also exposes the subject's real difficulty, which is unseen analysis. Paper 1 in Literature is guided analysis of an unseen literary passage, and at Higher Level that means two passages rather than one, typically including poetry. Poetry is the single most reliable place where Abu Dhabi candidates lose marks, and it is also the most fixable, because the loss comes from technique rather than from sensibility. A student who has written four unseen poems with marks against criterion letters is in a measurably different position from one who has read widely and written none.

Abu Dhabi's cohort gives this course a particular texture. Diploma classes here commonly contain students whose strongest language is not English, students who read fluently in Arabic and have never been asked to analyse a translated text, and students who arrived from an IGCSE route where close reading was marked against expected points rather than against criteria. All three sit the same unseen paper. The useful response is not a different reading list but a different first document: a marked unseen script with four numbers on it.

Everything below is written so a parent can check it. Components with their weightings and criterion mark allocations. The works requirements as a table. What a marked unseen poem actually tells you. What eight weeks of genuine movement looks like against what eight weeks of pleasant discussion looks like. And the authorship boundary on the Higher Level Essay, stated plainly, because finished essays are sold openly in this market and that is a risk to a Diploma rather than a service.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-literature-tut.programmesIntro: Three routes bring an Abu Dhabi student to a Literature A course, and each generates different evidence in a first session. The self-taught route in particular is poorly understood by families and worth reading if your household's strongest language is not English.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme English A: Literature
programmes.description: A Group 1 course studied at Standard or Higher Level, organised around three areas of exploration and seven central concepts. Assessment is a guided analysis of unseen literary text, a comparative essay on two studied works, an individual oral built on two works, and at Higher Level an essay on one work. All marks are criterion-referenced rather than awarded against a list of expected points.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi, Literature is often the smaller of the two Group 1 options, with Language and Literature taking the larger share of a cohort. That means a Literature class can be small, taught by one teacher, and short of anyone to argue with about an unseen poem, which is exactly the gap a second reader fills.

programmes.name: School-supported self-taught Literature
programmes.description: A Standard Level Literature course in a language the school does not teach, studied with school support rather than classroom teaching. It exists so a candidate can take their best language at Standard Level, and it carries the same components and the same criteria as a taught course, with far less contact time behind them.
programmes.countryNote: This route matters in Abu Dhabi because households here speak a wide range of first languages and the self-taught option is frequently the difference between a comfortable Group 1 grade and a stressful one. A family exploring it should raise it with the Diploma coordinator early, because works have to be selected and approved rather than simply chosen.

programmes.name: MYP Language and Literature into DP Literature
programmes.description: MYP reports against four criteria on a 1 to 8 scale, which gives a usable baseline before the Diploma begins. The specific habit that transfers is annotation: a student who marks a text while reading, rather than after, arrives able to produce evidence under time pressure. Students who have only ever discussed texts in class find the unseen paper a shock.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Abu Dhabi continuum school has reported MYP criterion scores for MYP 4 and 5, keep them. A parent holding two years of criterion-level history can see immediately whether a weak first Diploma unseen paper is new or long-standing, and that distinction changes what the first block of sessions should target.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-literature-tut.subjectsIntro: The components and reading skills an Abu Dhabi Literature family actually buys hours against, with the criterion that governs each and the failure that shows up in marked work.

subjects.name: Paper 1: guided analysis of unseen literary text
subjects.description: One unseen passage at Standard Level, two at Higher Level, each with a guiding question. Four criteria at five marks each. Candidates lose marks by cataloguing devices without building an interpretation, and by answering the guiding question only in the final paragraph.

subjects.name: Unseen poetry
subjects.description: The most feared and most improvable element of the course. A poem offers less material and demands more interpretation per line than prose. Students who have practised a repeatable opening move, usually establishing the speaker and the situation before any device is named, stop freezing.

subjects.name: Paper 2: comparative essay on two works
subjects.description: An unseen general question answered through two studied works. Knowledge and comparative analysis carry ten marks each, so the pairing decision matters as much as the writing. Two works chosen for thematic convenience with nothing formal in common produce a thin essay however well written.

subjects.name: Individual Oral
subjects.description: A fifteen-minute oral on a global issue examined through two works, one written in the language of the course and one read in translation, followed by questions. Forty marks across four criteria, so balance between the two works is structurally important.

subjects.name: Higher Level Essay
subjects.description: An essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words developing a line of inquiry about one literary work from the course. The only component drafted over weeks under supervision, which makes it the clearest documentary evidence of progress available in the subject.

subjects.name: Works in translation
subjects.description: A defined part of the reading must be works originally written in another language. Candidates often treat translation as a neutral window and lose the chance to discuss what a translator's choices do, which is legitimate analytical ground and frequently an untouched source of marks.

subjects.name: The works requirements
subjects.description: Form, period and region requirements determine which combinations are legal, and the school manages compliance. The student's job is narrower and still often undone: knowing which work is allocated to which component, so the oral and the comparative essay do not collide.

subjects.name: Annotation and evidence retrieval
subjects.description: Thirteen works at Higher Level cannot be re-read before a paper. A student needs a system for finding the four quotations that matter in a work read eighteen months earlier, and almost no one is taught one. This is a one-session fix with a two-year payoff.

subjects.name: The learner portfolio
subjects.description: A required record of the candidate's own work across the course and the raw material for both the oral and the Higher Level Essay. A thin portfolio in DP1 turns into a scramble in DP2; a full one makes the later components markedly cheaper to prepare.

subjects.name: Timed writing by hand
subjects.description: Both papers are handwritten under time pressure. A student producing strong untimed essays and weak timed ones has a planning and pace problem, which is visible in a single marked script and responds to drills rather than to more reading.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-literature-tut.regionsTitle: Abu Dhabi Literature students, reading time and the practical week
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-a-literature-tut.regionsIntro: A Literature candidate's constraint is reading hours rather than tuition hours, and reading hours are shaped by commute, siblings and the school's own timetable. The notes below describe what families in each area most often need help scheduling.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Short school runs and apartment living mean study happens at home in the early evening. Literature students here manage reading well in term time and lose ground over long holidays, so a holiday reading plan is often more useful than extra term-time sessions.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Schools with strong library provision and dedicated Group 1 staffing. Students arrive with their works read; the help they need is unseen technique and pairing decisions rather than comprehension of the set texts.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities with long weekday evenings and heavy weekend activity schedules. Many students here crossed from an IGCSE English route and have never written an unseen literary analysis against criteria, which a cold timed paper exposes in one sitting.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Continuum intake with criterion histories available from MYP. Families here can often establish a baseline from existing records rather than paying for a diagnosis, which shortens the first engagement.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Island neighbourhoods where the afternoon commute makes late-afternoon sessions unreliable. Reading happens late, and students frequently annotate nothing, so a session on retrieval systems pays for itself across thirteen works.

regions.name: Al Mushrif and Al Karamah
regions.note: Many bilingual households where Arabic is the home language. These students are often the strongest readers of works in translation in the class and the least confident about saying so, which is a marks issue in the oral rather than a confidence issue.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: Longer commutes to island schools cut into weekday reading time. A Saturday morning session with a fresh unseen passage tends to produce better work than a Thursday evening one after a forty-minute drive home.

regions.name: Al Reef and Al Falah
regions.note: Mainland communities where families are price-conscious and sensibly ask how few hours will do. For Literature the answer is usually a short unseen-technique block plus a works audit, not a standing weekly slot across two years.

sections.heading: Nine works or thirteen: the audit that should exist before any teaching happens
paragraphs: The works requirement is public, administrative and routinely misunderstood by the people it affects most. Standard Level candidates study nine literary works and Higher Level candidates thirteen, selected so that the set spans literary forms, historical periods and regions of the world, with a defined element read in translation. The school is responsible for compliance. The student is responsible for knowing what they have, and that is where the failure sits.

A works audit is a plain table. One row per work: title, author, form, period, region, read in translation or not, which component it is allocated to, and a frank self-rating of how well the student could write about it without the book in front of them. Producing it takes most of one session and it changes behaviour immediately, because it makes two things visible. First, collisions: a work used in the Individual Oral is not then available for the comparative essay, and candidates discover this late with distressing regularity. Second, decay: a novel read in the first term of DP1 and rated highly by the student often turns out to be a plot summary and two half-remembered quotations.

The audit also tells a tutor where the hours should not go. A student with strong recall across seven works and a persistent 11 out of 20 on unseen papers does not need more reading, and paying for literary discussion in that situation is comfortable and useless. The converse is also common: a student with excellent unseen marks and three works they genuinely cannot write about is three works short of a viable Paper 2, and the fix is reading rather than technique.

Parents can request the audit as a document and keep it. It is one of the few artefacts in this subject that a non-specialist can read usefully, and it makes the rest of the engagement checkable: a work rated two out of five in October should not still be rated two in February if sessions have been spent on it.

sections.heading: Paper 1 is where the grade is decided, and poetry is where Paper 1 is decided
paragraphs: Paper 1 asks for guided analysis of an unseen literary passage, one at Standard Level and two at Higher Level, each with a guiding question. All four criteria carry equal marks, which means a student who understands a poem beautifully and organises the answer poorly loses as much as one who organises a shallow reading well. It is the largest single component at both levels, and it is the component no amount of set-text revision touches.

Poetry is the recurring problem. A prose extract gives a candidate narrative to hold on to; a poem gives sixteen lines and no scaffolding. Abu Dhabi candidates in particular often arrive from systems where poetry was taught as the identification of devices, so under pressure they produce a list: alliteration here, enjambment there, a simile in line nine, and no claim about what the poem is doing. That script can be fluent, accurate and still sit in the middle of criterion B, because nothing has been evaluated.

The repeatable fix is unglamorous. Before naming a single device, the candidate states who is speaking, to whom, in what situation, and what changes by the end. That takes ninety seconds and converts the rest of the answer, because every device then has something to serve. Students who adopt it typically move one criterion mark on their next timed paper, and the change is visible on the script rather than inferred from a conversation. Alternating poetry and prose each session keeps both techniques live, since they are genuinely different tasks.

Marked scripts are the whole evidence base here, and Abu Dhabi schools will generally release one with criterion-level marks if a parent asks directly. If the school cannot, a cold timed passage written in the free trial lesson produces the same four numbers. Either way, the useful question after four sessions is not whether lessons are going well but whether the criterion the tutor named has moved on a comparable passage.

sections.heading: Components, weightings and the criterion marks behind each
paragraphs: Criterion-referenced marking is why parents struggle to read progress in this subject, and the published mark allocations are the remedy. The same four criteria appear across components, but they carry different numbers of marks in each, so a middling performance means something different depending on where it happened. A parent who knows that knowledge and analysis dominate the comparative essay, while organisation and language carry full weight in the oral, can direct hours sensibly.

The split also explains a pattern that confuses families. A student can be visibly better at Literature than a classmate and score the same, because the classmate pairs works intelligently for the comparative essay and keeps a tight thirteen minutes in the oral. Those are learnable, cheap, procedural advantages, and they are worth attending to before any additional reading.

At Standard Level the two written papers carry the bulk of the grade with the oral making up the remainder. At Higher Level the load spreads across four components, with the unseen paper the largest and the comparative essay, oral and essay each carrying a meaningful share. The strategic consequence is that a Higher Level student weak on unseen analysis is weak in the biggest component, and no amount of excellence on the Higher Level Essay compensates for it.

Treat the figures below as the shape of the assessment rather than the final word. Weightings and limits are revised between subject guide editions, and the authority for your child's cohort is their Diploma coordinator. The criterion letters and what each rewards are the stable part, and they are what a parent should ask about.

sections.heading: Works in translation, and the advantage most Abu Dhabi students do not use
paragraphs: Part of the reading in a Literature A course must be works originally written in another language, and the Individual Oral requires one work in translation alongside one written in the language of the course. Most candidates treat the translation as transparent: they analyse the text as though the English on the page were the author's own choice of word. That is a missed opportunity rather than an error, and in a multilingual city it is a particularly odd one.

A translated text carries two layers a candidate can legitimately discuss. There is what the work does, and there is what survives or shifts in the crossing. A student who can observe that a translator has flattened a register, or chosen one of several possible words for a concept with no English equivalent, is doing exactly the kind of evaluative work criterion B rewards. This does not require fluency in the source language, though it helps.

In Abu Dhabi a substantial number of Diploma candidates read fluently in Arabic, and some in Urdu, Russian, French or Malayalam. Those students are frequently the best-placed people in the room to notice what a translation has done, and they are frequently the quietest about it, because they have inferred that their home language is a side matter in an English class. Correcting that inference is one of the cheapest grade interventions available in this course, and it belongs in the oral preparation rather than in a pep talk.

There is a scheduling point attached. Works in translation tend to be the works a class covers at pace, because the teacher is less confident of the context. A student who does their own background reading on the period and place of one translated work, rather than on all of them, gets disproportionate return in the oral, where depth on two works beats coverage of nine.

sections.heading: What eight weeks of movement looks like on paper
paragraphs: Progress in Literature is often described as slow, and reading maturity genuinely is. Criterion-level improvement is not, and conflating the two is how a block of tutoring becomes a standing appointment nobody evaluates. The test of a working block is whether a named criterion has moved on a comparable piece of timed writing.

The pattern of a block that works is specific. Week one: a cold unseen passage, marked, four numbers, and the works audit begun. Week two: the single weakest criterion, applied to the student's own sentences, not discussed in the abstract. Week three: a second cold passage in the other form, poetry if week one was prose, and the marks compared rather than described. Weeks four and five: the comparative essay, where the mark allocation shifts and the pairing decision is made from the audit. Weeks six and seven: the oral, or the Higher Level Essay draft. Week eight: an honest comparison against week one and a stop-or-continue recommendation.

A block that has stopped working has signs that a parent can read without any literary expertise. No new timed writing in three weeks. Sessions that discuss the novel rather than the student's paragraph. Feedback that has become encouragement. A student who can repeat the tutor's point and cannot apply it alone. Any one of those is a reason to ask which criterion is currently being worked on, and a tutor who cannot answer in one sentence has lost the thread.

Grade movement lags all of this. A student can gain two criterion marks and hold the same overall grade for a term, which is normal and is not a failure of the work. That is precisely why the record we keep is criterion-level, and why an honest answer to how quickly a grade moves is that the school knows how close your child already was to a boundary and we do not.

sections.heading: The Individual Oral in Literature, and the thirteen-minute problem
paragraphs: The oral is examined inside the school, recorded, and marked out of forty with ten marks on each of the four criteria. A candidate selects a global issue and examines how it is presented in and through two works, one written in the language of the course and one read in translation, then answers examiner questions. Parents almost never hear it, which makes it the component where preparation is least supervised and most productive.

Two structural problems account for most lost marks. The first is a global issue pitched too broadly: stated at a level of generality where no specific passage from either work is actually required, which damages knowledge and focus simultaneously. Narrowing it is usually a single session's work and the highest-return change available in the component. The second is time. Candidates who know one work better than the other allocate time accordingly, and a run that gives eleven minutes to a novel and three to a translated play cannot score well on focus and organisation whatever the insight.

The remedy is mechanical and slightly unpleasant. Record a full practice run, with a clock, out loud, then listen back. Students discover that their sense of balance is wrong by minutes, that their opening is forty seconds longer than it needs to be, and that they have two extracts marked but no plan for moving between them. Most candidates cut their own opening after hearing it once, which is the sort of improvement no amount of discussion produces.

Because the words spoken in the examination are the candidate's own, this is work a tutor can support without any authorship question arising at all. A tutor may help narrow the issue, challenge the choice of extracts, time the practice, and question the student as an examiner would. That last part matters: the examiner questions at the end reward a candidate who deliberately left something unsaid, and very few students plan for that.

One work in the language of the course, one read in translation
A narrow global issue outscores a broad one almost every time
Record a timed practice run; internal sense of balance is usually wrong

sections.heading: Authorship on the Higher Level Essay, and what this market sells instead
paragraphs: The Higher Level Essay is 1,200 to 1,500 words developing a line of inquiry about one literary work from the course, produced over weeks under school supervision. The learner portfolio behind it is likewise the candidate's own record. Both are covered by the IB's academic honesty requirements, and an authenticity breach is a matter for the student's Diploma rather than a dispute between a parent and a tutor. The boundary therefore belongs on the page, stated in the terms a family can hold a tutor to.

Teaching is permitted broadly and is where the value sits. A tutor may explain what each criterion rewards, discuss whether a line of inquiry is answerable within the word range, read a dated draft and identify where the argument stalls, point out where a paragraph summarises rather than analyses, mark timed work honestly, teach cutting as a technique, and model analysis on a text the student is not submitting. That last approach is particularly efficient, because it builds analytical habits with no assessed material involved.

What is not permitted is supplying any part of the submitted text. No sentences for insertion, no paragraph rewritten into final form, no line of inquiry selected for the student, no previous candidate's essay offered as a template, and no editing pass that leaves prose the student could not have produced. The workable test is whether the student could have arrived at this version themselves and can explain why it is stronger. If either answer is no, the line has been crossed, and schools now commonly ask for dated drafts precisely so authorship can be shown.

This is not a theoretical concern in the UAE search results. Operations selling completed Internal Assessments and essays advertise openly in this market, one of them with a published price, which is an academic-integrity breach and a malpractice trigger for the student who submits it. A family comparing providers should expect a legitimate tutor to refuse that request plainly and in writing, and should treat a provider willing to take it as a risk to their child's Diploma.

sections.heading: Getting started in Abu Dhabi, including the permit question
paragraphs: The first step costs nothing. Ask the school for a marked unseen script with criterion marks, then take the free trial lesson, one per family with no card details taken, and bring the script to it. Where no script is available, the trial can be built around a cold unseen passage instead and produce the same four numbers. The session ends with a named weakest criterion, the start of a works audit, and an hours figure.

Sometimes the honest hours figure is zero. A student with balanced criterion marks whose real constraint is reading volume needs a holiday reading plan rather than weekly sessions, and we say that. A student weak only in criterion D because English is a third language needs a short targeted block, not a two-year commitment. Both answers are more useful to a family than a package, and both are checkable against the script.

Supply is reasonable in this subject. Experienced Diploma Literature teachers are easier to find than Theatre or Arabic A specialists, so matching is usually quick. Where nobody suitable is free for the level and component you need, you are told with a realistic date rather than matched to a generalist. Lessons are delivered one to one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India, which is why the choice of tutor is not limited by driving distance from your address.

On legality, two points cover almost every parent's question. Private tutoring in the UAE requires the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, with eligible categories including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18; tutoring without one attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published. Separately, ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar Abu Dhabi private and charter school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school. IB Gram holds no regulator licence or accreditation and operates no UAE office.

process.title: Say which component is in play
process.description: A message naming the level, the component and what evidence exists gets a better match than a request for a Literature tutor. Higher Level, 11 out of 20 on an unseen poem, no breakdown given, is enough to plan a first session. Without a document, the first paid hour goes on producing one.

process.title: Ask the school for the marked script
process.description: Abu Dhabi schools will generally release a marked script with criterion-level marks when a parent asks directly. It turns one report grade into four numbers, which is the difference between a diagnosis and a guess. If it cannot be released, a cold timed passage does the same job.

process.title: Use the free trial on an unseen passage
process.description: One trial lesson per family, no card details taken, no obligation to continue. The student writes or discusses an unseen passage and the tutor marks it against the four criteria, so the session produces evidence rather than impressions, and ends with a realistic hours figure including zero.

process.title: Build the works audit early
process.description: A written inventory of every work with form, period, region, component allocation and honest recall. It takes most of a session, it is a document the family keeps, and it regularly changes which works a student plans to pair for the comparative essay before that choice becomes irreversible.

process.title: Review against week one, with both scripts open
process.description: At the end of a block, a written comparison of the first marked script and the latest, criterion by criterion. If the named criterion moved, the next block starts from there. If it did not, the plan changes or the block ends, and we state which we believe is right.

whyPoints.title: An audit before an opinion
whyPoints.description: The first substantive output is a written works inventory with component allocations and honest recall ratings. It catches collisions and decay that no amount of literary discussion surfaces, and a parent can read it without being a specialist in the subject.

whyPoints.title: Unseen work marked, not just discussed
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 is the largest component at both levels and the one set-text revision never touches. Sessions produce cold timed passages with criterion marks attached, alternating poetry and prose, so the evidence of improvement is a second script rather than a fluent conversation.

whyPoints.title: Multilingual readers treated as an asset
whyPoints.description: A candidate who reads Arabic, Urdu, French or Russian is well placed to say what a translation has done to a text, and that is exactly the evaluative move criterion B rewards. In this emirate that is a common and badly underused advantage.

whyPoints.title: The authorship line stated in writing
whyPoints.description: On the Higher Level Essay a tutor teaches, marks and names problems. Nobody supplies sentences or rewrites a paragraph into final form. That is printed here because completed essays are sold openly in this search result and they put a Diploma at risk rather than help it.

Pages implying otherwise make a claim a regulator can test.

whyPoints.title: Scheduled around real Abu Dhabi weeks
whyPoints.description: Sessions are set in Gulf Standard Time around school runs, island traffic and weekend activity schedules. For students commuting from Yas or the mainland a Saturday morning slot with a fresh passage usually produces better writing than a weekday evening after a long drive.

faqs.question: How many works will my daughter read for English A Literature at Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Nine literary works at Standard Level and thirteen at Higher Level, chosen so the set spans literary forms, historical periods and regions of the world, with a defined element read in translation. The school manages compliance with those requirements. What a student needs to track personally is narrower and often neglected: which work is allocated to which component, because a work used in the Individual Oral is then unavailable for the comparative essay. Confirm the current requirements and your daughter's allocation with her Diploma coordinator rather than relying on any website.

faqs.question: Why does my son do well on set texts and badly on the unseen paper?
faqs.answer: Because they are different tasks. Set-text work rewards accumulated knowledge of a book studied over months; the unseen paper rewards building an interpretation of a passage read ten minutes earlier. A student can know nine works well and still produce a list of identified devices with no claim attached, which sits in the middle of criterion B by design. The fix is a repeatable opening move: establish speaker, situation and what changes before naming any technique. One marked script will show you whether that is the problem.

faqs.question: Is unseen poetry really harder than unseen prose?
faqs.answer: It is harder in a specific way. A prose extract supplies narrative a candidate can lean on while they find something to say; a poem supplies sixteen lines and demands interpretation almost immediately. Students who were taught poetry as device identification freeze under time pressure because the list runs out before the page does. Practising the two forms alternately is more effective than practising either alone, and poetry responds faster to technique work than almost anything else in the course, which makes it good value for a short block.

faqs.question: What is a works audit and why would I pay for one?
faqs.answer: It is a written inventory of every work your child has studied: title, literary form, period, region, whether it was read in translation, which component it is allocated to, and an honest rating of how well they could write about it without the book. It takes most of one session and it regularly surfaces two expensive problems: works committed to two components at once, and works the student believes they know and cannot actually quote. The output is a document you keep and update, which is more than most tutoring produces in a term.

faqs.question: How do I choose which two works to pair for the comparative essay?
faqs.answer: Start from what the works have in common formally rather than thematically. Two novels that both happen to concern family are easier to pair in conversation and harder to compare in an essay than a novel and a play with a shared structural device, because criterion B rewards comparative analysis rather than parallel description. The audit narrows the field quickly by eliminating works committed elsewhere and works the student cannot quote. The school's teacher will have views on viable pairings too, and those views are worth soliciting early.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the Higher Level Essay on a literary work?
faqs.answer: Yes, inside a firm boundary. A tutor may teach what each criterion rewards, say whether a line of inquiry can be answered in 1,200 to 1,500 words, read the student's dated draft and name where the argument stalls or where words are spent badly, and teach cutting as a transferable technique. A tutor may not supply sentences, rewrite a paragraph into final form, choose the line of inquiry, or hand over a previous candidate's essay as a model. The test is whether the student could have produced that version unaided and understands why it is better.

faqs.question: What is the school-supported self-taught route, and should we consider it?
faqs.answer: It is a Standard Level Literature course in a language the school does not teach, studied with school support rather than classroom teaching, and it exists so a candidate can take their strongest language at Standard Level. Components and criteria are identical to a taught course, with much less contact time behind them, so it suits a genuinely strong reader in that language and punishes a hopeful one. Works have to be selected and approved rather than simply chosen, so raise it with the Diploma coordinator early in DP1 rather than partway through.

faqs.question: My son reads Arabic fluently. Does that help with works in translation?
faqs.answer: It helps more than he probably realises. A candidate who can see what a translator has done, where a register has flattened or a concept has no clean English equivalent, is making exactly the evaluative move criterion B rewards. Many Abu Dhabi students assume their home language is irrelevant in an English class and stay quiet about it. In the Individual Oral, where one work must be read in translation, that instinct costs marks. Preparation should deliberately bring it into the oral rather than treating it as background.

faqs.question: How should a Literature student revise works read eighteen months ago?
faqs.answer: Not by re-reading them. Thirteen works cannot be re-read in DP2 alongside five other subjects, and attempting it is how students arrive at the papers exhausted and vague. What works is a retrieval system built once: for each work, a single page with the structural shape, four quotations that can serve several questions, and two critical angles. Building the first one takes a session and the student builds the rest. Students who annotated as they read have a head start; students with clean copies need the system more.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting Literature support in the second term of DP2?
faqs.answer: It depends which marks are still open. Unseen technique responds to focused work within weeks, so a late block aimed at Paper 1 is frequently worthwhile, and Paper 2 pairing decisions can still be improved. The Higher Level Essay is different: once the school's internal deadline has passed, that mark is fixed. The Individual Oral may also already be examined. The first useful step late in the course is establishing which components remain live, because hours spent on closed ones are the commonest way families waste money here.

faqs.question: What should I expect in the session notes?
faqs.answer: Four specific things: which criterion the session targeted, what was worked on in your child's own writing, what they are doing before the next session, and which document will show whether it worked. Notes go out the same day and are deliberately concrete enough to argue with. A note reporting good progress tells a parent nothing. A note saying criterion C was targeted through the structure of her own unseen response and a second timed passage is due on Sunday can be checked when the passage arrives.

faqs.question: Do Literature grades matter for UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: Equivalency is assessed against the certificate as a whole rather than one subject, and the published requirements differ by curriculum track. On the sourced British track, candidates must show five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that count, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels. The American track routes English proficiency through IELTS 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in SAT reading and writing. No IB points threshold is published here because we have not read one on an official Ministry page; verify on moe.gov.ae.

faqs.question: How do Ramadan and the Abu Dhabi school calendar affect reading schedules?
faqs.answer: Reading is the part that suffers. School days shorten across the UAE during Ramadan and evenings reorganise around Iftar, so the long uninterrupted blocks a novel needs become scarce while short analytical sessions remain perfectly workable. The practical response is to front-load reading before Ramadan and use the weeks themselves for unseen technique, oral practice and draft work, which fit a 60 to 75-minute post-Iftar slot. Mapping internal deadlines that fall in or just after those weeks is worth doing in advance.

faqs.question: Can one tutor cover both Literature and another Group 1 or Group 2 subject?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking rather than assuming. A Diploma English specialist may cover both Group 1 options competently, since the criteria and much of the technique overlap, though the works requirements and the oral differ. Pairing Literature with a Group 2 language is a different matter and usually needs a second tutor. The honest answer depends on who is available, and you are told what the matched tutor has actually taught before the trial lesson rather than after it.

Ask the school for a marked unseen script, take the free trial lesson, one per family with no card details taken, and leave with a named weakest criterion and the start of a works audit. From there the plan is specific: which criterion, which component, which passage will test it, and how many hours it should take, including none where the evidence says the reading plan matters more than a tutor. Sessions run one to one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, and the record is documents you can read in order.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-english-b-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below work on Diploma English B at Standard and Higher Level for students in Abu Dhabi schools: the writing task in Paper 1, the listening and reading papers in Paper 2, the individual oral, and at Higher Level the two literary works. Sessions run live online, timed to Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: Two different things are being sold at the same hourly rate
paragraphs: English B is the only Diploma subject where a parent can reasonably pay AED 50 an hour for something useful and AED 300 an hour for something else useful, and get value from both. That is because the course has two halves that look alike from outside and need completely different providers. One half is language itself: vocabulary range, listening fluency, confidence in speaking at length. The other half is examination technique: which text type the writing task requires, how the receptive papers distribute their marks, what the oral is actually assessed on.

Most families buy the second at the first's price or the first at the second's price, and both mistakes are expensive. A student booked with a cheap generalist for exam technique gets pleasant conversation and no understanding of why their writing task scored poorly. A student booked with an IB specialist at AED 250 an hour for conversation practice is paying a premium rate for something a well-chosen reading habit and a structured speaking routine would deliver for almost nothing. The money question in this subject is a sequencing question.

The published figures are worth putting on the page, because most competitor pages in this search publish none. Tutopiya advertises online sessions from around AED 33-52 and EdFlik from AED 45-65, both at the university-student end. Unitors lists IGCSE from AED 150 an hour and IB from AED 200. TutorChase publishes AED 270. Bestimate's 2026 tutoring cost table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180-350 and specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level work at AED 200-450 and above, with BartyED at AED 650 at the premium end. Those are other providers' published figures as read in October 2026, and none is an IB Gram price list.

Abu Dhabi changes the calculation in a way that is specific rather than decorative. ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection ratings, and the schools here teach a wide spread of curricula with intakes drawn from across the world. An English B class in this city routinely contains a student who has been in English-medium education since Year 1 and is in the wrong course, next to a student who arrived last year and genuinely needs the course. Those two should not be buying the same hours, and frequently are.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. English B support here is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which removes the drive from the fee: a visiting tutor quoting AED 250 for sixty minutes and driving from the island to Al Shamkha and back is being paid for a commitment of more than two hours, and that is priced in whether or not the invoice shows it. For a language course needing frequent short sessions, that difference compounds quickly.
