sections.heading: Filming in Abu Dhabi: where a student can actually point a camera
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi is an unusually photogenic city in which almost nothing is unowned. Malls, waterfront promenades, residential compounds, towers, cultural institutions and school grounds all have a manager, and a student who plans a shoot without asking is planning to be asked to stop. This is not a legal lecture: it is the single most common reason a Diploma Film project in this emirate slips, and it is entirely avoidable with two weeks of notice.

The practical approach is to treat location access as part of the project's scope rather than as logistics to be handled later. A project that depends on filming inside a public venue on a specific weekend is fragile. A project that can be shot on school grounds, inside a family home, or in a compound street with the neighbours informed is robust, and robust is what finishes. Students are frequently surprised by how much visual variety sits inside the permissions they already have.

Where a project genuinely needs a managed location, the request should come from the school rather than from a sixteen-year-old, and it should be specific about date, duration, crew size and equipment. The table below is a planning aid, not a statement of any venue's policy; every line should be checked with the actual site and with your child's teacher. A tutor's job here is to force the question early, while the script can still change, rather than to adjudicate access. A shoot that has been scoped around confirmed permissions is a shoot that happens on the weekend it was planned for.

sections.heading: Kit, software, and what genuinely limits a Film grade
paragraphs: Parents of Diploma Film students are asked for equipment with some regularity, and the honest position is that very little of it moves the grade. The tasks are marked on analysis, documentation and argument. A student with a phone, a tripod, a borrowed lavalier microphone and free editing software can produce submissions that score well. A student with an expensive camera and no shot plan cannot.

Two exceptions are real. Sound is the one technical area where cheap equipment is genuinely limiting, because unusable dialogue cannot be fixed in post and a reel with inaudible dialogue damages the work it is meant to demonstrate. The other is storage and backup, which is not glamorous and is the reason projects occasionally die outright. A single copy of a shoot on one memory card is a project waiting to be lost, and losing footage three weeks before an internal deadline is not a recoverable situation.

Software matters less than students believe, because every assessed judgement is about the decision rather than the tool. A session reviews the timeline in whatever the student already uses, and the tutor's questions are the same regardless. The table below separates the genuine needs from the expensive distractions, which is a conversation worth having before a purchase rather than after one. The pattern across the rows is consistent: anything that improves a decision earns its money, and anything that only improves the image rarely does. Before buying a camera, ask the subject teacher what the school already owns and what it is willing to lend over a weekend, because in most Abu Dhabi schools running Film the answer covers more than families assume.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a subject built on other people's footage
paragraphs: Film sits closer to the academic-honesty line than most Diploma subjects, because its raw material is work made by other people. Analysing an extract from a prescribed film is exactly what the textual analysis asks for and is entirely proper. Lifting a sequence into a student's own reel without acknowledgement is not. The boundary is acknowledgement and purpose, and students generally need it drawn once, clearly, early in DP1.

The same boundary governs what a tutor may do. A tutor teaches film language, questions an argument, reads a draft and gives marking-style feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor does not supply a script, voice a recording, cut a sequence for a student's portfolio, or hand over text for a project report. Every submitted artefact is the student's own, and a provider offering finished coursework is offering something that puts the student's diploma at risk while carrying none of that risk themselves. One page ranking in this search sells completed assessments outright.

There is a third strand specific to this subject: music and footage rights. A student who scores a short film with a commercial track has created a problem that is small inside a school submission and real outside it. Library music, creative-commons material and original composition all avoid it. A tutor's useful contribution is to raise it while the edit can still change, and to insist the source list for the comparative study is complete rather than decorative.

sections.heading: When your Abu Dhabi school does not run Film at all
paragraphs: A sizeable number of families reach this page because Film is the subject their child wants and their school does not offer. ADEK licenses and inspects the private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection ratings, but no regulator requires a school to run a particular Diploma subject, and arts options are the first to disappear from a small timetable. So the question is practical rather than regulatory.

There are three honest answers and none of them is tutoring. A student can move to a school in the emirate that runs the subject, which is a bigger decision than a subject choice. A student can take the subject by arrangement with another provider where their school permits it, which depends entirely on the school's own policy and the Diploma coordinator's view. Or a student can keep Film as the subject of their Extended Essay and build the analytical skills there, which is the route that works most often and costs least.

Outside support has a narrow and genuine role in the third option. An Extended Essay in Film written by a student who has never been taught film analysis needs the vocabulary before it needs a question, and that is teachable in a short block. What a tutor cannot do is register a candidate, substitute for a school's subject provision, or promise an outcome from an arrangement the school has not agreed to. Anything that implies otherwise should be read with real scepticism.

sections.heading: What a Film grade does, and does not do, after the Diploma
paragraphs: Parents in this emirate ask a reasonable question about Film: does it count. For a film, media or communications degree it counts directly, and a portfolio and reel built properly during the Diploma are genuinely useful in an application that asks for creative work. For most other degrees, Film is one subject among six and is treated like any other, with the Higher Level requirements that matter being whichever ones the course specifies.

The Ministry of Education equivalency question is separate and often conflated with admissions. Equivalency is a process run by the Ministry and the emirate's attestation channel, not something a tutoring provider performs or guarantees. For the British curriculum the published requirement includes five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count of five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. No IB points figure is published here, because none has been read on the Ministry's own pages.

The practical advice is narrower than the question. Check the subject requirements on the admissions pages of the universities your child is actually considering, because they vary and they change, and treat any tutoring page's summary of them, including this one, as a prompt to verify rather than as a source. Film is a strong Diploma subject for a student who wants to make things and can document their thinking. It is a weak choice for a student who wants a comfortable grade.

process.title: Say which task, and how far it has gone
process.description: Name the assessed task and its current state: textual analysis not started, comparative study question unsettled, portfolio pages reconstructed after the shoot, project report blank. A request phrased this way reaches a tutor who has worked on that task. A request for help with Film reaches a general media teacher, which is a different purchase.

process.title: Send the draft, the cut and the deadline
process.description: Before the free trial lesson, send whatever exists, a link to the current cut if there is one, and the school's internal deadline. The trial is then spent reading the real work against the real requirements rather than on introductions. One free trial lesson per student, booked without card details.

process.title: Fix the limit before the content
process.description: Every recorded submission has a stated running time and the written ones have word counts. The first session agrees what the limit is and what will have to be left out to meet it. Students who settle this at the start do not spend their final week cutting the analysis out of their own recording.

process.title: Test the shoot against real access
process.description: If a project still needs filming, the plan is checked against locations the student can actually use with permission in the weeks available. Scope changes are cheap now and impossible later. This is the single step that most often stops a reel being abandoned halfway through DP2.

process.title: Review against the submission, not the feeling
process.description: The block closes by checking whether the submission met its limit, cited its sources, and evidenced what it claims. That is checkable. A general sense that the sessions went well is not, and it is how open-ended arrangements survive long past the point they were useful.

whyPoints.title: Task-level work, not film appreciation
whyPoints.description: Sessions are attached to a named assessed task and its own requirements: the textual analysis, the comparative study with its sources, the portfolio and reel, or the Higher Level report. Open-ended enthusiasm for cinema is pleasant and does not move a grade that is awarded for argument and evidence.

whyPoints.title: Screen-shared review of real material
whyPoints.description: Timelines are scrubbed, frames are paused, portfolio pages are read beside the footage they describe. That work is easier on a shared screen than across a table, which is one reason the online format suits this subject rather than merely substituting for something better.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted as the market's, with sources named
whyPoints.description: The published market band for IB specialist tutoring runs at AED 200-450 an hour, with one-to-one visits published at AED 180-500 including the drive. Those are other providers' figures as published in October 2026. Three of the six competitor pages researched for this market publish no price at all.

whyPoints.title: A stated limit on what a tutor produces
whyPoints.description: Teaching, questioning and marking-style feedback on the student's own drafts and cuts. No supplied scripts, no edited sequences handed over, no text for a project report. The boundary is written down here because it is the differentiator in a search where completed coursework is openly sold.

whyPoints.title: Availability disclosed before booking
whyPoints.description: Film is among the thinnest subjects in this market. Where no UAE-resident specialist is free, the wider online pool is offered and the tutor's location is stated before anything is confirmed. No competitor page researched for this market discloses a coverage limit at all.

whyPoints.description: IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform with no office in the UAE. It holds no approval, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board. Regulators are explained on this page and never implied as endorsers.

faqs.question: What does an IB DP Film tutor in Abu Dhabi actually work on?
faqs.answer: Four things, depending on where your child is. The textual analysis, building an argument about a short extract and cutting the recording to its limit. The comparative study, framing a researchable question and finding sources the student can actually reach and cite. The film portfolio, turning three film roles into documented evidence rather than assertions. At Higher Level, the individual project report inside a group film. Camera technique and software training sit with the school and with practice. Sessions run one-to-one over live video, with timelines and portfolio pages read on a shared screen.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a Film tutor to our address in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Diploma Film support here is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For this subject the format is a genuine advantage rather than a substitute. A tutor needs to scrub through a cut, pause on a frame, and read a portfolio page beside the footage it describes, all of which is screen work. Removing the drive across the emirate also means the hour goes on the edit instead of the ring road.

faqs.question: Why does my child keep running over the time limit on the textual analysis?
faqs.answer: Because they are walking through the extract shot by shot instead of arguing about it. A chronological description of a four-minute sequence will always overrun, and when students then trim, they instinctively cut the analytical sentences and keep the description, which makes the recording shorter and weaker at the same time. The repair is structural. Open with a claim about what the sequence is doing, pick three or four timecoded moments that earn the claim, and leave the rest of the extract unmentioned on purpose. That version fits the limit without being squeezed.

faqs.question: How do we choose two films for the comparative study that will actually work?
faqs.answer: Start from the question rather than from the films. A workable question is narrow, answerable from a handful of specific moments, and could have come out differently. Then pick two films from genuinely different cultural contexts that can both answer it, and check before committing that there is citable writing about each one your child can reach. Many students in this emirate want to include a Gulf or Arab film, which is a strong instinct, provided the film is accessible and something has been published about it. The source list is marked, so reachability is not a detail.

faqs.question: My child's portfolio pages were written after the shoot. Is that recoverable?
faqs.answer: Partly, and the honest answer depends on which role. Evidence that existed and was not kept, a lighting set-up that was tried and photographed, two cuts of a sequence that still sit in the project file, can often be reassembled. Evidence that was never captured, the drafting decision nobody recorded, cannot be recreated credibly and reads as invention when it is attempted. The useful move is to stop reconstructing the past and start documenting whatever production work is still ahead, then build the strongest honest pages from what genuinely exists.

faqs.question: Which three film roles should my child pick for the portfolio?
faqs.answer: Three that sit at different points of the pipeline, not three that all happen in the edit suite. One in planning, one on set and one in post produces three distinct kinds of evidence and reads as a student who understood the task. Writer, cinematographer and editor is a common workable set. Director, sound designer and producer is another. Picking editor, sound designer and colourist feels safe and gives an examiner three variations of the same kind of page. The decision is cheap to make before a shoot and hard to repair afterwards.

faqs.question: Can my child film in a mall or on the Corniche for a school project?
faqs.answer: Treat every location in Abu Dhabi as owned and managed, because almost all of them are. Malls, waterfront promenades, towers and cultural venues each have their own permissions process, and a request carries far more weight coming from the school than from a student. Ask with a specific date, duration, crew size and equipment list, and allow two weeks. The stronger plan is to scope the project around locations the student already has access to, which in practice means school grounds, a family home, or a compound street with neighbours informed.

faqs.question: What equipment do we actually need to buy for Diploma Film?
faqs.answer: Much less than most families expect. A phone, a cheap tripod, a modest wired microphone and free editing software are enough for submissions that score well, because the tasks are marked on argument, documentation and decision-making. Two things are worth spending on. Sound, because unusable dialogue cannot be repaired and damages the reel it is meant to demonstrate. And backup storage, because a single copy of a shoot on one memory card is how projects die three weeks before a deadline. An expensive camera with no shot plan changes nothing.

faqs.question: Can a tutor cut a sequence or voice a recording for my child?
faqs.answer: No, and a provider willing to is selling something dangerous. Every submitted artefact in Diploma Film has to be the student's own: the recording, the script, the cut, the portfolio pages, the project report. A tutor teaches film language, questions an argument, reads a draft and gives marking-style feedback on material the student has produced. That boundary is stated here because it is the real differentiator in this search. One page ranking for these queries sells completed assessments, and the student carries the consequence, not the seller.

faqs.question: Can my child use a commercial song in their reel?
faqs.answer: It is better avoided, and it is worth settling while the edit can still change. Library music, creative-commons tracks and original composition by the student or a classmate all remove the question entirely, and a student composer on the same project usually improves the work as well. Raising it late is the problem: a reel locked around a commercial track is hard to re-score in the final fortnight. The same thinking applies to borrowed footage, which belongs in an analysis with acknowledgement and not in a student's own production.

faqs.question: Our school runs the Diploma but not Film. What are the real options?
faqs.answer: Three, and only one of them is cheap. Moving to a school in the emirate that offers it is a far bigger decision than a subject choice. Taking the subject through another provider depends entirely on your school's policy and the Diploma coordinator's view, and that conversation has to happen with the school rather than with a tutor. The option that most often works is keeping Film as the Extended Essay subject, which gives the student a 4,000-word research piece in the discipline. No regulator obliges a school to run any particular Diploma subject.

faqs.question: How does the Higher Level collaborative project get marked if the group underperforms?
faqs.answer: Each student submits their own project report, and that report is what carries the individual grade. A group film that turns out weak is survivable if a student can evidence their own contribution, the decisions they argued for, and what they would change. A group film that turns out well is not automatically good news if a student has nothing individual to point to. So the work worth doing is logging your own contribution as the shoot proceeds, with dates and specifics, rather than waiting until the report is due and trying to remember.

faqs.question: When in the two years should an Abu Dhabi Film student start outside support?
faqs.answer: DP1, and ideally before the first shoot. The cheap, high-leverage work is all early: choosing three portfolio roles that produce distinct evidence, framing a comparative study question that can be answered, and testing whether a planned shoot can actually be filmed with permission in the time available. All of that costs a handful of hours and removes most of the DP2 crisis. Support bought in the final fortnight of DP2 is triage. It can rescue a limit overrun or tighten an argument, and it cannot create documentation that was never captured.

faqs.question: Is Film a sensible Diploma choice for a child who wants to study medicine or engineering?
faqs.answer: It can be, with eyes open. Film is one Diploma subject among six and carries no penalty, but competitive science and engineering courses specify which Higher Levels they expect, so a student taking Film at Higher Level needs to check that their other Higher Levels still satisfy the course. Verify this on each university's own admissions pages rather than on any tutoring site, including this one, because requirements vary and change. Film is a strong choice for a student who wants to make things and document their thinking, and a poor one taken for an easy grade.

faqs.question: Do Film tutors working with Abu Dhabi students need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private tutoring in the UAE need a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years and covers school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount appears here. Because the permit is free, its absence is worth asking about.

faqs.question: What if no Film specialist is free when our deadline is close?
faqs.answer: You are told before anything is booked. Film is one of the thinnest subjects in this market and Higher Level project support is thinner still. Where no UAE-resident specialist covers the task, the match comes from the wider pool of Diploma Film tutors working to Gulf Standard Time, most often from India, in the same online format and on the same hourly basis, with the tutor's location stated upfront. Flexibility on timing widens the choice considerably: a 19:30 slot reaches a materially larger pool than a fixed 17:00 one.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-film-home-tutor.closingBody: An IB DP film home tutor in Abu Dhabi is worth buying when the request is specific. Say which of the four assessed tasks is the problem, send the current draft or cut and the school's internal deadline, and the free trial lesson will tell you whether a block is needed and roughly how long it has to be. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with timelines and portfolio pages read on a shared screen. Every recording, script, cut and report submitted stays your child's own work, and nothing on this page promises a grade.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-film-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors cover Diploma Film for Abu Dhabi students: textual analysis of a prescribed extract, the recorded comparative study, portfolio documentation across three production roles, and the Higher Level collaborative project report. Sessions are one-to-one over live video with work shared on screen.

intro.heading: Diploma Film is mostly writing, and that surprises everyone
paragraphs: The students who choose Film in Abu Dhabi are usually the ones already making things: short videos, edits, music clips, films for school events. The subject attracts them for the right reasons and then assesses something they did not expect. Three of the four components are written or spoken analysis, and the fourth, the Higher Level collaborative film, is marked largely on an individual written report about a process rather than on how good the film is. Capable film-makers are routinely predicted a 4 because nobody told them this.

The components are specific and their limits are hard. The textual analysis is a written analysis of a short extract from a prescribed film, inside a strict word limit. The comparative study is a recorded multimedia piece comparing two films from different cultural contexts, inside a strict time limit, with a documented source list. The film portfolio documents the student's work in three production roles across a set number of pages, with a short reel. Higher Level adds the collaborative film and its report.

That structure tells a parent exactly where to look. A student who talks fluently about cinema and writes vaguely about it will lose marks on two components. A student who shot an impressive short but kept no record of their decisions will lose marks on a third. Both problems are visible in Year 12 if anyone checks, and both are substantially cheaper to fix then than in the spring of Year 13 when the material has to be produced at once.

On delivery: IB Gram teaches UAE students one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time, with extracts, timelines, portfolio pages and drafts shared on screen. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are a service we run only in India. For this subject that is close to ideal. Reviewing a sequence frame by frame, pausing on a cut and asking why it is there, is work done better on a shared screen than over somebody's shoulder.

And the boundary. The student writes every word, shoots every frame, cuts every edit and records their own comparative study. A tutor teaches analysis, questions a film pairing, explains what a criterion asks for, and marks practice analysis against the published descriptors. Nobody at IB Gram scripts, edits, narrates or writes any part of a submission, and footage, music and generative tools used in any film must be credited exactly as the school requires. Providers in this market do sell finished coursework, and that risk is carried entirely by your child. A final note before the detail: nothing in this page requires a parent to know anything about cinema. Every check described here is a question about whether a document exists, how long it is, and whether its claims point at a specific moment with a timecode attached.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-film-tutor.programmesIntro: Film is examined in the Diploma, and the habits that decide the grade form earlier. Here is what each IB stage contributes for an Abu Dhabi student heading towards it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years producing a textual analysis, a recorded comparative study, a portfolio documenting three production roles and, at Higher Level, a collaborative film with an individual report. The marks reward precise analysis of how film form creates meaning and documented evidence of production decisions. They do not reward polish, and a beautiful short film with no record of its development scores poorly.
programmes.countryNote: Film provision in Abu Dhabi schools varies widely: some have an equipped media suite and a specialist teacher, others run the course on laptops and goodwill. The emirate's production environment is an asset students rarely use, and a second reading of a written component is most valuable where the department is a single person.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Middle Years Arts and Design both build the habit of documenting a creative process and reflecting on it in writing, which the Diploma assesses directly. A Year 11 who has written about why a shot was chosen, rather than only choosing it, arrives in DP1 with the one skill the course punishes hardest for lacking.
programmes.countryNote: In several Abu Dhabi schools media work at this stage is production-led with light written reflection. We check what a student has actually written before deciding whether a DP1 plan begins with analytical writing or with film language.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No bearing on a Diploma grade. What carries forward is the expectation that a film is talked about as a set of deliberate choices rather than as a story, which is usually formed by how a child is asked to discuss what they watch.
programmes.countryNote: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies run alongside the licensed international curriculum in UAE private schools under the federal requirement, so specialist arts and media time at Primary level differs sharply between schools in the emirate.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A sensible route for students combining Diploma courses with a media, production or communications career study, often building a showreel alongside. Film taken within it is assessed against the same subject guide, so the tutoring work is identical.
programmes.countryNote: Uncommon in Abu Dhabi, so families on this route rarely find anyone locally who has supported it. Online matching resolves a limitation that was only ever about distance rather than expertise.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-film-tutor.subjectsIntro: Film students in Abu Dhabi usually need one other subject supported in the same year. These are the Diploma courses our tutors cover alongside it, and where the skills genuinely transfer.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Textual analysis, comparative study, film portfolio and, at Higher Level, a collaborative film with an individual report. Marks go missing on analysis that retells plot instead of explaining technique, and on portfolios that show finished work without the decisions behind it.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The closest analytical neighbour, and the subject that most reliably predicts a strong Film grade. A student who can explain how a text produces an effect has exactly the skill the textual analysis rewards, applied to image and sound.

subjects.name: English A: Literature
subjects.description: Builds close reading and formal analysis with a tighter focus on structure. The transfer into writing about editing, framing and sound is direct, and one tutor can keep the analytical standard consistent across both.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Shares the documentation problem and much of the formal vocabulary. Students taking both must keep the two sets of written work distinct: one argues a curatorial intention, the other explains how a sequence creates meaning.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Useful for anything involving sound design and score. Students taking both write stronger analysis of soundtrack, which is the element most Film candidates ignore entirely in favour of the image.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Shares performance analysis and collaborative production. Students taking both need to separate theatrical and cinematic vocabulary, because describing a film shot in stage terms reads as imprecision to a Film examiner.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Valuable for the cultural-context requirement of the comparative study. Students taking both use context as evidence inside the argument rather than as background preceding it.

subjects.name: Digital Society
subjects.description: Overlaps around media, platforms and distribution. Students taking both often have the sharpest material for a comparative study involving contemporary production and circulation.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Included because it is the most common fourth subject among Film students we support in the emirate, and a weak grade here is what most often threatens an otherwise comfortable Diploma total.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Film is a strong choice for a student who can analyse a sequence and a poor one for a student who wants to write a director's biography. Support is process coaching and reading what the student has already written.

sections.heading: The four things a Diploma Film student submits
paragraphs: Families consistently imagine this subject as a making course with some writing attached. It is the reverse. Standard Level students submit a textual analysis, a comparative study and a film portfolio. Higher Level students add a collaborative film project with an individual report. Of those, only the portfolio reel and the Higher Level film involve submitting footage, and even the Higher Level film is assessed heavily through the written account of the process.

The limits are strict and losing marks to them is entirely avoidable. The textual analysis sits inside a 1,750-word limit on a short extract from a film on the prescribed list. The comparative study is recorded to a tight time limit and submitted with a list of sources. The portfolio is capped at a set number of pages and accompanied by a short reel. Confirm every figure against the guide version your child's school follows, because guides are revised and schools adopt revisions at different points.

The table below sets the components side by side with what is submitted, the limit that applies and what the marks reward. The right-hand column is the one worth reading twice. In every component credit attaches to specificity: a technique located by timecode, a comparison that produces a claim neither film would support alone, a production decision recorded with its reason at the time it was made. Notice what the table does not include: an examination at the end of the course. There is no paper to rescue a weak two years here, which is why the school's internal deadline calendar is the single most important document a Film family can hold.

sections.heading: Textual analysis: a few minutes of film and 1,750 words
paragraphs: The textual analysis is the component that most reliably separates grades, and the reason is that it looks easy. A student watches a short extract from a prescribed film and writes about it. What goes wrong is almost always the same thing: they write about what happens rather than about how the film makes it happen. Plot retelling is the single most expensive habit in this subject, and students arrive with it fully formed from years of writing about stories.

The second common failure is scope. A student who tries to cover an entire extract evenly produces 1,750 words of thin observation. A student who selects two or three moments and analyses them properly, with timecodes, in terms of framing, editing rhythm, sound and movement, produces an answer that can be credited. The limit is not a constraint to fight; it is an instruction to choose, and choosing is the analytical act.

The third is sound, which Abu Dhabi students ignore as reliably as students anywhere. Diegetic and non-diegetic sound, silence, the moment music enters, the volume relationship between dialogue and background: these are decisions the film-makers made deliberately and almost nobody writes about them. A student who analyses soundtrack competently stands out immediately, and it is among the easiest improvements to teach. The table below sets out weak and strong treatment across what the analysis must cover. The practice route we use is to start on a sequence the student knows by heart. Familiarity means they can find the moment instantly, so the only new skill being practised is the explaining, which is the part the marks are attached to.

sections.heading: The comparative study is an argument, not two reviews
paragraphs: The comparative study asks a student to compare two films from different cultural contexts in a recorded multimedia piece. The weak version is two descriptions placed end to end with a sentence of comparison at the join. The strong version makes a claim that only comparison could produce, and then evidences it with specific sequences from both films. The test is simple: if the study would still make sense with one of the films removed, it is not a comparative study.

Choice of films sets the ceiling on this component, and students choose badly for understandable reasons. They pick two films they like, or two films that are obviously similar, and then discover there is nothing to argue about. The productive pairing shares a problem and solves it differently: two films handling the same genre convention, the same kind of protagonist or the same historical moment from inside different traditions. We spend the first session on the pairing, because no amount of later work rescues a weak one.

Because the study is recorded rather than written, students assume the production values carry weight. They do not. A clear voice over well-chosen clips, with the argument audible and the evidence visible, scores better than an elaborate edit that buries a thin claim. What does cost marks is a sloppy source list and uncredited clips. Document every source as you go, in the format the school requires, and the final week becomes about the argument rather than about reconstructing a bibliography.

sections.heading: The portfolio, the three roles and the evidence problem
paragraphs: The film portfolio asks a student to document their own work in three distinct production roles, within a capped number of pages and with a short reel. This is where confident film-makers lose the most marks, because the portfolio is credited for documented decisions rather than for results. A student who directed something excellent and kept no record of why they chose a lens, a location or a cut has produced something unassessable in portfolio terms.

Role choice matters more than students expect. Three roles that genuinely demand different thinking, such as director, sound designer and editor, give a student three distinct bodies of evidence. Three overlapping roles on the same project produce one body of evidence described three times, which reads thin however much work went into it. We plan the roles against the projects available in DP1, so each one has a real chance to generate material.

The routine, again, is small and it is the whole game. During production, photograph set-ups, screenshot timelines, save versions rather than overwriting, and write two sentences after each session on what was decided and why. Ten minutes. That is what a portfolio page is built from. The table below sets out each common role, what the portfolio needs to show, the characteristic failure and what a session fixes. The page cap is the other thing to respect early. A capped portfolio rewards selection, so a student with a year of dated records chooses the strongest evidence, while a student with three weeks of records includes everything and still looks thin.

sections.heading: The Higher Level collaborative project when the group falters
paragraphs: Higher Level students make a film in a group and submit an individual report about it. The assessment follows the individual, which is the single most reassuring fact in this subject and the one students most often do not know. A group that fragments does not automatically sink everyone in it, because what is credited is each student's own contribution and reflection on the collaborative process, including the difficulties.

That does not make a failing group harmless. A student whose teammates stop working has less finished film to point at and more pressure in the final weeks, and the practical answer is to document their own contribution relentlessly from the start. Dated notes, message threads about decisions, drafts, call sheets, versions: all of it becomes evidence of what this student actually did. A student who can show their own process survives a difficult group far better than one who relied on a shared drive somebody else maintained.

Our advice to Abu Dhabi families is to assume some friction and plan for it. Agree roles in writing in the first week. Keep individual records as well as shared ones. Scope the film small enough that two committed people could finish it if a third disappears, because in a cohort of five or six students the chance of one dropping away is real. None of this is cynicism; it is the same risk planning a producer would do on any real production.

sections.heading: Filming in Abu Dhabi: permission, locations and sensible scope
paragraphs: Ambition is the most common cause of unfinished films in this emirate, and location access is usually what kills it. Filming in public and commercial spaces in Abu Dhabi normally requires permission from the venue or the relevant authority, and a student who plans a sequence in a mall, a museum or a managed waterfront without asking first will be moved on. Check the current requirements for any public or commercial location, and ask through the school, which can approach a venue with more standing than a sixteen-year-old can.

The good news is that constraint improves student films. A two-person scene in a flat on Al Reem Island, lit from one window and cut carefully, evidences more technical control than an unfinished action sequence shot across three locations. Villa communities in Khalifa City and Shakhbout City offer private exterior space without any permission question. Residential interiors, school grounds with permission, and private outdoor areas cover almost everything a Diploma project needs.

Two further practicalities. Anyone appearing on camera should agree to it, and for anyone under eighteen the school's own permission process applies, which is also the honest way to handle it. And heat is a real production constraint between spring and autumn: an outdoor shoot planned for April behaves nothing like the same shoot in December, and students planning long exterior sequences should schedule them for the cooler months rather than discover the problem on the day. Equipment is the last thing to plan around rather than the first. Schools in the emirate often hold cameras, microphones and lights bought for productions, and asking the department what exists and when it is free usually answers more questions than any purchase would.

sections.heading: Rights, credits and honesty in a borrowing medium
paragraphs: Film is built from other people's material, which makes the honesty rules less intuitive than in an essay subject. Clips used in a comparative study, music on a soundtrack, stock footage, fonts, images and anything produced with a generative tool all require proper crediting in the format the school specifies. A student who credits everything has nothing to fear. A student who uses a commercial track because it fits and says nothing has created a problem for themselves at submission.

On music specifically, the practical route is to use material the student has the right to use: compositions written by a friend taking Music, properly licensed library tracks, or clearly identified material used under the conditions the guide sets out for academic work. The school's film teacher is the right person to confirm what is acceptable for a submission, and the question should be asked before the edit is locked rather than after.

Our own boundary is the same as on every page. A tutor teaches analysis, questions a pairing or a scope, explains what a criterion asks for, and marks practice work. A tutor does not script, shoot, edit, narrate or write any part of a submission. There are providers in this market who will produce coursework, including for this subject, and the consequence of using one falls on your child rather than on them: the Diploma at risk is theirs. The administrative habit that prevents nearly all of this is a single running document listing every borrowed element with its source and date, kept from the first week. It takes seconds per entry and turns the final submission check into a formality.

sections.heading: Where Film leads, how it is sequenced, and what support costs
paragraphs: Three closing questions, in the order parents ask them. On destinations: film, media and communications degrees generally welcome the subject, and many ask for a showreel or portfolio in which the student's own work is central. Highly selective film schools select on a portfolio and an interview as much as on grades. Competitive science, engineering and medicine routes expect specific subjects and Film does not substitute for them, so the decision belongs in the Year 12 option conversation with the actual entry requirements on the table.

On sequencing: ask the film teacher for the internal deadline calendar at the start of DP1 and work backwards. The pattern that fails is spending DP1 shooting and DP2 discovering that three written components are due. The pattern that works puts analytical writing into DP1 at low intensity, keeps production documentation running continuously, settles the comparative study pairing by the end of DP1, and leaves DP2 to finish rather than to start.

On cost: published market figures for Diploma specialist support in this market run from roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, with qualified subject tutors online quoted from about AED 150 to AED 300, and in-home visits from around AED 180 to AED 500 because travel sits inside the rate. Those were read in October 2026 from providers in this market and are not an IB Gram price list. Our rate is quoted per 60 minutes in writing after a free trial lesson, with marking and a written note included.

faqs.question: What exactly does a Diploma Film student submit?
faqs.answer: At Standard Level: a textual analysis of a short extract from a prescribed film, a recorded multimedia comparative study of two films from different cultural contexts with a source list, and a film portfolio documenting the student's work in three production roles with a short reel. Higher Level adds a collaborative film made in a group, submitted with an individual report. Only two of those involve footage, and even the Higher Level film is assessed heavily through the written account of the process. Your school holds the current limits.

faqs.question: How long is the textual analysis and what is it analysing?
faqs.answer: It is a written analysis of a short extract from a film on the prescribed list, inside a 1,750-word limit. The subject of the analysis is how the film creates meaning: framing, editing, sound, movement and mise-en-scene, located precisely by timecode. It is not an essay about the film as a whole or about the director. Students who try to cover every second of the extract evenly write thin observation; those who select two or three moments and analyse them properly score far better within the same limit.

faqs.question: Why do capable students still lose marks on the textual analysis?
faqs.answer: Because they retell the plot. Years of writing about stories produces a reflex to describe what happens, and the component credits explanation of how the film makes it happen. The second cause is spreading 1,750 words evenly across the whole extract instead of choosing. The third is ignoring sound entirely, which almost every candidate does: when music enters, what is heard off screen, the balance between dialogue and background. Analysing soundtrack competently is one of the quickest ways to stand out.

faqs.question: What makes a comparative study score well rather than averagely?
faqs.answer: A claim that only comparison could produce. The average study is two descriptions placed end to end with a comparative sentence at the join; the strong one argues something about both films that neither would support alone, then evidences it with specific sequences. A useful test: if the study still makes sense with one film removed, it is not comparative. Context must work as evidence inside the argument rather than as background before it, and every clip and source must be credited as the school requires.

faqs.question: Does the choice of two films really matter that much?
faqs.answer: It sets the ceiling. Students pick two films they love, or two that are obviously alike, and then find there is nothing to argue. A productive pairing shares a problem and solves it differently: the same genre convention, the same kind of protagonist or the same historical moment handled from inside different traditions. The films must come from different cultural contexts. We spend the first session on the pairing rather than on the writing, because strong writing cannot outperform a pairing with no argument in it.

faqs.question: What are the three production roles, and can a student choose freely?
faqs.answer: Students document their own work in three distinct roles drawn from the production roles the guide sets out, commonly director, cinematographer, editor, sound designer, writer or producer. The practical advice is to choose three that demand genuinely different thinking, so each generates its own body of evidence. Three overlapping roles on one project produce a single body of work described three times, which reads thin. Plan the roles in DP1 against the projects actually available, and confirm the permitted list with your school.

faqs.question: Is my son marked on the group's film or on his own contribution?
faqs.answer: On his own contribution and his individual report. That is the most reassuring fact in this component and the one students most often do not know. A group that fragments does not automatically sink everyone, because what is credited is each student's role, decisions and reflection on the collaborative process, including its difficulties. The practical protection is to document his own work separately from any shared drive: dated notes, drafts, versions, call sheets and decision threads all evidence what he actually did.

faqs.question: Do we need permission to film in public places in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: For public and commercial locations, normally yes, and a student who arrives with a camera and no arrangement will be moved on. Check the current requirements for the specific location and authority, and ask through the school, which can approach a venue with standing an individual student does not have. Residential interiors, private villa exteriors and school grounds with permission cover almost everything a Diploma project needs. Anyone appearing on camera should consent, and for under-eighteens the school's own permission process applies.

faqs.question: What music can legally go on the soundtrack of a submitted film?
faqs.answer: Material the student has the right to use. The straightforward routes are a composition written by a friend taking Diploma Music, properly licensed library music, or clearly identified material used under the conditions the guide allows for academic work, credited exactly as the school requires. A popular commercial track dropped in because it fits is the common mistake and it creates a problem at submission. Ask the film teacher before the edit is locked rather than afterwards, when changing the soundtrack means recutting.

faqs.question: Is a phone good enough to shoot a Diploma film?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, and worrying about the camera is usually a way of avoiding harder questions. Modern phone footage is entirely capable of scoring well; what limits student films is sound, lighting and framing, in that order. A cheap external microphone and a single controlled light source improve a film more than a better camera would. What examiners credit is control and intention, visible in a small two-person scene shot carefully, rather than equipment visible in an ambitious sequence that was never finished.

faqs.question: How is an edit reviewed in an online session?
faqs.answer: The student shares their screen with the timeline open and drives the software while the tutor watches, pauses and asks why a cut is where it is. In practice this is closer to a proper edit review than sitting beside them, because both people see the same frame at the same timecode and nothing has to be described. Because the student operates everything, nothing produced in the session is anyone else's work, which is exactly the boundary the subject requires.

faqs.question: How many hours does the textual analysis usually take to get right?
faqs.answer: In our Abu Dhabi caseload, typically four to six across DP1 and early DP2: one or two learning located analysis on a familiar sequence, one on selecting which moments to analyse, one on sound, and one before the school's internal deadline checking criteria coverage and the word count. A student starting in the final term needs more hours for less movement, because the skill being taught is a habit of attention and habits do not form in a fortnight.

faqs.question: Is Film a weak subject for a university application?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the destination, and it should be checked against each course's published requirements rather than a general reputation. Film, media and communications degrees generally welcome it and often ask for a reel or portfolio in which the student's own work is central, which the Diploma conveniently produces. Selective film schools weigh portfolio and interview heavily. Competitive science, engineering and medicine routes expect specific subjects, and Film does not substitute for them, so the decision belongs in the Year 12 option conversation.

faqs.question: What does Diploma Film support cost in the Abu Dhabi market?
faqs.answer: Published figures for Diploma specialist support in this market run from roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, with qualified subject tutors online quoted from about AED 150 to AED 300, and in-home visits from around AED 180 to AED 500 because the drive is inside the rate. Those were read in October 2026 from providers in this market and are not an IB Gram price list. We quote per 60 minutes in writing after a free trial lesson, with marking and a written session note included, and no package is required.

faqs.question: Our comparative study has not been started and DP2 has begun. What is possible?
faqs.answer: A great deal, provided the pairing is settled quickly and well. Unlike the portfolio, the comparative study is produced rather than accumulated, so it does not depend on evidence that should have been captured last year. The realistic plan is one session on the pairing, two or three on building the argument and selecting sequences, and one before the internal deadline checking timing, sources and criteria coverage. What cannot be rebuilt late is portfolio evidence, so if both are behind, prioritise the study and document production from this week forward.

intro.heading: French looks familiar, which is the problem
paragraphs: French ab initio is the Diploma's beginner French course, Standard Level only, for students with little or no previous experience of the language. In Abu Dhabi it is chosen most often by students who arrived at an international school partway through, needed a Group 2 subject and had no realistic claim to French B. It is also chosen, less wisely, by students who picked it because the alphabet is the one they already read. That assumption is the central misunderstanding in the subject and it costs marks for two years.

Here is why. A beginner in French can read a printed word on day one and produce a plausible sound for it. That feels like progress and it is genuinely useful: French reading comprehension benefits enormously from English cognates, and an ab initio student can often extract the gist of a reading passage in week six. The listening paper offers no such help. Spoken French removes most final consonants, runs words together through liaison, carries four nasal vowels that do not exist in English, and silences the ending of every third-person plural verb. A student who has learnt the language by eye hears a continuous stream with no word boundaries and recognises almost nothing in it.

This matters because receptive skills carry half the grade. Paper 2 combines a 45-minute listening section with an hour of reading and is worth 50%. Paper 1, two short written tasks in one hour, is 25%. The individual oral, conducted and marked by the school and moderated by the IB, is the remaining 25% and starts from a photograph linked to one of the five prescribed themes. A student who is strong on reading and weak on listening is therefore sitting on a visible, fixable half of their grade, and almost nobody has told them that the fix is phonological rather than lexical.

The second organising fact is that the content is prescribed. Five themes — identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet — carry twenty topics between them, and the course does not go beyond that list. For a beginner this is a considerable advantage, because it turns a language into a finite syllabus with countable vocabulary. Not all twenty cost the same, though: some recycle words the student already has, while others introduce abstract vocabulary that appears nowhere else. Teaching them in list order rather than in order of overlap makes the course harder than it needs to be.

On delivery, we are plain: IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE, and no tutor will come to a UAE address. That service exists only in India. French ab initio sessions are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. For this subject the format is well matched to the work, because audio clips replay from the same window the student is writing in, pronunciation can be modelled and immediately imitated, and every session leaves a record of which sounds, structures and topics were covered.

programmes.description: French ab initio is a Group 2 language acquisition course at Standard Level, built for genuine beginners. It assesses productive, receptive and interactive skills across five themes and twenty prescribed topics, with no literary works and no Higher Level tier. The whole course is a controlled build from sound and spelling up to short accurate communication.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the ab initio group frequently sits in the same timetable block as French B, and in a school with a francophone intake a beginner can end up comparing themselves with heritage speakers down the corridor. That comparison is demoralising and meaningless, and it is worth naming early.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition French runs in phases rather than year groups. A student leaving MYP5 in phase 1 is close to the ab initio starting point; phase 3 or above generally points to French B. The recorded phase is the cleanest evidence available for which Diploma course fits, and schools will supply it on request.
programmes.countryNote: Students arriving in Abu Dhabi from outside the region in Year 10 or 11 often have no MYP French phase at all, which is the simplest route into ab initio. Schools on Saadiyat and Yas with high international turnover run the largest beginner groups for this reason.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Primary French is taught through inquiry as an additional language, building spoken familiarity, songs, numbers and basic reading. Children typically leave able to greet, count and recognise familiar written words, with no systematic grammar and no exposure to French at natural speed.
programmes.countryNote: A child who had two years of primary French in Abu Dhabi and then stopped is usually still an ab initio candidate, and should be presented as one honestly. Overstating that prior exposure to secure a French B place produces two years of a course the student cannot access.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme carries a language development component assessed by portfolio rather than by examination. For a student who wants usable workplace French without a listening paper, it removes the single hardest element of ab initio while still recording language learning.
programmes.countryNote: CP provision is limited in Abu Dhabi relative to the Diploma, but it is worth knowing it exists before a reluctant beginner is committed to two years of examined French. Where the goal is conversational competence rather than a grade, ab initio is not automatically the right answer.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tu.subjectsIntro: French beginners rarely need a second language tutor, but the evening time ab initio consumes competes directly with the subjects below. These are the requests that arrive alongside it from Abu Dhabi families.

subjects.name: French ab initio
subjects.description: Beginner Diploma French: sound and spelling, the twenty prescribed topics, two short writing tasks, a listening and reading paper worth half the grade, and a visual-stimulus oral. The limiting factor for most students is listening recognition rather than vocabulary size.

subjects.name: French B
subjects.description: The next course up, assuming real prior French and adding two literary works at Higher Level. Students sometimes ask about moving across after a strong ab initio year; it is rarely sensible mid-course, because French B assumes a reading range eighteen months of beginner work does not build.

subjects.name: Spanish ab initio
subjects.description: Structurally identical and the most common alternative. Spanish spelling maps onto sound far more transparently than French, so its listening section is kinder; French offsets that with richer cognate support in reading. The honest comparison is where each hides its difficulty.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: The other beginner option in Abu Dhabi, and the one with a visible rather than hidden obstacle. Arabic front-loads its difficulty into the writing system, which students can see; French defers its difficulty to the listening paper, which they cannot.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Taken where English is an additional language, with the same three-skill architecture and the same criteria as every Group 2 course. A student doing both English B and French ab initio learns the assessment model once and applies it twice.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The commonest companion request. The exploration is 20% of the grade and is written over weeks, so it can be scheduled around a language build. Students new to IB conventions often lose marks on presentation rather than on mathematics.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Reading-heavy with a pre-release case study on a fixed timetable. It competes with French reading practice for evening time, and because its deadlines are fixed and the language build is not, the French work should bend around it rather than the reverse.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Interdisciplinary and well served by UAE material on water, energy and urban growth. Its internal assessment is produced over weeks, which makes it one of the easier subjects to run alongside an intensive beginner language term.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Portfolio-driven across two years, with flexible studio time that can give way during a heavy French term. It is the subject most often paired with a demanding language build for exactly that reason.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Command-term discipline decides the grade, and the answer-shape skills transfer to French ab initio writing tasks, where the task prompt sets an audience and purpose that must visibly be addressed rather than ignored.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The exhibition and the 1,600-word essay contribute up to 3 points alongside the Extended Essay. Beginners in a second language often write well on knowledge and language, because the experience of hearing a language they cannot parse is a live example.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay. An ab initio student should not attempt it in French, and a good supervisor will say so. Support is narrowing the research question and giving feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplying text.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tu.regionsIntro: Beginner French requests in Abu Dhabi come mostly from the mainland communities and the newer developments, because that is where mid-course arrivals and mixed-curriculum school choices concentrate. The area affects timing far more than availability.

regions.name: Al Reef
regions.note: Large villa community near the airport road with a highly mixed intake and considerable family turnover. A student arriving here in Year 11 with no French is the typical ab initio profile in the emirate.

regions.name: Al Falah
regions.note: Mainland community with a strong Emirati and Arab resident base, where French is a deliberate third-language choice rather than a heritage one. Beginners here usually start from genuine zero, which simplifies the plan.

regions.name: Shakhbout City
regions.note: Villa district with long bus routes to island campuses, so sessions tend to start at 18:00 on school nights. Weekend mornings work better for a beginner who needs concentration for sound work.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Dense mainland residential district feeding a wide spread of schools. Students here often sit in combined French groups and benefit most from having the twenty-topic list made explicit.

regions.name: Al Ghadeer
regions.note: Community on the Dubai border with families commuting in both directions. Scheduling consistency is the main constraint, and a fixed weekly slot matters more here than the day it falls on.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Growing school population with small Diploma cohorts, so a beginner group may be tiny or merged with French B. Students frequently need the ab initio and French B content separated explicitly in their own notes.

regions.name: Al Samha
regions.note: Northern mainland district with long journeys to most campuses. Evening sessions after 18:30 are the norm, and listening work is better placed earlier in a session here than at the end.

regions.name: Baniyas
regions.note: Established mainland town with a mix of curricula nearby. French beginners here tend to be students taking a Group 2 subject by requirement rather than by enthusiasm, which changes how the course is best sequenced.

schoolClusters.city: Mainland communities: Al Reef, Al Falah, Shakhbout City and Al Samha
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's largest residential belt, feeding British, American and IB campuses. Beginner French groups here are small and often timetabled against larger French B cohorts, which is the usual trigger for one-to-one support.

schoolClusters.city: Yas and the eastern islands
schoolClusters.note: Newer campuses with high international turnover and very small Group 2 cohorts, where a single teacher may cover beginners and heritage speakers in one room. Beginners in that setting need their own material rather than differentiated worksheets.
schools: The British International School Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Island schools with an established French presence
schoolClusters.note: The island holds the emirate's francophone anchor and the older international campuses, which means a beginner may be learning French in a building where it is a first language for other students. Useful for exposure, unhelpful for confidence.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-ab-initio-home-tu.modesIntro: Beginner French breaks into four separable jobs and they need different intensities. Each runs one-to-one over live video, with audio and writing in the same shared window.

modes.title: Sound and spelling block
modes.description: The opening work, and the part most ab initio courses skip because the alphabet looks familiar. Silent endings, liaison, nasal vowels and the written forms that produce each sound are taught explicitly, with the student reading aloud and hearing the difference between what they said and what a French speaker would say.
bullets: Nasal vowels isolated and drilled, since English has no equivalent
Silent final consonants and the plural -ent ending taught as rules
Liaison practised on connected phrases rather than single words
The student reads aloud every session and hears the model immediately after

modes.title: Topic coverage, weekly
modes.description: Once sound and spelling are functional, sessions work through the twenty prescribed topics in order of vocabulary overlap rather than list order. Each session builds the words a short task needs and uses them the same hour in speech and writing, with the coverage ledger updated every week.
bullets: One topic per session, taught in overlap order not list order
New vocabulary used in a produced sentence the same hour
A ledger of topics covered, revisited and still open
Reading and listening material drawn from the topic itself

modes.title: Listening recovery block
modes.description: A dedicated block for the component beginners lose most on. Short graded audio on covered topics, played twice as the exam does, answered under time, then checked against the transcript with every word known by eye but missed by ear written down. Numbers get their own fifteen minutes every session.
bullets: Thirty to ninety seconds of audio, heard twice, no pausing
Transcript used only in review, never alongside
French numbers drilled separately every single session
Several different speakers across the block to break voice dependence

modes.title: Paper and oral technique block
modes.description: The final months, on the examination rather than the language. Both Paper 1 tasks written to time inside the printed word ranges, reading passages timed separately, and recorded oral rehearsals against the real preparation limit. Technique is the cheapest part of the course and usually the part nobody gets.
bullets: Both writing tasks produced under exam timing
Reading timed per passage to expose pace rather than comprehension
Oral rehearsals recorded and reviewed against the three criteria
Question-type drills: short answer, matching, true or false with justification

sections.heading: What a beginner French tutor in Abu Dhabi is actually being asked to do
paragraphs: The brief is narrow and has a deadline. A student with no French needs to reach a Group 2 Standard Level grade in roughly eighteen months, with five other Diploma subjects running, and the examination session will not move. Everything in a sensible plan follows from that: what is taught first, what is triaged, and what is honestly out of reach.

The order that works is not the order students expect. Sound and spelling first, because every listening mark and every piece of pronunciation in the oral depends on it, and because a student who learns vocabulary before sound learns it in a form they will never recognise in speech. Then the twenty prescribed topics, taught in order of how much their vocabulary reappears elsewhere. Then examination technique, which is quick once the first two exist. Courses that run in the reverse order — phrases and past papers first, pronunciation absorbed somehow — produce students who write reasonable French and cannot understand a question asked aloud.

There is an Abu Dhabi-specific complication worth naming. This emirate has a real francophone population, concentrated around the island's long-established schools and the Lycée Louis Massignon catchment, with families from France, Lebanon, Morocco, Algeria and West Africa. A beginner in a school with that intake will encounter students for whom French is a home language, and may be timetabled alongside French B in the same block. The comparison is corrosive and completely irrelevant to an ab initio grade. We address it directly, because a student who concludes in DP1 that they are hopeless at French stops doing the daily work that the course actually requires.

What is honestly out of reach is worth saying as clearly as what is not. Eighteen months of beginner French does not produce a student who follows a French film without subtitles, reads a newspaper or holds an unstructured adult conversation. It can produce a student who writes two short accurate tasks on familiar topics, extracts information from a short unseen text, follows clear speech on a prescribed theme, and talks about a photograph for four minutes with structure. That is what the course asks for and it is achievable. Anything promised beyond it should be questioned.
bullets: Fixed deadline, prescribed content, no Higher Level to plan around
Order: sound and spelling, then topics in overlap order, then technique
Beginners in francophone school settings need the comparison defused early
Realistic outcome: short accurate writing and structured speech on familiar topics

sections.heading: The gap between how French is written and how it sounds
paragraphs: This is the whole subject compressed into one problem. Written French gives a beginner a great deal: recognisable letters, visible word boundaries, and thousands of words that look like English equivalents. Spoken French takes most of it away. Final consonants are usually silent. The third-person plural verb ending is written and not pronounced. Words run into each other through liaison so that boundaries disappear. Four nasal vowels carry meaning and have no English equivalent, so an untrained ear hears them as the nearest English sound and loses the distinction.

The consequence is a student who scores respectably on reading and badly on listening, and who concludes they have a vocabulary problem. They do not. They have a recognition problem: the words are in their head in written form only. The diagnostic is simple and worth doing in a first session. Give the student a short transcript to read, which they manage. Then play the same passage as audio. If comprehension collapses between the two, the problem is phonological and no amount of additional vocabulary learning will touch it.

The fix is explicit teaching of the sound-to-spelling relationship, which most beginner courses never do because the alphabet is familiar. Nasal vowels isolated and drilled. The silent endings taught as rules rather than met as exceptions. Liaison practised on connected phrases so the student expects boundaries to vanish. Reading aloud every session, with the student hearing a model immediately afterwards and correcting towards it. None of this is advanced work and all of it is routinely skipped.

French numbers deserve separate treatment because they defeat beginners more reliably than anything else and they appear in almost every listening section. Seventy is expressed as sixty-ten, eighty as four-twenties, ninety-seven as four-twenties-ten-seven. A student who can read those on a page may not catch them at speed, and prices, dates, times and ages are exactly what listening questions ask for. Fifteen minutes on numbers in every session for a term is wildly disproportionate value and almost nobody does it.

sections.heading: English is a help in reading and a trap in writing
paragraphs: French and English share an enormous amount of vocabulary, and for an ab initio reader that is a genuine gift. Words ending in -tion, -ité, -ment and -able are usually transparent. Academic and abstract vocabulary tends to come from the same Latin stock. A beginner six weeks into the course can often extract the gist of a reading passage simply by recognising shapes, which is why reading is the component most ab initio students are least worried about.

In writing the same overlap turns hostile. Some words look identical and mean something different, and because they look safe a student uses them with confidence. A library is not a librairie, which is a bookshop. To attend is not assister in the sense English suggests. Actuellement means currently rather than actually. Sensible means sensitive. Rester means to stay, not to rest. A student who writes these in a Paper 1 task produces a sentence that is grammatically sound and communicates the wrong thing, which costs message marks rather than language marks and is therefore harder to spot in self-marking.

The second form of interference is structural and more expensive. English word order and English prepositions get imported wholesale: adjectives placed before the noun where French puts most of them after, possession expressed with an English pattern, and prepositions chosen by translating the English one rather than learning the French verb's own requirement. These are not careless errors. They are systematic, which means they can be taught out systematically, in about three sessions, once someone lists them.

What works is a short personal error list rather than a grammar course. The student writes, the tutor marks each interference error by category rather than individually, and the categories go on a list belonging to that student. Lists of this kind reach fifteen or twenty items, not hundreds, and they stop recurring within a term because the student is finally seeing the pattern instead of a page of red corrections. This is also where the online format pays off, because the list lives in the shared document and both parties can see it growing shorter.
