sections.heading: Gender, agreement and the three tenses ab initio actually needs
paragraphs: Beginners are often taught French grammar as though they were heading for A-Level, which wastes months. Ab initio needs a defined and surprisingly small amount of structure, used accurately, and it does not need the subjunctive, the conditional perfect or the literary past. Deciding what to leave out is as much of the job as deciding what to teach.

Gender comes first because it propagates. Every noun carries one, the article changes with it, adjectives agree with it, and past participles sometimes agree too. A student who learns nouns without their gender from the first week is building a structure that will produce errors in every sentence for two years. The practical rule is that a noun is never learnt alone: it is learnt with its article, said aloud with its article, and written with its article. This costs nothing at the start and is extremely expensive to retrofit later.

Three tenses carry almost everything ab initio asks for. The present, for description and routine. The perfect, for saying what happened, which requires the auxiliary choice and the past participle. And the near future, formed with the verb to go plus an infinitive, which gives a student a complete future with no new conjugation to learn. With those three, correct agreement and a handful of connectives, a student can address any of the twenty prescribed topics in writing and in the oral. The imperfect is worth recognising in reading and listening and is rarely needed in production at this level.

Connectives are the cheapest marks in the writing tasks and the most neglected item on this list. A beginner who can join clauses with because, but, then, however and for example produces writing that reads as developed rather than listed, and the message criterion responds to that immediately. Five connectives, drilled until automatic, change the appearance of a task more than fifty new nouns do. That trade is worth making explicit to a student who believes progress means a longer vocabulary list.
bullets: Never learn a noun without its article — gender propagates into everything
Three tenses cover the course: present, perfect, and near future
The imperfect is for recognition in reading and listening, not production
Five connectives, automatic, improve the message mark more than fifty nouns

sections.heading: Twenty prescribed topics, and which of them pay twice
paragraphs: French ab initio content is a finite list: five themes and twenty topics between them. That makes coverage auditable, which is unusual and useful. A student four months from the examination can be shown precisely which topics they have usable vocabulary for and which they do not, instead of experiencing the course as a sequence of unrelated weeks.

The topics do not cost the same, and sequencing by cost rather than by list order makes a measurable difference. Topics about the self, family, daily routine, food and school recycle vocabulary the student already has, and each one taught reinforces the others. Topics about technology, the environment and social organisation introduce abstract vocabulary that appears in that topic and nowhere else, and they need more time for less transferable return. A course that works through the list in published order spends its early, high-energy weeks on expensive topics and its tired final weeks on cheap ones, which is exactly backwards.

Overlap also determines what to protect when time runs short. If eight topics remain open with four months to go, the right move is to secure the ones whose vocabulary supports the others and accept thin coverage on the most specialised. That is a decision to make deliberately, with the ledger in front of you, rather than one that happens by default when the calendar runs out. Families are rarely shown the list at all, which means the triage never happens consciously.

The ledger itself takes a minute a week: twenty rows, each marked covered, revisited or open, updated at the end of every session and shared. It is the single most useful administrative habit in the course and the thing that makes an honest conversation about outcomes possible in March. A student who knows that fifteen of twenty topics are secure revises differently from one who has no idea, and the difference shows up in the writing tasks, where topic choice is the first decision the candidate makes.

sections.heading: Paper 1: two short tasks, and the audience nobody addresses
paragraphs: Paper 1 gives a beginner one hour and two short written tasks, with word ranges printed on the paper, and takes 25% of the grade. The temptation is to treat it as a vocabulary display and write as much as possible. That is the wrong instinct, and correcting it is one of the most reliable gains available in the course.

Writing less, accurately, scores better. A student attempting complex structures they do not control generates errors in every line, and the language marks fall accordingly. A student writing short declarative sentences with correct agreement, three tenses used appropriately and five reliable connectives produces a piece that reads as controlled. For a beginner, control is what the descriptors reward. The drill is unglamorous: write the task, then cut every clause that was attempted rather than known, and see the mark rise.

The element beginners miss entirely is the audience. Each task sets a text type and implies a reader — a message to a friend, a note for a school noticeboard, a short email to a host family, a post for a class blog. That implied reader determines the form of address, the level of formality, the opening and the closing. A task written as undifferentiated prose with no greeting, no addressee and no sign-off loses marks that have nothing to do with French ability. A student told once what each text type needs produces all of it next time at no extra cost.

The formality choice is specifically awkward in French, because the language forces a decision in the second word of most sentences: the familiar or the polite form of address. English lets a beginner avoid the question. French does not, and a task addressed to a school principal with the familiar form has told the examiner something about register before the content is even read. Teaching the two forms as a decision tied to the audience, rather than as a grammar point, fixes it quickly and permanently.
bullets: Two tasks, one hour, word ranges printed on the paper, 25% of the grade
Writing less accurately beats writing more ambitiously at this level
Each task implies a reader: greeting, address form, sign-off

sections.heading: Paper 2 at beginner level: why listening is harder than reading
paragraphs: Paper 2 carries half the grade and splits into a 45-minute listening section and an hour of reading. For French ab initio students those two halves behave completely differently, and treating them as one component is why so much revision time is wasted.

Reading is the kinder half. Cognates do real work, the text sits still, and a student can reread a sentence. The failures here are usually pace rather than comprehension: a student who understood the passage but did not finish it. The fix is volume and timing, not more vocabulary — short French texts read daily on familiar topics, with speed measured rather than comprehension quizzed, and passages timed individually in sessions so the student learns what twelve minutes feels like.

Listening is where ab initio grades are decided. The audio plays twice and then it is gone, the speakers are unfamiliar, and the sound-to-spelling gap described earlier means a student's vocabulary may be unavailable to them in audio form. Practice has to be graded and structured: thirty to ninety seconds on a topic already covered, clear speech, played twice as the exam does, answers written under time, and only then the transcript, with every word known by eye but missed by ear recorded. That list is the revision product, and it is usually short and highly repetitive.

Two further habits make a visible difference. Vary the speaker, because a student who has only heard their teacher's French has calibrated to one voice and the examination audio will not resemble it. And treat numbers, dates and times as a standing item, because they are what listening questions ask for most and French expresses them in a way that catches beginners at speed. Both are easy to arrange in an online session where any clip plays from the same window, and both are rarely arranged at all.
bullets: Reading fails on pace; listening fails on recognition — different fixes
Audio twice only, under time, transcript strictly afterwards
Keep the list of words known by eye but missed by ear
Vary the speaker, and drill numbers every single session

sections.heading: The individual oral: four minutes on a photograph, under pressure
paragraphs: The oral starts from a visual stimulus, a photograph linked to one of the five prescribed themes. The student gets supervised preparation time, presents on the image, then answers questions that widen beyond it. It is conducted and marked by the school, moderated by the IB, worth 25% of the grade and marked out of 30 on language, message and interactive skills. For most beginners it is the component with the most available upside, because it rewards structure rather than range.

The common failure is inventory. The candidate names everything visible in the photograph, in order, for four minutes, and finishes having said nothing. Message marks reflect that. The alternative uses no more vocabulary: name what is there, place it in a context, say what is being done and by whom, then give a view with one reason attached. That sequence can be drilled until it survives nerves, and it is deliberately mechanical because a beginner under examination pressure in a second language needs something to fall back on rather than something to improvise with.

Pronunciation matters here in a way it does not in the written papers, and this is where the sound work from the opening block pays its second dividend. A candidate who pronounces final consonants that should be silent, or who flattens the nasal vowels into English approximations, is harder to follow, and difficulty following affects the message mark as well as language. Reading aloud every week through the course is what prevents this, and it costs nothing except the discomfort of doing it.

Interactive skills carry 6 marks and are the ones beginners surrender out of embarrassment. If a question is not understood, the credited response is to ask for it to be repeated or rephrased, in French. Students instead guess, answer a different question, and lose message marks as well as interaction marks. Three fixed phrases for requesting a repeat, drilled until automatic, is a two-minute intervention with a measurable payoff. Recording rehearsals is what makes it stick, because the student hears themselves guessing and recognises the habit at once.

sections.heading: Placement, permits, and what French ab initio does not do
paragraphs: Placement first, because in a city with a real francophone population it goes wrong in both directions. Ab initio is for students with little or no previous experience of the language, and the judgement sits with the school within the IB's framework. A student who studied French for three years in middle school is not an ab initio candidate even if they remember little of it, and presenting them as one is both a regulatory problem for the school and a practical one for the student, who will be bored into disengagement. Equally, a student with two years of primary French and nothing since is a beginner in every meaningful sense and should not be pushed into French B to flatter the subject grid.

Private tutoring in the UAE requires a permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page calls it 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing' and lists a two-working-day completion time with no fee. Tutoring without it attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no schedule of amounts is published, so no figure appears here. Abu Dhabi adds a further point: reported ADEK professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid tutoring of students enrolled at their own school. ADEK itself supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools across the emirate.

On what the course does not do: ab initio records a credited beginner Group 2 language and no more. It does not make a student a bilingual candidate, it is not a route to the IB bilingual diploma, which involves two Language A courses, and it does not substitute for French B on any application that specifies the latter. Where Ministry of Education equivalency is relevant, the published British-track rules require five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels. No IB points threshold has been verified from the ministry's own pages, so none is published here, and equivalency is a process the authority runs rather than something a tutoring provider performs or accelerates.

Finally, how we work. A trial lesson comes first, one per subject, booked before any payment is taken, spent on actual sound and spelling rather than on introductions. Where no UAE-based French ab initio specialist is free at the hour you need, we say so and name the options: a different time, a wait for a named slot, or a specialist outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. Nobody is substituted quietly.

process.title: Establish what French there genuinely is
process.description: Has the student studied French before, for how long, and when did it stop? Can they read a short sentence aloud? Can they understand that same sentence spoken? Those four answers place a beginner accurately in ten minutes and prevent the two placement errors that cost a whole year.

process.title: Run the read-then-hear diagnostic
process.description: The student reads a short transcript, then hears the same passage as audio. If comprehension collapses between the two, the problem is sound recognition rather than vocabulary, and the plan starts with phonology. This single test reframes most beginner French plans and takes five minutes.

process.title: Fix the deadline and pick the order
process.description: Which session is being sat, and how many months away is it? Eighteen months allows a full sound block, all twenty topics and technique time. Eight months means sound and topics run in parallel with triage. We write the number down before choosing what to teach first.

process.title: Take the trial lesson on sound, not vocabulary
process.description: One trial per subject, before any payment, spent on nasal vowels, silent endings and reading aloud. By the end the student should hear a difference they could not hear at the start, and you should have the outline of the opening block. If it was a vocabulary lesson, the match is wrong.

process.title: Keep the ledger and the error list visible
process.description: Twenty topics marked covered, revisited or open, plus a short personal list of interference errors by category. Both live in the shared document, both get updated every session, and both are what make an honest conversation about outcomes possible in March rather than in July.

process.title: Re-test listening at the end of the block
process.description: The block closes by re-sitting a listening section under the same conditions as the baseline. Two scores side by side, then an explicit decision: continue on another component, change tutor, or stop. A block without an end test cannot tell you whether it worked.

whyPoints.title: Sound is taught before vocabulary
whyPoints.description: Words learnt by eye are unavailable in audio, which is why strong readers fail the listening section. Nasal vowels, silent endings and liaison are taught explicitly from the first block rather than left to be absorbed from exposure that never happens.

whyPoints.title: French numbers get their own slot, every session
whyPoints.description: Seventy as sixty-ten and ninety-seven as four-twenties-ten-seven are what listening questions are built from, through prices, dates, times and ages. Fifteen minutes a session for a term is disproportionate value and almost nobody does it.

whyPoints.title: Interference is treated as a pattern, not a page of corrections
whyPoints.description: False friends, adjective position, prepositions chosen by translation: these are systematic errors that go on one short personal list by category. Lists reach fifteen or twenty items and stop recurring within a term.

whyPoints.title: Topics are taught in overlap order
whyPoints.description: The cheap, transferable topics come first while energy is high, and the specialised abstract ones later. Working through the prescribed list in published order spends the best weeks on the least transferable vocabulary.

whyPoints.title: The francophone comparison gets defused early
whyPoints.description: A beginner in an Abu Dhabi school with French-speaking students can decide in DP1 that they are hopeless at French. They are not: they are eighteen months into a beginner course. Saying so plainly protects the daily work the grade depends on.

whyPoints.title: Timelines stated before you book
whyPoints.description: Eighteen months, twelve, eight or five produce different realistic outcomes, and we name which applies to your child. A late start is often still worth doing; it is not worth being told it is equivalent to an early one.

faqs.question: Is French ab initio an easier choice than it looks?
faqs.answer: It is easier to start and no easier to finish. The familiar alphabet means a beginner reads a printed word on day one and gets real help from English cognates in the reading section, which feels like rapid progress. The difficulty is deferred to the listening paper, where silent final consonants, liaison, nasal vowels and compound numbers make a student's own vocabulary unrecognisable in speech. Half the grade sits in Paper 2, so a course that never addresses sound explicitly leaves that half largely to chance while the student feels reasonably confident.

faqs.question: Why does my child understand written French but not spoken French?
faqs.answer: Because they learnt the words by eye. Written French shows letters, word boundaries and English-like shapes. Spoken French silences most final consonants, drops the written plural verb ending entirely, joins words together so boundaries vanish, and uses four nasal vowels with no English equivalent. A word stored only in written form is simply not available when it arrives as sound. The diagnostic takes five minutes: have the student read a transcript, which they manage, then play the same passage as audio. If comprehension collapses, the problem is phonological rather than lexical.

faqs.question: Why are French numbers such a problem in the listening section?
faqs.answer: Because French builds them compositionally above sixty: seventy is expressed as sixty-ten, eighty as four-twenties, ninety-seven as four-twenties-ten-seven. A student who reads those comfortably on a page can still fail to process them at speaking speed, and listening questions are full of prices, dates, times, ages and quantities. Fifteen minutes on numbers in every session for a term is one of the highest-return habits available in the course, and it is almost never built into a beginner's plan because it feels too basic to spend session time on.

faqs.question: What are the most damaging mistakes in French ab initio writing?
faqs.answer: False friends and imported English structure, in that order. A library is a librairie only if you mean a bookshop; actuellement means currently, sensible means sensitive, rester means to stay. These produce grammatically sound sentences that communicate the wrong thing, costing message marks rather than language marks. Structurally, English word order, adjectives placed before the noun, and prepositions chosen by translating the English one are systematic rather than careless, which means they can be taught out in two or three sessions once someone lists them by category.

faqs.question: How many tenses does my child actually need for French ab initio?
faqs.answer: Three, used accurately. The present, for description and routine. The perfect, for saying what happened, which means learning the auxiliary choice and the past participle. And the near future, formed with the verb to go plus an infinitive, which gives a complete future with no new conjugation. The imperfect is worth recognising in reading and listening and rarely needed in production at this level. Nothing beyond that is required, and beginners taught French grammar as though they were heading for A-Level lose months they do not have.

faqs.question: Can my child take French ab initio if they studied French in middle school?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and the school decides within the IB's framework. Ab initio is for students with little or no previous experience of the language, so three years of middle-school French disqualifies a student even if they remember little of it. A student with two years of primary French that stopped years ago is a different case and is a beginner in every meaningful sense. The honest route is a short diagnostic with the school rather than an assumption either way, and it needs to happen before subject choices are locked for DP1.

faqs.question: Is there a Higher Level option in French ab initio?
faqs.answer: No. Ab initio exists at Standard Level only, in French and in every other language offering it. A student needing a Higher Level Group 2 subject has to take French B, which assumes genuine prior French and requires two literary works at HL. This catches out families building a grid around three Higher Levels, so it is worth confirming early with the school. The absence of an HL tier is also part of why ab initio is a cleaner build: one syllabus, one set of components, twenty prescribed topics and nothing above them.

faqs.question: How should a beginner practise French listening at home?
faqs.answer: With graded, topic-linked audio rather than French television. Thirty to ninety seconds of clear speech on a topic already covered, played twice as the exam does, answers written under time, then the transcript read against the answers with every word known by eye but missed by ear written down. That list is short and repetitive, and it is the actual revision product. Vary the speaker across the term so the student is not calibrated to one voice, and keep numbers as a standing fifteen-minute item in every session.

faqs.question: What does the French ab initio oral involve and how is it marked?
faqs.answer: The student is given a photograph linked to one of the five prescribed themes, has supervised preparation time, presents on the image and then answers questions that widen beyond it. The school conducts and marks it and the IB moderates. It carries 25% of the grade and is marked out of 30 on language, message and interactive skills. Beginners often do better here than expected, because it rewards structure over range: naming what is there, placing it in context, saying what is happening, then giving a view with one reason attached.

faqs.question: What should my child do in the oral if a question is not understood?
faqs.answer: Ask for it to be repeated or rephrased, in French. That is credited behaviour under interactive skills, worth 6 of the 30 marks, and beginners almost never do it because it feels like admitting failure. Instead they guess, answer a different question, and lose message marks as well as interaction marks. Three fixed phrases for requesting repetition, drilled until they come out without thinking, is a two-minute intervention. Recorded rehearsals make it stick, because the student hears themselves guessing and recognises the habit immediately.

faqs.question: Does the familiar or polite form of address matter in a written task?
faqs.answer: Yes, and French forces the decision early in almost every sentence, which English lets a beginner avoid. Each Paper 1 task implies a reader: a friend, a host family, a school noticeboard, a class blog. A task addressed to a school principal using the familiar form has told the examiner something about register before the content is read. Teaching the two forms as an audience decision rather than as a grammar point fixes it permanently in one session, and it belongs with the text-type work rather than in a verb table.

faqs.question: Will a French tutor come to our villa in Abu Dhabi for beginner lessons?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. Ab initio sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For beginner French the format suits the work: audio replays from the same window the student writes in, pronunciation is modelled and imitated immediately, and each session leaves a record of the sounds, structures and topics covered. In-home tuition is available in this market at roughly AED 180-500 an hour by published UAE surveys and listings, with travel inside the rate.

faqs.question: How many French sessions a week does a beginner in Abu Dhabi need at the start?
faqs.answer: Twice a week during the opening sound-and-spelling block, which runs six to eight weeks, then weekly once listening recognition has started to move. Early recall decays fast, and a single weekly session spends half its time recovering the previous one. After that, weekly sessions with short daily reading and listening between them is the pattern that works, and the daily work matters more than the length of the session. Front-loading intensity costs less across the full course than spreading the same number of hours evenly.

faqs.question: My child chose French ab initio in DP1 and is already behind. What comes first?
faqs.answer: The read-then-hear diagnostic, before anything is bought. If written comprehension is fine and listening collapses, the plan starts with sound: nasal vowels, silent endings, liaison and numbers, with reading aloud every session. If both are weak, the issue is topic coverage and the twenty-item ledger comes first. If writing is the only weak component, it is usually interference and text-type conventions, which are two or three sessions of work. Buying general French lessons without that diagnosis is how families spend a year on the wrong component.

faqs.question: Is French ab initio or Spanish ab initio the better choice in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: They are structurally identical courses, so the decision is about where each hides its difficulty. Spanish spelling maps onto sound far more transparently, which makes its listening section kinder for a beginner. French offers much stronger cognate support in reading, which helps the reading section and the writing tasks. Local exposure in the UAE slightly favours French given the francophone population here, but the deciding factor should be which course the school can actually staff properly, since a well-taught beginner group beats a theoretically easier language taught in a combined class.

faqs.question: What will the first month of French ab initio sessions produce?
faqs.answer: After four weeks at twice weekly, a student should hear and produce the nasal vowels distinctly, know which final consonants are silent and why, read a short unfamiliar sentence aloud with plausible pronunciation, recognise numbers to one hundred in speech, and have working vocabulary for the first prescribed topic used in spoken sentences. You should also have the twenty-topic ledger started and a personal interference list begun. If after a month the sessions have been vocabulary lists and translation exercises, the sequence is wrong and worth challenging.

A trial lesson follows, one per subject, booked before any payment, spent on sound and reading aloud. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: Eligibility first: who the ab initio course is actually for
paragraphs: French ab initio is the Diploma's beginner language course, offered at Standard Level only. The IB intends it for students with no previous experience of the language, or so little that starting from the beginning is honest. Your child's school makes the placement decision and is accountable for it, which is why a parent cannot simply choose the easier-looking route. Abu Dhabi families ask about this constantly, because so many students arrive here having done two or three years of classroom French somewhere else and genuinely do not know where they stand.

The practical test schools apply is whether a student has studied the language as a taught subject and for how long. Two years of primary French taught once a week, forgotten over four years since, is a different case from two years of secondary French with written assessments. A short diagnostic settles it quickly: read ten words aloud, conjugate one regular verb in the present, write four sentences about a photograph, answer three questions on a slow audio clip. Take the result to the school rather than arguing from memory, because a coordinator looking at a marked page reaches a decision in minutes and a coordinator listening to a parent's recollection does not.

If the placement is right, the course itself is narrow and learnable. Five prescribed themes with set topics beneath them, three assessed components, and a strong emphasis on controlled accuracy rather than range. Paper 1 is written production and carries a quarter of the grade. Paper 2 holds listening and reading together and carries half. The individual oral, built on a visual stimulus, carries the remaining quarter and is recorded and marked inside your child's school before the IB moderates it.

The second question - what will we see by the end of DP1 - deserves numbers rather than reassurance. A beginner's progress in a language is unusually measurable in the first year: words known and retrievable, verbs controlled in the present and then the past, words produced in a fixed writing time, seconds of unscripted speech before a stall. The ledger further down this page sets out realistic figures at each checkpoint for a student working an hour a week with homework between sessions.

Lessons are delivered one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared document for written work. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home tutoring is a service we run only in India. That is a straightforward trade rather than a compromise. French ab initio is a small specialism, the visual-stimulus oral has its own technique, and a family in Shakhbout City should be able to reach someone who has taught it rather than someone who can reach Shakhbout City by five o'clock.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme

sections.heading: Is my child eligible for French ab initio? The honest answer
paragraphs: This is the question that brings most families to a page like this one, and it has a clear shape. Ab initio courses are intended for students beginning a language, and the school decides whether a particular student qualifies. The IB expects the course to be taught to beginners, so a school that places an experienced linguist into it is not doing the student a favour; it is creating a problem at moderation and an unfair comparison with genuine beginners elsewhere.

What counts as previous experience in practice is taught study rather than exposure. A student who did French once a week in a Dubai or Abu Dhabi primary six years ago, with no written assessment and no memory of it, is usually treated as a beginner. A student with two years of secondary French, graded reports and written assessments, generally is not. The grey zone is real and the school owns it, so arrive with evidence rather than an opinion.

The useful move is a twenty-minute diagnostic before the placement form goes in. Reading ten words aloud shows whether sound-to-spelling mapping exists. Conjugating one regular verb in the present shows whether grammar was ever taught. Four written sentences about a photograph show production. Three questions on a slow audio clip show comprehension. That evidence makes the conversation with the DP coordinator short and factual, and either outcome is better than a placement that has to be unpicked in January.

sections.heading: The course in outline: themes, topics and three components
paragraphs: Ab initio content sits under five prescribed themes with a set of topics beneath each one, and schools choose how deeply to go within them. The vocabulary load is finite and specified in a way that later language courses are not, which is genuinely good news for a beginner: the territory has edges. A student can hold the whole domain in view by the middle of DP1, which almost never happens in French B.

Assessment is in three parts and none of them is a coursework essay. Paper 1 is written production in prescribed text types and carries a quarter of the grade. Paper 2 combines listening and reading and carries half. The individual oral, built on a visual stimulus, carries the final quarter and is conducted and marked by your child's teacher in school before the IB moderates a sample. The number of written tasks, their word ranges and the current criterion wording are set out in the IB subject guide your school holds.

We work from that guide and do not reproduce or supply IB documents, past papers or mark schemes - those are the school's to provide and the IB's to publish. What we do instead is build practice material in the same shape and mark it against the published criteria. Ask your DP coordinator for the component breakdown in writing at the start of DP1; it takes one email and removes most of the confusion that otherwise lasts a whole term.

sections.heading: The first twelve weeks of French from zero
paragraphs: French has no script barrier, which makes the opening faster than Arabic and the first obstacle different: the gap between spelling and sound. Silent final consonants, nasal vowels, liaison, and the fact that four different endings can sound identical in speech while mattering enormously on paper. A beginner who learns vocabulary by eye and then cannot recognise the same words in the listening paper has met this problem, and it is better addressed in week two than in DP2.

Grammar in the first term is deliberately narrow. Gender and the article system, because they poison agreement everywhere if left vague. The present tense of regular verbs plus the handful of irregulars that appear in every sentence a human being actually says. Negation. Question formation. Adjective position and agreement. That is enough to produce real sentences about the first prescribed theme, and producing real sentences early is what keeps a sixteen-year-old beginner engaged.

Vocabulary is handled as a retrievable count rather than a list seen. Thirty words taught and not retrieved a week later are zero words. We test retrieval cold at the start of each session, record what came back, and reteach what did not. By week twelve a student working an hour a week with homework can usually write a short paragraph about a photograph without help, hold thirty seconds of unscripted speech, and answer questions on a slow clip. Those are the figures the ledger tracks, and they are the ones a parent can read without knowing any French themselves.
bullets: Sound-to-spelling mapping taught from week one, not assumed
Gender and the article system before anything that depends on them
Present tense plus the irregulars that appear in real speech
Vocabulary counted as retrieved, never as covered

sections.heading: Where ab initio candidates lose marks
paragraphs: Beginner-course losses are different from French B losses and much more systematic. The biggest is attempting range beyond control: a student reaches for a complex structure they half-know, the sentence collapses, and a simpler correct version would have scored better. Ab initio rewards controlled accuracy, and teaching a student to write deliberately within their secure range is worth more marks than teaching them two new tenses.

Second is the text type. Paper 1 names one, and a note, a message, a short letter and a blog entry each have expectations about opening, closing and who is being addressed. Beginners frequently produce undifferentiated prose and lose conventions marks they did not know existed. Third is listening wasted on first-pass writing: a candidate who tries to write full answers during the first hearing arrives at the second with nothing to check.

Fourth is the oral, where recited material runs out. A student who has memorised a description can deliver it fluently and then stall completely when the conversation turns, because nothing in the preparation rehearsed responding. Fifth is agreement - gender, number, adjective position - dropped under time pressure in longer sentences. All five are habits, and habits move faster under one-to-one attention than vocabulary breadth does. The useful consequence is that a beginner's marked work becomes predictive within three tasks. If the same two habits appear each time, the next six weeks write themselves, and nobody has to guess which part of the course to revisit. A student who can name their own two habits is already most of the way to fixing them, which is why the marked task comes back with the pattern written on it rather than only the errors.

sections.heading: The visual-stimulus oral at beginner level
paragraphs: A quarter of the grade is a recording made in your child's school. The candidate works from a visual stimulus, describes it, relates it to a prescribed theme and to the target culture, and then holds a conversation with the teacher. It is marked in school against criteria for language, message and interaction, with the exact letters and allocations set out in the subject guide, and the IB moderates a sample afterwards.

For a beginner the task has a particular trap. Description is learnable and rehearsable, so a student can sound competent for ninety seconds and then meet a question they have not prepared for. The marks for interaction are precisely there to catch that. Preparation therefore has to include unscripted exchange rather than only polished description: unfamiliar images, questions the student has not seen, and the specific phrases that buy thinking time without sounding evasive.

The cultural link is the other commonly missed piece. The task is not only to say what is in the image but to connect it to the theme and to life in a French-speaking context, and a student who describes a market scene without ever mentioning where such a scene sits in the culture has left message marks unclaimed. Three or four transferable linking phrases, drilled until automatic, do more for the mark than another fifty words of vocabulary. Those phrases also survive nerves, which recited content famously does not, and a recording made in a school office on a Tuesday afternoon is a nervous occasion for most sixteen-year-olds.

sections.heading: The progress ledger: what is measurable, and when
paragraphs: Parents of beginners get the least informative school reports of anyone, because a comment like making steady progress is true of almost every beginner and tells you nothing. A beginner language is unusually measurable, so we measure it. Four numbers, taken the same way each time, at fixed checkpoints: words retrieved cold in two minutes, verb patterns controlled in a written task, words produced in a fixed ten minutes of timed writing, and seconds of unscripted speech before a stall.

The figures in the table below are what we see from a DP1 student working an hour a week with homework between sessions, and they are a guide rather than a promise. A student with two other new subjects and a heavy Higher Level load will sit lower; a student who does ten minutes of retrieval daily will sit higher. The value is not the absolute number but the direction across checkpoints, measured the same way each time.

No aggregate outcome statistics appear anywhere on this site, because we could not show you the data behind them. What we can show you is one student's ledger, with the dates, the measures and the marked tasks attached. That is also the document to take into a parents evening, because it gives the teacher something specific to respond to rather than a general worry about French. Teachers engage with a marked task and a set of dated measures in a way they cannot engage with a question about whether a child is doing all right, and the conversation that follows is usually more useful to everyone in the room.

sections.heading: Switching language or level after the Diploma has started
paragraphs: Switches happen and they are survivable if they happen early. A student placed in French B who cannot cope moving down to ab initio, or an ab initio student who is clearly beyond the course moving up, are both normal events in DP1. The school controls them, there are registration implications with the IB, and the window narrows as the first year goes on. Term one is uncomfortable; term three is expensive.

The two switches are not symmetrical. Moving down to ab initio from French B means a student has partial knowledge and now needs it systematised rather than extended, which is usually fast. Moving up from ab initio to French B SL means a genuine content gap, broader vocabulary and a longer written task, and it needs a term of concentrated work. Anyone who tells you either switch is painless has not supervised one.

What tutoring can do here is produce evidence for the conversation. A timed task at both course lengths, a listening attempt, a short oral sample, all marked against the published criteria, give the DP coordinator something concrete. The decision is the school's and we would not pretend otherwise, but a school asked to decide on evidence decides faster and more accurately than one asked to decide on a parent's impression. Ask for the deadline too. Every school has an internal cut-off for level changes that sits well before the IB's own, and knowing that date turns a vague worry into a scheduling problem with an answer.

faqs.question: Who is actually eligible to take IB French ab initio?
faqs.answer: Ab initio is intended for students beginning the language, and your child's school decides whether a particular student qualifies. In practice schools look at taught study rather than casual exposure: years in a timetabled French class, whether work was assessed, and what the student can currently do. A term of primary French years ago is usually treated as exposure. Two years of secondary French with graded reports usually is not. Arrive at that conversation with a short diagnostic in hand and it becomes a factual discussion rather than a negotiation.

faqs.question: My child had two years of French in Years 7 and 8 and remembers almost nothing. Can they start from scratch?
faqs.answer: This is the grey zone, and the school owns the decision. Taught study exists on paper, so some schools will say French B, while others will accept that nothing was retained and place the student in ab initio. What settles it quickly is evidence of current capability: reading words aloud, conjugating one regular verb, writing four sentences, answering questions on a slow clip. If the diagnostic shows almost no retained grammar, say so with the evidence attached rather than asserting that the French has been forgotten.

faqs.question: Is French ab initio an easier subject than French B?
faqs.answer: It is a narrower course rather than a soft one. The vocabulary domain has edges, the written tasks are shorter, and the oral works from a visual stimulus rather than a literary extract. What it demands in exchange is controlled accuracy: marks come from doing simple things correctly, so a student who reaches beyond their secure range loses more than they gain. Students who treat it as an easy option and coast tend to find the listening paper and the conversation section of the oral unforgiving in DP2.

faqs.question: Can an ab initio student reach the top of the grade scale?
faqs.answer: The full grade range is available in ab initio as in any Diploma subject, and the grade reflects performance against that course's criteria. Nobody can promise a particular grade in this subject or any other, and a tutor who does should concern you. What is reliably achievable is removing avoidable losses: conventions marks on Paper 1, the second hearing on listening, the interaction section of the oral. Those are the pieces where beginners most often leave marks behind, and they are teachable within a term.

faqs.question: How does the ab initio oral differ from the French B oral?
faqs.answer: Both start from a visual stimulus at Standard Level, but the expectations differ in scope. The ab initio task asks a beginner to describe the image, connect it to a prescribed theme and to life in a French-speaking context, and then hold a conversation, with marks for interaction specifically. French B assumes a much broader base and a longer, more analytical exchange, and at Higher Level the stimulus is replaced by an extract from a literary work entirely. Preparing for one does not prepare a student for the other.

faqs.question: How much vocabulary does a French ab initio student actually need?
faqs.answer: Less than families fear, and it has to be retrievable rather than merely covered. The prescribed themes and their topics define a finite domain, which is why a beginner can hold the whole territory in view by mid-DP1 in a way a French B student cannot. The useful measure is words retrieved cold in two minutes, tested rather than reviewed. Thirty words taught and not retrieved a week later are worth nothing, so we count retrieval at the start of each session and reteach what did not come back.

faqs.question: What does the ab initio written paper ask a beginner to produce?
faqs.answer: Written production in prescribed text types, worth a quarter of the grade. The current subject guide held by your child's school sets out the number of tasks and the word ranges, and those are the figures to work from rather than anything a tutoring site states. What matters for preparation is that text type carries marks in its own right: a note, a message, a short letter and a blog entry each have expectations about opening, closing and who is addressed, and beginners routinely produce undifferentiated prose and lose those marks unknowingly.

faqs.question: Can my child move from French B down to ab initio partway through DP1?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and earlier is far better. The school controls the change and there are IB registration implications, so the window narrows as the first year progresses. The practical advantage of moving down is that the student already has partial knowledge which now needs systematising rather than extending, and that is usually quick work. Bring marked evidence to the conversation - a timed task, a listening attempt, a short oral sample against the published criteria - because a school deciding on evidence decides faster and more accurately.

faqs.question: Does taking a beginner language limit university options later?
faqs.answer: A language acquisition grade contributes to the Diploma total that universities read, and most courses do not distinguish between ab initio and language B when they state requirements. Some specific programmes, particularly modern languages degrees, do set their own expectations, so check the individual course page rather than relying on a general answer. For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency, the British-track rules are published but no IB points figure has been read on an official Ministry source for this page, so verify that on moe.gov.ae.

faqs.question: What does a French ab initio tutor charge per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published UAE rates are mostly quoted for Dubai and describe a wide market. Tutopiya advertises from about AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the budget end. Unitors lists IB tutoring from around AED 200, TutorChase quotes about AED 270, and Bestimate's 2026 rate table puts specialist exam-year support at roughly AED 200 to 450 and above. A beginner-language specialism sits in the upper half of the online band because fewer tutors have taught the course. Those are their figures, not our price list.

faqs.question: How often should a true beginner have lessons?
faqs.answer: Two half-hours a week generally beats one hour at the start, because sound-to-spelling mapping, verb patterns and vocabulary all depend on retrieval spaced across days rather than massed in one sitting. A thirty-minute session also survives a long Abu Dhabi school run far better than a sixty-minute one. Once the mechanics are secure, usually around week twelve, a single weekly hour with a fortnightly measured checkpoint works well and is easier to protect through activity season.

faqs.question: What should I expect to see by the end of DP1?
faqs.answer: For a student working an hour a week with homework between sessions, a realistic end-of-DP1 picture is a complete Paper 1 task in a known text type with conventions in place, roughly sixty to ninety words produced in ten minutes of timed writing with agreement mostly intact, and thirty to sixty seconds of unscripted speech before a stall. Those are indicative figures rather than promises, and they vary with the rest of the Diploma load. The direction across checkpoints matters more than any single number.

faqs.question: Is French ab initio offered at Higher Level anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. Ab initio courses in the Diploma exist at Standard Level only, which is a design feature rather than an oversight: the course assumes a beginner, and a Higher Level beginner course would not be coherent. A student wanting a Higher Level language acquisition subject takes a language B course at HL, which assumes genuine previous experience and adds literary works. For most Diploma students this is not a constraint, because the Higher Level requirement is about the number of subjects overall rather than which ones.

faqs.question: Can lessons be timed around a long mainland school run?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is where online delivery earns its place. Families in Shakhbout City, Al Shamkha and Al Reef often finish the school run late and unpredictably, so a fixed slot with no travel variable attached is the only arrangement that holds for a full term. Shorter, more frequent sessions survive a late bus better than one long one. During Ramadan school hours shorten and sessions usually move to a post-iftar slot for the month before returning to the normal pattern.

faqs.question: What is a tutor allowed to do with work my child will submit for assessment?
faqs.answer: Teach, question, model and give feedback - nothing more. A tutor may rehearse the oral against unfamiliar images, mark practice tasks to the published criteria and explain the descriptors, and build a vocabulary list from the student's own errors. A tutor may not attend the assessed recording, supply content for the student to reproduce in it, or shape assessed written work into something the student could not have produced alone. We say this to the student in the first lesson, because stating it plainly is more useful than assuming it.

intro.heading: The price of French B in Abu Dhabi is a supply question, not a quality one
paragraphs: French tuition in Abu Dhabi is priced by how many people can do the job, and in this emirate that number is smaller than the equivalent number in Dubai. The francophone population here is concentrated rather than spread: around the Lycée Louis Massignon catchment, in the diplomatic and energy-sector households on the island, and in the newer island communities where internationally mobile families cluster. A tutor who can teach conversational French is easy to find. A tutor who has taught Diploma French B, knows what the 6 conceptual-understanding marks on Paper 1 reward, and has prepared an HL individual oral from a literary extract is not, and the rate reflects that scarcity rather than any claim about teaching quality.

That distinction is the first thing to hold on to, because it explains quotes that otherwise look arbitrary. AED 120 an hour usually buys a French speaker — often a university student or a parent with a teaching background in general French. AED 250 to 300 usually buys someone who has taught the Diploma course. AED 450 and above usually buys someone whose experience is narrow and specific, such as HL oral preparation or examiner-level familiarity with how the criteria are applied. None of those three is the right purchase in all circumstances. A DP1 student who needs vocabulary breadth and reading volume is wasting money at AED 450; a DP2 student eight weeks from the papers with a collapsing oral is wasting money at AED 120.

Published market figures give you something to hold a quote against. Platform listings in the UAE advertise online tutoring from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour, and one regional platform from around AED 33 to 52. One UAE agency publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. A UK-based agency publishes AED 270. A UAE cost survey puts specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level tutors at AED 200 to 450 and above, in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, and home-tutor listings reach AED 500. One Dubai provider publishes AED 650 for premium named tuition. Monthly packages circulate at around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Those are market numbers from the pages that published them, not our price list, and the honest use of them is comparative. If someone quotes AED 400 an hour, the question is not whether AED 400 is a lot. The question is what is inside it: is marking of work submitted between sessions included, is the hour 60 minutes, is VAT inside the figure, what happens if the match is wrong after two sessions, and does the tutor hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit. A provider answering those five cleanly at AED 300 is better value than one answering none at AED 200.

On delivery, be clear what you are buying: IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in Abu Dhabi, and in-home visits are a service we run only in India. French B sessions are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. That has a direct effect on price, because an in-home rate carries travel in it whether the invoice itemises it or not. Forty minutes of Abu Dhabi driving between Khalifa City and the island does not teach your child French, and somebody is paying for it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French B is the Group 2 course for students with prior French, at Standard or Higher Level. Paper 1 is one written task worth 25%, Paper 2 combines listening and reading for 50%, and the individual oral takes the remaining 25%. Higher Level adds two literary works, studied in French, which feed the oral rather than the written papers.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi cohorts are small, so a school may run one combined SL and HL French B group. That is the usual reason families start paying for outside support: not weak teaching, but a single teacher differentiating across two levels and a wide range of prior French in one room.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition French runs in phases, and the phase recorded at the end of MYP5 is the best predictor of French B cost. A student finishing in phase 4 needs examination technique. A student finishing in phase 2 needs vocabulary and reading volume first, which is more hours and therefore more money.

They often need fewer hours than their parents expect, aimed narrowly at criteria and text types rather than at the language itself.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Primary French is taught as an additional language through inquiry, building spoken familiarity and basic literacy without systematic grammar. programmes.description: The Career-related Programme includes language development with a portfolio rather than examined papers. For a student whose goal is workplace French rather than a Diploma grade, it carries no Paper 2 and therefore none of the receptive-skills cost that dominates a French B budget.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: French B is rarely the only line on a family's tutoring budget, and the sequencing of subjects across two years affects total spend more than any hourly rate. These are the subjects most often funded alongside it in Abu Dhabi.

subjects.name: French B
subjects.description: Paper 1 writing at 25%, Paper 2 listening and reading at 50%, individual oral at 25%. The money question is which of the three is failing, because receptive skills need volume over months while technique gaps close in one or two sessions at any rate you pay.

subjects.name: French ab initio
subjects.description: The beginners' course, Standard Level only. Cheaper to support per hour in this market because the pool of tutors able to teach beginner French is far wider, but it typically needs more hours across the two years than French B does.

subjects.name: French A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Group 1 course for students working at first-language level, often taken by students arriving from the French national curriculum. It costs more to support than French B because the specialist pool is narrower, and it is the route towards a bilingual diploma rather than French B.

subjects.name: Spanish B
subjects.description: Structurally identical to French B with the same weightings and criteria, so a household running both does not pay twice for assessment-technique teaching. Learning how Paper 2 is marked once covers both languages.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: Commonly taken by the same students in Abu Dhabi. Arabic B rates sit slightly higher at the specialist end because the pool of Diploma-experienced Arabic teachers is smaller, and the two orals need separating in preparation to avoid cross-contamination.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The single biggest competing claim on a tutoring budget, and the one where rates run highest. Sequencing matters: maths support is most valuable in DP1 when content is being laid down, while French B support pays best closer to the components.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Three internal assessment commentaries spread across the two years, which makes it schedulable. Families who plan the calendar rather than the hourly rate tend to run economics support in the terms when French B needs least.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy with a 20% internal assessment. Often funded in the final year only. A family budgeting across two years should expect science and language support to peak in different terms, which flattens the monthly total considerably.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Highest-rate subject in most UAE markets at the specialist end, which is worth knowing when a household needs both physics and French B. The honest sequencing answer is usually physics in DP1 and French B concentrated in DP2.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source-based Paper 1 and essay-driven Paper 2, both of which reward the same reading-under-time skill French B Paper 2 needs. Students doing both often get a return on reading practice in two subjects at once.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The 1,600-word essay and the exhibition contribute up to 3 points with the Extended Essay. Rarely worth paid support in isolation, and the cheapest intervention is usually one or two sessions on the essay's prescribed title rather than a block.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words of independent research. A French B student may write it in French under a Group 2 category, which narrows the supervisor pool and raises the rate. Support is question narrowing and feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplied text.

sections.heading: What French B tuition costs in Abu Dhabi, by provider model
paragraphs: No competitor page in this market publishes a rate table, which is why parents compare quotes with nothing to compare them against. The table below is organised by provider model rather than by brand, because model is what determines the rate. Every figure in it is a published market figure attributed to where it came from, and none of it is an IB Gram price list.

Reading it, three things stand out. The gap between the budget online tier and the specialist tier is roughly sixfold, which is a far wider spread than families expect and means the word 'tutor' is doing a great deal of work in these conversations. In-home rates sit above comparable online rates everywhere in the band, because travel is inside the rate whether or not the invoice says so. And the premium tier — AED 500 and above — is justified only by genuinely narrow expertise, which for French B means HL oral preparation or detailed familiarity with how the criteria are applied, and not by general seniority.

What the table deliberately does not do is tell you which row is right. That depends on the component failing and on how long is left. A DP1 student whose reading range is thin needs volume, consistency and a tutor who will set and check work between sessions, which the mid band supplies perfectly well. A DP2 student whose oral is collapsing six weeks out needs someone who has prepared that exact component repeatedly, and underpaying there is false economy because the component is 25% of the grade and there is no second attempt.

One honest note about group classes. A tuition centre group rate is the cheapest formal option in Abu Dhabi and is genuinely good value when a student's need matches the group's level. It is poor value when it does not, because a French B group containing both an SL student needing vocabulary and an HL student needing literary-extract technique serves neither. Ask what level the group is working at and what happens if your child is outside it, before the term's fees are paid.

sections.heading: Why Abu Dhabi French rates behave differently from Dubai's
paragraphs: The same qualification, forty minutes up the road, prices differently, and the reason is supply density rather than anything about the emirates themselves. Dubai's private school sector is very large — 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering seventeen different curricula, with International Baccalaureate students making up 7% of the total. A market that size supports a deep freelance tutoring layer: more French speakers, more former teachers, more competition, and therefore more price pressure at every tier.

Abu Dhabi's francophone and French-teaching population is smaller and geographically concentrated. The practical effect is that the mid band thins out. There are plenty of people who will teach general French at the budget end, and a small number who have genuinely taught Diploma French B, with comparatively little in between. Families notice this as a strange jump in quotes: AED 130, then AED 320, with nothing at AED 200 that is actually a Diploma specialist. That gap is the market structure, not a negotiating position.

In-home delivery amplifies it. A visiting tutor in Dubai can often reach three or four clients within a short radius in one evening, so travel is spread across several paid hours. In Abu Dhabi, with Diploma families spread between the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor and the mainland communities, a tutor might manage two. Fewer paid hours per evening of work means a higher rate per hour, which is why the published in-home band of AED 180 to 500 tends to sit in its upper half for Diploma subjects in this emirate.

School fees are the other piece of context, and the two emirates differ there too. Dubai's regulator announced in May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package, and that announcement is Dubai-specific. Abu Dhabi families should check ADEK's published position for their own year rather than assume the same applies. The relevance to a tutoring budget is simple: tuition is a discretionary line sitting beside a large fixed one, and knowing whether the fixed line is moving changes how much room there is.
bullets: Dubai: 387,441 private school students across 227 schools in 2024-25, IB at 7%
A larger market supports a deeper freelance layer and more price competition
Abu Dhabi's mid band is thin — the jump from general French to Diploma specialist is abrupt
In-home rates run higher here because a visiting tutor fits fewer paid hours into an evening

sections.heading: Six things that genuinely move a French B quote in this emirate
paragraphs: Quotes vary for reasons, and knowing which reasons are legitimate stops a family paying a premium for something that does not affect their child's grade. These six account for almost all of the variation we see in Abu Dhabi, and only four of them are worth paying extra for.

Level is legitimate. Higher Level French B carries two literary works and a literary-extract oral, so an HL tutor needs to have read and taught those works, and the pool narrows. Component is legitimate too: oral preparation and Paper 2 receptive-skills work require different experience, and a tutor who has prepared HL orals repeatedly earns the upper band for those sessions specifically. Timing is legitimate in the other direction: demand for the same early-evening slots is intense in Abu Dhabi, and a family able to take a 15:30 or a weekend-morning slot has real negotiating room that a family needing 18:00 does not.

Marking inclusion is the variable families most often fail to ask about and the one that moves real cost most. A rate of AED 250 that includes marking a timed paper submitted between sessions is cheaper than AED 200 plus a marking fee per script, and across a two-year course the difference is substantial. Ask it explicitly, in those words, and get the answer before the first invoice.

Two variables are usually not worth paying for. Native-speaker status on its own does not predict Diploma competence, because the course assesses criteria rather than fluency, and a native speaker with no Diploma experience will teach French rather than French B. And a provider's brand tier — the difference between a well-known agency and an equally qualified independent — is a marketing variable rather than a teaching one. Judge on whether the tutor can mark a script and explain the 12 / 12 / 6 split on Paper 1.

sections.heading: What you are actually buying: where the French B marks sit
paragraphs: A rate means nothing without knowing what the hour is aimed at, and French B distributes its marks in a way that should direct the spending. Paper 1 is a single written task worth 25%, at 250 to 400 words at Standard Level and 450 to 600 at Higher Level, marked out of 30 with language carrying 12 marks, message 12 and conceptual understanding 6. Paper 2 combines listening and reading for 50% of the grade. The individual oral is the remaining 25%, also marked out of 30, with 12 for language, 12 for message and 6 for interactive skills.

Half the grade in Paper 2 is where most of the money should go for most students, and it is where least of it goes. Listening and reading are the skills that require volume rather than explanation, which makes them feel like poor value per hour: nobody wants to pay a specialist rate for someone to sit while their child listens to audio. The resolution is that the tutor's job in receptive skills is to set the right material, run it under exam conditions, and diagnose the gap between what the student knows by eye and recognises by ear. That is a specialist job compressed into perhaps six sessions, with the volume happening unpaid in between.

The two 6-mark criteria are the cheapest marks in the subject. Conceptual understanding on Paper 1 credits choosing the right text type for the audience and purpose the task sets, and using its conventions — a blog post with a title and a reader addressed, a formal letter with the right opening and closing. Interactive skills in the oral credit responding to what was actually asked and requesting clarification rather than guessing. Both are learnable in a session or two at any rate you are paying, and both are routinely surrendered by students who never had them explained.

The practical budgeting conclusion is a sequence rather than a sum. One session to diagnose which component is losing marks, using a marked script and a timed Paper 2 score. One or two sessions on whichever 6-mark criterion is leaking. Then a block on the component carrying the biggest gap. A family that follows that order usually spends less in total than one that buys a weekly hour for two years and hopes.
bullets: Paper 1: 25%, marked out of 30 — language 12, message 12, concepts 6
Paper 2: 50%, listening plus reading, where volume beats explanation
Individual oral: 25%, out of 30 — language 12, message 12, interaction 6
The two 6-mark criteria are the cheapest available gains in the subject

sections.heading: Costing two Diploma years instead of the next lesson
paragraphs: Families ask for an hourly rate and then budget by the month, which is how a reasonable decision becomes an unreasonable total. French B runs for two years. The useful question is what the whole thing costs under different plans, and the answer is less about the rate than about how many months the arrangement stays open.

The expensive pattern is a standing weekly hour from the start of DP1 to the final paper, at a mid-band rate, with no stated target. It feels prudent and manageable. Over roughly sixty teaching weeks it is the largest total on the table, and much of it is spent on general practice during terms when the student did not need support. The cheap pattern is a short diagnostic, then two or three closed blocks timed to the components, with nothing in between. It has higher monthly peaks and a markedly lower two-year total.

The scenarios in the table use published market bands rather than our prices, and they are deliberately rough. Their purpose is to show the shape, which is that the number of months an arrangement stays open dominates everything else. A family paying AED 300 an hour for twenty well-targeted sessions spends less than a family paying AED 180 for sixty sessions of general practice, and the first family usually gets more grade movement because the sessions had a target.

Two further points for Abu Dhabi families specifically. The summer between DP1 and DP2 is the cheapest study time in the course and the most commonly wasted: reading volume done then costs nothing and removes paid hours later. And Ramadan planning matters financially as well as practically, because families who improvise lose three or four weeks and then buy an intensive block to recover them. Agreeing a post-Iftar slot in advance is free.

sections.heading: What the school should already be providing at no extra cost
paragraphs: Before anything is bought, it is worth establishing what has already been paid for inside the school fees, because families routinely purchase things their school supplies and never asked for things it does not. The pattern differs by school, so this is a list of questions rather than a list of answers.

Most French B teachers will mark an extra timed paper if a student asks and hands it in. Most will run or allow mock individual orals. Most schools publish an internal assessment calendar showing when the oral will be conducted and when internal deadlines fall. Many give access to the subject guide's assessment criteria, which parents are often surprised to learn they can simply read. All of that is included in the fees and none of it needs a tutor. A family that collects those four things first often discovers the gap is narrower than it looked.

What schools in small-cohort settings frequently cannot supply is differentiated time. A single combined SL and HL French B group with one teacher cannot run separate literary-extract oral preparation for three HL students and vocabulary building for eight SL students in the same lesson. Nor can a teacher with a full timetable mark a timed Paper 2 every week for one student. That is the genuine gap, and it is the gap worth paying for.

The table below splits the job into what is usually covered and what usually is not. Use it as a checklist in the next conversation with the subject teacher. The question to ask is not whether your child needs a tutor; it is which of these rows the school is not going to cover this year. Anything in the covered column that you are being invoiced for separately is worth questioning.

sections.heading: Native speaker, trained teacher, examiner: what each is worth paying for
paragraphs: Three claims appear in French tutoring adverts in this market and they are priced as though they were interchangeable. They are not, and understanding the difference is the easiest way to stop overpaying for the wrong attribute.

A native French speaker brings pronunciation, idiom and cultural reference, and for conversation practice that is exactly the purchase. What native-speaker status does not predict is knowledge of how French B is assessed. The course does not credit fluency; it credits language, message and conceptual understanding against published descriptors. A native speaker with no Diploma experience will deliver good French lessons and may never mention the 6 conceptual marks your child is losing on every Paper 1. Paying a premium for native-speaker status alone is paying for the wrong variable.

A trained Diploma teacher brings the criteria, the text types, the component timings and the experience of seeing where candidates lose marks. For most French B families this is the right purchase, and it is what the AED 200 to 450 specialist band is actually describing. The useful questions are narrow: which level have you taught, how recently, and can you mark a script and show me the 12 / 12 / 6 split? A tutor who answers those three concretely is worth the band regardless of nationality.

Examiner status is the claim to treat most carefully. Current examiner status is difficult to verify, so we do not describe tutors as examiners unless it can be evidenced, and nobody should imply that examiner experience grants access to marking, grade boundaries or paper content, because it does not. Where someone has recent marking experience and can evidence it, their value is specific: they know how descriptors are applied in practice, which is genuinely useful for a borderline candidate. It does not justify a premium for routine teaching, and a page that uses examiner status as a general selling point is selling you something it cannot deliver.
bullets: Native speaker: right for conversation, does not predict criterion knowledge
Trained Diploma teacher: the right purchase for most French B families
Examiner status: only meaningful if evidenced, and never implies access to marking
Three questions that settle it: which level, how recently, can you mark a script?

sections.heading: VAT, permits, cancellations and the five questions that stop a quote drifting
paragraphs: A quoted rate is the start of a cost, not the whole of it, and most of the difference between an expected total and an actual one comes from terms rather than from the hourly figure. Five questions settle almost all of it, and any provider unwilling to answer them in writing has told you something useful.

First, is the rate per hour or per lesson, and how many minutes is a lesson? A 50-minute lesson quoted as an hourly rate is a 20% increase that nobody mentions. Second, does the rate include marking of work submitted between sessions, and is written feedback included or extra? Third, does the quoted figure include VAT? We limit ourselves to whether our own quoted AED figures include it; the VAT treatment of education services in the UAE is a matter for the Federal Tax Authority and not something a tutoring page should assert. Fourth, what is the cancellation and rescheduling policy, in hours of notice? Fifth, what happens if the match is wrong after two sessions, and is anything refundable?

Two regulatory points belong in the same conversation. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a permit: the private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years, covering registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists a two-working-day completion time and no fee. Tutoring without the permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and since no schedule of amounts is published, treat any page quoting a figure with scepticism. In Abu Dhabi there is a second point: reported ADEK professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, so your child's own French teacher is not the answer, whatever the rate.

Finally, what we do not charge for. There is no fee for the consultation in which we read a marked script and say which component is failing. The trial lesson is one per subject, booked before any payment is taken, so the condition is simply that it precedes a block. And if no UAE-based French B specialist is free at the hour you need, we say so and offer the alternatives — a different time, a wait for a named slot, or a specialist outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time — rather than quietly substituting someone and letting you find out in week three.
