process.title: Say what you want the money to fix
process.description: Not 'French B help' but a component: the writing task, the listening and reading paper, or the oral. Send the last marked script and the most recent Paper 2 mark split if the school provides one. A quote without a target is a quote for an open-ended arrangement, which is the expensive kind.

process.title: Get the diagnostic before the block
process.description: We read the marked work and say which component is losing marks and roughly how many sessions it should take, before anything is booked. There is no charge for that conversation. A provider who quotes a term of weekly sessions without reading any of your child's work is pricing a habit, not a job.

process.title: Compare quotes on the five terms, not the rate
process.description: Per hour or per lesson, marking included or extra, VAT inside or outside, cancellation notice, and what happens if the match is wrong. Write the five answers down for each provider. The cheapest headline rate is frequently the most expensive total once those five are filled in.

process.title: Take the trial lesson, then decide the shape
process.description: One trial per subject, before any payment, spent on real work. Afterwards choose the shape deliberately: weekly standing hour, a closed component block, or a short intensive. The shape determines the two-year total far more than the hourly rate does.

process.title: Put an end date on the block
process.description: Every block gets a stated number of sessions and a re-test of the component it targeted. At the end, the decision is explicit: continue on something else, change tutor, or stop. Arrangements that never close are how a reasonable monthly figure becomes an unreasonable two-year one.

whyPoints.title: Published rates, with their sources attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page names where it came from — a platform listing, an agency page, a UAE cost survey. No competitor page in this market publishes a rate table at all, and a figure without a source is not information.

whyPoints.title: Market rates are not presented as our prices
whyPoints.description: The bands here describe what the Abu Dhabi and wider UAE market charges so you can judge any quote, ours included. Where this page needs to talk about our own model it points to the consultation and the trial lesson rather than inventing a price list.

whyPoints.title: You do not pay for Abu Dhabi traffic
whyPoints.description: Online delivery removes the travel premium that sits inside every in-home rate. Forty minutes of driving between the mainland and the island teaches nobody French, and in this emirate that drive is why in-home rates sit in the upper half of the published band.

whyPoints.title: Blocks close, so totals stay knowable
whyPoints.description: Sessions are booked as a defined block aimed at one component, with a re-test at the end and an explicit decision about whether to continue. Open-ended weekly arrangements are the single biggest driver of two-year spend in this subject.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you what the school should cover
whyPoints.description: If the thing your child needs is an extra marked paper or a mock oral, the school usually supplies it inside the fees. We say so, even when saying so means fewer booked sessions, because the alternative is selling you something you already own.

whyPoints.title: No claims we cannot evidence
whyPoints.description: No examiner status without evidence, no grade guarantees, no statistics without a source, and no implied approval from ADEK, the IB or any school. Those are the four things this market does most often and all four are liabilities rather than selling points.

faqs.question: What does a French B tutor in Abu Dhabi charge per hour in AED?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market bands put budget online platforms at roughly AED 33-65, a qualified subject tutor working online at AED 150-300, and IB specialists at AED 200-450 and above. In-home one-to-one runs AED 180-500 because travel sits inside the rate, and one Dubai provider publishes AED 650 for premium named tuition. Those are market figures from the pages that published them, not our price list. In Abu Dhabi specifically, Diploma-level French quotes tend to sit in the upper half of each band, because the pool of tutors who have actually taught French B here is small.

faqs.question: Why is French B tuition more expensive in Abu Dhabi than in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Supply density. Dubai's private school sector had 387,441 students across 227 schools in 2024-25, which supports a deep freelance tutoring layer and real price competition. Abu Dhabi's francophone and French-teaching population is smaller and concentrated in a few areas, so the middle of the market thins out: plenty of general French at the budget end, a small number of genuine Diploma specialists, and comparatively little between. In-home rates are also pushed up because a visiting tutor here fits fewer paid hours into an evening than one working a dense Dubai radius.

faqs.question: Does a native French speaker justify a higher rate for French B?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Native-speaker status predicts pronunciation, idiom and cultural reference, which is the right purchase for conversation practice. It does not predict knowledge of how French B is assessed, and the course credits language, message and conceptual understanding against published descriptors rather than fluency. A native speaker with no Diploma experience may never mention the 6 conceptual marks your child loses on every Paper 1. The questions that actually matter are which level the tutor has taught, how recently, and whether they can mark a script and show the 12 / 12 / 6 split.

faqs.question: Is French B Higher Level more expensive to support than Standard Level?
faqs.answer: Usually, and for a legitimate reason. Higher Level requires two literary works studied in French, and the individual oral starts from an extract from one of them. A tutor supporting HL needs to have read and taught those works, which narrows the available pool and pushes the rate up. Paper 1 also demands 450 to 600 words at HL rather than 250 to 400, and Paper 2 runs two hours rather than one hour forty-five. For the written papers the rate difference is small; for the oral and the literary works it is real and worth paying.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest way to get French B help that actually works?
faqs.answer: A diagnostic followed by closed blocks, rather than a standing weekly hour for two years. The weekly-hour pattern feels prudent and produces the largest two-year total, because much of it funds general practice in terms when nothing specific needed fixing. A family paying a specialist rate for around twenty well-targeted sessions typically spends less than one paying a mid rate for sixty untargeted ones, and gets more movement, because each block had a baseline, a target component and a re-test at the end.

faqs.question: Which French B component deserves most of the budget?
faqs.answer: Paper 2, in most cases, because listening and reading carry 50% of the grade and receive the least deliberate practice. The money there does not buy explanation, it buys the right graded material, sessions run under real exam conditions, and a diagnosis of the gap between what the student knows by eye and recognises by ear. That is roughly six sessions of specialist time with unpaid volume in between. The two 6-mark criteria — conceptual understanding on Paper 1 and interactive skills in the oral — are the cheapest gains and should come first.

faqs.question: Are monthly French tuition packages in Abu Dhabi good value?
faqs.answer: They can be, if you check what counts as a session. Packages circulating in this market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. The questions to ask are how long a session is, whether unused sessions roll over, whether marking between sessions is included, and what notice a cancellation needs. A package is predictable, which has real value for budgeting, but it also keeps an arrangement open by default — and arrangements staying open is the main driver of two-year spend.

faqs.question: What should my child's school already be doing for French B free of charge?
faqs.answer: Teaching the five themes, running at least one mock individual oral, publishing the internal assessment calendar, and in most cases marking an extra timed paper that a student hands in voluntarily. The criteria themselves are published in the subject guide and parents can read them. What a small-cohort school often cannot supply is differentiated time: separate literary-extract oral preparation for three HL students while eight SL students build vocabulary. That gap is what outside support is actually for, and it is worth collecting the free items before buying anything.

faqs.question: Will a French tutor visit our home in Khalifa City?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. We do not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service runs only in India. French B sessions for Abu Dhabi families are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The cost consequence is direct: published in-home bands of AED 180-500 carry travel inside them, and in this emirate the drive between the mainland and the island is long enough that it occupies a meaningful share of what you pay. In-home tuition is a real option with real advantages for younger children; for a Diploma component it buys less per dirham.

faqs.question: Do Abu Dhabi school fees affect what we should spend on tutoring?
faqs.answer: Indirectly, as context for a discretionary line sitting beside a large fixed one. Dubai's regulator announced in May 2026 that private school fees there would not increase for 2026-27 under an economic incentives package, but that is specific to Dubai. Abu Dhabi families should check ADEK's published position for their own year rather than assuming it applies, since fee decisions in the emirate sit with its own authority. The practical point is that knowing whether the fixed line is moving tells you how much room the discretionary one has.

faqs.question: Does the rate include marking work submitted between sessions?
faqs.answer: Ask, in those words, before booking. It is the single variable that moves real cost most and the one families most often leave unasked. A rate of AED 250 that includes marking a timed paper handed in between sessions is cheaper over two years than AED 200 plus a per-script fee, and French B generates a lot of scripts if it is being taught properly. Get the answer in writing alongside the hourly figure, the lesson length, the VAT position, the cancellation notice and what happens if the first match is wrong.

faqs.question: Is VAT included in French B tuition quotes?
faqs.answer: That depends on the provider and you should ask directly. We will tell you whether our own quoted AED figures include it. What this page will not do is state the UAE VAT treatment of education services as settled fact, because that is a matter for the Federal Tax Authority and any page asserting it without citing the authority is guessing on your behalf. The practical approach is to ask every provider whether the number they quoted is the number you will pay, and to get that answer before the first session rather than with the first invoice.

faqs.question: Do French tutors in Abu Dhabi need a permit, and does it affect the price?
faqs.answer: They need one, and it costs nothing, so it should not affect the price. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE lists a two-working-day completion time and no fee. Anyone citing permit costs as a reason for a higher rate is mistaken, and tutoring without one attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

faqs.question: Can we pay for French B support in DP2 only and save a year?
faqs.answer: Often yes, with one caveat. If DP1 was solid and the gap is technique — text types, oral structure, question handling on Paper 2 — then DP2-only support is efficient and considerably cheaper than two years of weekly sessions. The caveat is receptive skills. Listening and reading improve by volume over months, so a student whose Paper 2 is weak and who starts in DP2 is buying the diagnosis late. In that case the cheapest intervention is not more paid hours, it is daily reading and graded listening started immediately, with paid sessions aimed at direction rather than quantity.

faqs.question: What happens if no French B specialist is available at our time?
faqs.answer: You get told, with the options stated. Abu Dhabi demand concentrates into the same early-evening hours, and there are weeks when no UAE-based French B specialist has an 18:00 slot. The alternatives are a different time with an available specialist, a wait for a named slot to open, or a specialist based outside the UAE teaching on Gulf Standard Time. A family able to take 15:30 or a weekend morning has far more choice and, in this market, more negotiating room. What does not happen is a general French tutor being substituted without being named.

faqs.question: Is paid French B support worth it if my child is already at a 5?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on where the 5 is coming from, which is why the diagnostic matters more than the rate. A 5 built on strong reading with a weak oral is two or three sessions away from a 6, because the oral is 25% and its structure is learnable. A 5 built on a competent oral and a weak Paper 2 is a volume problem that paid hours cannot shortcut. Both are worth knowing before any money moves. We will read a marked script and tell you which one you have, at no charge, and sometimes the honest answer is that the school's own marking is enough.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send the marked work and we will price the job, not the hour
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-home-tutor.closingBody: Send the last marked French B script, the most recent Paper 2 result, and the examination session your child is sitting. We will say which component is costing the grade, roughly how many sessions it should take, and what your child's school should be covering inside the fees already. There is no charge for that conversation, and it is the part that determines what you spend. A trial lesson follows, one per subject, booked before any payment. Sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, so you are not funding a drive across the emirate.

intro.heading: French B is a marks problem before it is a language problem
paragraphs: Most Abu Dhabi students who struggle in French B are not bad at French. They are losing marks in predictable places: a Paper 1 task written in the wrong register for its text type, an oral that describes a photograph beautifully and never links it to a theme, a listening section attempted at the pace of the reading section. The language itself is often adequate. The marks are leaking through the assessment design, and that is a far more tractable problem than fluency.

The course is assessed in three parts. Paper 1 is written production and carries a quarter of the grade at both levels. Paper 2 holds listening and reading and carries half. The individual oral carries the remaining quarter, is conducted and marked inside the school, and is then moderated by the IB. Higher Level adds two literary works written in French and changes the oral entirely: an extract from one of those works replaces the visual stimulus that Standard Level candidates face.

Each of those pieces is marked against criteria identified by letter, and the letters reward genuinely different things. Language is one criterion. Message is a second. Conceptual understanding - whether the student has controlled audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation - is a third, and it is the one students are least often taught explicitly. Six marks on a thirty-mark paper sit there. A student who writes fluent French and ignores the text type is throwing those six away before the examiner reaches the grammar.

In Abu Dhabi the cohort is unusually mixed. Some students come from Lycee Louis Massignon or from francophone households and find the language easy but the academic conventions unfamiliar. Others have four years of secondary French from a British curriculum school and can handle the conventions but run out of vocabulary under time. A third group picked French up in MYP and sits in the middle. The same syllabus produces three different tutoring jobs, and the first session should establish which one applies. Getting that wrong is expensive: a francophone student given grammar drills makes no progress at all, while a vocabulary-short student handed register work loses the term. One timed task and one listening item settle it inside twenty minutes, which is why the trial lesson contains both rather than a conversation about goals.

Delivery is online, one to one, over live video with a shared document for written tasks. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home tutoring is a service we run only in India. For French B that is no loss at all. The scarce resource in this subject is a tutor who has prepared the HL oral and knows what the literary extract discussion actually sounds like, and geography should not decide whether your child gets one.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-tutor.programmesIntro: French appears in three IB programmes in this emirate, and the handover between them is where most preparation gaps start. The notes below are about that handover rather than about the programmes in the abstract.

Three components carry the grade: written production, a listening and reading paper, and an individual oral assessed in school. Higher Level adds two literary works and a different oral task. Tutoring here is component-led, because the marks are component-specific and a student rarely loses them evenly.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools often run French B SL and HL in a shared timetable block, with the HL literary works covered in a fraction of the time the task deserves. That single scheduling fact explains most of the HL oral requests we receive from the emirate.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP Language Acquisition runs in phases, and a student finishing phase 4 is usually ready for French B SL while a phase 5 or 6 leaver can consider HL. The MYP assessment criteria reward comprehending spoken and written text and communicating in response, which maps onto the Diploma components less directly than parents assume.

programmes.description: The Career-related Programme includes language development as part of its core, so a CP student in a school that offers it may be building French alongside a career-related study rather than sitting a Diploma language examination. abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-tutor.subjectsIntro: On a subject page the useful breakdown is not a list of other subjects but a list of the things actually marked. Each entry below is a component, a skill or a criterion that carries French B marks, with what it rewards.

subjects.name: Paper 1: written production
subjects.description: One task chosen from three, each tied to a prescribed theme and a named text type. Marked out of thirty across language, message and conceptual understanding. The text type is not decoration: its conventions carry marks that fluent French alone cannot recover.

subjects.name: Paper 2: listening comprehension
subjects.description: Recorded passages at increasing difficulty with questions in French. This is the component Abu Dhabi students most often underestimate, because classroom listening is usually teacher-paced and the paper is not. Accent variety and speed are the two levers.

subjects.name: Paper 2: reading comprehension
subjects.description: Authentic-style texts with question stems that vary from locating stated detail to inferring attitude. Students who read front to back at constant speed lose time they needed for the inference questions at the end.

subjects.name: Individual oral at Standard Level
subjects.description: A visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes, with supervised preparation, a short presentation and then a discussion. Marked on language, message and interactive skills. The theme link is where the marks hide.

subjects.name: Individual oral at Higher Level
subjects.description: An extract from one of the two literary works studied, presented and then discussed, followed by a wider conversation. A different task from the SL oral in kind rather than degree, and it needs the works genuinely read rather than summarised.

subjects.name: The two literary works
subjects.description: Works written originally in French, studied across the two years. They feed the oral and deepen the language, and they are the part of HL most likely to have been compressed into a few weeks by a crowded timetable.

subjects.name: Conceptual understanding
subjects.description: Audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation. A separate criterion worth six of Paper 1's thirty marks, and the one least often taught as its own skill. Teachable in a handful of sessions, which makes it unusually good value.

subjects.name: Text-type repertoire
subjects.description: Blog post, formal letter, article, interview, set of instructions, diary entry, speech and more. Each has layout, salutation and register expectations. Practising two text types properly beats skimming eight.

subjects.name: The five prescribed themes
subjects.description: Identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation and sharing the planet. Schools choose depth within them, so a student can be fluent on daily life and silent on the environment, which shows up in the oral first.

sections.heading: What French B means on an Abu Dhabi timetable, and what it is not
paragraphs: French B is the Diploma's language acquisition course for students with previous experience of French. It sits at Standard or Higher Level, and it is not a literature course at SL, not a conversation class, and not the same animal as ab initio. The distinction matters because the three profiles we meet in this emirate get placed into the same class and then need different things. A francophone student needs conventions. A four-years-of-French student needs vocabulary under time. An MYP continuer needs both, in that order.

The course content runs through five prescribed themes - identities, experiences, human ingenuity, social organisation, sharing the planet - with schools choosing which topics to cover in depth. That choice is invisible to parents and consequential for tutoring. A student who has done three units on health and family and none on technology or the environment will meet a stimulus or a reading text in that gap, and vocabulary built for one theme does not transfer across.

Higher Level is not Standard Level with extra homework. It adds two literary works written in French and replaces the oral task with an extract-based one. The written task grows from the 250 to 400 word range to 450 to 600, and the listening component lengthens. A student choosing between the levels in DP1 should see a timed task at both lengths before deciding, because the honest answer usually becomes obvious within one session and saves a painful switch in January.

sections.heading: The three components, and how the marks divide at SL and HL
paragraphs: The grade comes from three places and they are not equally weighted. Paper 1, written production, is a quarter. Paper 2, holding listening and reading together, is a half. The individual oral is the remaining quarter and is the only component assessed inside the school, by your child's own teacher, before the IB moderates a sample. Papers 1 and 2 are marked externally. There is no coursework essay in this subject.

What changes between the levels is worth laying out side by side, because schools do not always do so and families make the level decision on a vague impression of difficulty. The written task is longer at HL. The listening section is longer at HL. The oral task is different in kind at HL. The reading section and the overall weightings stay the same. Exact timings and current criterion wording sit in the IB subject guide, which your child's school holds; we work from it and do not reproduce or supply IB documents.

The practical consequence for tutoring is that an hour spent on Paper 2 technique is worth twice an hour spent on Paper 1 technique, in pure mark terms, and almost nobody allocates time that way. Most students arrive wanting help with writing because writing is what feels hard and what gets handed back with red on it. Listening is the component that feels fine until the mock, which is exactly why it deserves the clinic rather than the leftovers of a session.

sections.heading: Paper 1: the text type is half the task
paragraphs: Candidates choose one task from three. Each names a text type and sits inside a prescribed theme, and the text type carries marks in its own right. A blog post, a formal letter, an article, an interview, a speech and a set of instructions all have expectations about layout, opening, closing, register and how directly they address a reader. A student who writes excellent continuous prose in response to a formal letter task has lost marks before the examiner judges a single verb ending.

This is the cheapest improvement available in the subject, and it is why we teach two or three text types properly rather than skim the whole list. A checklist for each - how it opens, how it closes, whether it addresses the reader directly, what register it holds, what visual features it needs - takes one session to build and can be rehearsed in ten minutes before a mock. Students who have one tend to use it; students told to remember the conventions do not.

Register is the subtler half. Abu Dhabi students with francophone exposure at home often write in a conversational register that is natural, fluent and wrong for a formal task, and the loss appears under language and under conceptual understanding simultaneously. The repair is a substitution list drawn from the student's own marked work: the phrases they actually reach for, with the formal equivalents next to them. Generic textbook lists do not stick because they are not the student's own habits.

sections.heading: The individual oral: a photograph at Standard Level, an extract at Higher
paragraphs: A quarter of the grade is decided in a room in your child's school, recorded, marked by their teacher and moderated by the IB. At Standard Level the candidate receives a visual stimulus connected to one of the prescribed themes, prepares under supervision, presents for a few minutes and then holds a discussion. At Higher Level the stimulus is an extract from one of the two literary works studied, and the discussion moves from the extract to the work as a whole and then outwards to the themes.

The most common Standard Level failure is a beautiful description with no argument. A candidate narrates what is in the photograph - the people, the place, the weather - and never says what it suggests about identity, or ingenuity, or how a society organises itself. The marks for message and for conceptual understanding are sitting in that unmade link. Two or three drilled phrases that move from description to theme change the mark more than a month of vocabulary work.

At Higher Level the failure is different: the works have been summarised rather than read. A candidate who knows the plot can describe the extract and cannot discuss how it works, which collapses the moment the teacher asks why the author chose that moment. Preparation here means reading properly, holding three or four passages in mind with something to say about each, and practising the handover from extract to work to theme. That is a block of focused sessions, not a term of them.

sections.heading: Criterion letters: where the marks actually are
paragraphs: Every mark in this subject is awarded against a lettered criterion, and students who know the letters perform differently from students who do not. Paper 1 is marked out of thirty: twelve for language, twelve for message, six for conceptual understanding. The individual oral is also marked out of thirty, with twelve for language, twelve for message and six for interactive skills - the ability to sustain a real exchange rather than deliver a monologue and stop.

Reading those numbers changes priorities. A student with excellent grammar and weak task response is capped at roughly half the paper regardless of accuracy, because message and conceptual understanding together carry eighteen of thirty. A student with imperfect French who answers the task precisely, in the right text type, for the right audience, can score well above where their accuracy alone would place them. That is not a loophole; it is what a language acquisition course is designed to reward.

In practice we mark practice work with the letter written beside each comment, so a parent and a student can see which criterion is leaking. Three tasks marked that way produce a pattern within a fortnight. Current criterion wording and mark allocations sit in the IB subject guide held by your child's school - ask the DP coordinator for the breakdown in writing, and bring it to the first session if you have it. A student who can name the three letters and say what each rewards behaves differently in a timed task, because they stop treating accuracy as the only thing being judged and start answering the question that was set.

sections.heading: Paper 2: why listening is the weaker half
paragraphs: Half the grade sits in one paper, and students consistently rate it as the component they worry about least. Classroom listening is teacher-paced, teacher-accented and usually repeated on request. The paper is none of those things. Passages run at natural speed, voices vary, and the question stems move from locating a stated detail to inferring an attitude that is never stated. The gap between those two experiences is where the marks go.

The repair is exposure plus technique. Exposure means listening to French well outside the textbook: news bulletins, interviews, regional accents, people talking over each other. Technique means knowing what to do with a second hearing. A candidate who tries to write full answers on the first pass loses the thread and then has nothing left to check; a candidate who marks question numbers against moments in the audio on the first pass and writes on the second finishes with answers and time.

Reading has its own pacing trap. The stems are not arranged so that working front to back at constant speed is optimal, and inference questions often sit late in the paper where a slow reader arrives with four minutes left. Planning an order of attack, and logging marks by question type rather than as one total, turns a vague 'reading is hard' into a specific and fixable list. Two or three sessions of this usually produce the largest single mark movement available in the subject, and it holds for the rest of the course once learned.
bullets: Listening is natural pace and varied accents, unlike most classroom practice
Mark the audio on the first hearing, write on the second
Plan a reading order rather than working front to back
Log marks by question type to find the repeating loss

sections.heading: What one hour a week fixes in six weeks, and what it does not
paragraphs: Honesty about pace is more useful than enthusiasm. In six weeks of one hour a week, with homework between sessions, a French B student can reliably learn two or three text types to checklist level, be taught conceptual understanding as an explicit skill, change their listening technique, and plan a reading order. Those four things are technique rather than knowledge, and technique moves fast. They are also where most of the recoverable marks are.

What six weeks does not do is build vocabulary breadth across five themes, repair systematic grammar gaps from three years of partial learning, or turn a student who has summarised two literary works into one who has read them. Those need two or three terms, and anyone promising otherwise is selling something. No tutor can promise a grade in this subject or any other, and we do not publish outcome statistics anywhere on this site because we could not show you the data behind them.

The sensible plan, then, is technique first and content second, with the fortnightly marked task running throughout so the evidence stays comparable. If your child is in DP2 with the oral deadline close, the order inverts: the oral block comes first because it is a quarter of the grade with a fixed internal date, and Paper 1 work resumes afterwards. Tell us the deadline in the first message and the plan builds backwards from it rather than forwards from a syllabus list.

process.title: Send the level, the school and the next deadline
process.description: Tell us whether your child is in SL or HL, which school, and what is coming next - a mock, the internal oral recording, or simply the May session. French B tutoring is component-led, so the deadline decides which component gets the first four weeks. A line about where marks were lost last term helps more than a general description.

process.title: A free trial lesson with a timed task inside it
process.description: One lesson, free, with no card details and no obligation to continue. Your child writes a short task under time and attempts a listening item, which is enough to see whether the problem is language, task response or pacing. You get the marked task afterwards either way, with the criterion letters on it.

process.title: Technique first, in the order the marks sit
process.description: Text types and conceptual understanding for Paper 1, then listening and reading technique for Paper 2, because half the grade sits there and it is usually the least practised half. Vocabulary and grammar work runs underneath rather than instead, built from the student's own marked errors rather than from a generic list.

process.title: The oral block, timed to the school's internal date
process.description: Once the school names its recording window, a focused block covers the task your child actually faces: unfamiliar visual stimuli at Standard Level, the literary extract and the handover to theme at Higher Level. Rehearsals are recorded and reviewed against the criteria. The tutor has no part in the assessed recording itself.

process.title: If no French B specialist is free, we say so

If we cannot match your child to a tutor who has prepared that oral, we will tell you rather than put a general French tutor in front of them. A date when someone is free is more useful than a booking that underdelivers.

whyPoints.title: Component-led, because that is how marks are awarded
whyPoints.description: Sessions are planned against the component that is leaking rather than against French in general. A student losing eighteen marks to message and conceptual understanding does not need more grammar, and three marked tasks with criterion letters on them show which it is within a fortnight.

whyPoints.title: Both versions of the oral, prepared properly
whyPoints.description: The Standard Level visual stimulus and the Higher Level literary extract are different tasks needing different rehearsal. We match to tutors who have prepared both and will tell you which they have actually done. Ask about the oral in the trial lesson - the answer is diagnostic.

whyPoints.title: Listening treated as half the grade
whyPoints.description: Paper 2 carries fifty per cent and is the component most often left to the textbook. Exposure beyond classroom audio, plus a technique for using the second hearing, produces the largest single mark movement we see in this subject and takes two or three sessions rather than a term.

whyPoints.title: Online, stated plainly

faqs.question: My child did four years of French at a British curriculum school. Is French B SL or HL the right level?
faqs.answer: Four years of secondary French usually places a student comfortably in Standard Level and plausibly in Higher Level, and the honest test is a timed task at both lengths. SL asks for 250 to 400 words, HL for 450 to 600, and the difference in sustained register is where the decision really lies. Higher Level also adds two literary works and a different oral task. One session with a timed task at each length normally settles it, and settling it in DP1 is far cheaper than switching level in January.

faqs.question: How is IB French B assessed, component by component?
faqs.answer: Three components. Paper 1 is written production and carries a quarter of the grade at both levels. Paper 2 holds listening and reading together and carries half. The individual oral carries the final quarter, is conducted and marked by your child's teacher in school, and is then moderated by the IB. Papers 1 and 2 are externally marked and there is no coursework essay. Ask your DP coordinator for the component breakdown in writing at the start of the course; schools provide it readily and it answers most family questions at once.

faqs.question: What exactly happens in the French B individual oral?
faqs.answer: At Standard Level your child receives a visual stimulus connected to one of the prescribed themes, prepares under supervision, presents for a few minutes and then holds a discussion with the teacher. At Higher Level the starting point is an extract from one of the two literary works studied, and the discussion moves from the extract to the whole work and then to the themes. It is recorded, marked in school against language, message and interactive skills, and moderated by the IB. Exact timings are in the current subject guide your school holds.

faqs.question: Why does French B HL include two literary works when it is a language course?
faqs.answer: The works are there to deepen language through sustained, authentic text and to give the Higher Level oral something substantial to discuss. They are written originally in French and studied across the two years. In practice they are the element most often squeezed by a crowded Abu Dhabi timetable, which is why HL candidates often arrive able to summarise both works and unable to discuss how either one works. Reading them properly, with three or four passages held in mind, is the single most useful HL preparation there is.

faqs.question: My child writes good French but keeps losing Paper 1 marks. What is going wrong?
faqs.answer: Almost always the text type. Each task names one - a formal letter, a blog post, an article, a speech - and its conventions carry marks independently of the French. A student who writes fluent continuous prose in response to a formal letter task loses marks for layout, salutation, closing and register before accuracy is judged. Message and conceptual understanding together carry eighteen of Paper 1's thirty marks, so task response outweighs grammar. A text-type checklist built in one session usually recovers most of it.

faqs.question: What is conceptual understanding in French B, and can it be taught?
faqs.answer: It covers audience, context, purpose, meaning and variation: whether the student has written the right kind of text for the right reader for the right reason. It is a separate criterion worth six of Paper 1's thirty marks and it is rarely taught as its own skill, which makes it unusually good value for tutoring. Yes, it can be taught, and quickly. Two or three sessions spent asking who this text is for and what it is trying to do, against the student's own marked work, moves it measurably.

faqs.question: Which accents and speeds appear in the French B listening paper?
faqs.answer: Recorded material uses natural pace and a range of voices rather than the single teacher accent most classroom listening relies on, and that gap is the real problem. The fix is exposure well beyond the textbook - news bulletins, interviews, people talking over one another - plus a technique for the second hearing. Mark question numbers against moments in the audio on the first pass and write answers on the second. Students who try to write full answers immediately lose the thread and have nothing to check afterwards.

faqs.question: Is French B Higher Level much harder than Standard Level?
faqs.answer: It is longer and broader rather than simply harder. The written task roughly doubles in length, the listening section extends, and two literary works are added along with an extract-based oral. A student with solid accuracy who reads willingly usually copes well. A student who is already managing the Standard Level word count with difficulty will find the sustained register at 450 to 600 words the real obstacle. Write one task at each length under time before choosing, and make the decision on evidence rather than ambition.

faqs.question: Do Abu Dhabi schools actually offer French B at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Several do, often with small candidate numbers, and some run SL and HL together in one timetabled block. That arrangement is the practical reason many HL requests reach us from the emirate: shared teaching time means the literary works and the extract-based oral get a fraction of the attention their weight deserves. Ask your child's school two questions - whether HL runs this year, and how many hours are timetabled for the literary works. The answers tell you whether outside support is sensible.

faqs.question: What do French B tutors charge per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published UAE market rates, mostly quoted for Dubai, set the range. Budget online providers advertise from roughly AED 33 to AED 65 an hour. Unitors lists IB tutoring from about AED 200, TutorChase quotes around AED 270, and Bestimate's 2026 tutoring-cost table puts specialist exam-year support at roughly AED 200 to AED 450 and above. In-home visits run higher once travel is priced in, from about AED 180 to AED 500. Those are those providers' figures, not ours - ask for a quote and take the free trial first.

faqs.question: Can a tutor prepare my child for the oral without crossing an academic honesty line?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is firm. A tutor may rehearse with unfamiliar stimuli or extracts, time the presentation, teach the phrases that move from description to theme, record practice attempts and review them against the published criteria. A tutor may not be present at the assessed recording, may not supply content for the student to reproduce in it, and may not script a response. Everything submitted is your child's own work, and we state that to the student in the first lesson rather than leaving it implied.

faqs.question: My child speaks French at home but is in French B. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: The school decides placement, and a home-language speaker in French B is common enough in this emirate. Fluency helps with listening and with the oral and is no help at all with text types, register or the written conventions, so these students often score lower than their speaking suggests. The work is conventions and conceptual understanding rather than language, and a substitution list built from their own marked writing - the conversational phrases they reach for, with the formal equivalents - is the practical tool.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the May session should French B revision start in earnest?
faqs.answer: Technique work should start as early as possible because it keeps paying back: text types, conceptual understanding, listening method and reading order are all teachable in six weeks and then available for the rest of the course. Intensive timed practice is better placed in the final term, once content coverage is complete. The fixed point to plan around is the school's internal oral recording window rather than the written session, because that date is set locally and often arrives earlier than families expect.

faqs.question: Can sessions work around the Abu Dhabi school day and shift during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes. Island schools finishing around 15.15 and mainland activity blocks ending later produce different realistic slots, and online delivery means no travel time is lost either way. During Ramadan school hours shorten and the useful window for a Diploma student often sits after iftar, so sessions move for the month and move back afterwards. The thing worth protecting through it is the fortnightly marked task, since that is what keeps the comparison across the term meaningful.

faqs.question: Will a French B grade help with university applications from the UAE?
faqs.answer: A language acquisition grade contributes to the Diploma total that universities read, and some courses state a modern-language requirement or preference, so check the specific programme rather than relying on a general answer. For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency, the British-track rules are published but no IB points threshold has been read on an official Ministry source for this page, so verify that on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority. Equivalency is a process you handle through the official channel; a tutoring service does not perform it for you.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-tutor.closingHeading: Find out which criterion is leaking
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-french-b-tutor.closingBody: If your child is losing French B marks and nobody has said which criterion they are coming off, one timed task answers it. The trial lesson is free, takes no card details and carries no obligation, and you keep the marked task with the criterion letters on it whatever you decide next. Tell us the level, the school and the date of the internal oral recording, and we will match a French B tutor who has prepared that exact task to a slot that fits the Abu Dhabi school run - or tell you honestly when the next one is free.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-geography-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma Geography at Standard and Higher Level. Each profile names the optional themes they have taught and whether they work on the fieldwork report, because the optional themes are a department choice and the report is a separate skill from classroom teaching.

intro.heading: Geography is marked on specificity, and that is where the marks go
paragraphs: A Diploma Geography answer that is true of anywhere scores in the lowest band available. That is the single most useful sentence a parent can be given about this subject, and it explains most of the disappointing marks. A student writes that rapid urbanisation puts pressure on infrastructure, that coastal ecosystems are vulnerable to development, that water scarcity drives investment in new supply. Every statement is correct. None of it is geography, because geography requires a named place, a figure, a date and a mechanism.

The structure the subject is examined through is straightforward once stated. Both levels sit a core theme of three units covering changing population, global climate vulnerability and resilience, and global resource consumption and security. Both levels sit a paper on optional themes chosen by the school from a list of seven, with Standard Level students answering two and Higher Level students three. Higher Level students sit an additional paper on global interactions, covering power and networks, human development and diversity, and global risks and resilience. Everyone writes a fieldwork report inside a 2,500-word ceiling.

The optional themes are the thing to establish first, because they determine whether a tutor can help at all. A tutor who has taught freshwater drainage basins and geophysical hazards through several cohorts is a specialist for a student sitting those and a reader for a student sitting leisure, tourism and sport. There are seven themes and a school teaches two or three of them, so the probability of a random match is poor. One email to the department settles it.

Abu Dhabi contributes something genuinely valuable here that almost no tutoring page mentions: case material. A student in this emirate lives beside coastal mangrove systems, a water supply built on desalination, large-scale solar generation in the Al Dhafra region, oasis agriculture and falaj irrigation at Al Ain, rapid planned urban expansion at Al Shamkha and Khalifa City, and a population structure that behaves unlike any textbook demographic transition model. Examiners reward specific, well-understood local examples, and a student who can deploy them is writing something the mark scheme has not seen a hundred times already. Lessons run online, one to one, over live video; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi, because home visits are a service we provide only in India.

What follows takes the components in order, says where each one loses marks, and then deals with the fieldwork report and the local material a student here can actually use. Cost is at the end, because an hourly rate means nothing until you know what the hour has to produce. The order is deliberate: case material first, because an answer cannot be lifted out of the middle bands without specific places and figures available to put into it, and technique second, because technique applied to nothing produces a well-structured answer with nothing in it.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-geography-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Geography is examined at Diploma level, but the habit of writing about specific places is built earlier and the fieldwork report sits in the core with everything else. These are the stages that matter here.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years covering three core units, two or three optional themes, and for Higher Level students an additional global interactions paper. Everyone produces a fieldwork report within a 2,500-word ceiling, marked against criteria covering the fieldwork question, the methods, the treatment of information, the written analysis, the conclusion and the evaluation.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi Geography cohorts are frequently small and the optional themes are chosen at department level. Ask which themes are taught, whether the Higher Level global interactions units have been started, and when the fieldwork data collection is scheduled, because the heat in this emirate makes that date a real constraint rather than an administrative one.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Individuals and Societies in the middle years teaches investigation and communication against criteria that already distinguish evidence from assertion. Students who learned to attach a place name and a figure to a claim arrive in DP1 writing in the bands the Diploma rewards rather than unlearning a general-statement habit.
programmes.countryNote: Students arriving into Diploma Geography in this emirate often come from courses where graphical skills were taught as presentation rather than as analysis. A short block on reading data from a map, a graph and a photograph, and saying what it shows, is the cheapest intervention available before DP1 starts.

programmes.name: The Diploma core: IA, EE and TOK
programmes.description: The fieldwork report, an Extended Essay that Geography students often write in the subject, and Theory of Knowledge. The fieldwork report is unusual among internal assessments because it depends on primary data the student collected on a specific day, which cannot be recovered later if the design was wrong.
programmes.countryNote: Fieldwork in Abu Dhabi is weather-constrained in a way few guides acknowledge. Collection in the hottest months is impractical for anything outdoors, which compresses the viable window and pushes it against the school's internal deadline. Plan the data collection date before the research question is finalised, not after.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-geography-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Geography pairs with a recognisable set of subjects in this emirate, and the combination affects both the reading load and the university routes. These are the ones seen most often.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Three core units, two or three optional themes, a Higher Level global interactions paper, and a fieldwork report within a 2,500-word ceiling. Marks are lost to statements that are true of anywhere and to graphs described rather than interpreted.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: An interdisciplinary course spanning the sciences and individuals and societies, with substantial overlap on resource and climate content. Students sometimes take it instead of Geography; confirm how target universities treat it, because recognition varies by course rather than by institution.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Cells, physiology, genetics and ecology with an internally assessed investigation. The ecology content maps onto Geography's coastal and extreme-environment themes, and the two reports demand the same discipline about data quality.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Micro, macro and the global economy with a portfolio of commentaries. Pairs well with the resource security and global interactions content, and students find the development material covered twice from different angles.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: A source paper, essay papers and a 2,200-word historical investigation. Shares Geography's demand for specific evidence, and a student who writes well in one is usually one technique away from writing well in the other.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Political concepts examined through a source booklet and extended responses, plus an engagement project. Overlaps directly with the Higher Level global interactions paper on power, networks and global risks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and financial mathematics. The statistics content is exactly what the fieldwork report's treatment of information needs, and students taking both should be using one subject to teach the other.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Five content units, two written papers and a research project worth a quarter of the grade. A common third choice in a block containing Geography, and the lightest for reading volume.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Offered at several levels across the emirate's schools and mandatory alongside the licensed curriculum for the groups the regulations specify. A genuine constraint on the hours available for Geography fieldwork write-up in a crowded term.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: A comparative study, a process portfolio and an exhibition. Taken alongside Geography by students who want a practical subject, and the comparative study rewards the same contextual precision Geography demands.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-geography-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Delivery is online, so the community a family lives in does not affect which tutor is available. It does affect the fieldwork a student can reach, which in this subject is a practical matter rather than a scheduling one. These are the areas the enquiries come from.

regions.name: Eastern Mangroves
regions.note: Beside one of the most useful fieldwork environments in the country. Mangrove systems support work on coastal margins, sediment and ecosystem services, and a student here can design a transect study that does not require a long journey to reach.

regions.name: Hudayriyat Island
regions.note: A rapidly developed leisure and residential island, which makes it live case material for the leisure, tourism and sport theme as well as for urban environments. Students who live on a site under active development have access to change over time that textbooks describe second-hand.

regions.name: Al Wathba
regions.note: Inland community near wetland and desert environments, relevant to the extreme environments theme and to water management content. Scheduling here is driven by a long school commute, and a fixed evening slot works better than a variable one.

regions.name: Al Shahama
regions.note: Northern community on the route towards Dubai, with students travelling substantial distances to school. The local Geography specialist pool is effectively empty, which makes online delivery the difference between a subject specialist and a generalist.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Oasis city within the emirate, with falaj irrigation systems and agricultural land use within walking distance of several schools. Students here have the best primary fieldwork access in the country for water management and land use, and frequently do not know it.

regions.name: Al Mirfa
regions.note: Coastal town in the Al Dhafra region, a long way from the island school cluster and from any visiting tutor. For families here the realistic choice has always been online or nothing, and for a subject with seven possible optional themes that choice determines the quality of the match.

sections.heading: The three core units and the case studies an examiner expects to be named
paragraphs: Both Standard and Higher Level sit the core theme, which covers changing population, global climate vulnerability and resilience, and global resource consumption and security. The paper that assesses it mixes short answers on each unit with a question built on a visual stimulus and an extended answer chosen from a pair. The short answers reward precision, the stimulus question rewards reading what is actually in front of the student, and the extended answer rewards the thing this whole subject rewards: specific places doing specific things.

Changing population is where UAE students have an unusual advantage and rarely use it. The textbook demographic transition model describes a population changing through its own births and deaths. This country's population structure is shaped overwhelmingly by migration, is heavily weighted towards working ages, and is unevenly distributed by sex in a way no classical model predicts. A student who can explain why the standard model does not describe where they live has demonstrated exactly the analytical control the upper bands ask for.

Global climate vulnerability and resilience is the unit where general statements do the most damage. A vulnerable coastline somewhere is worth nothing. A named stretch of coast, its elevation, the assets behind it, the specific adaptation measures in place and their limitations is worth the band. Abu Dhabi supplies this: a low-lying coastal capital, mangrove systems that both protect shoreline and store carbon, and adaptation investment that can be described concretely.

Global resource consumption and security is the unit where this emirate is close to a case study in itself. A water supply dependent on desalination raises every question the unit asks about security, energy intensity and strategic reserve. Large-scale solar generation in the Al Dhafra region sits beside a hydrocarbon economy. Food security in a country importing most of what it eats, with oasis agriculture at Liwa and Al Ain on groundwater, is a genuine tension rather than a textbook example. Students should use what is around them, with figures checked against official sources rather than remembered.

sections.heading: Optional themes: how many your child answers, and which ones are on the timetable
paragraphs: The first paper is set on the optional themes the school teaches. There are seven in the guide: freshwater and drainage basins, oceans and coastal margins, extreme environments, geophysical hazards, leisure, tourism and sport, food and health, and urban environments. A Standard Level student answers two and a Higher Level student three, and the school chooses which. This makes the themes the first question to ask and the single biggest determinant of whether a tutor is useful.

Departments choose for sensible local reasons. Coastal margins and extreme environments are natural choices in this country, and urban environments is close to unavoidable given how fast the emirate's communities have been built. Geophysical hazards is sometimes chosen precisely because it is remote from local experience and therefore has to be taught properly rather than assumed. None of that helps a tutor who has not taught the particular combination, which is why the question has to be asked before the match rather than after.

Each theme has its own command vocabulary and its own classic failures. Coastal margins punishes students who describe processes without landforms attached. Urban environments punishes students who write about urbanisation in general rather than about a named city's specific problem. Extreme environments punishes the assumption that a desert is a desert: the guide wants the physical processes and the human responses in specified places. Food and health punishes answers with no data in them at all.

The practical approach is to treat each theme as a separate subject with a separate case-study bank, and to resist the temptation to revise them together. Two themes done properly outscore three done vaguely, and for a Standard Level student that is not even a trade-off, since only two are required.

sections.heading: The Higher Level paper on global interactions, and why it is sat cold
paragraphs: Higher Level students sit an additional paper on global interactions, covering power, places and networks, human development and diversity, and global risks and resilience. It is conceptually the most demanding part of the course and it is the part most often taught last, because the core and the options have examination priority through DP1 and most of DP2.

The paper is shorter than the others and the questions are structured in two parts, with the second part carrying the larger share and requiring extended argument. Content covers globalisation and its measurement, the geography of power and influence, flows of people, capital and information, development measured in more than one way, cultural diffusion, and the risks that arise from interconnection. Students find it abstract because it has fewer physical landforms to hold on to.

What makes it answerable is the same discipline as the rest of the subject: named examples with figures. Globalisation indices are measurable and comparable. Development indicators are specified and each one has a known blind spot. Flows have origins, destinations and volumes. A student who has three or four concrete examples per unit can write this paper; a student with a conceptual understanding and no examples cannot, however well they understand it.

There is a useful overlap worth exploiting for students taking Global Politics alongside Geography. Power, interdependence, development and global risk appear in both courses, and a case prepared for one can serve the other with its framing adjusted. For a student carrying both subjects in a crowded DP2 this is not a marginal saving.

sections.heading: Graphical and statistical skills: the marks nobody revises for
paragraphs: A share of the marks in this subject is awarded for handling data, and students almost never revise it because it does not look like content. The guide expects a student to read and interpret maps, graphs, photographs and infographics, to construct appropriate graphical representations, and to apply statistical techniques to field data. Confirm with your school which techniques the department teaches, because the list in the guide is wider than any one cohort covers.

The distinction that earns marks is between describing data and interpreting it. A student who writes that the graph rises from 2010 to 2020 has described it. A student who writes that the rise is steepest between two named years, that it coincides with a specific event, and that one data point breaks the pattern for an identifiable reason has interpreted it. Examiners can tell the difference instantly and the band difference is substantial.

On the statistical side, the common failures are mechanical and fixable. A correlation technique applied to data that does not meet its assumptions. A result calculated and then not interpreted against the hypothesis. A significance level quoted without saying what it means for the conclusion. These are a handful of sessions of work and they pay in both the written papers and the fieldwork report, because the report's treatment of information criterion is precisely this skill assessed directly.

The visual stimulus question deserves its own drill. Students arrive at it with revised content and try to answer from memory rather than from the material provided, which is the one thing the question does not want. The habit to build is to annotate before writing: what does this show, what is anomalous in it, what can be inferred and what cannot. Three or four practised examples and most students stop answering a different question from the one that was asked.
bullets: Describing data earns little; interpreting it earns the band

sections.heading: The fieldwork report: 2,500 words, primary data and one decisive question
paragraphs: The internally assessed component is a written report on fieldwork the student conducted, inside a 2,500-word ceiling, marked against criteria covering the fieldwork question and its geographic context, the methods of investigation, the quality and treatment of the information collected, the written analysis, the conclusion and the evaluation. Confirm the current criteria and mark allocations with your school's Diploma coordinator rather than relying on figures from a tutoring page.

One decision determines most of the outcome: the fieldwork question. It has to be answerable with data a student can actually collect, narrow enough to analyse inside 2,500 words, and grounded in a geographic context the student can describe properly. A question that is interesting and uncollectable produces a report that fails on three criteria at once, and the problem is only visible after the data has been gathered, by which point the collection day has gone.

The treatment of information criterion is where technically weaker students lose most. It asks for data presented appropriately, processed where processing is warranted, and presented in forms that support the analysis. Students either present raw tables with no processing or produce a sequence of decorative charts that nothing in the analysis refers to. The test to apply to every figure in a report is simple: which sentence of my analysis does this support? A chart that answers nothing should not be there.

The evaluation is the second common weakness and it is written as apology rather than as analysis. The criterion wants the method, the sample and the data assessed specifically, with the consequences for the conclusion identified. A student who says the sample was small has said nothing. A student who says a sample of a stated size at a single site on a single morning limits the inference to that site and that time, and explains what a second site would have added, has written an evaluation.

sections.heading: Fieldwork a student in this emirate can realistically collect
paragraphs: The practical constraint on fieldwork in Abu Dhabi is not access but climate and calendar. Outdoor data collection in the hottest months is impractical for anything requiring sustained time in the open, which compresses the viable window into the cooler part of the academic year and pushes it hard against the school's internal deadline. The date should be chosen before the question is finalised, because a question that needs summer collection is a question to replace.

Within that window, what is available is better than students assume. Coastal and mangrove environments along the Eastern Mangroves and the wider shoreline support transect work on vegetation, sediment and ecosystem characteristics. The Corniche and the developed beaches support profile and management studies. The planned expansion at Al Shamkha, Al Falah and the Khalifa City corridor supports urban land-use, housing density and microclimate work with genuine change to measure. Al Ain's oases and falaj systems support water management and land-use studies that very few students anywhere can do with primary data.

Human geography fieldwork is often easier to design here than physical, and it is underused. Pedestrian and traffic counts at specified points and times. Land-use mapping along a transect from a centre outwards. Questionnaire work on travel behaviour or service provision, with the school's permission and proper consent where respondents are involved. Environmental quality surveys using a defined index applied consistently. All of these produce quantitative data a student can process and defend.

Two cautions. First, anything involving questionnaires or people needs the school's involvement and proper consent, and personal data should be kept to the minimum the design requires, with identifiers separated at collection and a deletion plan afterwards; the UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection governs personal data generally. Second, access to some sites requires permission that has to be sought in advance, and a report built on data a student was not permitted to collect is worse than no report.

sections.heading: Abu Dhabi Geography cohorts and what to ask the department
paragraphs: ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in this emirate and publishes inspection ratings. Those ratings describe schools rather than departments, and a strongly rated school can run a Geography group of six students whose optional themes were chosen by one teacher in a single afternoon. The ratings are useful for choosing a school and not for diagnosing a subject.

The questions worth asking are specific. Which optional themes are taught. Whether Higher Level global interactions has been started and when it will finish. When fieldwork collection is scheduled and at which site. Which statistical techniques the department teaches. Whether anonymised past reports at different mark bands can be shown. The last of these is the single most useful document a Geography parent can obtain and it is almost never requested.

Mandatory UAE subjects run alongside the licensed curriculum for the groups the regulations specify, and they consume hours that a fieldwork write-up also needs. Dubai's regulator requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies in all private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students and specified languages of instruction, and requires that teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education hold the appropriate approval from that regulator. The federal position is that private schools must follow Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their own curriculum. Abu Dhabi families should confirm the local detail with their school.

The national regulator map, since families move between emirates: Dubai with KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain with ADEK, Sharjah with the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah with its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah with the federal Ministry of Education. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from any of them, nor from the IB, and claims none; they are named here to explain who governs what.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in a fieldwork report
paragraphs: Fieldwork reports have an honesty exposure the other internal assessments do not, because the data is invisible to the examiner. A student who did not collect enough readings, or whose results are messier than expected, is a short step from filling in the gaps. That is academic misconduct, it is more detectable than students think because invented data behaves too well, and it is unnecessary, since the criteria reward the handling of the data rather than its tidiness.

The second exposure is shared data. Where a class collects together, which is normal and permitted, the write-up must still be entirely individual: the question, the analysis, the conclusion and the evaluation are the student's own work. Reports from the same cohort that share phrasing as well as data are a straightforward malpractice problem for everyone involved, and it is worth saying to a student before the write-up rather than afterwards.

The tutor boundary is the same across every Diploma subject. A tutor may teach method, explain what each criterion asks for, interrogate a question before collection, explain a statistical technique, read a student's own draft and say where the analysis describes rather than argues, and point at a figure that supports nothing. A tutor may not supply text, process the data on the student's behalf, rewrite a section into its final form, or produce any part of the assessed work.

One site in the competitor research sells completed internal assessments outright, and the consequence of buying one falls on the student rather than the seller. Ask any provider for a written statement of what they will refuse to do before booking hours. A provider who names specific refusals has given you the most useful comparison point available between quotes.
bullets: Invented data behaves too well and the criteria do not reward tidy results
Shared collection is fine; shared write-up is malpractice for everyone involved

sections.heading: What Geography support costs here, and how the lessons run
paragraphs: Market rates for a qualified subject tutor working online across the UAE run roughly AED 150-300 an hour, IB specialists are quoted from about AED 200 to AED 450 and upwards, and in-home visits sit at roughly AED 180-500 because the tutor's travel is priced inside the hour. Those bands come from published provider pages and from Bestimate's Dubai rate table, read in October 2026. They describe the market and are not an IB Gram price list.

Two questions separate quotes in this subject. Is marking inside the rate, since extended answers improve through being marked against the published markbands rather than discussed. And which optional themes has the tutor taught, since there are seven and a school teaches two or three. A provider who cannot answer the second question is offering a generalist, whatever the hourly figure says.

On delivery, stated plainly: every UAE lesson is one-to-one and online, over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an address in Abu Dhabi and does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. For this subject the format has a specific advantage, because map work, graph interpretation, data processing and report drafting are all screen activities, and a shared screen with annotation is a better working surface than a printout on a table.

On availability, honestly. For core-unit work and extended-answer technique a match usually takes a few days. For a specific pair of optional themes it can take longer, and near internal deadlines the whole emirate wants the same fortnight. Where nobody is free we say so and offer a tutor based elsewhere on the same specification at the same rate, or give a date rather than a maybe. No competitor in the researched set discloses a coverage limit at all, and several conceal non-UAE delivery behind an overseas number.
