sections.heading: Abu Dhabi History cohorts, the department's choices and the single-teacher class
paragraphs: ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in this emirate and publishes inspection ratings. Those ratings are awarded to schools rather than to departments, so they will not tell you whether the History teaching is strong, and a school with a high rating may have a History group of five students taught by someone covering two subjects.

The questions that do tell you something are narrow and the department will answer them. Which prescribed subject is the source paper set on. Which world history topics will the essays come from. At Higher Level, which regional option. How many students sit the subject this year and whether both levels share a room. Whether anonymised past investigations at different mark bands can be shown. The last of those is the most valuable and the least often requested.

Mandatory UAE subjects run alongside the licensed curriculum for the groups the regulations specify, and they consume real hours in a History student's week. Dubai's regulator requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies in all private schools regardless of curriculum, organises separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, and specifies the language of instruction for each. The federal position is that private schools must follow Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their own curriculum. Abu Dhabi families should confirm the local detail with the school and count those hours before agreeing to a weekly essay commitment.

The regulator map nationally, since families move between emirates: Dubai with KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain with ADEK, Sharjah with the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah with its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah with the federal Ministry of Education. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities also approve fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods, so the regulator's role goes beyond inspection. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or licence from any of them, nor from the IB, and claims none.

sections.heading: Academic honesty in the historical investigation
paragraphs: The investigation is the Diploma component most exposed to the finished-coursework market, because it is a self-contained piece of writing on a student-chosen question and because a competent graduate could produce one in a day. One site in the competitor research sells completed internal assessments outright. For a family weighing options, the position needs stating without euphemism: buying assessed work is malpractice under the IB's rules and the consequence falls on the student rather than on the seller.

What a supervisor or tutor may properly do is substantial. They may question whether a research question is answerable, ask what sources the student will actually read, explain what each of the three sections is marked on, read a student's own draft and say where a claim is unsupported or where the structure has collapsed into narrative, point out referencing failures, and ask the questions that make a student revise their own work. All of that is teaching and it is what the specialist rate buys.

What they may not do is supply text, restructure a section into its final form, select and summarise the sources so the student need not read them, or produce the reflection. The reflection is a particular temptation because it sounds generic and is easy to write for somebody else, and a reflection written by anybody other than the student is both detectable and worthless, since it reflects on a process that did not happen.

Ask any provider for a written statement of what they will refuse to do before any hours are booked. Providers who answer in general language about integrity while describing a service that returns completed drafts have answered the question. A provider who names the specific actions they decline has given you the most useful comparison point available between quotes.
bullets: A tutor questions, explains and comments on the student's own draft
A tutor does not supply text, restructure to final form or write the reflection

sections.heading: What History support costs in this emirate, and how the lessons run
paragraphs: Start with the numbers a parent can verify. Published provider pages and Bestimate’s Dubai rate table, read in October 2026, put a qualified subject tutor working online across the UAE at roughly AED 150-300 an hour, IB specialists from about AED 200 to AED 450 and upwards, and in-home visits at roughly AED 180-500 - the gap being the tutor’s travel, priced inside the hour. These are market observations, not an IB Gram price list.

In this subject one question separates quotes more than any other: is marking inside the rate. History improves through marked written work, and an hour of lesson time with the essay marked by nobody is a materially different product from an hour that includes a timed essay read against the published markbands with the band named. Those two are frequently quoted at the same number, and the cheaper-looking one is usually the first.

On delivery, the position plainly stated: every UAE lesson is one-to-one and online, over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an address in Abu Dhabi and does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. The gain is the match. A student sitting History of Africa and the Middle East at Higher Level needs a tutor who has taught that option, and the number of people in the emirate who have is not large enough to choose from by driving distance.

On availability, the honest answer. For Standard Level essay work and the source paper, a match usually takes a few days. For a specific regional option at Higher Level it can take longer, and near internal coursework deadlines the whole emirate wants the same fortnight. Where nobody is free we say so and offer a tutor based elsewhere on the same specification at the same rate, or give a date rather than a maybe. No competitor in the researched set discloses a coverage limit at all.

process.title: Send one marked source paper
process.description: A marked first paper with the marks shown question by question localises the problem in minutes. It distinguishes a four-mark technique gap from a nine-mark integration failure from a complete absence of paper structure, and those three need different numbers of hours and different kinds of work.

process.title: Get the department's three choices
process.description: The prescribed subject, the world history topics and, at Higher Level, the regional option. One email to the Diploma coordinator. Those three decide which tutors are specialists for your child, and a provider who matches without asking has told you how carefully they are doing it.

process.title: Free trial with the marked script open
process.description: Held by the tutor who would take the weekly slot, with your child's own marked work on the shared screen. It ends by naming the band the writing sits in and the one move that reaches the next band. A general closing statement is a reason not to book the block.

process.title: Agree what each session hands back
process.description: Hours rather than terms, with the marked document each session returns specified in advance, what is included in the rate, and the date on which somebody reports whether the band has moved. Written down before any money moves.

process.title: Audit at six weeks against the marked work
process.description: Lay the marked essays out in order. If the band moved on the component being worked, continue. If the same feedback appears three times, the habit is being described rather than repaired and the recommendation should be a different approach, a different tutor, or stopping.

whyPoints.title: Every session returns a marked document
whyPoints.description: Written work comes back marked against the published markbands with the band named and one specific move to the next band stated. In a subject where every component produces a number, that is the only honest evidence that something changed, and it is auditable by a parent who knows no history.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the department's actual choices
whyPoints.description: The prescribed subject, the world history topics and the Higher Level regional option are school decisions. We name which the tutor has taught and for how many cohorts, because a History specialist for the wrong regional option is reading the syllabus alongside your child.

whyPoints.title: Feedback that is not allowed to repeat
whyPoints.description: If the same comment lands on three consecutive essays, the sessions are describing a habit rather than fixing it. We treat repetition as a failure of the teaching and change the approach, which is the opposite of the incentive a weekly open-ended arrangement creates.

whyPoints.title: A published boundary on the investigation
whyPoints.description: A tutor questions a research question, explains the criteria and comments on a student's own draft. A tutor does not supply text, restructure sections or write the reflection. The boundary is published because a market in completed coursework operates alongside this one.

whyPoints.title: No regulator used as a credential
whyPoints.description: ADEK licenses and inspects private schools in this emirate; the other emirates sit with KHDA, SPEA, the Ras Al Khaimah Department of Knowledge or the federal Ministry of Education. IB Gram holds no approval or accreditation from any of them, nor from the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and claims none.

whyPoints.title: A review that can end the arrangement
whyPoints.description: At six weeks the marked work either moved or it did not, and the recommendation can be a different component, a different tutor or stopping altogether. A review that can only recommend renewal is not a review, and in a subject this measurable there is no excuse for one.

faqs.question: How will I know whether History tutoring has actually moved the grade?
faqs.answer: By reading marked documents rather than progress updates. Ask for a marked source-paper answer with the marks shown question by question in the first two weeks, then timed essays marked against the published markbands with the band named. Two things should be visible over six weeks: the band on the component being worked should move, and the same feedback should not appear three times, because repeated feedback is feedback that was not acted on. This subject is unusually easy to audit, since every component produces a document with a number on it.

faqs.question: What should a marked History essay show me after four weeks?
faqs.answer: A band, a reason for that band, and one named move to the band above. Not a paragraph of encouragement and not a list of content the student could add. The published markbands reward focus on the question, accurate and specific knowledge, analysis rather than narrative, and a sustained argument. A useful marked essay says which of those is missing and what the student should do differently in the next one. If four weeks of marking has produced no named move, the sessions are conversations rather than teaching.

faqs.question: Which prescribed subject is my child's Abu Dhabi school teaching for the source paper?
faqs.answer: Ask the department, because the school chooses it and the whole first paper is set on it. While you are asking, get the world history topics the essays will come from and, at Higher Level, the regional option. Those three answers decide whether any given tutor is a specialist for your child or someone reading the syllabus alongside them. In this emirate the Higher Level regional option is frequently History of Africa and the Middle East, and the number of tutors who have taught that option through several cohorts is smaller than for the European options.

faqs.question: How are the marks divided across the four questions on the source paper?
faqs.answer: Twenty-four marks in one hour, split across four questions with different allocations: two short comprehension items worth three marks and two marks, a four-mark question assessing a source's value and limitations through its origin, purpose and content, a six-mark comparison and contrast of two sources, and a nine-mark answer that must use the sources together with the student's own knowledge. Because the allocations differ, the technique for each differs too, and a diagnostic marked paper tells you immediately which of the four is leaking marks.

faqs.question: Why does my child's essay keep stalling at nine out of fifteen?
faqs.answer: Three causes account for nearly all of it. The essay narrates: it recounts what happened accurately and never turns the material into an argument about the question. The evidence is generic: economic conditions worsened, opposition grew, rather than a named measure with a date and a figure. And the counter-argument is absent, because stating an objection feels like weakening the case. Each is a single repair visible in a marked script, and the usual sequence is a forced plan in which every paragraph opens with a claim about the question.

faqs.question: What does the Higher Level regional option paper actually require?
faqs.answer: Three essays of fifteen marks each across two and a half hours, on a regional option the department chooses, with no source booklet. The difficulty is breadth and stamina rather than depth: students who revise intensely on three topics find nothing to write on the third question. The strategy that works is breadth-first, aiming to be able to produce a competent plan on every section of the option within ten minutes, with full essays written only on the sections the plans reveal as weak. That plan count is itself a measure of readiness a parent can check.

faqs.question: How are the twenty-five marks on the historical investigation divided?
faqs.answer: Across three sections, each with its own criterion: an identification and evaluation of sources, the investigation itself, and a reflection on what the process revealed about the methods and limitations of historians. The second section carries the largest share. Confirm the current mark allocations and the weighting at your child's level with the Diploma coordinator rather than relying on a figure from a tutoring page. The structure is the useful thing to know, because almost every weak investigation is weak structurally rather than historically.

faqs.question: Does the 2,200-word ceiling include footnotes and the bibliography?
faqs.answer: What counts towards the ceiling is specified in the subject guide and is worth confirming with your school's coordinator, since treating the question casually causes real damage. The common failure is a student who writes to the limit on the investigation body and then has to cut the reflection to fit, losing marks allocated to a section that is quick to write well. The sensible approach is to budget the words across the three sections at the planning stage rather than discovering the problem during a final edit the night before an internal deadline.

faqs.question: What should a tutor hand back after each History session?
faqs.answer: A marked document. For paper work that means a timed answer marked against the published markbands with the band named and one move to the next band written out. For the investigation it means the section commented on with the criterion it is marked against identified and the specific weakness pointed at. A session note describing what was discussed is not evidence of anything. Specify what will be handed back before booking the block, because a provider who will not specify is telling you what to expect.

faqs.question: Can a tutor suggest the research question for the investigation?
faqs.answer: A tutor can and should question a proposed question hard: is it answerable, is it narrow enough for 2,200 words, what sources will the student actually read, and does it allow all three sections to be written properly. That interrogation is the highest-value hour in the component. What a tutor should not do is hand the student a question, because the choice is part of the assessed work and because a question the student does not own produces a reflection with nothing genuine in it. The distinction is between questioning and supplying.

faqs.question: How far ahead of the May session should History revision really start?
faqs.answer: Earlier than feels necessary for the essay papers and considerably earlier for the investigation, because the investigation's internal deadline usually sits months before anything external. The practical sequence is source-paper technique first, since it is mechanical and produces an early mark gain, then essay band repair across the middle of DP2, then breadth revision for the Higher Level option. Get the actual dates from your school's Diploma coordinator: the IB's own site blocks automated checking, so no session or results date in this project is confirmed and none is published here.

faqs.question: Is the investigation moderated, and can anyone predict the mark it will get?
faqs.answer: Internally assessed work is marked by the school and subject to the IB's moderation process, which means a school's mark can be adjusted. That is precisely why nobody should offer you a predicted mark for an investigation, and a provider who does is making a claim they cannot support. What a supervisor can tell you honestly is which criterion the current draft is weak against and what would have to change, which is more useful than a number. Treat any confident mark prediction as a reason to ask what it is based on.

faqs.question: Can an Abu Dhabi student get the sources a good investigation needs?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and the constraint is knowing where to look rather than availability. School library subscriptions frequently include academic databases nobody has shown the cohort how to use. Published document collections in translation exist for most syllabus periods, digitised newspaper archives cover the twentieth century in depth, and several national archives publish scanned material openly. One supervised hour spent learning to search properly saves a fortnight. A question requiring untranslated material or a physical archive visit is a question to change rather than to fight.

faqs.question: What does Diploma History support cost in the Abu Dhabi market?
faqs.answer: A qualified subject tutor working online across the UAE is quoted roughly AED 150-300 an hour, IB specialists from about AED 200 to AED 450 and upwards, and in-home visits roughly AED 180-500 because travel sits inside the hour. Those figures come from published provider pages and Bestimate's Dubai rate table, read in October 2026, and they describe the market rather than our prices. The question that actually separates quotes in this subject is whether marking is inside the rate, since marked written work is the entire mechanism by which History marks move.

faqs.question: What happens if the marks have not moved after six weeks?
faqs.answer: Then the arrangement should change, and a provider who cannot say so has an incentive problem. Lay the marked essays out in order and look at the feedback: if the same comment recurs, the habit is being described rather than repaired and the teaching approach is wrong rather than the student. The honest options are a different component to work on, a different tutor, or stopping. A review that can only ever recommend renewal is not a review, and in a subject where every component produces a number there is no excuse for one.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-home-tutor.closingHeading: Send one marked paper and the department's three choices
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-home-tutor.closingBody: A marked source paper with the marks shown question by question, plus the prescribed subject, the world history topics and the Higher Level regional option from your school's Diploma coordinator, is everything needed to say what the first block should do and roughly how many hours it should take. The trial that follows is free and is held by the tutor who would take the slot, with your child's own marked work on screen. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one online over live video on Gulf Standard Time; we do not make home visits in the UAE. At six weeks you will be shown the marked work and told plainly whether it moved.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB Diploma History at Standard and Higher Level to Abu Dhabi students over live video. Each profile names the prescribed subject and world history topics they teach most, the regional option they cover at Higher Level, and the hours they can hold during an Abu Dhabi term.

intro.heading: History is marked on argument, and that is a teachable skill
paragraphs: History looks like the Diploma subject that rewards knowing things. It is not. Every mark in every component is awarded for what a student does with evidence, and almost all of the lost marks in an Abu Dhabi cohort come from the same three habits: answering a source question without using the source, writing a narrative when the question asked for a judgement, and submitting an investigation that describes an event rather than examining a historical question about it. None of those is a knowledge gap. All three are structural, which is why they move quickly under one-to-one attention.

The mark arithmetic explains why. Paper 1 is a one-hour source paper worth 24 marks across four questions, and the marks are not evenly spread: three, two, four, six and nine, depending on the question set. The nine-mark question alone is worth more than the first three combined, and it is the one students practise least because it is the one that takes longest to mark. Paper 2 asks for two essays from different world history topics at 15 marks each. At Higher Level, Paper 3 adds three more essays from a regional option, also 15 marks each, over two and a half hours.

Weightings follow from that. At Standard Level, Paper 1 carries 30 per cent of the grade, Paper 2 carries 45 per cent and the historical investigation 25 per cent. At Higher Level the same investigation drops to 20 per cent, Paper 1 to 20 per cent, Paper 2 to 25 per cent, and Paper 3 takes 35 per cent. A Higher Level student who neglects the regional option is neglecting the largest single block of marks in the subject. Confirm these weightings with your child's Diploma coordinator, because the IB revises subject guides on a rolling cycle and a stale figure is worse than none.

Abu Dhabi cohorts have one local peculiarity worth naming. The regional option many schools in the emirate teach is the history of Africa and the Middle East, which has thinner commercial revision material behind it than the Europe or Americas options. A student taking it cannot simply buy a workbook and work through it. That makes the choice of tutor matter more here than in a subject with uniform resources, and it is the reason we ask which regional option a school teaches before matching anybody.

Lessons for UAE families run live online, one to one, with a shared screen. There are no home visits in Abu Dhabi; in-home tutoring is something we offer only in India. For this subject the online format carries a specific advantage: a student's essay can be annotated paragraph by paragraph during the lesson, against the band descriptors, and the annotated version saved. Source questions are worked the same way, with the examiner's wording on screen beside the student's answer.
bullets: Paper 1 is 24 marks in one hour across four questions with unequal mark values
Paper 2 and Paper 3 essays are marked out of 15 against published band descriptors
The historical investigation is 25 marks across three sections, inside 2,200 words
Higher Level Paper 3 carries the largest single weighting in the subject
Ask your school which regional option and prescribed subject it teaches before booking
Lessons are delivered online, one to one, on Gulf Standard Time

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.programmesIntro: History students in Abu Dhabi arrive from several routes, and each route leaves a different gap in the first weeks of DP1. These are the three programmes that most often precede or surround a Diploma History class in this emirate.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: History is examined by a source paper, an essay paper on world history topics, a Higher Level regional option paper, and one internally assessed historical investigation. The command vocabulary is narrow and precise: evaluate, examine, discuss, to what extent. Students who treat those verbs as synonyms write the same essay for every question and sit in the middle bands regardless of how much they know.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools differ in which prescribed subject and which world history topics they teach, so two students in neighbouring communities can be sitting materially different papers. A tutor matched without that information will teach the wrong content competently. We ask for the prescribed subject, the two world history topics and the regional option before suggesting anybody.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP individuals and societies builds genuine source-handling instincts through criterion-based investigations, and students arrive able to research and present. What they have usually never done is write to a 15-mark band descriptor under timed conditions, or answer a four-mark question about the value and limitations of one source in six minutes.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Abu Dhabi school runs MYP into its own Diploma, continuity of staff hides the step change in assessment. The first marked Paper 1 attempt in DP1 is often the moment the gap appears. A short autumn block on source questions costs far less attention than the same work attempted in the spring of DP2 alongside the investigation.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: CP students may take Diploma History as one of their DP courses and sit the identical papers under the identical descriptors. The difference is the surrounding commitments, including the career-related study and the reflective project, which compete for exactly the hours a History essay needs.
programmes.countryNote: CP cohorts in Abu Dhabi are small, so a CP History student often has nobody on the same pathway to pace against. One-to-one work gives them the calibration a class normally provides: how long a 15-mark essay should take, and what a band-five paragraph actually looks like next to a band-three one.

programmes.name: Extended Essay in History
programmes.description: A 4,000-word independent research essay on a focused historical question, supervised in school. History is a popular choice because the reading is available, and a frequent source of difficulty because students pick questions that are either unanswerable from accessible sources or so broad that no argument fits the word count.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi students have unusually good access to regional primary material through the National Archives and the emirate's museums, which makes genuinely original questions possible on Gulf and wider Middle Eastern topics. Supervision from a tutor is feedback on drafts the student has written and coaching on process; no part of the text may come from anybody else.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.subjectsIntro: History sits in Group 3 and rarely travels alone. These are the components and neighbouring courses Abu Dhabi families most often ask about in the same conversation, with the specific skill each one shares or competes with.

subjects.name: History Paper 1
subjects.description: Four questions on a prescribed subject, 24 marks in total. The value-and-limitations question wants origin, purpose and content used as evidence, not described. The compare-and-contrast question wants linked comparisons across both sources, not two separate summaries. The nine-mark question wants sources and own knowledge in the same argument.

subjects.name: History Paper 2
subjects.description: Two essays from two different world history topics, 15 marks each. The commonest loss is chronological narrative with an evaluative sentence bolted on at the end. The bands reward a thesis sustained across paragraphs, each supported by specific, dated evidence.

subjects.name: History Paper 3
subjects.levels: HL only, two and a half hours
subjects.description: Three essays from one regional option at 15 marks each, carrying 35 per cent of the Higher Level grade. Time management is a real component skill here: three full essays in 150 minutes means roughly 45 minutes each with planning, and students who overrun the first lose marks on the third.

subjects.name: Historical investigation
subjects.description: Twenty-five marks across identification and evaluation of sources, the investigation itself, and a reflection on the methods of the historian. Most lost marks sit in the first and third sections, which students treat as preamble and afterword rather than as 10 of the 25 marks.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Shares the vocabulary of power, sovereignty and intervention, and the two subjects reinforce each other on twentieth-century material. The risk is importing political theory into a History essay that needs dated evidence and historiographical awareness instead.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Taken alongside History by students heading for politics, law or international relations degrees. The industrialisation and Cold War topics benefit directly from economic literacy, provided the student keeps diagrams out of a History answer and keeps causation historical.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The closest skill neighbour History has. Both reward close reading of a text for purpose and audience, which is exactly what the Paper 1 value-and-limitations question asks for. Students strong in English A often improve fastest on source questions once the transfer is made explicit.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: History is the standing TOK case study on evidence, perspective and the limits of knowledge. The reflection section of the historical investigation is effectively a short TOK exercise, so the two can be prepared together and save a student several hours.

subjects.name: Arabic and UAE social studies
subjects.description: Private schools in the UAE are required to teach Arabic, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed curriculum under federal rules. These sit on top of the Diploma load rather than inside it, and students sometimes need help protecting History essay time from them.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: A common second Group 3 subject in Abu Dhabi where the school allows it. Psychology trains a student to cite a study and its findings, which transfers well to source use, but its essay structure is shorter and more formulaic than a 15-mark History response needs.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.regionsTitle: Abu Dhabi communities, archives and where a History student can actually find a primary source
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.regionsIntro: This emirate gives a History student something most do not: reachable primary material and institutions that hold it. These notes cover where students in each community tend to study, and what is genuinely on their doorstep for an investigation or an Extended Essay.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah and the Corniche
regions.note: Walking distance from Qasr Al Hosn, the oldest standing structure in the city and a documented site with published material. Students here have the easiest route to a locally grounded investigation question rather than a recycled Cold War topic.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Louvre Abu Dhabi sits here with catalogued collections and published exhibition scholarship. For an investigation on representation, collecting or cultural diplomacy, the material is on the island rather than behind a paywall.

regions.name: Al Maryah Island and Al Reem
regions.note: Dense apartment communities with large Diploma cohorts and tight evening schedules. Sessions here work best in 45-minute blocks on fixed evenings, which online delivery makes practical in a way a travelling arrangement does not.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: The corridor that sends us the most Diploma enquiries in the emirate. Higher Level students here are frequently sitting the Africa and the Middle East regional option, which needs a tutor who has actually taught it rather than one improvising from a Europe workbook.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Inside the same emirate and the same regulator's remit, with the oasis sites and falaj systems of the Al Ain cultural landscape close by. Students here have strong material for questions on water, settlement and the pre-oil economy, and thin local access to specialist History teaching.

regions.name: Bain Al Jessrain and Between the Two Bridges
regions.note: Villa communities positioned between the island and the mainland, so an in-home tutor's drive is unpredictable in either direction. Fixed online slots remove the variable, which matters when a timed essay has to start on the hour.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Newer schools and younger Diploma cohorts, with several families booking two children at once. Separate slots per student work better than a shared hour, because Paper 1 technique and Paper 2 essay structure need different lesson shapes.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Mussafah
regions.note: Well off the main school-run routes, which keeps the pool of locally reachable Group 3 specialists small. These are the communities where the difference between the nearest History tutor and the right one is largest.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi island, Al Bateen and the Corniche
schoolClusters.note: Students we support in these neighbourhoods attend established island schools, several running the Diploma alongside other pathways. Which prescribed subject and regional option each school teaches changes with staffing, so ask the History department rather than assuming.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.modesIntro: Three formats cover almost every History request we receive from this emirate. Each is shaped around a component rather than around a number of hours, and none of them involves a tutor travelling to a UAE address.

modes.title: Source-skills block for Paper 1
modes.description: A short, intensive run on the four question types, taken one at a time rather than as whole papers. The student answers under the clock, the tutor marks against the published expectations on a shared screen, and the same question type is repeated the following week until the mark pattern changes. This is the fastest-moving work in the subject.
bullets: One question type per session, worked to time before it is discussed
Origin, purpose and content used as evidence rather than labelled
Compare-and-contrast answers built as linked statements, not two summaries
The nine-mark question practised as a short essay with sources embedded

modes.title: Weekly essay coaching for Paper 2 and Paper 3
modes.description: A fixed weekly slot in which the student plans, writes and then re-plans essays against the 15-mark band descriptors. For Higher Level students the regional option gets its own rotation, because three essays in two and a half hours is as much a timing skill as a content one.
bullets: Band descriptors read with the student, not quoted at them
Thesis-first planning in five minutes, practised until it is automatic
Dated, specific evidence required in every paragraph
Timing drills for three consecutive Paper 3 essays

modes.title: Historical investigation supervision
modes.description: Sessions covering question choice, source selection, the evaluation of two sources, structuring an argument inside 2,200 words, and the reflection section. The tutor reads drafts the student has written and returns comments naming the section and the marks at stake. No part of the submitted text comes from the tutor, and the student is told that in the first session.
bullets: Question narrowed to something answerable from available sources
Two sources chosen for evaluative richness, not convenience
Word budget allocated across the three sections before writing starts
Reflection drafted as historiography, not as a diary entry

sections.heading: Paper 1 question by question: where the 24 marks actually sit
paragraphs: Paper 1 gives a student one hour, a small set of sources on a prescribed subject, and four questions worth 24 marks between them. The marks are deliberately unequal. The opening comprehension questions are worth three and two marks and take a few minutes. The value-and-limitations question is worth four. The compare-and-contrast question is worth six. The final question, which asks the student to use the sources and their own knowledge to assess a claim, is worth nine. That last question is worth more than the first three put together and is the one most students have attempted least often.

Each question has a failure mode that repeats across every Abu Dhabi cohort we see. The value-and-limitations answer describes a source instead of reasoning from it: a student writes that the author was a government minister and stops, rather than explaining what that position makes the source good evidence for and what it makes it poor evidence for. The compare-and-contrast answer produces two paragraphs, one per source, with no linking statements, which cannot reach the upper band however accurate it is. The nine-mark answer either forgets the sources or forgets the own knowledge, and loses roughly half the available credit either way.

The repair is mechanical, which is why this block of work moves fastest of anything in the subject. Each question type gets its own session, answered to time first and marked afterwards, with the student watching the mark being awarded or withheld sentence by sentence. Four sessions of that typically changes a mark profile more than a term of content revision, because nothing in it depends on knowing more history. It depends on doing something specific with the history already known.
bullets: Practise the nine-mark question first, not last: it carries the most credit
Value and limitations means reasoning from origin and purpose, not stating them
Compare and contrast needs linked statements covering both sources in each point
Answer to the clock before discussing, or the timing skill never develops

sections.heading: Paper 2: two essays, 15 marks each, and the narrative trap
paragraphs: Paper 2 asks for two essays in 90 minutes, drawn from two different world history topics the school has taught. Each is marked out of 15 against band descriptors that reward a clear, sustained argument, specific and accurate evidence, and an awareness that historians disagree. Nothing in those descriptors rewards coverage. A student who writes everything they know about the causes of a war, in order, with a conclusion that picks one cause, has written a competent narrative and will be marked as one.

The structural fix is to decide the judgement before writing rather than during. Five minutes of planning that produces a thesis and three or four supporting claims converts the same knowledge into a higher band, because every paragraph then argues towards something instead of arriving somewhere. The second common loss is vagueness: 'in the late nineteenth century' where a date and a name were available. Band descriptors use the word specific, and examiners apply it literally.

The third loss is the one students resist most. Both essays must be finished. Forty-five minutes each, planning included, is the budget, and an essay that runs to sixty minutes guarantees a weak second answer worth the same 15 marks. We practise this as a timing skill with a visible clock, because no amount of content revision rescues an unfinished second essay. The table below maps the twelve world history topics to the kind of question each tends to produce, so a student can see what their own topics usually demand.
bullets: Decide the judgement in planning, then argue it; do not discover it in the conclusion
Every paragraph needs at least one dated, named, specific piece of evidence
Historiographical awareness is credited; name the debate rather than quote a historian
Budget 45 minutes per essay and practise finishing both

sections.heading: Higher Level Paper 3: the regional option that carries 35 per cent
paragraphs: Paper 3 is the largest single block of marks in Higher Level History and the one most often under-prepared. The student writes three essays in two and a half hours from one regional option: the history of Africa and the Middle East, the Americas, Asia and Oceania, or Europe. Each essay is worth 15 marks under the same descriptors as Paper 2, so the skill is identical and the volume is triple. Thirty-five per cent of the final grade turns on whether a student can produce three sustained arguments in a row without the third collapsing.

For Abu Dhabi families there is a specific consideration. A number of schools in the emirate teach the history of Africa and the Middle East, which is pedagogically sensible and commercially inconvenient: there is markedly less published revision material for it than for the Europe or Americas options. A student taking it cannot work through a widely available workbook, and a tutor who has only ever taught Europe will teach the right technique against the wrong content. This is the first question we ask on a Higher Level History enquiry.

Preparation that works for this paper is sequenced rather than crammed. Early in DP2, essays are written one at a time without a clock so the argument structure is sound. Then they are written to 45 minutes. Then two consecutively, then three. The failure mode is almost never ignorance of the third topic; it is fatigue and poor time discipline in the final forty minutes of a long paper. That is trainable, and it is trained by doing it, not by reading about it.
bullets: Three essays at 15 marks each, in 150 minutes, from one regional option
Thirty-five per cent of the Higher Level grade sits in this single paper
Ask the school which regional option it teaches before choosing a tutor
Build from single untimed essays to three consecutive timed ones

sections.heading: The historical investigation: 25 marks across three sections
paragraphs: The internally assessed component is a 2,200-word historical investigation on a question of the student's own choosing, marked out of 25 marks in three sections. Section one is the identification and evaluation of sources, worth six marks. Section two is the investigation itself, worth fifteen. Section three is a reflection on what the process revealed about the methods and limitations of historians, worth four. Ten of those twenty-five marks therefore sit outside the essay most students think of as the work.

That is where the predictable losses are. Section one is routinely written as a bibliography with adjectives: two sources named, described, and called useful. The marks are for evaluating each source's value and limitations in relation to this specific investigation, which means the evaluation has to refer to the question being asked. Section three is routinely written as a personal diary about how hard the research was. The marks are for engaging with the methods of the historian, using the student's own experience as the example rather than the subject.

Section two fails more rarely but more expensively. The usual cause is a question too broad for 1,300 words of argument, which produces description. A question like 'What were the causes of a named war' cannot be answered in that space; a question about one specific disagreement between historians over one decision can. Narrowing the question is the single most valuable hour a tutor spends on this component, and it has to happen before the research, not after the first draft. A tutor comments on drafts the student has written and names the section and marks at stake; no part of the submitted text comes from anybody else.
bullets: Six marks for source evaluation, fifteen for the investigation, four for the reflection
Source evaluation must refer to this question, not to the source in general
The reflection is historiography about the student's own process, not a diary
Narrow the question before researching; it is the cheapest fix available

sections.heading: Abu Dhabi as a source base: archives, museums and a better investigation question
paragraphs: Most historical investigations submitted worldwide are about the same dozen twentieth-century topics, researched from the same secondary books. A student in this emirate has an alternative that costs nothing and marks better: regional material that is physically and institutionally reachable. Qasr Al Hosn in Al Khalidiyah is a documented site with published scholarship behind it. Louvre Abu Dhabi on Saadiyat Island holds catalogued collections and publishes exhibition research. The Al Ain cultural landscape, with its oases and falaj irrigation systems, carries a long documentary and archaeological record.

Questions built on that material are narrower by nature, which is exactly what the mark scheme rewards. A question about how one institution has represented a particular period, or about a specific historiographical disagreement over the pre-oil Gulf economy, fits inside 1,300 words of argument. A question about the causes of a world war does not. The source evaluation section also becomes easier to write well, because the student is evaluating sources they have actually handled rather than sources they have read about.

There is a practical caution. Access to collections and archives needs arranging in advance, often through the school, and nothing in that process can be promised by a tutoring provider. What a tutor can do is say which of several possible questions is answerable from what is genuinely available, which is a judgement about scope rather than an administrative favour. Students who settle their question in the first term of DP2 have time for this; students who settle it in the spring do not, and that is the real reason regional questions get abandoned for a safe Cold War topic.
bullets: Qasr Al Hosn, Louvre Abu Dhabi and the Al Ain cultural landscape are documented, reachable material
Narrow regional questions fit the 1,300-word investigation better than broad global ones
Evaluating sources the student has handled is easier to write at band level
Arrange any access through the school, and settle the question early in DP2

sections.heading: Command terms, band descriptors and the vocabulary that decides a grade
paragraphs: Every History question is built on a command term, and the terms are not interchangeable. Examine asks for an argument that considers the components of an issue. Evaluate asks for a judgement that weighs strengths against limitations. Discuss asks for a balanced review that offers a conclusion. To what extent asks for a judgement about degree, which means a measured answer rather than a yes or a no. Students who read all four as 'write about this' produce one essay shape for every question, and that shape fits the middle bands only.

The band descriptors themselves are public documents, and reading them with a student rather than at them changes behaviour quickly. The descriptors use three words repeatedly: clear, specific and sustained. Clear means the argument is identifiable in the opening lines. Specific means named people, dated events and concrete detail rather than period generalisation. Sustained means the argument is still being made in the final paragraph, not restated there for the first time since the introduction.

A productive session on this looks unspectacular. The student brings a marked essay. The tutor and student put the descriptor beside it and identify, line by line, the sentences that earn credit and the sentences that merely occupy space. Then the same question is re-planned in five minutes with the descriptor visible. Most students make a visible gain within three or four cycles of that, because the work is not about learning more history; it is about learning what the marks are for.
bullets: Examine, evaluate, discuss and 'to what extent' require different essay shapes
Band descriptors reward clear, specific and sustained argument, in those terms
The argument must be visible in the first two sentences of the essay
Re-planning a marked essay against the descriptor is the highest-yield exercise

sections.heading: Academic honesty: what a History tutor may and may not touch
paragraphs: History carries a particular integrity risk because its assessed coursework is prose, and prose can be supplied. A commercial provider in this market advertises completed internal assessments for sale. Buying one is a malpractice matter under IB rules, and the consequence lands on the candidate rather than on the seller. Any family being offered assessed work as a product should treat the offer itself as disqualifying information about the provider.

The legitimate boundary is well defined and worth stating in plain terms. A tutor may teach source evaluation, explain what a band descriptor rewards, discuss the historiography around a topic, challenge the scope of a research question, read a draft the student has written and return comments naming the section and the marks at stake. A tutor may not author any portion of a submitted text, may not supply sentences to insert, and may not hand over a finished investigation or Extended Essay. Our tutors state that boundary to the student in the first session.

There is also a copyright boundary that providers cross casually. Past papers, mark schemes, subject guides and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB and to the examination boards, and reproducing or distributing them as downloads is infringement. We reference them and link to the official source: ibo.org for IB material, and the school's Diploma coordinator for anything the IB releases through schools. A provider sending you a folder of scanned mark schemes is telling you something about how it operates.
bullets: Completed coursework sold as a product is a malpractice risk carried by the student
A tutor teaches, questions, and comments on the student's own drafts
No portion of a submitted investigation or Extended Essay comes from a tutor
Official papers and mark schemes are referenced and linked, never redistributed

sections.heading: Who may lawfully tutor a History student in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. u.ae states that it is granted free of charge for two years and that eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page describes the application route through its smart app, website and e-services system, with a two-working-day completion time and no fee listed.

u.ae also states that individuals offering private tutoring without a MoHRE permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No schedule of amounts is published, so no figure appears on this page, and a provider quoting one is guessing. Because the permit is free and quick, asking a prospective tutor whether they hold it is a reasonable question with no reasonable objection to it.

In Abu Dhabi, ADEK is the Department of Education and Knowledge, and the u.ae guidance on private schools states that it supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Gulf News has reported that ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, and that the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also prohibits serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Treat that as press-reported and verify it on adek.gov.ae before relying on exact wording. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or licence from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, operates no UAE office, and claims none of those things.

process.title: Free first lesson, terms stated up front
process.description: One 50-minute online lesson in one subject at no charge, with no card details taken and no obligation. The tutor marks a recent Paper 1 question or an essay paragraph by paragraph against the descriptors and names what is costing marks. You decide afterwards whether to continue.

process.title: A written plan mapped to components
process.description: After the free lesson you receive a plan that names the sessions, the component each one targets, and the rate in AED. If the honest recommendation is four source-skills sessions rather than a term of weekly lessons, that is what the plan will say. Nothing recurring begins before you agree it.

process.title: Fixed weekly slot that survives the term
process.description: Sessions hold the same hour each week on Gulf Standard Time and shift around mock weeks, examination periods and Ramadan timings rather than lapsing. Session notes record the question types practised and the marks achieved, so the record is specific rather than impressionistic.

process.title: Review on marks, and change course if they do not move
process.description: Every few weeks the tutor reviews marked work with you by component and band. If the mark profile is static after a fair run, the right answer is sometimes a different tutor or a different format, and we would rather recommend that than keep a booking running out of inertia.

whyPoints.title: Component-level teaching, not generic History help
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 source questions, Paper 2 world history topics, Paper 3 regional options and the historical investigation are four different skills with four different mark schemes. Matching starts from which of those is failing, which is why we ask for the school's prescribed subject and topics before suggesting anybody.

whyPoints.title: The regional option question, asked first
whyPoints.description: Schools in this emirate commonly teach the history of Africa and the Middle East at Higher Level, where commercial revision material is thin. A tutor who has taught only the Europe option will deliver correct technique against the wrong content, and a parent has no easy way to detect that until mocks.

whyPoints.title: Marked work as the unit of progress
whyPoints.description: Every session produces something marked: a timed source question, an essay paragraph, a redrafted investigation section. Annotated work is saved from the shared screen so the following week starts from evidence rather than from memory of what went wrong.

whyPoints.title: A stated coursework boundary
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, questions and comments on drafts the student has written, naming the section and marks at stake. No part of a submitted investigation or Extended Essay comes from the tutor, and the student is told that in the first session rather than in terms and conditions.

whyPoints.title: Sourced regulatory facts, no borrowed authority
whyPoints.description: Permit rules are quoted from u.ae and mohre.gov.ae, the ADEK position is flagged as press-reported until verified, and no IB examination date is published here because the IB's own site cannot be checked automatically. IB Gram claims no regulator or board approval.

whyPoints.title: A tutor pool that is not limited by driving distance
whyPoints.description: Because lessons are online, a family in Al Ain or Mussafah chooses from specialists free at that hour rather than from whoever is willing to drive. In a subject where the right Higher Level option matters, that difference decides whether a suitable tutor exists at all.

faqs.question: What does an IB DP History tutor in Abu Dhabi actually work on first?
faqs.answer: Almost always Paper 1 source questions, because they are the fastest-moving marks in the subject and the clearest diagnostic. A student who scores four out of nine on the final source question usually has the historical knowledge and is losing credit on structure: using sources without own knowledge, or own knowledge without sources. Four focused sessions on the four question types typically changes that profile. Essay work on Paper 2 and Paper 3 follows, and investigation supervision runs alongside whenever the school's internal deadline requires it.

faqs.question: How are the marks distributed across the four History Paper 1 questions?
faqs.answer: Twenty-four marks across four questions in one hour, and they are deliberately uneven. The opening comprehension questions carry three and two marks. The value-and-limitations question on one source carries four. The compare-and-contrast question across two sources carries six. The final question, requiring the sources and the student's own knowledge in a single judgement, carries nine. That final question is worth more than the first three combined, which is why we practise it first rather than last. Confirm the current structure with your child's History teacher.

faqs.question: Why does my child's Paper 2 essay score in the middle band despite good knowledge?
faqs.answer: Because the band descriptors reward argument rather than coverage. An essay that narrates events in order and names a cause in the conclusion is a competent narrative, and it is marked as one. The upper bands require a judgement stated early and sustained through every paragraph, supported by specific dated evidence, with some awareness that historians disagree. The fix is five minutes of planning that produces a thesis and three supporting claims before any prose is written. Most students move a band within three or four marked attempts once that habit sticks.

faqs.question: Which Higher Level regional option do Abu Dhabi schools usually teach for Paper 3?
faqs.answer: Several schools in the emirate teach the history of Africa and the Middle East, which suits the cohort and has noticeably less published revision material than the Europe or Americas options. That matters when choosing a tutor: technique transfers between options, content does not. A tutor who has taught only Europe will coach essay structure correctly against the wrong material, and the gap usually surfaces at mocks. Ask the History department which option and which sections they teach, then ask any prospective tutor the same question.

faqs.question: How long is the IB History historical investigation and how is it marked?
faqs.answer: It is written to a 2,200-word ceiling and marked out of 25 across three sections: six marks for the identification and evaluation of sources, fifteen for the investigation itself, and four for a reflection on the methods of the historian. Ten of the twenty-five marks therefore sit outside the central essay, which is where students most often lose credit by treating section one as a bibliography and section three as a diary. Confirm the current marks and ceiling with your child's teacher, since the IB revises guides periodically.

faqs.question: How do we narrow an investigation question that is too broad?
faqs.answer: By testing it against the word budget. Section two gives roughly 1,300 words for argument, which is not enough to answer anything beginning 'what were the causes of'. A workable question targets one specific disagreement, decision or representation, so that evidence can be weighed rather than listed. The practical test is whether two named sources can meaningfully disagree about it. Narrowing is the cheapest intervention available in this component, and it has to happen before research begins rather than after a first draft exists.

faqs.question: Can an Abu Dhabi student use local archives and museums for a History investigation?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it usually produces a better question than a recycled global topic. Qasr Al Hosn, Louvre Abu Dhabi's catalogued collections and the Al Ain cultural landscape all carry published documentary and scholarly material, and questions built on them are naturally narrow enough to argue inside 1,300 words. Access to collections or archives has to be arranged in advance, normally through the school, and no tutoring provider can arrange or promise it. Settle the question early in DP2 so there is time for that process.

faqs.question: What is the difference between examine, evaluate and 'to what extent' in a History question?
faqs.answer: They demand different essay shapes. Examine asks for an argument that considers the components of an issue. Evaluate asks for a judgement that weighs strengths against limitations. Discuss asks for a balanced review ending in a conclusion. To what extent asks for a judgement about degree, so the answer is measured rather than absolute. Students who read all of them as 'write about this' produce one shape for every question and sit in the middle bands. Twenty minutes spent separating these terms is reliably worth more than a revision session.

faqs.question: Is Higher Level History much harder than Standard Level for an Abu Dhabi student?
faqs.answer: It is longer rather than conceptually different. Higher Level adds Paper 3: three essays from a regional option in two and a half hours, carrying 35 per cent of the grade, which is the largest single block of marks in the subject. The descriptors are the same as Paper 2, so the skill is identical and the volume triples. The real difficulty is endurance and time discipline in the final forty minutes. That is trainable by building from single untimed essays to three consecutive timed ones over several months.

faqs.question: Can a History tutor help with the Extended Essay without crossing IB rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a boundary we state to the student in the first session. A tutor may challenge the research question, discuss the historiography, explain what the criteria reward, and comment on drafts the student has written. A tutor may not author any part of the submitted text, supply sentences to insert, or hand over finished work. The school supervisor remains the formal supervisor throughout. Providers advertising completed coursework are selling a malpractice risk that falls on the candidate, not on them.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a History tutor to a home in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. There are no home visits in Abu Dhabi or elsewhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Lessons are one to one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared screen used to annotate essays and source answers line by line. For this subject the format has a practical benefit: the marked version is saved, so the following week begins from the annotated evidence rather than from a recollection of what the tutor said.

faqs.question: Do History tutors working in Abu Dhabi need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is issued through MoHRE. According to u.ae it is granted free of charge for two years, with eligibility extending to registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. u.ae also states that tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no amounts are published. MoHRE's service page lists a two-working-day completion time and no fee.

faqs.question: Can my child's school History teacher give them private lessons in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: You should not be offered that arrangement. Gulf News has reported that ADEK's professional-ethics rules prohibit private and charter school staff from giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, and that the MoHRE permit code of conduct similarly bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. That is press-reported, so verify the current wording on adek.gov.ae. Beyond the rule, there is a practical reason to avoid it: the same person should not both mark internal work and be paid privately to improve it.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a DP2 History student usually need before mocks?
faqs.answer: A common pattern is four sessions concentrated on Paper 1 question types, then weekly essay coaching through the mock period, with investigation supervision folded in when the school's internal deadline approaches. Higher Level students generally add a Paper 3 timing rotation in the second term. We would rather agree a fixed block with a stated end point than open an indefinite weekly booking, and if the marked work stops improving after a fair run we will say so rather than keep the slot filled.

faqs.question: Can History lessons work around Ramadan timings and school mock weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Slots are held rather than fixed, so they move to post-Iftar timings during Ramadan and lighten or pause during school mocks and examination periods without the booking lapsing. Online delivery makes that straightforward because no journey has to be replanned around the change. Families who travel between Abu Dhabi and abroad during holidays normally keep the same tutor and the same hour, adjusting only for the time difference, which protects continuity through the weeks when essay practice most often stops.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.closingHeading: Bring one marked source question and one essay paragraph
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-history-tutor.closingBody: The quickest way to find out what is actually costing your child marks in Diploma History is to put two pieces of work in front of a specialist: a marked Paper 1 answer and one paragraph from a recent essay. That is what the free 50-minute online lesson is built around, in one subject, with no card details taken and no obligation to continue. You will leave it with a written plan naming the component each session targets, the rate in AED, and a straight answer about whether source skills, essay structure or investigation supervision is the right place to spend the time. Lessons run online from any community in the emirate, on Gulf Standard Time.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These are Diploma subject specialists, matched by subject and level rather than by how far they live from your community. The rate you are quoted depends on the level, the component and how rare the specialism is, which is what the tables on this page break down.

intro.heading: Pricing a Diploma year properly, before anyone quotes you an hour
paragraphs: A Diploma student takes six subjects. That single fact is what makes Diploma tutoring a budgeting problem rather than a shopping problem, and it is the thing most rate comparisons ignore. A rate of AED 250 an hour sounds reasonable in isolation. Two subjects at one weekly hour each for thirty teaching weeks is a different conversation, and a family that has not done that arithmetic before the first phone call tends to make the decision twice: once optimistically in September and again, under pressure, in February.

The Abu Dhabi market quotes in several incompatible ways, which is the second reason families overpay. Some providers quote an hourly rate with marking included and some do not. Some quote a monthly package against a session count and leave the session length vague. Visiting tutors quote a rate that has travel inside it without saying how much, so a family comparing an in-home rate to an online rate is comparing two different products and usually concludes the online one is cheaper for the wrong reason. The honest comparison is per hour of teaching actually received, with marking, and that is the comparison this page sets out.

Abu Dhabi has its own cost drivers, and distance is the obvious one. The emirate is geographically spread in a way Dubai is not: the island, the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, Yas and Saadiyat, and the mainland communities out towards Shakhbout City and Mohammed Bin Zayed City. A visiting tutor crossing from one of those to another at five in the afternoon is spending real time, and that time is in your rate whether or not the invoice names it. Nobody drives forty minutes each way for free, and a tutor who appears not to be charging for it is either charging for it somewhere else or will not last the term.

The second Abu Dhabi driver is cohort size. Diploma cohorts in this emirate are smaller than in Dubai, and for less common Higher Level subjects a school may have three or four candidates. That thins the local supply of anyone who has taught that subject, and thin supply raises the price of the few people who have. It is why a Mathematics HL hour and a Film HL hour are not the same purchase in Abu Dhabi even though both are Diploma hours, and why availability rather than price often becomes the real constraint in February.

What follows is the whole cost picture: the market bands and who publishes them, the travel hour priced out across Abu Dhabi's actual distances, the nine variables that move a Diploma quote in this emirate, how monthly packages compare to paying per session, and where tuition sits inside a Diploma budget alongside school fees and examination registration. IB Gram's figures are not in these tables, because we do not publish a price list: our model is a free first lesson and then a quote that depends on the subject, the level and the rarity of the specialism. What we will do is show you how to read everyone else's.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: The programme your child is in changes the rate before anything else does. These are the IB programmes Abu Dhabi families price, with what each one costs differently and why.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The most expensive hour in the IB range, because the tutor needs subject depth at Higher Level plus familiarity with a specific internally assessed component and its published criteria. Market figures put IB specialist tutoring at roughly AED 200 to 450 an hour, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and BartyED AED 650 at the premium end.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the Diploma premium is sharpened by cohort size. A school with four candidates in a Higher Level subject produces almost no local pool of people who have taught it, so the rate for that subject sits at the top of the band while a Mathematics or Biology hour sits in the middle. Families on Saadiyat Island and Al Reem Island report the widest spread in quotes, which usually reflects subject rarity rather than any difference in quality.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Cheaper per hour than the Diploma and usually cheaper in total, because an MYP student rarely needs more than one or two subjects supported and there is no external examination driving an intensive block. Qualified subject tutors working online sit around AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 as the nearest comparable band.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi parents often start spending at MYP 4 or 5, when criterion-referenced grades begin to look like they matter for Diploma entry. Spending here is better value than spending in DP2, for an unglamorous reason: an MYP hour fixes marking-language problems that would otherwise cost Diploma hours at double the rate two years later.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The lowest rates in the range and the shortest sessions, typically forty-five minutes rather than sixty because that is the limit of useful concentration for a primary-age child. Market budget and generalist online bands apply here, which run from roughly AED 33 to 150 an hour depending on the provider, per EdFlik's and Tutopiya's published figures.
programmes.countryNote: The Abu Dhabi complication at primary level is sibling bookings. Families in Al Raha Gardens, Khalifa City and Al Reef frequently have two or three children in the same primary school and ask whether one session can cover them. It can, at a per-student rate below the one-to-one rate, but only where the children are within a year of each other and working on the same thing.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: Priced like the Diploma for the Diploma courses a student takes, and generally unsupported for the career-related study itself, which is school-specific. The reflective project is coached as a process rather than taught as content, which is slower work and usually priced accordingly.
programmes.countryNote: Few Abu Dhabi schools run the Career-related Programme, so families who need it tend to find no local tutor at all for the career-related element and only subject specialists for the Diploma courses. That is a coverage problem rather than a pricing one, and it is worth establishing before a budget is set.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Diploma subjects do not cost the same amount, and the reason is supply rather than difficulty. These are the subjects Abu Dhabi families ask us to price, with where each sits in the market band and why.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The deepest local pool and therefore the most competitively priced Diploma hour in Abu Dhabi, usually mid-band. Higher Level carries a premium over Standard Level because proof, calculus and the harder optional content narrow the field of people who can teach it confidently.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mid to upper band. Supply is reasonable at Standard Level and thinner at Higher Level, where fields and modern physics plus uncertainty treatment in the exploration are the specialist part. Expect a quote above the Mathematics equivalent in this emirate.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Upper-mid band, with organic mechanisms and the exploration's research-question design being the work families actually pay for. Chemistry HL is the single most requested Higher Level subject we see from Abu Dhabi, which keeps its rate firm through the autumn.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Mid-band and well supplied. Much of the paid work is command-term and timing technique rather than content, which means fewer total hours than Chemistry or Physics for the same grade movement, and a lower overall bill.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Mid-band for teaching and upper-band for commentary supervision, because the three commentaries are slow criterion-driven work on the student's own text. Families who budget for subject teaching and then discover commentary support is separate are a common pattern.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Mid-band, with the individual oral and the higher-level essay being the components that attract a premium. Supply in Abu Dhabi is adequate rather than deep, and the better specialists are booked early in the autumn.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.levels: A and B, HL and SL
subjects.description: Variable and often upper-band, because the A and B routes need genuinely different teachers and the pool for language A literary analysis at Higher Level is small. KHDA's published guidance requires schools to teach Arabic in separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, which is the same distinction that governs who can usefully tutor your child.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Top of the band and frequently unavailable locally. Three internally assessed components and no written papers means the whole grade is criteria work, and the number of people in Abu Dhabi who have marked a process portfolio is very small.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Mid-band, with the Higher Level pre-released case study creating a short, expensive window of demand in the spring. Booking that window in the autumn costs considerably less than trying to buy it in March.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Mid to upper band. Much of the paid work is the internally assessed experimental study, where the statistics have to be chosen before the design is fixed, and that is slower than content teaching and priced as such.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi's distances are the hidden line item in every in-home quote. These are the communities Diploma families ask from, with what the geography does to a visiting rate and to the hour a session can start.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: A short run to the island schools and a long one to anywhere on the mainland. In-home quotes here tend to sit at the top of the band because tutors factor the causeway and the limited number of households they can serve in an evening.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Dense towers, so a visiting tutor can in theory serve several families in one building. In practice the bridge traffic at 5pm decides the start time, and quotes reflect the one-trip-per-evening reality rather than the theoretical density.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Shakhbout City
regions.note: A large villa population a genuine drive from the island. Visiting rates here carry the longest travel component in the emirate, which is why these are the communities where the online comparison is most lopsided in cost terms.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Close to the airport road and reasonably central for a tutor working the corridor, so travel loading is moderate. This is also one of the few areas where enough IB families cluster to make group pricing a real option.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Short commutes and dense school provision, so in-home supply is better here than anywhere else in Abu Dhabi and quotes are correspondingly softer. A 4pm start is realistic, which widens the number of tutors who can take the booking.

regions.name: Yas Island and West Yas
regions.note: A newer population with fewer tutors living locally. Families here frequently receive in-home quotes with an explicit travel surcharge, and just as frequently find that no specialist in a thin Higher Level subject will make the trip at all.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City and Mussafah
regions.note: The furthest regular drive from the island schools, and the area where in-home rates and the practical start time both suffer most. Weekend blocks are more realistic than weekday evenings for most households here.

regions.name: Al Reef and Al Falah
regions.note: Settled villa communities out past the airport. The travel loading is substantial and the local pool is thin, so families here are the most likely to end up paying a premium for a generalist rather than a standard rate for a specialist.

schoolClusters.city: Island and Saadiyat schools
schoolClusters.note: Where the shortest commutes and the deepest in-home supply sit. School fees at this end of the market are also the highest, which matters when tuition is added to an existing budget rather than considered alone.
