sections.heading: ADEK's ethics rule, the MoHRE permit, and what a cheap unpermitted hour really costs
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit, not left to the market. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and the eligible categories are broad: teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing and lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the ministry's app, website and e-services.

Because the permit costs nothing, a tutor who does not hold one is not saving money by skipping it. People offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so no amount is quoted here; figures circulating online could not be verified against a ministry source. The practical point for a parent is narrower: a permit is free and quick, so its absence tells you something about how the arrangement is being run.

Abu Dhabi adds a second rule that matters specifically here. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics framework for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with the MoHRE permit's code of conduct carrying a similar restriction. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it. Either way, the implication for a Music student is clear: the obvious cheap option, your child's own classroom music teacher taking a paid evening slot, is the option to leave alone.

sections.heading: What no amount of money buys in Diploma Music
paragraphs: Some things in this subject are not for sale at any rate, and a provider willing to sell them is a provider to walk away from. The clearest is assessed work. Every word of the written exploration, every recording linked to the experimentation report, every item in the presenting music submission and every artefact of the Higher Level project has to be the student's own. A tutor teaches, questions, reviews and gives feedback on work the student has produced. Anyone offering finished components is offering malpractice, and the consequence lands on the student, not on the seller.

The second is a grade. No tutor can promise a 7, and any page that does is telling you something about itself rather than about your child. Marks in Music follow research quality, documentation and justification, all of which take time the student has to spend personally. A page that promises a specific score in exchange for a specific fee should be read with real scepticism, whatever the fee is.

The third is a shortcut through the school's own process. Internal deadlines, moderation and the subject teacher's judgement sit with the school, and no external tutor sits inside that. What an outside specialist can honestly add is narrower and still valuable: component interpretation that is accurate, feedback early enough to act on, and a plan that survives the term it was written in. Priced at the market specialist band, that is a reasonable purchase. Priced as a guarantee, it is a fiction.

sections.heading: When no Abu Dhabi Music specialist is free
paragraphs: Arts subjects are the thinnest part of the tutoring market in every emirate, and Diploma Music is thinner than Visual Arts. Pretending otherwise would be the easiest thing on this page and the least useful, so here is the position as it stands. Requests for Standard Level component work are usually matched quickly. Requests for Higher Level project supervision in a specific week take longer, and requests that insist on a UAE-resident tutor in a 17:00 slot sometimes cannot be met at all.

The fallback is disclosed rather than hidden. Where no UAE-based specialist covers a component, IB Gram matches from its wider pool of Diploma Music tutors working to Gulf Standard Time, most often from India, at the same online format and the same hourly basis. Families are told where the tutor is before a session is booked, not after. Several providers in this search route UAE parents to non-UAE numbers without saying so; the disclosure is the difference, not the arrangement.

What this means for the money is simple. Availability, not price, is the binding constraint on arts subjects in this emirate, so flexibility on timing buys more than negotiation on rate. A family that can take a 19:30 slot has a materially wider choice of specialist than a family that can only take 17:00, and at the same published band. The table sets out what to expect by request type, so the trade-off between a convenient hour and a specialist one is visible before anything is booked.

process.title: Name the component, not the subject
process.description: Tell us which component is the problem: the written exploration, the experimentation report, presenting music, or the Higher Level project. A request phrased as the component gets matched to someone who has worked on it. A request phrased as help with Music gets matched to a general music teacher, which is a different purchase at a similar price.

process.title: Send a draft, a score and one recording
process.description: Before the free trial lesson, send whatever exists: a partial draft, a score, a single recording, and the school's internal deadline. The trial is then spent reading the actual work against the actual criteria instead of on introductions. One free trial lesson per student, booked without card details.

process.title: Agree the hours and the finish line
process.description: We quote by the hour at the market specialist band and agree how many sessions the block contains and what it ends with. Open-ended arrangements drift and cost more over a Diploma year than bounded ones. If the work finishes early, the block ends early rather than rolling on.

process.title: Keep the instrumental teacher
process.description: Nothing in a Diploma Music block replaces instrumental teaching, and paying a Diploma tutor to run technique work is paying the specialist band for the wrong lesson. The two bills cover different jobs. Where a student has no instrumental teacher, the school's department is the first place to ask, not us.

process.title: Review on the submission, not on a feeling
process.description: At the end of the block, the test is whether the submission met its own limits, carried its documentation, and justified its material. That is checkable. A general sense that sessions were going well is not, and it is how rolling arrangements survive long past the point they were useful.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted as the market's, with the source named
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page is attributed to the provider or rate table that published it, with the month it was read. Three of the six competitor pages researched for this market publish no price at all, and two quote in US dollars. A number you can trace is worth more than a number that sounds reassuring.

whyPoints.title: Component limits treated as part of the task
whyPoints.description: Word counts, timings and evidence requirements are checked against the current subject guide at the start of a block, not discovered in the final week. Overrun is the cheapest failure to prevent and one of the most expensive to fix late, which makes it the first thing a session should settle.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery stated plainly, with no travel premium
whyPoints.description: Lessons for UAE families run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses, so no drive is being priced into the hour. The saving is real and it buys additional sessions rather than additional kilometres.

whyPoints.title: Availability disclosed before a booking, not after
whyPoints.description: Arts subjects are thin in this market. Where no UAE-resident specialist covers a component, the wider online pool is offered and the tutor's location is stated before anything is confirmed. No competitor page researched for this market discloses a coverage limit at all.

whyPoints.title: Submitted work stays the student's own
whyPoints.description: Teaching, questioning, marking-style feedback and process coaching on drafts the student has produced. No supplied text, no finished components, no editing to completion. One page ranking in this search sells completed assessments outright; that is an academic-integrity breach and a risk carried entirely by the student.

whyPoints.title: No accreditation claimed that we do not hold
whyPoints.description: IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. It holds no approval, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE as an institution, the IB or any examination board, and it has no office in the UAE. Regulators are explained on this page, never implied as endorsers.

faqs.question: How much does an IB DP Music tutor cost per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published market bands put specialist IB tutoring at roughly AED 200-450 an hour and above. Unitors lists IB from AED 200, TutorChase publishes AED 270, and Bestimate's 2026 tutoring cost table puts specialist IB, IGCSE and A-Level work at AED 200-450 and higher, with one-to-one visits at AED 180-350. Cheaper online options exist from around AED 33-65 an hour, but those sit at the university-student end and rarely work at component level on Diploma Music. Those are other providers' figures as published in October 2026. IB Gram prices by the hour at the specialist end and starts with a free trial lesson rather than a package.

faqs.question: Why would a Music hour cost more than a Maths hour for the same student?
faqs.answer: Because the supply is thinner and the knowledge is narrower. Maths tutors who know the Diploma syllabus are plentiful in this emirate. Tutors who can say what the experimentation report asks for, what the presenting music programme notes are marked on, and how a Higher Level project has to be evidenced are not. Scarcity shows up in the rate. The counterweight is that Music hours are usually fewer and attached to a named component with a deadline, so the total spend across a Diploma year is often lower than for an examined subject that needs weekly support for two years.

faqs.question: Does my child still need an instrumental teacher if we book Diploma Music support?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they are separate purchases. An instrumental teacher builds technique, repertoire and performance readiness. A Diploma Music tutor works on the assessed components: research for the exploration, documentation for the experimentation report, selection and rationale for presenting music, and scope and evidence for the Higher Level project. No part of the Diploma grade is awarded for grade-exam standard. Paying a Diploma specialist at the specialist band to run scales is paying a premium rate for the wrong lesson, and dropping the instrumental teacher to afford it removes the thing that makes the student's own material credible.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a Music tutor to our villa in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India. Diploma Music support for families here is delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with scores, drafts and recordings opened on a shared screen. For this subject the online format is not a compromise. Score and audio work is easier to do well on a shared screen than across a kitchen table, and removing the drive means a Khalifa City family can book a component specialist rather than whoever can reach the community by six.

faqs.question: How many hours does a Diploma Music component usually take to sort out?
faqs.answer: A written exploration commonly takes six to ten hours spread across two terms. The experimentation report takes five to eight, front-loaded, because the documentation has to happen while the work is happening. Presenting music is shorter, four to six hours near the deadline. The Higher Level project is the big one at eight to fourteen hours across DP2, mostly spent on scope and evidence rather than on music. At AED 250 an hour, the middle of the published specialist band, those ranges give a usable budget shape, and they are ranges rather than quotes.

faqs.question: Which term of the Diploma is the expensive one for Music?
faqs.answer: DP2 autumn, consistently. Internal deadlines for the written components cluster there, the Higher Level project is usually mid-flight, and every student in the cohort wants the same slots in the same fortnight. DP1 autumn is the cheapest and highest-leverage term: two to four hours spent settling the exploration's direction and the experimentation plan prevents most of the DP2 scramble. DP2 spring is close to free for Music because the submissions are closed and attention moves to examined subjects. Budgeting across the two years rather than reacting to deadlines is what lowers the total.

faqs.question: My child plays to a high standard. Will Diploma Music be easy for them?
faqs.answer: Not automatically, and this is the most common misreading of the course. The Diploma assesses research, experimentation, documentation and justification, delivered through written work and curated recordings. A student with a strong instrument can submit a weak exploration, because the exploration is a research task that happens to be about music. Instrumental fluency helps with the presenting music component and with producing credible experimentation material, so it is a real advantage. It is not the grade. The students who struggle most are often the strongest players, because nobody warned them the written half was the half that counts.

faqs.question: Can a tutor look at my child's experimentation report and tell us what it is missing?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is a normal first session. The tutor reads the draft against what the component asks for and names what is absent, which in this component is almost always the abandoned attempt. A report that describes a clean path from idea to outcome reads as written afterwards, because the credit sits in the decisions that did not work. The feedback is on the student's own draft and the student makes the changes. A tutor never supplies text for a submitted component, and anyone offering to is offering something that puts the student's diploma at risk.

faqs.question: Is a cheaper tutor at AED 60 an hour ever the right choice for this subject?
faqs.answer: For general music theory or help catching up on missed content, possibly. For an assessed Diploma component, rarely. The lower bands in this market are staffed largely by university students and generalists, and the thing a Music submission needs is someone who knows the component's limits and failure modes. Buying four cheap hours that produce a tidy but unjustified draft costs less than two specialist hours and achieves less. The honest version of the trade-off is that the cheap hour is good value for content and poor value for criteria.

faqs.question: Do tutors working with Abu Dhabi students need a MoHRE permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private tutoring in the UAE need a MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years and covers school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here. Since the permit is free, its absence is a signal worth asking about.

faqs.question: Can we book my child's own school music teacher for paid evening sessions instead?
faqs.answer: That is the option to leave alone in this emirate. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct is reported to carry a similar restriction. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on the detail. The practical answer is that it creates a problem for the teacher and an awkward conflict around moderation of your child's own submitted work, for no educational gain.

faqs.question: What should the free trial lesson actually produce for a Music student?
faqs.answer: One concrete change and a limit to work to. Send the current draft, a score and a recording beforehand, plus the school's internal deadline. The trial is then spent reading the real work against the real criteria rather than on introductions, and it should end with the student knowing what the next version has to do differently. One free trial lesson per student, booked without card details. If the component turns out to need less help than feared, saying so is a better outcome than selling a block nobody needed.

faqs.question: Is Higher Level Music worth the extra spend for a university application?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the degree direction, and it should be checked on the university's own admissions pages rather than taken from any tutoring site. Conservatoire and music-degree routes usually weigh audition and portfolio alongside grades, and a Higher Level project can be useful evidence of independent practice. For a non-music degree, Higher Level Music is one Higher Level among three and carries no special weight. What it reliably does add is a documented piece of real-world creative work, which is a different kind of asset from a points total.

faqs.question: Our school has only one Higher Level Music candidate this year. Does that change anything?
faqs.answer: It changes the cost, yes. A cohort of one has no precedent to lean on: no classmate who has already scoped a project, no accumulated departmental sense of what works. The conversation a larger cohort has for free is the conversation those families end up buying, usually three to five hours early in DP2 spent pressure-testing scope and evidence requirements. It is the single best-value purchase in this subject, because a project scoped around a venue or collaborator who later says no is very hard to rescue late.

faqs.question: Can sessions move during Ramadan and around school production weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for Music they usually have to. Ramadan shifts school hours and family routines across the UAE, and post-Iftar slots work better than late afternoon for many households. School concert and production weeks matter here more than in other subjects, because the music department and its spaces are fully committed and a student's own recording time disappears. Blocks are planned around both, with the heavier documentation work placed in the quieter weeks either side rather than scheduled into a fortnight nobody is free in.

faqs.question: What happens if no Abu Dhabi-based Music specialist is available?
faqs.answer: You are told before anything is booked. Arts subjects are the thinnest category in this market, and Higher Level project supervision is thinner than Standard Level component work. Where no UAE-resident specialist covers the component, the match comes from the wider pool of Diploma Music tutors working to Gulf Standard Time, most often from India, at the same online format and the same hourly basis. The tutor's location is stated upfront. Flexibility on timing widens the choice considerably: a 19:30 slot reaches a materially larger pool than a fixed 17:00 one.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-music-home-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the component and the deadline, not with the hourly rate
abu-dhabi/ib-dp-music-home-tutor.closingBody: An IB DP music home tutor in Abu Dhabi is a straightforward purchase once the question is framed properly. Name the component, send the current draft and one recording, state the school's internal deadline, and the free trial lesson will tell you whether a block is worth buying and roughly how big it needs to be. Market rates in this emirate run at AED 200-450 an hour at the specialist end, and this page shows where every one of those figures comes from. Lessons run one-to-one online on Gulf Standard Time, every word submitted stays your child's own, and nothing on this page promises a grade.

intro.heading: Why a strong player can be a weak Music candidate
paragraphs: The call that brings most Abu Dhabi families to an IB DP Music tutor sounds the same every time. The student has played an instrument for a decade, performs in the school production, possibly passed a high practical grade, and is predicted a 4. Nothing is wrong with the musician. What is wrong is that the course measures three things and the family has been investing in one of them, usually for years, without anyone explaining that the other two carry most of the marks.

Diploma Music asks a student to operate as researcher, performer and creator across four areas of inquiry, and almost everything assessed is submitted as a document, a recording or a report rather than performed in a room. There is written analysis of music in context. There is a record of experimentation in which the student has demonstrably tried things with music rather than only talked about them. There is a presented programme of performing and creating with programme notes. Higher Level students add a real-world project.

The consequence for a parent is uncomfortable but useful. Instrumental lessons, however good, do not address two of the three roles, and a tutor who simply plays alongside your child will not either. The useful work in this subject is analysis taught like an essay subject, experimentation structured so it leaves evidence behind, and a programme chosen and documented to show range rather than to show off. That is what this page is about.

On delivery: IB Gram teaches UAE students one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time, with scores, recordings, notation files and written drafts shared on screen. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home visits are a service we run only in India. For the written and analytical work that carries most of the grade, a shared screen with the score open is the precise tool for the job. Instrumental technique is better served by your child's existing teacher, and we say so rather than pretending otherwise.

The boundary, stated plainly. The student performs, composes, experiments and writes. A tutor teaches analysis and technique of writing, questions a programme choice, explains what a criterion is asking for, and marks practice analysis against the published descriptors. Nobody at IB Gram composes, arranges, records or writes any part of a submission, and generative tools used in any creative work must be acknowledged exactly as the school requires. Providers in this market sell finished coursework; the risk of using one is carried entirely by your child. One practical reassurance before any of the detail: monitoring this subject requires no musical training. Every check on this page is a question about whether a document exists, how long it is, and whether the claims in it point at a specific moment in a specific piece.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-music-tutor.programmesIntro: Music is examined in the Diploma, and the skills that decide the grade build earlier. Here is what each IB stage contributes for an Abu Dhabi student heading towards it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two years working as researcher, performer and creator across four areas of inquiry, submitting written analysis, a record of experimentation and a presented programme, with an additional project at Higher Level. Marks are lost by students who perform well and document nothing, and by students who write about music in general terms without showing the specific moment in the score that justifies the claim.
programmes.countryNote: Music departments in Abu Dhabi schools vary more than any other subject we support. Some have a full department and an active ensemble programme; some run the Diploma course with one part-time specialist. That gap, rather than any difference in student ability, explains most of the variation in results we see across the emirate.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Middle Years Arts introduces the process journal and the habit of reflecting on musical decisions in writing, which is exactly what the Diploma later assesses. A Year 11 student who has analysed a piece in writing and documented a composition arrives in DP1 ready for the components rather than surprised by them.
programmes.countryNote: In several Abu Dhabi schools music at this stage is largely performance and production based, with light written work. We check what a student has actually written before deciding whether a DP1 plan starts with analysis skills or with content.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No bearing on a Diploma grade. What carries forward is aural confidence and the expectation that music is talked about as well as played, both of which are established far earlier than any formal theory teaching.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: A route that suits students combining Diploma courses with a music, production or performing-arts career study. Music taken within it is assessed against the same subject guide, so the work a tutor does is identical.
programmes.countryNote: Rare in Abu Dhabi, which means a family on this route seldom finds anyone locally who has supported it. Online matching answers a problem that was only ever about distance.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-music-tutor.subjectsIntro: Music students in Abu Dhabi commonly need a second subject supported in the same year. These are the Diploma courses our tutors cover alongside it, and where the skills genuinely transfer.

subjects.name: Music
subjects.description: Researcher, performer and creator roles across four areas of inquiry, with written analysis, documented experimentation and a presented programme. Marks go missing on general claims about style unsupported by a specific moment in the music, and on experimentation that was done but never recorded.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The nearest analytical neighbour. A student who can explain how a text produces an effect has the skill the Music written components need, applied to sound instead of words. Students strong here usually need the least help with analysis.

subjects.name: Film
subjects.description: Shares the problem of writing analytically about a time-based medium and of documenting a creative process for assessment. Students taking both often reuse analytical vocabulary about structure and effect across the two subjects.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Shares the discipline of documenting process and defending a selection. The two sets of written work must stay distinct in purpose: one argues a curatorial intention, the other a musical one.

subjects.name: Theatre
subjects.description: Overlaps around music for dramatic impact and entertainment. Students taking both have ready-made material for one area of inquiry, provided the musical analysis is genuinely musical rather than theatrical.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Useful for the sociocultural and political dimension of the course. Students taking both write stronger contextual sections because they treat context as evidence rather than as introduction.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Listed because it is the most common fourth subject among Music students we support in the emirate, and a weak grade here is what most often threatens an otherwise comfortable Diploma total.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: Relevant for students researching regional repertoire, where primary sources, lyrics and performance practice may be in Arabic. A student who can read the sources writes a different quality of contextual analysis.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: Questions about interpretation, authenticity and cultural ownership arise in both. A single tutor can keep the student's position consistent across a Music component and a TOK exhibition.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Music is a strong choice for students who can analyse a score, and a poor one for students who want to write a biography of a composer. Support is process coaching and reading what the student has already written.

sections.heading: What Diploma Music actually asks a student to submit
paragraphs: Parents consistently underestimate how much of this course is writing and documentation. The three submitted strands at Standard Level cover exploring music in context, experimenting with music, and presenting music, and each combines written work with musical material the student has produced. Higher Level adds a project rooted in a real-life musical context. There is no single examination hall moment that carries the subject; there are deadlines, and work that exists or does not.

The written limits matter because they are hard. Exploring music in context allows a substantial written submission; the experimenting report is much shorter; the programme notes attached to the presented programme are shorter still. Students routinely write to the limit on the component they enjoy and skimp the one they do not, which is a predictable way to lose marks in two places at once. Confirm every figure with your school, because guides are revised and schools adopt revisions at different points.

The table sets the components side by side with what must be submitted, the written limit and what the marks actually reward. The right-hand column is the one to read first. In every component the credit goes to specificity: a named moment in a named piece, a documented experiment with a stated outcome, a programme choice justified by what it demonstrates. General admiration of music scores nothing anywhere in this subject. It is also worth noticing what the table does not contain: an examination that can be revised for in the usual sense. There is no paper at the end of this course to rescue a weak year, which is why the internal deadline calendar is the document that governs the subject.

sections.heading: Three roles, and finding the one that is failing
paragraphs: The most useful hour in this subject is usually diagnostic. The course assesses a student as researcher, performer and creator, and a candidate is rarely weak in all three. A student with a high practical grade is typically strong as performer, adequate as creator and untrained as researcher. A student who composes in software all weekend is often the reverse. Identifying which role is dragging the grade turns a vague worry into a plan.

The researcher role is where Abu Dhabi students most often lose ground, and the reason is structural rather than musical. Analysis of music is a written skill taught in English lessons and almost never in instrumental ones, so a student who has had a decade of excellent instrumental teaching may never once have been asked to explain how a passage works. That is not a deficiency in the student; it is a gap in what they have been taught, and it responds quickly to teaching.

The table sets out each role, what a strong version looks like, the characteristic weakness, and what a session actually does about it. Families should read the third column carefully and decide which line describes their child. Booking a tutor without that answer tends to produce pleasant sessions about music in general, which is the most common way money is wasted in this subject. The diagnosis is also worth repeating later in the course. A student whose researcher role was the weakness in DP1 can reach DP2 with that fixed and a new problem in the creating strand, and a plan written in September that is never revisited stops matching the student by February.

sections.heading: The analysis gap: playing well is not explaining well
paragraphs: Written analysis is the part of this course that most reliably separates grades, and it is a teachable skill rather than a talent. The weak version asserts: the piece is dramatic, the harmony is interesting, the rhythm drives the music forward. None of these can be credited because none of them points at anything. The strong version locates: at this timing, the bass drops out, which removes the harmonic anchor and makes the entry two bars later feel unresolved.

The mechanism we teach is deliberately mechanical, because students under pressure need a procedure rather than inspiration. Hear it, locate it, name it, explain its effect, connect it to the context. Five steps, applied to anything. A student who can run that sequence on a recording they have never met before has the researcher role solved, and the same sequence serves the programme notes and the Higher Level project.

Score reading helps and is not strictly necessary at the level this course requires. A student who learned by ear can locate events by timing instead of bar number and still score well, provided they are precise. What does not work is vagueness in either system. We usually build minimal score literacy alongside aural location, because the two reinforce each other and because being able to point at a bar makes a written claim far harder to dispute. The fastest way to build the habit is to practise on music the student already knows intimately. A piece they have performed gives them the ear and the fingers to find the moment instantly, so the only new skill being learned is the explaining, which is the part that is actually assessed.

sections.heading: Choosing contexts, and the Gulf repertoire advantage
paragraphs: The course is framed by four areas of inquiry covering music for sociocultural and political expression, music for listening and performance, music for dramatic impact and entertainment, and music technology in the electronic and digital age. A student must range across them rather than retreat into the one their instrument lives in. The commonest failure is a portfolio that is four variations on Western classical repertoire with one token world-music example attached at the end.

Students in Abu Dhabi have an advantage here they consistently fail to use. Regional and Arabic musical traditions, the recorded and live music of the Gulf, and the local presence of international performance and production offer genuine, accessible material for at least two areas of inquiry. A student writing about music for sociocultural expression with reference to repertoire they have heard performed locally is on stronger ground than one summarising a textbook account of a tradition they have only read about.

Two cautions. First, respect is not optional: writing about a tradition requires engaging with how its own practitioners describe it, not imposing Western analytical categories and calling it analysis. Second, sources in Arabic are an asset rather than an obstacle for students who read the language, and should be cited properly. The school's music teacher is the right person to confirm referencing requirements for each component, and the student must acknowledge every source and every generative tool used. A sensible way to plan coverage is to map the four areas against the student's own repertoire early in DP1 and look for the gap. Whichever area has nothing in it is the one to build a context around, and choosing it deliberately in Year 12 is far cheaper than discovering the hole during DP2.

sections.heading: Recording in Abu Dhabi: what is judged and what is not
paragraphs: Recorded material is how the performing and creating work reaches an assessor, and students lose marks to recording problems that cost nothing to solve. The thing being judged is the music, not the production value, but a recording in which the instrument is distorted, the room swamps the detail or a phone microphone clips on every loud passage prevents the music from being heard at all. Those are avoidable losses rather than aesthetic preferences.

Apartment living across Al Reem Island, the Corniche and Al Raha Beach creates the two usual problems: hard reflective surfaces and neighbours. Both have cheap answers. Soft furnishings, a duvet over a reflective wall, recording away from the corner of a room, and a microphone placed further from a loud instrument rather than closer deal with most of it. School music rooms are usually available by arrangement and are the better option for anything amplified or percussive.

The table sets out the situations we meet most often in this emirate, the specific problem each creates, the cheapest workable fix and what it changes about the submission. None of it requires buying equipment. Students who test a recording set-up in Year 12 rather than on the day of the deadline avoid the single most frustrating category of lost marks in this subject. One further point specific to this emirate: schools here often have better-equipped music rooms than families realise, including interfaces and microphones bought for productions. Asking the music teacher what is available, and when it is free, is usually more productive than buying anything.

sections.heading: Experimenting with music, and the evidence it leaves behind
paragraphs: Experimentation is the component families understand least and lose most marks on. Students assume it means trying things, and they do try things constantly: a different voicing, a sample slowed down, a rhythmic idea borrowed from something they analysed. The problem is that experimentation which leaves no trace cannot be credited. A student who spent six months genuinely exploring and recorded none of it has, for assessment purposes, done nothing.

The useful definition is narrower and more actionable than students expect. An experiment starts from something encountered in the music studied, tries it practically, produces a result that can be heard, and leads to a stated decision about what to do next. That chain is what the report needs to show. A list of things attempted without outcomes reads as activity, and activity is not the same as experimentation.

The routine that works is small. After each working session, export or record whatever exists, however rough, note in two sentences what was tried and what happened, and date it. Ten minutes. Over a year that produces a body of evidence no retrospective write-up can match, and it makes the report straightforward to assemble because the material is already there. Students in Abu Dhabi working largely in software have the easiest version of this, since project files already carry a history if they are saved as separate versions rather than overwritten. Students working on paper or at an acoustic instrument need the equivalent discipline: a voice memo of the attempt, a photograph of the sketched bars, and the two sentences. The medium does not matter; the dated trace does.

sections.heading: Sequencing the two years without a crisis in February
paragraphs: Music is a subject in which almost everything is submitted, which makes sequencing the main management problem. Schools in Abu Dhabi set their own internal deadlines and those are the dates that matter, because a component reviewed before an internal deadline can still change and one reviewed afterwards can only be explained. Ask the music teacher for the internal calendar at the start of DP1 and plan backwards from it rather than forwards from today.

The pattern that goes wrong is consistent. DP1 is spent performing and enjoying the subject, DP2 begins with written work that has not been practised, and February arrives with three components half-done and school examinations in the same fortnight. The pattern that works puts analytical writing into DP1 at a low intensity, keeps the capture routine running throughout, and leaves DP2 for consolidating the programme and the project rather than discovering the components.

The table below is a typical shape rather than an official one. Treat it as a template to adjust against your school's calendar. The useful feature is the right-hand column: the parental check at each stage requires no musical knowledge at all, only the ability to ask whether a document exists and how long it is. That is the whole of what monitoring this subject requires, and it is why the question to ask at a parents' evening is which component is behind rather than how the student is getting on. Build school examination weeks and production weeks into the shape from the start as well. In Abu Dhabi those two tend to collide with component deadlines in the same fortnight, and a plan that has no slack in it fails at precisely that point.

sections.heading: Where Diploma Music leads, and what support costs
paragraphs: Two questions close almost every first conversation. On destinations: a Diploma Music grade is evidence of musical literacy and sustained work, and it is accepted on music and music-technology degree routes, but conservatoires and competitive performance courses select by audition and by a separately prepared repertoire. The course helps and does not substitute. Families planning an audition route should treat it as a parallel project with its own timetable, and should check each institution's published requirements rather than assuming.

On cost: published market figures for Diploma specialist support in this market run from roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, with qualified subject tutors online quoted from about AED 150 to AED 300, and in-home visits from around AED 180 to AED 500 because the drive sits inside the rate. Those are figures providers published, read in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list. Our rate is quoted per 60 minutes in writing after a free trial lesson, with marking and a written note included.

Worth adding a note about permits, because parents ask. A tutor resident in the UAE giving private lessons, online included, needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years. Tutoring without a permit carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published schedule of amounts. IB Gram is not approved, endorsed or certified by ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and any provider claiming such status should be asked for the number.

faqs.question: What does the Diploma Music course actually ask a student to submit?
faqs.answer: At Standard Level, three strands: exploring music in context, which combines written analysis with the student's own creating and performing excerpts; experimenting with music, which is a report plus practical musical evidence; and presenting music, a recorded programme of performing and creating with programme notes. Higher Level adds a multimedia presentation of a real-world musical project. Almost nothing is performed live to an examiner. Each strand carries a written limit, and your school holds the current figures for your child's cohort because guides are periodically revised.

faqs.question: Which of the three musical roles do Abu Dhabi students find hardest?
faqs.answer: The researcher role, consistently. Analytical writing about music is taught in English lessons and almost never in instrumental ones, so a student with a decade of excellent instrumental teaching may never have been asked to explain how a passage achieves its effect. That is a gap in what they have been taught rather than a limitation in the student, and it responds quickly to teaching. The performer role is usually the strongest and the creator role sits between the two, depending on whether the student composes in software.

faqs.question: My son plays to a high standard but cannot analyse a score. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters a great deal, because performing is one of three assessed roles and analysis feeds two of them. A student who cannot locate and explain a musical event will struggle with the written components and with programme notes, which means a technically strong candidate can be predicted a 4. The good news is that this is the fastest-moving weakness in the subject. A term of weekly practice analysis, marked against the descriptors, usually produces visible change, because it is procedure rather than talent.

faqs.question: Can a student who learned by ear cope with the written components?
faqs.answer: Yes. Precision matters more than notation. A student who locates an event by timing rather than bar number loses nothing, provided the timing is exact and the description of what happens is accurate. We usually build minimal score literacy alongside aural location anyway, because the two reinforce each other and a bar number is harder to dispute than a timing. What does not work in either system is vagueness: a claim that cannot be pointed at cannot be credited, however musically true it is.

faqs.question: How much music theory does the course assume?
faqs.answer: Less than families expect and more than some students arrive with. The course needs enough theoretical vocabulary to describe what is happening accurately: harmony, texture, metre, timbre, structure. It does not require advanced harmony or counterpoint exercises. The gap we most often fill is vocabulary rather than theory itself, because students can frequently hear a change perfectly well and have never been given the words to name it. Two or three sessions of targeted vocabulary work usually closes that gap.

faqs.question: Can Arabic and Gulf musical traditions be used as a context for the research?
faqs.answer: They can, and students in Abu Dhabi underuse them. Regional and Arabic repertoire gives genuine, accessible primary material for more than one area of inquiry, particularly music for sociocultural expression, and a student who has heard the music performed locally writes with authority a textbook summary cannot match. Two conditions apply: engage with how the tradition's own practitioners describe it rather than imposing borrowed analytical categories, and cite every source properly, including Arabic-language material.

faqs.question: Where can a student in Abu Dhabi record a performance submission?
faqs.answer: The school music room is usually the best option and is often available by arrangement, particularly for amplified or percussive work that is impossible in an apartment. At home, natural sound is improved cheaply: record away from a room corner, add soft furnishings or a duvet against a reflective wall, and move the recording device further from a loud instrument rather than closer. The most valuable step is testing the set-up during Year 12 and keeping the settings, so the deadline week is about music rather than technology.

faqs.question: Our school runs Music with one part-time teacher. Can tutoring fill the gap?
faqs.answer: Partly, and it is worth being precise about which part. A tutor can teach analysis, structure the experimentation documentation, review components against the criteria before internal deadlines and mark practice work. A tutor cannot run an ensemble, supervise a recording session on site or replace the relationship with the subject teacher who submits the work. In small departments the most valuable use of outside hours is an independent reading of each component, because a single familiar reader stops seeing what a moderator will notice immediately.

faqs.question: Is a recording judged on sound quality or on musicianship?
faqs.answer: On the music. Production polish earns nothing. The reason recording quality still matters is that a distorted, clipped or heavily reflected recording stops the music from being heard, so phrasing, articulation and dynamic control simply do not reach the assessor. Those are avoidable losses rather than aesthetic judgements, and fixing them costs nothing: better microphone placement, a quieter room, soft furnishings and a test run weeks before the deadline resolve almost every case we see in this emirate.

faqs.question: What does the Higher Level project add, and who should take it on?
faqs.answer: Higher Level students present a multimedia account of a project rooted in a real-life musical context: working with a community ensemble, a production, an event, a collaboration outside school. The marks follow evidence of genuine engagement and a documented process rather than a well-described intention. It suits students who are already active musically outside the classroom. It goes wrong when a student invents a plausible project in DP2 and then cannot evidence having done it, which is visible immediately.

faqs.question: Where is the line between teaching composition and composing for a student?
faqs.answer: A tutor may explain a technique, analyse how a composer achieved an effect, ask what the student is trying to do and why a passage is not doing it, and mark a practice exercise. A tutor may not write, arrange, orchestrate, edit or record any part of submitted creative work. The distinction is practical as well as ethical: a student who is handed material cannot document how it developed, so the help destroys the very evidence the component is credited for. Generative tools used in creative work must be acknowledged as the school requires.

faqs.question: Will my daughter still need to prepare an audition separately from the course?
faqs.answer: Yes, if she is applying to a conservatoire or a competitive performance programme. Those institutions select by audition against their own published repertoire requirements, and a Diploma Music grade is supporting evidence rather than a route in. Treat the audition as a parallel project with its own timetable and its own teacher, usually her instrumental teacher, and check each institution's requirements directly. Music and music-technology degrees that do not audition generally treat the Diploma grade as solid evidence of literacy and sustained work.

faqs.question: How many sessions does an Abu Dhabi Music student usually book?
faqs.answer: The common shapes in our caseload are a weekly hour through DP1 and the first term of DP2, concentrating on analysis and documentation, which comes to roughly forty hours; or a lighter plan of one review per component placed before each internal deadline, which is closer to eight to twelve hours in total. Students starting in DP2 with little documented need more hours for less movement. Published specialist rates in this market run roughly AED 200 to AED 450 an hour, read in October 2026.

faqs.question: Can sessions work around school productions and Ramadan rehearsals?
faqs.answer: They have to, in this subject more than most. Production weeks consume evenings entirely, and our practice is to pause rather than push a session into a week when the student is rehearsing until 9pm. During Ramadan sessions commonly move to after Iftar, planned at the start of the term rather than negotiated weekly. Nothing is charged for a session that does not run, and the slot is held rather than released. Families who agree the term's shape in advance lose far fewer sessions than those who reschedule as they go.

faqs.question: We are a term into DP2 and the folder is nearly empty. What now?
faqs.answer: Partly, and honesty about which parts serves better than optimism. What can still move is the written analysis, the programme choice and its notes, and any experimentation documented from this week forward. What cannot be recovered is a year of exploration that was never captured, because the report is credited for evidence rather than for recollection. The sensible plan is an audit, a sustainable capture routine starting immediately, and effort concentrated on components that remain open rather than spread evenly.

intro.heading: Philosophy marks move when somebody marks the writing, not when the reading list grows
paragraphs: Philosophy is the Diploma subject where effort and attainment come apart most visibly. A student reads Descartes, follows the lesson, argues confidently at the dinner table in Al Bateen, and then scores a 4 on a mock Paper 1. Parents in Abu Dhabi tell us the same story in almost identical words: the child understands the material, so the problem must be nerves or timing. It is almost never either. The problem is that an IB Philosophy essay is marked on a short list of named qualities, and reading more philosophy does not by itself produce any of them.

That is why this page is built around evidence rather than promises. The only way to know whether Philosophy tutoring is working is to look at marked writing: the same student, the same command term, four weeks apart, with a marker's comments in the margin and a criterion-by-criterion breakdown underneath. If a tutor cannot show you that, you are buying conversation. Good conversation, often — Philosophy tutors tend to be enjoyable company — but conversation is not what the examiner sees in May.

A Philosophy session that earns its fee looks fairly dull from the outside. The student writes to time. The tutor marks what was written, against the criteria, in front of them. They identify one specific habit that cost marks — an undefended premise, a paragraph that explains a theory instead of using it, a conclusion that repeats the introduction in different words — and the student rewrites one paragraph with that habit removed. Then the next piece of writing tests whether the habit has actually gone. Over six to eight weeks that produces a visible line on a chart. Over six to eight weeks of enthusiastic discussion it does not.

Abu Dhabi adds its own constraints to that work. Philosophy is a small-cohort subject here. At several schools ADEK licenses the Diploma Philosophy class runs with a handful of students, sometimes as an option block that collides with a science, occasionally as a self-taught course supervised rather than taught. A student in that position has nobody to compare their writing against and no second opinion on a mark. One-to-one online lessons are a direct answer to that: the student gets a subject specialist who marks to the published criteria weekly, and you get a written record you can hold against the school's own predicted grade.

IB Gram is an independent tutor-matching platform. We hold no accreditation from the IB, from ADEK or from any Abu Dhabi school, and we do not claim any. What we do is match a Diploma Philosophy student in Abu Dhabi with a tutor who has taught the current syllabus, run the lessons live online, and keep the marked work where a parent can read it.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-philosophy-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Philosophy sits in Group 3 of the Diploma, but the thinking it tests is built earlier. These are the programme stages our Abu Dhabi Philosophy tutors work across, and what each one needs.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Philosophy
programmes.description: The course that this page is about. Students study the core theme on what it is to be human, at least one optional theme, and one prescribed philosophical text. Higher Level students add a second optional theme and a paper on the practice of philosophy itself. Every component is assessed on argument rather than on coverage, which is why essay technique carries so much of the grade.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi, Diploma Philosophy is usually offered as one choice inside a crowded Group 3 block alongside Economics, Business Management, Geography and Psychology. Cohorts are small, and in some schools ADEK licenses the subject is supervised rather than timetabled as a full class. Confirm with your child's IB coordinator which optional themes and which prescribed text the school has registered for this cohort before any tutoring plan is written.

programmes.name: MYP Individuals and Societies
programmes.description: The MYP route into Philosophy. Students are assessed on four criteria, including investigating and critical thinking, which is the closest thing the Middle Years Programme has to a philosophy essay. A Year 11 student who scores well on criterion D here usually has the raw material for Diploma Philosophy; one who scores well only on knowledge and understanding tends to struggle in Year 12.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi IB continuum schools in the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor run MYP through Year 11, so students arrive in Diploma Philosophy from an MYP background rather than from IGCSE. The gap is specific: MYP students are used to structured criteria and command terms but have rarely written a 1,200-word argumentative essay to time. That single difference is worth two or three sessions in September.

programmes.name: Theory of Knowledge
programmes.description: Compulsory for every Diploma student and heavily adjacent to Philosophy. TOK asks how knowledge is produced and justified across areas of knowledge, and the TOK essay is marked on whether a claim is examined rather than asserted. Philosophy students often assume TOK is free marks and then approach the TOK essay in a philosophy register, which the TOK criteria do not reward.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools timetable TOK very differently from one another: some give it a weekly lesson across both years, others compress it into blocks around the exhibition and essay deadlines. A Philosophy student can gain in both subjects at once if the tutor keeps the two registers separate, and can lose in both if nobody points out that a TOK prompt is not an invitation to summarise Kant.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-philosophy-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Philosophy is rarely the only subject a family is worried about. These are the Diploma courses our Abu Dhabi tutors most often pair it with, and what each one actually punishes.

subjects.name: Philosophy
subjects.description: Assessed on four components at Higher Level and three at Standard Level. Marks are lost for describing positions rather than evaluating them, and for essays that never state which premise is being rejected.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge
subjects.description: The 1,600-word essay plus the exhibition. The commonest failure is a well-written essay that answers a question the prescribed title did not ask, which no amount of polish recovers.

subjects.name: Extended Essay
subjects.description: Four thousand words on a self-chosen question. Philosophy students often pick a title that is too large to defend; narrowing it is the single most valuable hour of supervision available.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Shares the analytical habits Philosophy needs. Students who can handle the Paper 1 guided analysis usually transfer well, provided they stop treating a philosophical text as a literary one.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: The Group 3 subject most often taken alongside Philosophy in Abu Dhabi. Evaluation marks hinge on using studies as evidence rather than listing them, which is the same discipline Philosophy Paper 1 rewards.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Common option-block partner. Diagram accuracy and evaluation carry the paper; students coming from Philosophy tend to write strong evaluation and weak diagrams.

subjects.name: History
subjects.description: Source work and the HL essay both reward handling counter-evidence. Philosophy students usually find the HL essay easier than the source paper, where the marks sit in close reading under time pressure.

subjects.name: Global Politics
subjects.description: Offered in a small number of Abu Dhabi schools. The engagement project and the HL extension both need a defensible claim, so the skill overlap with Philosophy is high.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: Taken by many students in Abu Dhabi alongside a Group 3 choice. Productive skills, not comprehension, decide the grade, and the written tasks reward exactly the structural discipline Philosophy demands.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-philosophy-home-tutor.regionsIntro: Lessons are delivered online, so the practical question in Abu Dhabi is not distance but timing. These are the communities we most often schedule Diploma Philosophy sessions for, and what shapes the slot.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Families here often finish the school day late because of co-curricular commitments on campus. A 7pm or 7.30pm Philosophy slot usually works better than an immediate after-school session, and it leaves the student fresher for timed writing.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment living and short commutes mean students are home early, so a 5pm start is realistic. We tend to use the earlier slot for timed essay writing and keep marking discussion for a shorter midweek follow-up.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: The eastern corridor school run is the constraint, not the lesson. Students arriving home after 4.30pm do better with a 6.30pm session, and many Philosophy students here are in small cohorts where weekly marked writing is the only external feedback they get.

regions.name: Al Raha Beach and Al Raha Gardens
regions.note: A dense cluster of Diploma students in a small area, several in schools where Philosophy runs as a supervised option. Sibling scheduling is common: two back-to-back slots in one evening rather than two separate evenings.

regions.name: Al Bateen and the Corniche
regions.note: Older, island-side communities with a long-established Diploma population. Students here frequently take Philosophy alongside English A Literature, so sessions often cover transfer of close-reading technique to Paper 2.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Larger mainland catchment with longer bus routes. Weekend morning sessions are more productive than weekday evenings for students on a 45-minute bus home, especially for the two-hour timed Paper 1 practice.

regions.name: Yas Island

modes.title: Weekly marked-essay cycle
modes.description: The default, and the one that produces evidence. One session a week across a term: the student writes under timed conditions between sessions, the tutor marks against the criteria before the lesson, and the lesson is spent on the gap the marking exposed. Suits a student sitting at a 4 or 5 who needs technique rather than content.

modes.description: A short block of sessions around the philosophical analysis of a non-philosophical stimulus. The tutor works on choice of stimulus, the philosophical issue being extracted, and the structure of the analysis. The student writes every word themselves; the tutor reads drafts and gives feedback, which is what IB rules permit.

sections.heading: What a marked Philosophy script actually tells you
paragraphs: A marked Philosophy essay is the most useful document a parent in Abu Dhabi can hold. Not the mark at the top: the annotations. They tell you precisely where the essay stopped doing philosophy and started doing summary, and that point is almost always identifiable to the sentence. Once you can see it, you can see whether it is still happening six weeks later.

Diploma Philosophy essays are assessed on a short set of named qualities. Expressed plainly, the examiner is asking: does this student understand the issue, have they used philosophical argument to address it, have they considered a serious objection, and is the whole thing organised so the argument is followed rather than reconstructed by a sympathetic reader. A student can know a great deal and satisfy only the first of those. That is the shape of nearly every stuck Philosophy grade we see in Abu Dhabi.

So the first session with a new student is not a syllabus overview. The tutor asks for two pieces of recent writing — a mock answer and a class essay are ideal — and marks them cold against the criteria. What comes back is a diagnosis in writing: which criterion is already secure, which is costing the grade, and what the single highest-value change is. Parents regularly tell us this is the first time anyone has shown them why a confident, well-read child is sitting on a 4.

The second thing a marked script shows is whether the student is writing to time. Philosophy papers are long and the pressure is real; an essay written over two unhurried evenings proves nothing about performance in a hall. Every piece of evidence in this process is produced under exam conditions for that reason, and the first timed script is usually a full band below the coursework the school has seen.

sections.heading: How the Philosophy grade is assembled, component by component
paragraphs: Before any plan is made, it is worth knowing where the marks physically sit. Under the current subject guide, Standard Level Philosophy is assessed on three components and Higher Level on four, and the weightings are not evenly spread. A Standard Level student who ignores the internal assessment has written off a quarter of the grade; a Higher Level student who treats the unseen paper as a bonus has written off a fifth.

The table below sets out the structure as published in the subject guide. Durations and weightings should be confirmed with your child's IB coordinator, because the IB revises subject guides on a cycle and a school may be teaching a different cohort year to the one you are reading about. That caution matters more in Philosophy than in most subjects, because the prescribed text list changes and a tutor working from the wrong text is worse than no tutor at all.

The practical consequence of the weighting is that tutoring should be sequenced, not spread. For a Year 12 student, the internal assessment and the core theme are where early work pays, because both are still open. For a Year 13 student in January, the only rational focus is the examined papers, since the internal assessment has usually been submitted internally by then and no amount of tutoring changes a mark already banked.

One more consequence, specific to Higher Level: the fourth component is the one with no obvious revision material attached. It asks the student to engage with an unseen passage about the practice of philosophy itself, and it rewards a habit rather than a body of content. Habits take weeks of short, repeated practice, which is exactly the kind of work that drops off a revision timetable built around content.

sections.heading: Six ways an Abu Dhabi Philosophy student loses marks, in the order a marker meets them
paragraphs: These are drawn from marked scripts, not from a list of general study tips. They appear in roughly this order as you read down a page, and each one is fixable inside two or three sessions once it has been named.

The first is the undefended premise. The essay asserts something that a philosopher would immediately challenge and moves on. The second is the explanatory paragraph: a clear, accurate account of a theory that is never applied to the question. The third is the missing objection. A student who presents one position well but never meets a serious challenge to it has capped the evaluation marks, no matter how elegant the prose. The fourth is the decorative philosopher, named in a subordinate clause with no argument attached.

The fifth is scope. Abu Dhabi students, many of whom are strong English writers, tend to open with a question large enough to need a book. The essay then has to retreat, and the retreat eats the time that should have gone on evaluation. The sixth is the closing paragraph that restates the opening in new words rather than resolving the argument the body has set up. It is the most common single reason a good essay reads as a 5 rather than a 6.

A tutor who marks weekly can tell you which of those six is live this month. That is a different conversation from the one most families have with us at the start, which usually begins with the belief that the student needs to read more. Occasionally they do. Far more often the reading is sufficient and the writing is doing something the criteria do not reward.
bullets: Undefended premise: the claim a philosopher would attack first goes unexamined
Explanatory paragraph: the theory is described accurately and never used
Missing objection: no serious challenge is met, so evaluation marks are capped
Decorative philosopher: a name appears with no argument attached to it
Scope: the opening question is too large to defend in the time available
Restating conclusion: the final paragraph repeats the introduction instead of resolving it

sections.heading: A four-week marked-work cycle you can audit yourself
paragraphs: This is the mechanism behind every claim on this page. It is deliberately boring and deliberately legible: a parent who has never read a philosophical text should be able to open the folder and see whether anything is improving.

Each cycle runs on one timed piece of writing per week plus one lesson. The writing is done at home under exam conditions and sent before the lesson. The tutor marks it against the criteria, in writing, with a mark for each and a one-line reason. The lesson then works on one thing — not six — and the student rewrites a single paragraph applying it. The next week's piece is chosen to test whether the fix survived without being prompted.

By the end of four weeks you have four marked scripts on the same criteria, written to the same time limit, with one named target per fortnight. If the criterion scores have not moved, the plan is wrong and should be changed; that is a conversation worth having in week five rather than in April. If they have moved, you know which part of the work caused it. This is also the record that lets you sanity-check a school predicted grade, which in a cohort of four students is based on a very small sample.

Families often ask how long a change takes to appear. In our experience with Diploma humanities students, structural habits such as the missing objection move within two or three marked pieces, because the fix is a rule the student can apply. Scope and evaluation depth take longer, usually six to eight weeks, because they require judgement rather than compliance. Anyone who tells you otherwise has not marked much Philosophy.

sections.heading: Small cohorts, option blocks and the supervised Philosophy student
paragraphs: Philosophy in Abu Dhabi is a minority subject, and that shapes everything about how tutoring should be used. In a school where Economics runs three Diploma classes, Philosophy may run one group of five, taught by a teacher whose main subject is something else, inside an option block that forces awkward trade-offs against a science or a second language.

Three consequences follow. The first is calibration: with five students in a cohort, the school's internal mark distribution carries almost no information. A predicted 5 might mean the student is the second strongest of five, which tells you nothing about where they would sit against a full examination cohort. An external marker working to the published criteria is the only practical cross-check available.

The second is coverage. Where a subject is supervised rather than taught — a legitimate arrangement that several schools use for very small option choices — the student is carrying the syllabus themselves with a teacher checking in. Those students need the tutor to behave like a teacher, not a polisher: sequencing the optional theme, setting the reading, and testing it, as well as marking the essays.

The third is the timetable. A single Philosophy group often sits in the least convenient block in the week, and the student may have a long gap between lessons. Online sessions are scheduled around that rather than against it, and because the tutor is not crossing Abu Dhabi at five in the afternoon, a 7.30pm Tuesday slot costs nothing extra to arrange. That is the practical reason families here end up choosing online delivery even when they started out searching for someone local.

sections.heading: What Diploma Philosophy support costs in the Abu Dhabi market
paragraphs: Published rates for private tuition in the UAE vary by a factor of ten, and almost nobody ranking for these searches prints a figure at all. The bands below are market rates collected from providers' own published prices and from a Dubai rate survey, not an IB Gram price list. They are here so you can tell whether a quote you have been given is normal.

Three things reliably move the number for Philosophy specifically. Scarcity is the first: there are far fewer Diploma Philosophy specialists in the Gulf than Maths or Chemistry tutors, so the subject sits at the upper end of the band for its level. Marking is the second, and it is the one parents forget to ask about. An hour of lesson time plus a properly marked essay is roughly ninety minutes of tutor work, and a quote that includes marking is not comparable with one that does not. The third is the format: an in-home visit anywhere in the UAE carries the tutor's travel inside the rate, which is why those bands sit higher for the same teaching.

Two figures are worth holding alongside the rate. The Knowledge and Human Development Authority confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package; Abu Dhabi fee regulation sits with ADEK separately. Against a school fee measured in tens of thousands of dirhams, a weekly subject session is a small marginal cost — but it is a recurring one, and it should be bought against a target, not indefinitely.

For IB Gram's own arrangements, the honest answer is that it depends on the tutor's experience and the number of sessions, and the only way to find out whether the match works is the free trial lesson, which happens before any payment. We will not publish a tariff on a page like this and then quote something different on the phone, which is a pattern the competitor research found repeatedly.

sections.heading: The Diploma Philosophy year counted backwards from the May session
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi schools sit the May examination session. Nobody ranking for these searches publishes a calendar, which is odd, because the calendar is what decides whether tutoring arrives in time to be useful. The table below counts backwards from the examinations rather than forwards from today.

Two cautions about dates. Exact IB examination and results dates are published by the International Baccalaureate and set per session; we do not restate them here, because an incorrect date on a page like this is worse than no date, and your child's IB coordinator holds the authoritative version for their cohort. Internal deadlines — the ones that actually bite — are set by the school, not the IB, and they usually fall weeks before the IB's own upload deadlines so that teachers have marking time.

The pattern worth noticing is how early the internal assessment closes. For most Abu Dhabi cohorts the Philosophy analysis is finished during Year 13's first term, which means the window for useful support on a quarter of the Standard Level grade opens in Year 12 and closes long before anyone starts revising. Families who come to us in February asking for internal assessment help are usually too late for that component and should be spending the money on Paper 1 technique instead.

The second pattern is the Ramadan overlap. Ramadan moves roughly eleven days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar, so for the next several cycles it falls in the revision term for the May session. Abu Dhabi school hours shorten, evenings restructure around Iftar, and a 5pm session stops being viable. Sessions move to post-Iftar slots, typically from 8.30pm, and the students who plan that in advance lose nothing; the ones who improvise lose three or four weeks of the most valuable revision time in the course.
