abu-dhabi/ib-dp-spanish-ab-initio-home-t.modesIntro: Three delivery patterns cover almost every ab initio plan we are asked for in Abu Dhabi. The difference between them is not price but what evidence each one produces, which is the thing a beginner language plan lives or dies on.

modes.title: Twice-weekly short contacts
modes.description: Two sessions of 45 minutes, placed at least two days apart, is the pattern that suits a beginner language best through DP1. Vocabulary decays fast at this stage and a single weekly hour spends most of its first fifteen minutes recovering ground. The short-contact pattern also produces twice as many marked artefacts per month, which is what makes progress visible.
bullets: Each session opens with a cold recall test on the previous one
One short written task per week, marked against a criterion letter
A running error log the student can see, not a tutor's private note

modes.title: Weekly session with an oral focus
modes.description: A single 60-minute session, built around the individual oral, suits DP2 students whose written accuracy is already stable. Half the hour goes on a visual stimulus under timed conditions, the rest on the follow-up conversation, which is where beginners lose most of the available marks because they prepared a monologue and were asked a question.
bullets: Recorded stimulus responses the student can hear back
A rotating bank of images across the five prescribed themes
Conversation questions pitched one band above current performance

modes.title: Pre-mock intensive block
modes.description: Four to six sessions compressed into a fortnight ahead of school mocks or the May session. The block is diagnostic rather than instructional: timed papers under exam conditions, marked and returned with the mark scheme logic written out, so the remaining weeks are spent on the two or three error classes that are actually costing marks.
bullets: Full timed writing and reading papers in the first two sessions
A written summary of the three highest-cost error classes
A revision sequence the student can run without a tutor present

sections.heading: What a Spanish ab initio candidate has to produce by May of DP2
paragraphs: A Spanish ab initio candidate has to produce four things: a written paper of two tasks chosen from a short list of text types, answers to a recorded listening paper, answers to a reading paper based on authentic texts, and an individual oral in which they describe a visual stimulus and then hold a conversation about it. Each of the four carries a quarter of the grade. Nothing else counts, and there is no internal assessment to carry a weak paper.

That even split is the most useful planning fact available to an Abu Dhabi family, because it tells you where tuition is worth buying. A student who writes reasonably and cannot hear Spanish at speed is not a weak linguist; they are a candidate losing a quarter of their grade in a skill that responds to practice faster than any other. Listening improves on volume of exposure, which is cheap, so it is close to negligent to spend a term of paid hours on writing while the listening paper stays untouched.

The ceiling is also worth stating plainly. Ab initio is designed for a beginner, so the language demanded is narrow and the marks reward control rather than range. A student who learns twelve more tenses will not score higher than one who uses the present, the preterite and the near future accurately across all five themes. Tutors who were trained on Spanish B instinctively push range, and that instinct quietly costs ab initio candidates marks they would otherwise have kept.

Where families get the biggest surprise is the reading paper. The texts are authentic, which means they contain words no ab initio student has met, and the task is to locate and manipulate information rather than to understand everything. Students taught to translate before answering run out of time and then answer the easy questions badly. The skill is procedural and it is teachable in about four sessions, which makes it the best-value fortnight in the course.

sections.heading: The diagnostic that happens before anyone is quoted an hourly rate
paragraphs: A beginner language plan written without a diagnostic is a guess with an invoice attached. The diagnostic we run first takes about forty minutes and is deliberately boring: it produces numbers rather than impressions, because numbers are the only thing you can compare against the same test in March.

It has five probes. A four-minute unprompted speaking sample, timed and recorded. A short cold writing task in a known text type. Five reading questions on an authentic text the student has not seen. A listening passage at exam speed. And a theme audit, where the student says what they can produce about each of the five prescribed themes, which almost always reveals that two themes have never been taught at all.

What comes out of it is a short file: a word count for unprompted speech, a ranked error list, a theme coverage grid with gaps marked, and a reading time-per-question figure. That file is the baseline. Everything after it is measured against it, and at the end of each term the same probes are rerun so the comparison is like for like rather than a new test that happens to be easier.

The diagnostic also decides whether tuition is the right purchase at all. A student who produces ninety words of comprehensible Spanish in four minutes and loses marks only on preterite endings does not need two sessions a week for a year. They need four sessions on verb endings and a written revision sequence, and saying so costs us hours we would otherwise have billed. A tutor unwilling to tell you that is not measuring anything.

sections.heading: Vocabulary as a measured quantity rather than a feeling
paragraphs: Ask most beginners how their Spanish vocabulary is going and the answer is a feeling. Ask them to write for five minutes about food and health and you get a number, and the number is usually much lower than the feeling. The gap between those two is where ab initio grades go missing, because the student who feels fine stops revising and the student who feels hopeless revises the wrong thing.

The useful distinction is between recognition and production. A student can recognise two or three times as much Spanish as they can produce. Paper 2 rewards recognition. Paper 1 and the oral reward production only. A plan that drills word lists improves recognition and leaves production flat, which is why vocabulary apps produce such disappointing results in a course that is half productive.

So production is tracked directly. Each term the student writes the same timed task on a rotating theme and the output is counted: total words, distinct verbs used, correct past-tense forms, and errors per hundred words. Four numbers, same conditions, three times a year. A rising word count with a rising error rate is a different problem from a flat word count with a falling error rate, and the two need opposite teaching.

None of this is exotic. It is what a school department would do if it had the time, and the reason an outside tutor can do it is that they have one student in the hour rather than twenty-two. An Abu Dhabi DP teacher carrying two Group 2 classes and a TOK slot is not going to count distinct verbs in a mock script, and nobody should expect them to.

sections.heading: The visual stimulus: the task Abu Dhabi beginners under-rehearse
paragraphs: The individual oral is worth a quarter of the grade and is the only assessment where a beginner is alone with an examiner in real time. It starts from a visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes, which the student describes, and then moves into a conversation about the image and the theme behind it. Both halves are marked, and the second half is where the marks are lost.

The reason is predictable. A student who knows the oral is coming prepares a description. They rehearse it until it is fluent, deliver it well, and then meet a follow-up question they have not prepared and answer it in four words. The description was the easy half. The conversation is where the examiner finds out whether the language is owned or memorised.

Rehearsal therefore has to be built the other way round. Sessions run the conversation first, on an unseen image, with questions pitched slightly above the student's current band, and the description is drilled last once the student has something to say. Recording matters here more than in any other part of the course: a beginner cannot hear their own hesitation, and playing back ninety seconds does more than a paragraph of written feedback.

There is an Abu Dhabi scheduling wrinkle worth naming. Orals in the emirate's Diploma schools are often held in a compressed window around the end of the first DP2 term, sometimes the same fortnight as internal assessment deadlines in three other subjects. A student who starts oral rehearsal when the window is announced has already lost the useful preparation period. The right time to start is the term before, at a low intensity, when nothing else is competing for the evening.

sections.heading: Why there is no self-taught route, and what that means in Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Families sometimes ask whether a student can take Spanish ab initio independently, with a tutor instead of a class, when the school's Group 2 column does not include it. The answer families should get from their DP coordinator is that ab initio courses require school-supported teaching and are not available to a candidate studying alone. Confirm it with the coordinator for your own cohort before making any plan that depends on it, because this is the kind of rule that decides a timetable.

That matters a great deal in a small market. Abu Dhabi Diploma cohorts are modest in size, and a school will only run a beginner Spanish class if enough students choose it. Where it does not run, the realistic options are a different Group 2 language, a different course in the same language, or a school conversation about provision, and an outside tutor cannot substitute for the registration itself.

Where a tutor is genuinely useful is in the opposite situation: the class exists, it is taught well, and your child is the only beginner in a room where several students already speak some Spanish. That is common in the emirate's international schools and it is the single most reliable reason an Abu Dhabi family hires beginner Spanish support. The class is not wrong. The pace is set by the median student, and the median student is not a beginner.

The honest version of this page includes what we cannot do. We cannot register a candidate, approve a placement, or influence a school's option blocks. We can produce a dated diagnostic script that makes the placement conversation evidence-based rather than anecdotal, and in our experience that is what shifts those conversations.

sections.heading: Home tutoring in Abu Dhabi, and what online delivery changes for a beginner
paragraphs: In-home tutoring is a real and busy market in Abu Dhabi. A tutor arrives at a villa in Khalifa City or an apartment on the Corniche, teaches for an hour or two, and leaves. Published market comparisons put that service at roughly AED 180 to AED 350 an hour, with monthly in-home packages advertised around AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions. Those figures are what the market charges, cited from published rate tables rather than quoted by us.

IB Gram does not sell that service in the UAE. We do not send a tutor to an Abu Dhabi address, and we do not run home visits in Abu Dhabi; home tutoring at the door is something we offer only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one online, over live video, on Gulf Standard Time. Saying so plainly is more useful than the alternative, which is a page that lets a parent assume otherwise until the first booking.

For a minority subject the trade is clearly favourable. The pool of in-home Spanish tutors who have taught the ab initio course specifically, in one emirate, within reasonable driving distance of your area, at the hour your child is free, is very small. Online, the constraint is only the hour. The practical result is that a Saadiyat family and an Al Reef family get the same tutor, which is not true of any in-home arrangement.

There is also the evidence point this whole page rests on. A screen-shared session produces artefacts by default: the shared document, the recorded oral, the marked script in a folder both sides can open. A kitchen-table lesson produces a tutor's memory of it. For a subject where the parent cannot assess the work directly, that difference is the whole argument.

sections.heading: Reading an ADEK school report on a beginner linguist
paragraphs: ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate of Abu Dhabi, and publishes its own inspection outcomes for them. That is the regulator your child's school answers to, and it is the authority whose published listings you should read rather than any claim made on a tutoring site, including this one.

What ADEK does not do is standardise the internal report you receive each term. Those reports vary widely between the emirate's IB schools, and a beginner language report is among the least informative documents in the set. A grade band, an effort score and a sentence are typical. None of the three tells you whether your child can write a controlled past-tense paragraph about health, which is the thing the examiner will ask for.

So the report is read for three specific things and nothing else. Whether a predicted grade has moved since the last one. Whether the comment names a skill or a behaviour, because 'needs to revise vocabulary' is not a diagnosis. And whether the report distinguishes between the four assessments, because a student can be fine in three of them and still lose a quarter of the grade in the fourth.

Where the report is thin, the ask is simple and schools generally agree to it: a marked piece of work with the criterion letters on it, and the raw score on the most recent listening and reading papers. Those two documents tell you more than three terms of reports, and requesting them politely in writing after a parents' evening is ordinary practice rather than an escalation.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, and what a beginner-language tutor will not do
paragraphs: The IB's academic honesty rules apply to every piece of assessed work a Diploma student submits, and language courses carry a particular temptation: the work is short, the student's own Spanish is limited, and a fluent adult could improve a script in ten minutes. A tutor who does that has produced work that is not the student's, which under IB rules is malpractice and puts the candidate's diploma at risk rather than the tutor's income.

The line is straightforward in practice. A tutor may teach a text type, model an example on a different topic, mark a student's own draft against criterion letters, explain why a sentence costs a mark, and test whether the correction has been learned. A tutor may not supply sentences for the student to insert, rewrite a paragraph into better Spanish, or translate the student's English draft. We will not do those things on request, and a tutor who offers to is a liability wearing a solution's clothing.

Machine translation sits in the same place and deserves naming, because it is the live issue in beginner languages. A student who drafts in English and runs it through a translation tool submits language they could not have produced, and in a course built on a narrow controlled range the mismatch is visible to any experienced examiner. Sessions treat translation output as something to be analysed, not used: comparing what the tool produced with what the student can defend is a genuinely good teaching exercise.

None of this is a reason to avoid outside help with assessed work. It is a reason to be specific about what the help is. Feedback, teaching, process coaching and timed practice are all available and all legitimate. Production of the work is not, in any subject, at any price.

sections.heading: The Spanish year counted backwards from the May session
paragraphs: UAE Diploma students sit the May session, and planning a beginner language forwards from September never works, because the first two terms always feel like there is time. Counting backwards from the examination window makes the real constraints visible: the oral is earlier than families expect, the last useful intervention point is earlier still, and the final six weeks are for consolidation rather than new learning.

IB session and results dates in this project are not independently verified, because the IB's own site blocks automated checking, so this page publishes no specific date. Confirm every date for your cohort with your DP coordinator, who works from the current assessment procedures. What is safe to plan around is the order of events and the gaps between them, which do not change.

The order runs like this. Group 2 placement is settled in the first weeks of DP1. Theme coverage should be complete, with no untaught theme, by the end of DP1. Oral rehearsal begins a term before the oral window rather than inside it. Timed full papers start at the beginning of DP2. The last fortnight in which a new error class can be fixed is roughly two months before the written papers, and after that the work is maintenance of what already exists.

Cambridge and Pearson publish their dates openly and are worth naming as a contrast, because many Abu Dhabi families have an IGCSE sibling in the same house. Cambridge's March 2027 series, for instance, has exams running from 3 February to 4 March 2027 with final entries due on 27 November 2026 — an entry deadline more than two months before the first paper. That gap is the general lesson: administrative deadlines sit far earlier than the exam a family is counting down to.

process.title: Tell us the starting point, honestly
process.description: A short message with the school, the year group, whether Spanish ab initio or Spanish B is on the timetable, and what the last report said. If you have an MYP phase descriptor or a marked script, send it. The more documents arrive first, the less of the trial lesson goes on discovery.

process.title: Free trial lesson, used as a diagnostic
process.description: The trial is a working session, not a sales call, and it runs the five diagnostic probes rather than teaching a topic. It is free with no card required and no obligation to book afterwards. You receive the baseline file whether or not you continue, because it is your child's data.

process.title: A plan with numbers in it
process.description: Within a day or two you get a written plan: the ranked error classes, the theme gaps, the recommended session pattern and the number of weeks before the next measurement. If the honest recommendation is four sessions rather than a year of weekly hours, that is what the plan says.

process.title: Sessions, with artefacts after each one
process.description: Lessons run online, one-to-one, over live video on Gulf Standard Time. After each session a short note goes to the shared folder: what was tested cold, the result, what was taught, and the task set. Marked scripts come back with criterion letters written on them.

process.title: Termly remeasurement against the baseline
process.description: At the end of each term the same probes are rerun under the same conditions and the numbers are compared with the baseline. Word count, distinct verbs, errors per hundred words, listening raw score, reading seconds per question. The plan changes on those numbers rather than on how the sessions felt.

whyPoints.title: A beginner course taught as a beginner course
whyPoints.description: Ab initio rewards a narrow range used accurately. Tutors who work on this course resist the instinct to widen the language, because widening it is what loses beginners marks. That single discipline is the difference between a Spanish teacher and an ab initio tutor.

whyPoints.title: Measurement before method
whyPoints.description: Nothing is taught until the diagnostic says what is costing marks. Four numbers, retaken under identical conditions each term, make progress checkable by a parent who does not read Spanish. An opinion about progress is not evidence of it.

whyPoints.title: Every lesson online, and we say so
whyPoints.description: UAE delivery is one-to-one online over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to an Abu Dhabi address; home visits are an India-only service. You will not discover that after booking, because it is on the page before you book.

whyPoints.title: Named limits on what a tutor may do
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches, models, marks and tests. A tutor does not write, rewrite or translate assessed work, and will decline if asked. Under IB academic honesty rules the risk of the alternative falls on the student, which is why the line is published rather than implied.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling built around Abu Dhabi, not around us
whyPoints.description: Slots are set on Gulf Standard Time, around school-bus arrival times in the corridor you actually live in, and move to post-Iftar hours through Ramadan. Travel weeks are covered rather than paused, which matters most in a subject where vocabulary decays in a fortnight.

whyPoints.title: An honest answer when nobody is free
whyPoints.description: Beginner Spanish is a minority course and specialist availability is finite. If no ab initio specialist is free at your hour, we say so and offer the nearest honest alternative, including waiting. We do not fill the slot with a Spanish B tutor and let you find out in March.

faqs.question: Is Spanish ab initio available at Higher Level for an Abu Dhabi Diploma student?
faqs.answer: No. The ab initio courses are offered at Standard Level only, and that applies in every school, in every emirate. If a Higher Level language is needed for a university route, the course required is a language B at HL, which assumes prior study. Families sometimes hope extra tuition can convert an ab initio registration into an HL one; it cannot. What tuition can do is make an ab initio grade strong enough that the Group 2 column stops being the weak point in the total, which for most beginners is the better use of the money.

faqs.question: Can my child study Spanish ab initio with only a private tutor if the school does not offer it?
faqs.answer: Ab initio courses require school-supported teaching and are not intended for candidates studying alone, so a private tutor cannot substitute for a class that is not running. Confirm the current position with your DP coordinator for your cohort before building any plan on it. Where a school does not run beginner Spanish, the realistic routes are a different Group 2 language, a different course in the same language, or a conversation with the school about provision. An outside tutor supports a registered course; it cannot create a registration.

faqs.question: What should we see after six weeks of Spanish ab initio tuition in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Four documents, not an impression. A baseline file from the diagnostic, with a word count for unprompted speech and a ranked error list. At least four marked scripts with criterion letters written on them. A theme coverage grid showing which prescribed themes have been taught and which are still open. And one repeat measurement, under the same conditions as the baseline, showing whether errors per hundred words moved. If after six weeks the only evidence is that your child enjoys the sessions, you have bought company rather than teaching.

faqs.question: How is the individual oral marked in a beginner Spanish course?
faqs.answer: The oral runs in two parts: a description of a visual stimulus connected to one of the prescribed themes, then a conversation with the teacher about the image and the theme. Both parts are assessed, and beginners typically perform well in the first and badly in the second, because they rehearsed a monologue rather than the ability to answer. Ask to hear a recording of a practice attempt. Fluent description followed by four-word answers is the signature of preparation aimed at the wrong half of the task.

faqs.question: My daughter can read Spanish but freezes in the listening paper. Is that fixable before the mocks?
faqs.answer: Usually, and faster than any other part of the course. Listening responds to exposure volume more than to explanation, so the fix is structural rather than clever: short daily audio at exam speed outside sessions, and session time spent on where attention actually breaks rather than on vocabulary. Take a raw score on a past listening paper cold first, date it, and retake a comparable one after four weeks. Listening is a quarter of the grade, which makes it the highest-value place to spend a month of attention.

faqs.question: How much vocabulary does an ab initio student genuinely need to produce?
faqs.answer: Less than most families assume, used far more accurately than most students manage. The course works from five prescribed themes and rewards control of a narrow range, so a candidate who can write correctly about all five themes with ordinary words scores better than one reaching for unusual language and losing accuracy. The practical test is production rather than recognition: ask for a timed written task on a theme chosen at random and count the words, the distinct verbs and the errors. Recognition from a vocabulary app flatters a student whose production is flat.

faqs.question: Does Spanish ab initio count towards a bilingual diploma?
faqs.answer: No. The bilingual diploma recognises study of two languages at Language A level, or a Group 3 or Group 4 subject taken in a language other than the candidate's Language A. An ab initio course sits in Group 2 as language acquisition for beginners, so it is outside that route by design. Confirm the current wording with your DP coordinator, as award conditions are set in the IB's own assessment procedures. For most Abu Dhabi beginners this is academic anyway: the useful goal is a solid Group 2 grade, not an award the course cannot reach.

faqs.question: Will a university accept Spanish ab initio as evidence of a second language?
faqs.answer: That depends entirely on the university and the course, and it is a question to put to the admissions office in writing rather than to a tutor. Some institutions treat any Group 2 grade as satisfying a general language requirement; others specify a B course, a level, or a separate proficiency test. Get the answer before DP2, because it occasionally changes a subject choice. What a tutor can do is make the grade as strong as the course allows and be honest that an ab initio grade cannot be presented as advanced proficiency.

faqs.question: My son has done two years of Spanish in MYP. Is ab initio still the right course?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and the MYP phase descriptor usually settles it. A student finishing MYP in Phase 1 or Phase 2 is a genuine beginner by the course's definition, whatever the number of years on the timetable suggests, because two lessons a week for two years produces limited production. Bring the phase descriptor and a cold timed writing sample to the placement conversation. A dated script showing what your child can actually produce carries more weight with a DP coordinator than a parent's or a student's estimate.

faqs.question: How many Spanish sessions a week do Abu Dhabi families usually start with?
faqs.answer: Two short contacts rather than one long one, at least two days apart, is the pattern that suits a beginner through DP1. Vocabulary decays quickly at this stage and a single weekly hour spends its first fifteen minutes recovering ground lost since the last. Two 45-minute sessions also produce twice as many marked artefacts a month, which is what makes progress visible to a parent. In DP2, once written accuracy is stable, families usually move to one 60-minute session focused on the oral.

faqs.question: Can Spanish lessons move to post-Iftar times during Ramadan in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for a language they probably should. School days shorten, afternoons get harder, and a beginner asked to speak Spanish at 16:00 while fasting will produce less than the same student at 21:00. Sessions move to post-Iftar slots for the month, and the content shifts with the timing: listening and reading work in the shorter afternoon slots, speaking rehearsal after Iftar. Stopping entirely for a month is the thing to avoid, because a fortnight of silence in a beginner language costs more than it appears to.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a Spanish tutor to our home in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE, and no tutor is sent to a villa, apartment or compound here; in-home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. UAE lessons are one-to-one online, over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. For a minority course like beginner Spanish that is the better arrangement anyway, because the tutor is chosen from everyone free at your hour rather than from those who can drive to your community.

faqs.question: What does private tuition for a beginner language cost in the Abu Dhabi market?
faqs.answer: Published comparisons put a qualified subject tutor working online at roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour in this market, in-home visits at around AED 180 to AED 350, and specialist exam-year support higher again. Monthly online packages have been advertised from about AED 799 for eight sessions. Those are market figures from published rate tables, not IB Gram prices, and they are the benchmark to read any quote against. Ask what a quoted rate includes: marking, session notes and termly remeasurement are often not in it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write the Spanish written assignment if my child's language is weak?
faqs.answer: No, and an offer to do so should end the conversation with that tutor. Under IB academic honesty rules the submitted work must be the student's own, and a fluent adult improving a beginner's script produces language the candidate could not have written. A tutor may teach the text type, model an example on a different topic, mark the student's draft against criterion letters, explain why a sentence costs a mark, and test the correction later. Translation tools fall on the same side of the line and are treated as material to analyse rather than to use.

faqs.question: What happens if no Spanish ab initio specialist is free at the hour we need?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and we tell you before you pay rather than after. Beginner Spanish is a minority course, specialist availability is finite, and the honest options are a different slot, a short wait for a named tutor, or a recommendation to look elsewhere. What we will not do is fill the hour with a Spanish B tutor and let the mismatch surface in a March mock. If a wait is involved we will say roughly how long and what the student should be doing in the meantime, which for a beginner is daily listening exposure.

intro.heading: Counting the weeks before you plan the lessons
paragraphs: Spanish ab initio is the Diploma's beginner Spanish course, available at Standard Level only. The thing nobody says out loud at the start is how little time there actually is. A student beginning in September of DP1 reaches the written papers around eighteen months later, and that eighteen months is not eighteen months of teaching. Take out the school holidays, the examination weeks, the Ramadan period, the trips that Abu Dhabi families take, and the internal deadlines in other subjects, and the real figure is closer to sixty teaching weeks.

Sixty weeks is enough. It is not enough to waste, which is why this page starts with the calendar rather than with the syllabus. Everything in the course has a natural place in that sequence: the sound system in the first fortnight, the present-tense verb system before anything that depends on it, the past tenses in the middle of DP1, theme vocabulary spread across both years, and the oral technique concentrated before the school's internal recording window. Teaching the same material in the wrong order costs a term.

Spanish is unusually front-loaded in good news and back-loaded in difficulty. Its spelling is close to one-to-one with its sounds, so a beginner can read aloud, recognisably and accurately, within a couple of weeks - something that takes far longer in French or Arabic. Its verb system is the opposite: rich, regular, extensive, and genuinely demanding to control under time. Students who are encouraged by the early reading progress and then meet the past tenses in February are the most common disappointment in this course, and it is predictable enough to prepare for.

The second thing this page does is name the stalls. Beginners do not decline steadily; they progress and then stop, at fairly reliable moments. Around week six, when phrase memory stops being enough and grammar has to become a system. Around week fourteen, when the second past tense arrives and the first one destabilises. Around week twenty-six, when vocabulary load across five themes outruns whatever revision habit the student has. All three are survivable if the family knows they are coming, and all three are routinely mistaken for a child who is simply not good at languages.

Lessons are delivered one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared document for written work. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi; home tutoring is a service we run only in India. That matters less here than the calendar does. What matters is that a beginner gets frequent short contact with someone who has taught this exact course before, and that the plan survives a family that spends three weeks of the summer away from the emirate.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-spanish-ab-initio-tutor.programmesIntro: Where a student joins the Spanish sequence changes everything about the plan. These notes are about the handover points between programmes rather than about the programmes themselves.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Spanish ab initio is a Group 2 subject at Standard Level for beginners. Five prescribed themes with set topics, three assessed components, no coursework essay. The work is sequenced rather than surveyed: sound system, present tense, past tenses, theme breadth, oral technique, in that order, because each stage depends on the one before it.
programmes.countryNote: Many Abu Dhabi schools run ab initio with one small group spanning both Diploma years, which means a DP1 beginner is often in a room with DP2 students revising. That arrangement is efficient for the school and leaves a new beginner short of the basics, which is the gap most families here are trying to fill.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: A student arriving from MYP Spanish phase 1 is a legitimate ab initio candidate and has a genuine head start: the sound system is probably in place and some core vocabulary survives. The gain is roughly four to six weeks of the sequence, which is worth having and not worth overestimating.
programmes.countryNote: Spanish is often introduced later than French or Arabic in this emirate's schools, so MYP Spanish records here tend to be short. A student with one year of phase 1 Spanish usually still belongs in ab initio, and the school will confirm that.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Primary Spanish is exposure: songs, numbers, colours, greetings. It leaves a usable accent and almost nothing else measurable, and it should not be reported as prior study years later. Where it helps is confidence - a student who has heard the language spoken is less startled by natural speed in DP1.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi primaries run Spanish as a short enrichment unit. Mention it on a placement form for completeness, and do not let it push a child towards Spanish B when a beginner course is the honest fit.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-spanish-ab-initio-tutor.subjectsIntro: The ab initio content is defined by five prescribed themes with set topics beneath them, plus the grammatical machinery needed to say anything about them. Here is that territory, with what each part demands of a beginner.

subjects.name: Identities
subjects.description: Self, family, daily routine, physical description, health. The theme most beginners handle first and best, because the vocabulary is concrete and the grammar needed is mostly present tense. Also the theme students over-rely on in the oral.

subjects.name: Experiences
subjects.description: Holidays, travel, food, festivals, past events. This is where the past tenses become unavoidable, which is why it sits naturally after the first stall rather than before it.

subjects.name: Human ingenuity
subjects.description: Technology, transport, media, entertainment. Vocabulary-heavy and abstract enough that beginners stall here if the theme is taught before their grammar is stable. Rich material for the visual-stimulus oral.

subjects.name: Social organisation
subjects.description: School, work, neighbourhood, services. Useful because a student can describe their own Abu Dhabi context in it, which makes the vocabulary stick far better than textbook settings do.

subjects.name: Sharing the planet
subjects.description: Environment, climate, community, global issues. Consistently the thinnest theme in a beginner's vocabulary and the one most likely to appear as the image they cannot describe. Worth deliberate attention in DP2.

subjects.name: The present-tense verb system
subjects.description: Three regular patterns, the high-frequency irregulars, and the reflexives needed for daily routine. Everything else in the course stands on this, so it is taught to automatic recall rather than to recognition.

subjects.name: The past tenses
subjects.description: The preterite, then the imperfect, then the choice between them. The second one destabilises the first on arrival, which is the week-fourteen stall. Expect a dip in accuracy before the system settles.

subjects.name: Core vocabulary retrieval
subjects.description: Measured as words retrieved cold under time, not as lists seen. The whole ab initio domain is finite, which means a beginner can genuinely hold it all by DP2 if retrieval is tested rather than reviewed.

subjects.name: Written text types at beginner level
subjects.description: Notes, messages, short letters, blog entries. Each has an opening, a closing and a reader, and each carries marks for those conventions independent of the Spanish. Two taught properly beats six skimmed.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-spanish-ab-initio-tutor.regionsIntro: The shape of a week differs sharply across the emirate, and for a beginner language - where frequency matters more than session length - that shape decides what is possible. These are the patterns we see.

regions.name: Madinat Zayed and Al Zahiyah
regions.note: Central and dense, with short school runs and heavy after-school activity. Two short sessions a week fit here far more comfortably than one long one, which suits beginner work anyway.

regions.name: Al Muroor and Al Manaseer
regions.note: Long-settled areas with students spread across several schools. Siblings finish at different times, so staggered half-hour slots are common and much easier to arrange online than any other way.

regions.name: Al Rawdah and Al Mushrif
regions.note: Quiet villa streets with reliable study space at home, which matters for the daily ten minutes of retrieval that beginner vocabulary depends on far more than the lesson itself does.

regions.name: Baniyas and Mussafah
regions.note: Longer commutes to the island schools and a later end to the day. Evening slots work best, and the plan should assume the weekday session is the shorter of the two each week.

regions.name: Al Jubail Island and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: Newer communities with small cohorts and long runs in both directions. Fixed slots with no travel variable are what hold across a term, and the Saturday session is often where new grammar lands.

regions.note: A cluster of IB and British schools serving the same streets. Spanish is usually the second language option here behind Arabic, so beginners are carrying two language courses and the interference needs naming early.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Larger Diploma cohorts and often a single ab initio group spanning both years. A DP1 beginner in that room needs the first-term sequence faster than the class can deliver it, which is usually why a family calls.

sections.heading: Eighteen months from zero: what the calendar actually allows
paragraphs: Start with the arithmetic, because it changes decisions. From the first week of DP1 to the written papers is about eighteen calendar months. Subtract the long summer, the winter and spring breaks, Ramadan and Eid, the school's own examination weeks, and the fortnight either side of internal deadlines in other subjects, and a realistic figure for a student having one session a week is somewhere around sixty teaching weeks with sixty hours of contact. That is the resource, and it is finite.

Sequencing that resource matters more than filling it. The sound system has to come first because everything else is learned through it. The present-tense verb system has to be secure before the past tenses arrive, or the student ends up with two unstable systems rather than one stable one. Theme vocabulary spreads across both years because it decays without revisiting. Oral technique concentrates at the end because it is a performance skill with a fixed local deadline attached.

The table below is the version we give to Abu Dhabi families at the start of DP1, and it is deliberately conservative. No IB session or results dates appear on it, because the IB's own site is the only place to confirm those and your child's DP coordinator holds the school's version. What the table does contain is the internal milestones a school controls, and those are the ones worth asking about in writing in September rather than discovering in February.

sections.heading: Why Spanish reads easily and conjugates hard
paragraphs: Spanish spelling maps onto Spanish sound with unusual consistency. Five vowel sounds, each almost always pronounced the same way, and a small set of consonant rules that cover nearly everything a beginner meets. The practical effect is that a student can read aloud, intelligibly and accurately, within a fortnight. That is a genuine motivational gift at the start of a course, and it is also a trap, because it makes a beginner feel further along than they are.

The verb system is where the real work sits. Three regular patterns, each with a full set of person endings, plus the irregulars that occur in almost every sentence anyone says. Then two past tenses, with a choice between them that depends on how the speaker is framing the event rather than on when it happened. Then the subjunctive, which ab initio touches lightly but which appears in listening and reading material regardless of whether a beginner produces it.

Planning around that asymmetry is the whole trick. Reading aloud goes in from week one, cheaply, because it costs little and returns confidence and listening accuracy together. Verb work is spaced daily in small amounts rather than massed weekly, because endings become automatic through retrieval rather than through explanation. And the arrival of the second past tense is scheduled deliberately, with the family warned that accuracy will dip for a fortnight before the system settles. Warning a parent in advance costs nothing and prevents the conversation in which a student who is actually on track is told they have gone backwards.

sections.heading: The vocabulary build, term by term
paragraphs: Ab initio vocabulary is finite, which is the single most encouraging fact about the course. The prescribed themes and their topics define edges, so unlike Spanish B there is a point at which a student has genuinely covered the territory. What makes this real rather than theoretical is measuring retrieval instead of coverage: words a student can produce cold, under time, without a prompt, counted at the start of each session.

The targets in the table are what we see from a DP1 student having one session a week and doing ten minutes of retrieval on most days. They are indicative rather than promised, and they move with the rest of the Diploma load. Two things reliably change them. A daily habit, even a very short one, roughly doubles retention against weekend-only revision. And describing the student's own Abu Dhabi context in the target language sticks far better than textbook settings do, which is why social organisation is often the theme that lands fastest here.

The number to watch is not the total but the distribution across themes. A student with a strong Identities vocabulary and nothing for Sharing the Planet has an even total and a serious exposure in the oral, because the image they draw is as likely to come from one theme as another. Tracking by theme rather than in aggregate is what catches that, and it is the sort of thing a term-by-term table makes visible immediately.

sections.heading: Listening from zero: a difficulty ladder, in order
paragraphs: Listening is half of Paper 2 with reading, and it is the component beginners leave until it is too late because early listening is demoralising. The answer is a ladder rather than a leap. Begin with material that is slow, clearly articulated and about a known topic, and move up in deliberate steps: speed first, then unfamiliar vocabulary, then accent variety, then overlapping speakers. Changing two variables at once is why students conclude they are hopeless at listening.

Technique sits alongside exposure. On a first hearing, a candidate should mark where in the audio each question is answered rather than trying to write full answers, then write on the second hearing. Students who attempt complete answers immediately lose the thread and arrive at the second hearing with nothing to verify. This single change in method is worth more marks in three weeks than a term of additional vocabulary, and it is almost never taught explicitly in a crowded class.

Spanish has one specific advantage for a beginner here. Because spelling and sound align closely, a student who hears a word they have read can usually recognise it, which is far less reliable in French. So vocabulary learned by eye transfers to the ear better in this language, and the early listening ladder can climb faster than families expect, provided the steps stay one variable apart. The one thing to avoid is leaving listening out of the first term altogether on the grounds that there is not enough vocabulary yet. Two minutes of slow audio a week from week two builds the habit cheaply, and a habit is far easier to extend later than to establish under exam pressure.

sections.heading: The oral: describing an image in a language met last year
paragraphs: A quarter of the grade is a recording made inside your child's school, marked by their teacher and moderated by the IB. The candidate works from a visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes, describes it, connects it to the theme and to life in a Spanish-speaking context, and then holds a conversation. For a student who met the language eighteen months earlier, the description is learnable and the conversation is the real test.

That asymmetry drives the preparation. Polished description is worth rehearsing and is not sufficient, because the marks for interaction exist precisely to distinguish a student who can speak from one who can recite. So rehearsal uses images the student has not seen, follow-up questions they cannot predict, and a short list of phrases that buy thinking time without sounding evasive. Recovery after a stumble is a trainable skill and shows up directly in the mark.

The cultural connection is the piece most often left unmade. A candidate who describes a street market in careful Spanish and never says anything about where such a scene sits in a Spanish-speaking context has left message marks on the table. Three or four transferable linking sentences, drilled until they arrive without thought, do more for the mark than another hundred words of vocabulary - and they survive nerves, which memorised content reliably does not. Worth asking the school one question early: when the internal recording window falls. It is set locally, it often arrives earlier than families expect, and everything in the final term arranges itself around that date.
bullets: Describe, link to the theme, link to the culture, then converse
Interaction marks catch recitation, so rehearse unseen questions
Thinking-time phrases are worth drilling to automatic recall
Recovery after a stumble is trainable and visible in the mark

sections.heading: The three weeks where beginners stall
paragraphs: Beginners do not improve smoothly. They improve, stop, and then improve again, and the stops are predictable enough to warn a family about in advance. Around week six, phrase memory stops working. Up to that point a student can hold enough set expressions to produce sentences, and then the material outgrows memory and grammar has to become a system instead. Students who are not told this is normal conclude they are bad at languages.

Around week fourteen the second past tense arrives and accuracy visibly drops. The imperfect destabilises the preterite, and for perhaps a fortnight a student who was writing correct narrative starts making errors they had stopped making. This is the system reorganising rather than deteriorating, and the fix is patience plus narrative tasks marked for tense choice alone. The worst response is to drill both tenses harder in isolation, which is what most students do unprompted.

Around week twenty-six the vocabulary load across several themes outruns whatever revision habit exists. The student has covered three themes and can retrieve one and a half. The fix is structural rather than motivational: retrieval tested per theme at the start of each session, with what fails being retaught rather than reassigned. Naming these three weeks in advance changes how a family reads a bad fortnight, which is most of the value of knowing. It also changes what a parent says at the kitchen table, and that is not a small thing in a two-year course.

sections.heading: What eighteen months cannot do, and what it reliably can
paragraphs: Honesty about the ceiling is more useful than enthusiasm. Eighteen months from zero does not produce a fluent speaker, will not give a student the range to improvise comfortably about an unfamiliar abstract topic, and will not fully stabilise the subjunctive in free production. Anyone suggesting otherwise is selling something. No tutor can promise a grade in this course or any other, and no outcome statistics appear anywhere on this site because we could not show you the data behind them.

What sixty well-sequenced teaching weeks reliably produce is different and still substantial. A secure present tense and a working past-tense system. Several hundred retrievable words spread across all five themes rather than bunched in one. Written text types known to checklist level. A listening method that does not waste the second hearing. And an oral that can survive a question the student did not expect, which is where the interaction marks live.

If your child is already in DP2 with less time than that, the plan compresses rather than collapses. The first fortnight finds out exactly which stalls were never resolved, and then the work goes only there - usually the past tenses and the thin themes - plus the oral block, because it is a quarter of the grade with a fixed internal date. A late start buys fewer avoidable losses, which is a smaller claim than a grade promise and a more honest one. It is also the claim we would rather be judged on.

process.title: Send the start date, not just the year group
process.description: Tell us when your child actually began Spanish, what the school's weekly timetable gives them, and whether the ab initio group spans both Diploma years. Those three facts decide where in the eighteen-month sequence the plan starts. Add the school's internal oral deadline if you have it, since everything in DP2 arranges itself around that.

process.title: A free trial lesson with a placement check inside it
process.description: One lesson, free, no card details and no obligation. Reading aloud shows whether the sound system is in place. One verb conjugated shows whether grammar is a system yet. Two minutes of cold retrieval gives a baseline word count. You keep the result whatever you decide about continuing.

process.title: The written sequence, shared in September
process.description: A term-by-term plan with the phases named and the internal deadlines marked, in writing, so you can see what is meant to be true by December and by March. It also names the three stall weeks in advance, which changes how a family reads a difficult fortnight when it arrives.

process.title: Short frequent sessions first, longer ones later
process.description: Two half-hours a week through the foundation phase, because verb endings and vocabulary become automatic through spaced retrieval rather than one long sitting. From the past tenses onward a single weekly hour with a fortnightly marked task is usually the better shape.

process.title: If no ab initio specialist is free, we say so
process.description: Teaching this course from zero inside two years is a specific skill, and availability tightens when internal oral windows cluster across the emirate. If we cannot match your child to someone who has done it, we will give you a date rather than put a general Spanish speaker in front of a beginner and hope.

whyPoints.title: The calendar comes before the syllabus
whyPoints.description: Sixty real teaching weeks is the resource, and sequencing it is the job. You get the term-by-term plan in writing in September, with the phases, the internal deadlines and the stall weeks marked, so the work is ordered rather than improvised lesson by lesson.

whyPoints.title: The stalls are named in advance
whyPoints.description: Week six, week fourteen, week twenty-six. Knowing those are coming changes how a family reads a flat fortnight, and it stops a capable student concluding they are bad at languages at exactly the moment the course asks them to shift from memory to system.

whyPoints.title: Vocabulary measured by retrieval
whyPoints.description: Words retrieved cold under time, counted at the start of the session and tracked by theme rather than in aggregate. An even total hiding one empty theme is a real exposure in the oral, and only per-theme tracking finds it.

whyPoints.title: Online, stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not run in-home visits in Abu Dhabi, and this page says so rather than letting you discover it after booking. For a beginner the gain is reach: a specialist rather than the nearest Spanish speaker.

whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page names the provider that published it. IB Gram holds no accreditation, licence or partnership from the IB or from any UAE regulator and claims none. Any IB session date must be confirmed with your child's DP coordinator or on the IB's own site.

faqs.question: Can a complete beginner really sit a Spanish examination eighteen months later?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is what the ab initio course is designed for. What makes the difference is sequencing rather than hours: the sound system first, the present tense secure before the past tenses arrive, theme vocabulary spread across both years, and oral technique concentrated before the school's internal recording window. Realistically a student having one session a week gets around sixty teaching weeks once holidays, examination weeks, Ramadan and family travel are removed. That is enough time, and it is not enough to spend in the wrong order.

faqs.question: Is Spanish the easiest language to begin from scratch in the Diploma?
faqs.answer: It is the easiest to read and among the harder to conjugate. Spanish spelling maps onto its sounds with unusual consistency - five vowel sounds, each nearly always the same - so a beginner can read aloud accurately within a fortnight, which French and Arabic do not allow. The verb system is where the work sits: three regular patterns with full person endings, the high-frequency irregulars, then two past tenses with a choice between them that depends on framing rather than timing.

faqs.question: How many Spanish words does an ab initio student actually need?
faqs.answer: The domain is finite, defined by the five prescribed themes and their topics, which is the most encouraging fact about this course. For a student having one session a week with short daily retrieval, a realistic picture is 150 to 250 retrievable words by the end of the first term and upward of 900 spread evenly across all five themes by the final term. Those are indicative figures, not promises. What matters more than the total is the spread, because a thin theme becomes the image your child cannot describe.

faqs.question: Why does my child read Spanish well and still get verb endings wrong?
faqs.answer: Because those are different skills with different learning curves. Reading benefits from Spanish orthography being transparent, so it arrives early and feels like general progress. Verb endings become automatic only through spaced retrieval - small amounts most days rather than a long weekly session - and until they are automatic they consume attention that should be going on the message. Expect reading to run ahead of production for the first term, and expect the gap to close once the present tense is secure.

faqs.question: Which Spanish accents will a beginner meet in the listening material?
faqs.answer: Material is drawn from across the Spanish-speaking world rather than one country, so a beginner will meet Peninsular and Latin American voices and sometimes faster or more clipped varieties. The way to handle it is a ladder rather than a leap: slow and clear on a known topic first, then normal pace with vocabulary held constant, then unfamiliar vocabulary, then a second variety, then interviews with overlapping speakers. Changing two variables at once is why students decide they cannot do listening.

faqs.question: What does the beginner oral actually involve in the room?
faqs.answer: Your child works from a visual stimulus linked to one of the prescribed themes, describes it, connects it to the theme and to life in a Spanish-speaking context, and then holds a conversation with their teacher. It is recorded in school, marked there, and moderated by the IB. Description is rehearsable and the conversation is the real test, which is why preparation has to include images the student has not seen and follow-up questions they cannot predict rather than only a polished opening.

faqs.question: When do beginners usually hit a wall, and what should we do about it?
faqs.answer: Three fairly reliable moments. Around week six, phrase memory runs out and grammar has to become a system - slow down and build one verb pattern to automatic recall. Around week fourteen the imperfect arrives and destabilises the preterite, so accuracy dips for a fortnight; narrative tasks marked for tense choice alone fix it. Around week twenty-six vocabulary across several themes outruns the revision habit. Knowing these are coming stops a capable student concluding they are hopeless at languages.

faqs.question: Can my child take Spanish ab initio if they already study French at school?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and the school decides. What is worth naming early is the interference: two language acquisition courses running together produce vocabulary substitutions and verb-pattern confusion that look like carelessness and are structural. Teaching the two systems contrastively rather than pretending they are unrelated is the practical answer, and it takes a session or two. Some students handle both well and find the second easier for having learned how to learn a language; others should drop to one, and the marked work shows which.

faqs.question: Does a beginner language count as a full Diploma subject?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ab initio is a Group 2 language acquisition subject and contributes to the Diploma in the same way any Standard Level subject does. It exists at Standard Level only, which is a design feature rather than a limitation, since the Higher Level requirement in the Diploma concerns how many subjects are taken at that level overall rather than which ones. A small number of university courses state modern-language expectations of their own, so check any specific target course rather than assuming.

faqs.question: What do beginner Spanish tutors charge per hour in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published UAE rates, mostly quoted for Dubai, give the range. Tutopiya advertises from about AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the budget end. Unitors lists IGCSE tutoring from around AED 150 and IB from AED 200, TutorChase quotes about AED 270, and Bestimate's 2026 rate table puts specialist exam-year support at roughly AED 200 to 450 and above, with the premium end quoted as high as AED 650 by BartyED. Those are their figures, not our price list.

faqs.question: Should we start lessons in the summer before DP1 begins?
faqs.answer: If the summer is settled rather than spent travelling, a few weeks on the sound system and the first verb patterns before term starts is genuinely valuable, because it moves the whole sequence forward by the amount that would otherwise be spent on mechanics in September. If the summer involves three weeks abroad and inconsistent internet, it is better to start in week one of term and keep the rhythm unbroken. Consistency matters more for a beginner than a head start does.

faqs.question: What if the school only runs Spanish ab initio in alternate years or in a mixed-year group?
faqs.answer: Both arrangements are common in this emirate and both have the same consequence for a DP1 beginner: part of each lesson is spent listening to material they have not met. The school is managing small numbers sensibly and the gap is real. Outside support is most useful in the first term in that situation, because the sequence a beginner needs - sound system, then present tense, then past tenses - is exactly what a shared group cannot deliver at the right pace.

faqs.question: How do we keep Spanish alive during long summer trips away from the UAE?
faqs.answer: With retrieval rather than lessons. Ten minutes most days of cold vocabulary recall, by theme, does more for retention than two long sessions on return would, and it needs no internet connection or timetable. Reading aloud is the other low-cost habit worth keeping, since Spanish orthography makes it productive even without a teacher present. Tell us the dates and the plan absorbs them, with the first session back used to re-measure retrieval rather than to resume where the syllabus stopped.

faqs.question: Where is the line between helping my child and doing their assessed work?
faqs.answer: The tutor teaches, questions, models and gives feedback; the student produces every mark-bearing word. In practice that means a tutor may rehearse the oral with unfamiliar images, mark practice tasks against the published criteria, explain descriptors and build vocabulary lists from the student's own errors. A tutor is not present at the assessed recording, supplies no content for it, and sees no assessed written work before the school does. We state this to the student in the first lesson rather than leaving it implied.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if my child is already in DP2?
faqs.answer: No, and the plan looks different. The first fortnight finds out which of the beginner stalls were never resolved - usually the past-tense choice and one or two thin themes - and the work goes only there. The oral block comes next because it carries a quarter of the grade against a fixed internal school deadline. Nobody can promise a particular grade from a late start, and anyone who does should concern you. What a compressed plan reliably buys is fewer avoidable losses on the paper.

abu-dhabi/ib-dp-spanish-b-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Diploma Spanish B at Standard and Higher Level. Sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and each one returns a marked piece of work or a recorded rehearsal rather than a verbal summary.

intro.heading: Spanish B is marked on decisions, not on fluency
paragraphs: The commonest Spanish B conversation in Abu Dhabi starts with a contradiction. The student spent a year in Madrid, or has Spanish-speaking family, or simply picked the language up fast and talks happily in class. The teacher reports good participation. The grade sits at 4. Nothing has gone wrong, and the explanation is in how Group 2 courses are marked: Paper 1 is scored out of 30 with 12 marks for language, 12 for message and 6 for conceptual understanding, and the individual oral uses the same shape with 6 marks for interactive skills instead. Fluency is not a criterion. Accuracy, appropriateness and control are.

In Spanish that distinction has a specific shape, because the language forces decisions a confident speaker can bluff past in conversation and cannot bluff past in writing. Which of the two verbs meaning 'to be' belongs here. Whether this past event takes the preterite or the imperfect. Whether this clause triggers the subjunctive. Whether this relationship needs por or para. A student who guesses on all four produces fluent Spanish that drops language marks in nearly every sentence, and the marked script looks like a page of small deductions rather than one identifiable problem.

Half the grade then sits somewhere else entirely. Paper 2 combines listening and reading for 50%, with a 45-minute listening section and an hour of reading at Standard Level and an hour of each at Higher Level. Spanish B candidates generally do better on reading than their peers in other Group 2 languages, because Spanish spelling maps onto sound transparently and English shares a great deal of Latin-derived vocabulary. They do worse than they expect on listening, because natural Spanish is fast, elides word boundaries and uses regional vocabulary that classroom audio avoids.

At Higher Level there is one more component families routinely misunderstand. Spanish B HL requires two literary works studied in Spanish, and those works are not examined on Paper 1 or Paper 2. They feed the individual oral, where the starting point is an extract from one of them. HL students who read the works carefully and then prepare only for the written papers have left 25% of the grade to chance; students who treat them as a literature course have over-prepared for a component that assesses language, message and interaction rather than literary analysis.

On delivery, we are direct. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses in Abu Dhabi, and in-home visits are a service we run only in India. Spanish B sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with the student's writing annotated on a shared screen and audio replayed from the same window. For a subject where the work is marking decisions sentence by sentence, having the script visible to both people is worth more than being in the same room.

Paper 2: listening plus reading, 50%, 1h45 at SL and 2h at HL

sections.heading: What a Spanish B tutor in Abu Dhabi is actually hired to fix
paragraphs: Three diagnoses cover almost every Spanish B student who comes to us, and they need completely different work. The first is the confident speaker whose marked script is covered in small deductions: grammatical decisions guessed rather than known. The second is the accurate writer whose listening score is half their reading score: a recognition problem, not a knowledge problem. The third is the student whose written papers are fine and whose oral mark is well below them: a component never rehearsed to time.

Distinguishing between them takes one session and a marked script, and it determines everything that follows. For the first student the work is a grammar clinic on their own sentences, which moves measurably over six sessions. For the second it is graded listening under exam conditions, which takes a term because recognition is built by volume. For the third it is three recorded rehearsals, which is the cheapest intervention in the subject and often worth a grade on a component carrying 25%.

What gets in the way is that the school report describes none of these. A Spanish B report that says a student participates well and should revise vocabulary is accurate and useless, because vocabulary is rarely the limiting factor for a student who can already hold a conversation. The marked script is the document that matters, with the criterion marks visible if the school supplies them, and the most valuable question a parent can ask at a Diploma parents' evening is which of language, message and conceptual understanding is losing the marks.

On delivery: IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE, and no tutor will arrive at a UAE address. That service runs only in India. Spanish B is taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For a subject whose work is marking decisions sentence by sentence and replaying audio until a word is recognised, both people needing to see the same screen matters more than both being in the same room. In-home tuition is a real market here, published at roughly AED 180-500 an hour with travel inside the rate, and the table below sets out honestly what that buys.

sections.heading: The four decisions that decide a Spanish B language mark
paragraphs: Spanish asks a learner to choose, repeatedly, where English does not. Four of those choices account for most of the language marks lost by Spanish B candidates at both levels, and all four are teachable to automaticity rather than to understanding. Understanding them is easy and is not the point; a student who has to think about the choice mid-sentence in an examination will get it wrong often enough to matter.

The two verbs meaning 'to be' divide essentially between what something is and what state it is in, and confident speakers often get the common cases right and the tested cases wrong, particularly with adjectives whose meaning changes depending on which verb is used. The past-tense split between the preterite and the imperfect is the single biggest source of errors in Spanish B writing, because English uses one simple past for both and a student narrating a holiday has to make the choice in every clause. The rule is about the kind of past being described rather than about time elapsed, and once it is framed that way it becomes reliable.

The subjunctive is where candidates most often decide not to try. It is triggered by identifiable structures rather than by feel: expressions of doubt, wishes and emotion, impersonal expressions, certain conjunctions, and some time clauses referring to the future. A Spanish B student does not need every subjunctive form in the language; they need the present subjunctive after about ten triggers, used accurately. That is a finite, learnable list, and using it once correctly in a written task demonstrates range to an examiner in a way that a longer vocabulary cannot.

The fourth decision, between the two words for 'for', is lower stakes individually and high in volume, because it appears constantly and each error is a small deduction. The useful approach is not a rule list but a short set of frequent collocations learnt whole. Across a two-year course these four decisions probably account for more lost language marks than every other grammatical issue combined, which is why the table below exists and why one of them gets a whole session at a time.

sections.heading: Paper 1: the task choice matters as much as the writing
paragraphs: Paper 1 offers three tasks and asks for one, within a word range of 250 to 400 at Standard Level and 450 to 600 at Higher Level, and takes 25% of the grade. It is marked out of 30: language 12, message 12, conceptual understanding 6. The first decision a candidate makes is which task to attempt, and it is made in about ninety seconds under pressure, usually badly.

Students choose by topic familiarity, which is the wrong criterion. The better choice is by text type and by the structures the task invites. A task that asks for a narrative lets a student show the past tenses they have drilled. A task that asks for a proposal or a speech invites the subjunctive naturally through recommendations and wishes. A task on an unfamiliar topic with a text type the student has practised is almost always a better bet than a comfortable topic in a form they have never attempted. Teaching that comparison takes one session and changes the ninety-second decision permanently.

The conceptual understanding marks are the cheapest on the paper. Each task implies an audience, a context and a purpose, and the text type carries conventions that signal it: a blog post with a title and a reader addressed, a formal letter with an appropriate opening and closing, a speech with a greeting and rhetorical questions, an interview laid out in turns. A task written as undifferentiated prose loses most of those 6 marks regardless of how good the Spanish is. A one-page reference and three timed attempts fixes it.

Register is the Spanish-specific wrinkle. The language forces a choice of address form early in most sentences, and the variety a student has learnt affects which plural form is available to them. The examination accepts any standard variety provided it is used consistently, which is the important word: a task that mixes a peninsular plural address with Latin American vocabulary and then switches halfway has created an inconsistency the examiner can see. Choosing one variety and sticking to it is a free mark-protection decision that many students have never been asked to make deliberately.

sections.heading: Paper 2: strong reading, weak listening, and why that gap exists
paragraphs: Paper 2 carries 50% of the Spanish B grade across a 45-minute listening section and an hour of reading at Standard Level, and an hour of each at Higher Level. Spanish B candidates tend to arrive with an unusual profile: reading comfortably ahead of listening, by a wider margin than students of most other Group 2 languages.

The reading advantage is real and comes from two sources. Spanish spelling maps onto pronunciation transparently, so a reader is never unsure which word they are looking at. And English shares a very large Latin-derived vocabulary with Spanish, so abstract and academic words are frequently transparent on sight. A Spanish B student can often read a passage on an unfamiliar topic and extract most of it, which is why reading is rarely the component families worry about.

Listening removes both advantages at once. Natural Spanish is fast, runs words together, drops consonants in several major varieties, and uses regional vocabulary that classroom material tends to avoid. A student whose Spanish has come mostly from reading and from one teacher's voice hears an unbroken stream. The gap between reading and listening scores is therefore diagnostic: if listening is around half of reading, the issue is recognition rather than knowledge, and more vocabulary learning will not close it.

What closes it is graded, deliberate practice that includes variety rather than avoiding it. Short clips on covered themes, played twice as the exam does, answered under time, and only then checked against the transcript, with every word known by eye but missed by ear written down. The list is short and repetitive, and it is the revision product. Alongside that, deliberate exposure to more than one Spanish variety across a term, because a candidate calibrated to a single accent is relying on the examination choosing that accent. Both are straightforward to arrange in an online session where any clip plays from the same window.

sections.heading: Latin American or peninsular Spanish: does the variety matter?
paragraphs: This question comes up in almost every first conversation with an Abu Dhabi family, usually because the household speaks one variety and the school teaches another, or because a tutor's accent differs from the teacher's. The short answer is that the examination accepts any standard variety of Spanish provided the student is consistent, and that consistency is the part worth attending to.

The practical differences a Spanish B student meets are limited and learnable. The plural form of address differs between Spain and most of Latin America, which affects verb endings in writing and speech. Some regions use a distinct second-person singular form with its own verb forms. Pronunciation of certain consonants differs, which matters for listening rather than for writing. And there is everyday vocabulary that varies by region — the words for a car, a computer, a mobile phone, a bus. None of this is an obstacle to a good grade; all of it is an obstacle to an inconsistent candidate.

Where it genuinely matters is the listening section, because the examination does not undertake to use the variety your child is used to. A student who has only ever heard peninsular Spanish and meets Caribbean or Argentine audio will lose marks that have nothing to do with their Spanish. This is the strongest argument for deliberately varied listening practice across the course, and it is an argument almost no classroom makes, because a single teacher provides a single accent for two years.

For writing and the oral, the guidance we give is simple. Choose the variety the student is most comfortable in, usually the one their household or their school uses, and be consistent in address forms, verb endings and vocabulary within a single piece of work. Mixing varieties mid-task is the only version of this that costs marks. A tutor whose own variety differs from the student's is not a problem and can be an advantage, provided they are explicit about which forms belong to which variety rather than correcting silently towards their own.
